conceptSelection.selectionReason: The complete Packet Journey matches the addressing table and every cable endpoint. Forward and return stages separate a successful exchange from a controlled filtering observation.

walkthrough.why: The destination is PC2, not PC1's own address or the gateway. A self-ping would not test this path.
walkthrough.action: On paper, draw PC1 - Switch - Router - PC2 and the reverse reply path.
walkthrough.whatHappens: PC1 at 192.168.1.10/24 sends toward PC2 at 192.168.2.10/24. They are different IP networks. PC1 therefore uses its local gateway, Router at 192.168.1.1.

walkthrough.why: Record the actual two interface names before any changes. Every configuration and rollback command must use that recorded mapping.
walkthrough.action: Label Router's Switch-facing cable LAN1 and its PC2-facing cable LAN2 on your drawing.
walkthrough.whatHappens: These are role names, not commands. Before configuration, Lab Step 2 requires Router's actual interface inventory and cable mapping in your baseline notes. GigabitEthernet0/0 is only the example LAN1 name.

walkthrough.why: The four-layer TCP/IP model groups ICMP with IP at the internet layer. Ethernet delivery belongs to link; some teaching conventions split link into two layers.
walkthrough.action: Trace PC1's frame to Switch and Router, then trace the new frame from Router to PC2.
walkthrough.whatHappens: Switch handles the local frame. Router reads the packet's destination IP and selects its directly connected PC2 network. Router creates an outgoing frame for PC2; it does not forward the incoming frame unchanged.

walkthrough.why: A reply supports this ICMP round trip. It does not test TCP/UDP ports or an application. Initial ARP delay is possible, but intermittent or persistent loss needs investigation.
walkthrough.action: Trace the reply from PC2 through Router and Switch back to PC1.
walkthrough.whatHappens: PC2 uses gateway 192.168.2.1 for the return path. In the real lab, repeated peer replies establish a baseline only after both endpoints and mapped router ports are configured.

walkthrough.why: An ACL number identifies a rule list. Never append into an existing 199, replace an existing binding or claim a cause from one timeout.
walkthrough.action: Mark a prediction that the lab-only ACL blocks PC1's echo request at Router; do not configure it during this paper exercise.
walkthrough.whatHappens: Lab Steps 7-10 first require a clean baseline with ACL 199 unused, then attach the complete new list to mapped LAN1. Expected peer loss must agree with the exact deny counter and attachment; the gateway test is not the full peer path.

walkthrough.why: Remove only the changes you own. Never erase all configuration or use a startup-to-running merge as a substitute for rollback.
walkthrough.action: Draw the restored path and write the cleanup order: detach our binding, delete our list, repeat peer tests, compare the baseline.
walkthrough.whatHappens: Lab Step 11 provides the full Router console sequence; Steps 12-14 verify both peers and the saved configuration. This paper prediction does not establish that an actual router was repaired.

beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: A missing reply is a symptom, not a diagnosis. Layer names help organize questions about the cable, local delivery, IP routing and application. Compare a working baseline with one controlled change so you can explain which evidence supports your conclusion.

firstPractice.hint: Compare your drawing with the visual's node labels and addressing table. Follow the reply as well as the request. Use the later lab to measure results only after recording a stable baseline.
firstPractice.task: Using paper only, write PC1's own address and PC2's destination address beside your drawing. Trace both directions. Circle the planned filter and write two other possible causes of a timeout. Do not change a live network. Perform later tests only in the isolated lab setup, not on networks with production traffic or shared use.
firstPractice.expected: PC1 is 192.168.1.10 and PC2 is 192.168.2.10. The planned filter is at Router. Missing replies can also involve endpoint settings, either route direction, ARP/link trouble or ICMP filtering. These are predictions, not captured results.

beginnerGuide.startingPoint: Read the definitions above first; no command experience is assumed. This introductory walkthrough is a paper prediction using PC1, Switch, Router and PC2. Do not type commands yet. The later Practice network section supplies all installation, console, addressing, baseline and rollback steps in order. A paper prediction is not a tested network result.

checkUnderstanding.hint: Separate the internet-layer ICMP exchange from transport ports and the application. Neither a self-ping nor a gateway-only test reaches PC2.
checkUnderstanding.answer: No. Repeated peer replies support the tested IP/ICMP exchange and its underlying path at that time. They do not establish TCP/UDP service availability or application health. A web application needs its own authorized test; this lab contains no web-server test.
checkUnderstanding.question: After rollback, PC1 repeatedly receives ping replies from PC2. Does this prove PC2's web application works?

everydayComparison.whereItStops: This is a memory aid, not a literal network rule or fault detector. A device can silently drop a packet. Neither a parcel story nor one ping result proves where a network failed; delivery of ICMP does not prove an application works.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: In the real network, Switch handles Ethernet frames and Router selects an IP path and builds a new frame. PC2 receives the request and needs a return path. Each parcel comparison is an organizational metaphor, not a literal device action; our test uses ICMP, not postal delivery.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: Imagine a parcel-delivery checklist. This is a memory aid, not a literal delivery process; real devices do not forward packets like parcels. Reading an address or asking about a reply organizes questions, not device actions.

prerequisites: For clicking, typing and notes, read https://www.qcsstudio.com/courses/ccna/start-here. Recap Day 2's device roles; this lesson reintroduces every console action.
Use a computer that can run GNS3 and a legally permitted Cisco IOS router image with two routed Ethernet ports and extended IPv4 ACL support.
Without a permitted image or suitable computer, follow the labelled paper exercises only. Do not type lab commands or claim observed results.
content.learnerOutcome: Use OSI and TCP/IP as troubleshooting checklists. Trace an ICMP exchange, explain its limits and compare a safe lab baseline before, during and after a controlled filter.
content.metaDescription: Understand OSI and TCP/IP with a guided GNS3 lab. Trace a packet, interpret ping results, test an isolated ACL and safely restore your baseline.

terms.meaning: A layered model is a diagram or checklist that organizes troubleshooting steps by grouping related network jobs. A layer is one such group. The OSI model has seven layers; the four-layer TCP/IP model groups jobs differently. Models structure questions; they do not detect or indicate a fault on their own and are not physical boxes.

Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) describes physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation and application jobs. This lesson uses four TCP/IP layers: link, internet, transport and application. Some teaching sources split link into physical and data link, giving five layers. These are grouping conventions, not different networks. TCP/IP means Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol.

A frame carries data across one local link. An IP packet carries data toward an IP destination, inside a frame on Ethernet. A router reads the destination IP and builds a new outgoing frame; a switch forwards local frames.

An IP address identifies a network interface. With /24, the first three octets (numbers) identify the network: 192.168.1.x uses mask 255.255.255.0. A default gateway is the local router address used to reach another network. A MAC address identifies an Ethernet interface on a local link.

An interface is a device connection such as GigabitEthernet0/0. A local Ethernet segment lets devices exchange frames without routing. Router separates the two IP networks. Administratively down means an interface is disabled by configuration; no shutdown enables that mapped port but does not repair a cable. Up/up is local physical and protocol status, not proof of end-to-end delivery.

Virtual PC Simulator (VPCS) is GNS3's lightweight practice computer. A Console is its text-control window: right-click the node and choose Console. A prompt such as PC1> means it is ready. Type only the command, then press Enter. The built-in Switch has no IOS console.

The router's prompt may use its configured hostname. A > prompt is user EXEC; enable opens privileged EXEC (#), which permits inspection and changes. configure terminal enters (config)#; interface selects (config-if)#. exit goes back one level; end returns to #. Never type the prompt.

Ping sends an Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) echo request and waits for an echo reply. ICMP belongs with IP at the TCP/IP internet layer, not TCP/UDP transport. A host is a network-connected computer. No reply means the exchange timed out, not proof of a failed layer. Host settings, filters and either path direction can affect it. A self-ping tests the local IP stack, not the peer path; a reply does not prove application health.

Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) finds a local Ethernet MAC address for an IPv4 next hop. An initial request can time out during discovery. Repeat the same peer test; intermittent loss can also reflect links, load or filtering. Persistent failure needs evidence, not a guess.

An ACL is an ordered permit/deny rule list. access-list 199 identifies a numbered list; ip access-list extended LAB_FILTER identifies a named list. An ip access-group line binds a list to an interface: in means arriving through that port, out means leaving. A rule's sequence number is not its ACL identifier. A per-rule match counter counts matched packets since initialization or clearing, not the number of rules; availability varies by image.

A baseline records the known configuration, cabling and successful tests before a change. Running-config is active; startup-config is the saved boot configuration. Rollback returns only our changes to that recorded state. Copying startup-config into running-config merges settings; it is not a reliable rollback.

This router ACL checks ICMP and IP addresses, not TCP/UDP port numbers or application health. After the specific deny, permit ip any any permits other IPv4 traffic evaluated by this ACL. It does not create routes or expose services by itself. Use this permissive teaching policy only in the fully disconnected lab; never copy it to a production or shared network.

teachingPrelude.explanation: Use these definitions before the diagram, walkthrough or commands. First establish a working peer exchange, then change one known rule and compare observations. An analogy can help remember a job, but it is not literal forwarding behavior. Our checklist narrows possibilities; it does not prove a faulty layer from one symptom.
teachingPrelude.labBoundary: Lab boundary: Use a disconnected, disposable GNS3 project with PC1, Switch, Router and PC2. Do not add Cloud, NAT or real-network adapters or connect company, production, shared or Internet traffic. This IPv4/ICMP exercise does not test applications, wireless or a firewall product.

practiceQuestions.answer: Inspect the tested forward and return path, including the relevant ACL binding and supported rule counters.
practiceQuestions.question: PC1 cannot ping PC2, although Router's mapped ports show up/up and addresses match the plan. What read-only evidence could you inspect next?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Up/up is local interface evidence, not proof of peer connectivity. The ACL is one hypothesis. Compare the exact source and destination, gateway settings and policy; real host firewalls, link problems or rate limits can also affect replies.

practiceQuestions.answer: Initial ARP discovery may have delayed a test. Repeated replies alone do not prove ARP caused the earlier timeout.
practiceQuestions.question: A first peer ping times out, then repeated tests reply. Name one possible explanation and what the observation does not prove.
practiceQuestions.explanation: ARP resolves the local next-hop MAC address. On PC1's cross-subnet request, that next hop is its gateway, not remote PC2. Transient loss can have other causes, so record the observation and establish a stable baseline before the controlled fault.

practiceQuestions.answer: No. A gateway test covers a shorter exchange and does not establish the full PC2 forward and return path.
practiceQuestions.question: PC1 receives gateway replies but not PC2 replies. Does that prove Router's ACL is the cause?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Check actual peer addresses, both gateways, the remaining links and policy evidence. General hosts may also block ICMP or be unavailable. Those are conceptual alternatives; this VPCS lab does not simulate a host firewall product.

practiceQuestions.answer: No. Stop without changing it, because the list is not proven to belong solely to this exercise.
practiceQuestions.question: During isolated-lab cleanup, you discover an unfamiliar second reference to ACL 199. Should you detach every reference and delete the list?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Perform rollback only in the isolated lab, never on production or shared networks. The required baseline had no 199. This lab authorizes only its known LAN1 inbound binding; another interface or feature reference breaks that ownership assumption. Detachment-before-deletion is a safety procedure, not a guarantee enforced by IOS.

practiceQuestions.answer: Verify the actual source and destination, mapped LAN1 inbound binding, exact rule match and whether this image exposes current counters.
practiceQuestions.question: The deny counter does not change after PC1's failed peer ping. Which checks prevent an unsupported conclusion?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Read the complete running configuration and relevant interface output in the Router console. A wrong port, direction, source or target can prevent a match; unavailable counters are also a measurement limitation. Do not invent a count or conclude that missing counts prove routing is broken.

practiceQuestions.answer: The tested IP/ICMP exchange replies again. Web-service availability or performance is not established.
practiceQuestions.question: After the isolated rollback, PC1 receives repeated replies from PC2. What is verified, and what still needs a separate test?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Compare the same peer test and the recorded configuration baseline before calling the lab restored. Successful ICMP does not establish TCP/UDP services or application health. Any application test belongs to a separately authorized environment; there is no web server in this lab.

realWorldScenario.title: Investigate an Office Ping Report Without Removing Its Controls
realWorldScenario.takeaway: A layered model guides evidence collection, not automatic removal of security controls. Separate observations from hypotheses, preserve intended policy and get the appropriate authorization. The concrete ACL creation and rollback sequence in this lesson belongs only to its isolated lab.
realWorldScenario.situation: An office reports that a server no longer replies to ping. This is a paper incident discussion, not an instruction to run the lab fault on that office. The responsible operator first confirms permission to inspect the relevant systems and gathers evidence without changing security policy.
walkthrough: Record the reported source, destination, time and affected service. A web-service complaint and an ICMP timeout are different observations; ask which was actually measured.
Within the approved read-only scope, compare cable and interface state, addresses, gateways and the recorded path with the known baseline. An up/up port alone does not prove the server is reachable.
Consider both directions and endpoint behavior. Missed ping replies may involve host firewalls, link problems or rate limits, not only router ACLs.

Ask the authorized operator to inspect the relevant ACL identifiers, interface directions and supported match counters. Treat deliberately filtered ICMP as possible intended policy, not automatically a fault to remove.
Report what is known and what remains uncertain. An approved service-specific test may be needed; this lesson's isolated lab does not run a production web-service test.

Do not detach or delete office ACLs as a diagnostic shortcut. Any real change requires the organization's approval and rollback process. Reproduce the educational before/fault/after exercise only in the fully disconnected disposable lab.

title: Encapsulation: what changes hop by hop
moduleTitle: Network Foundations and the Packet Journey

lab.goal: Build a disposable Ethernet path from PC1 through Switch, Router1 and Router2 to PC2. Capture the same ICMP request on all three routed segments, compare its frame addresses and IPv4 fields, then test and recover one controlled link fault.
setup: Create a fresh GNS3 desktop project named CCNA-Day-05. Add two VPCS hosts named PC1 and PC2, one built-in Ethernet Switch, and two fresh IOS/IOS XE router instances named Router1 and Router2. Do not attach Cloud, NAT or external links.

Use legally entitled router appliances with two routed Ethernet ports each, not Layer 2 switch ports. Before this lab, complete appliance installation and verify both routers boot. If an initial configuration dialog appears, answer no and press Enter to reach the console.

The example maps Router1 LAN to GigabitEthernet0/0 and transit to GigabitEthernet0/1; Router2 transit to GigabitEthernet0/0 and LAN to GigabitEthernet0/1. Inventory the actual names in steps 1–2 and substitute them consistently in every later command and cable selection. If two routed ports are missing, stop and correct the appliance template.

Use Add a Link to connect the exact endpoints in the topology. Keep the two used Switch ports in the same default access segment. The built-in Switch has no IOS console; do not type router commands into it. Use Ethernet only, not serial connections.

Install and open Wireshark before starting. Start all four endpoint/router nodes with the green start control. Right-click a node and choose Console. Keep its GNS3 node name visible so the two router consoles cannot be confused.

Start only from unused router ports with no IP addresses, NAT, access filters or custom routes. Steps 1–2 confirm this. If existing settings appear, stop and use fresh disposable instances rather than overwrite them. Keep the original project untouched.

Write the addressing table and port mapping in a separate note. /24 is 255.255.255.0 on the host LANs; /30 is 255.255.255.252 on the router link. PC1 gateway is 192.168.1.1; PC2 gateway is 192.168.2.1. No Internet access is expected.

Type only command text, one line at a time, followed by Enter. A pager prompt accepts Space for the next page or q to quit. On an error, stop and check the device, mode and port mapping. If a requested password is unknown, resolve your lab access before continuing.

steps.title: Configure Router1 only
steps.instruction: Open the Router1 console at # after its inventory step. Apply only this router's lines in order, pressing Enter each time. Replace example interface names with your recorded mapping. The route belongs to global configuration mode, reached after the second exit.
steps.expectedResult: Router1 returns to # with both addresses configured and a static route toward the remote /24 LAN. Verify actual link state in the later display step; no shutdown alone is not proof of connectivity.
commandExplanations: configure terminal enters global configuration mode, shown by (config)#, so subsequent lines can change this lab router.

interface selects the PC1 LAN port, GigabitEthernet0/0, and enters (config-if)# mode. GigabitEthernet names the port type; slash-separated numbers identify its slot and port. Use your verified mapping if different.
ip address assigns 192.168.1.1 to this PC1 LAN interface. Mask 255.255.255.0 is /24, making the first three address numbers the network part. The dots separate four decimal address bytes.
no shutdown removes the administrative disable from the selected lab interface. A working cable and running peer are still required for an up/up state.
exit leaves this interface context and returns to global configuration mode; it does not delete the settings.

interface selects the transit port, GigabitEthernet0/1, and enters (config-if)# mode. GigabitEthernet names the port type; slash-separated numbers identify its slot and port. Use your verified mapping if different.
ip address assigns 10.0.0.1 to this transit interface. Mask 255.255.255.252 is /30, making 10.0.0.0 the transit network with usable hosts .1 and .2. The dots separate four decimal address bytes.
no shutdown removes the administrative disable from the selected lab interface. A working cable and running peer are still required for an up/up state.
exit leaves this interface context and returns to global configuration mode; it does not delete the settings.

ip route adds a route to remote network 192.168.2.0. Mask 255.255.255.0 selects that /24 network; 10.0.0.2 is the other router's directly reachable transit address, the next hop. This is not an address assigned to the local port.
end returns from configuration mode to privileged EXEC, shown by #, for display commands.

steps.why: Explicit host addressing and gateways make the route usable from the endpoints. Using a router command in VPCS would not configure the intended setting.

steps.instruction: Right-click PC1 and choose Console. Confirm this is the VPCS window, not a router or your computer's terminal. Enter each line and press Enter. Compare the displayed address, mask and gateway with this host's table row before continuing.
steps.expectedResult: PC1 shows 192.168.1.10/24 and gateway 192.168.1.1. Record its MAC address for the later capture comparison.
commandExplanations: ip assigns this VPCS host address 192.168.1.10. Mask 255.255.255.0 is /24. The last value, 192.168.1.1, is its local router gateway for remote networks. Dots separate address bytes; spaces separate the three values.
show ip displays this VPCS host's address, mask, gateway and MAC address. It verifies local settings only; it does not send a reachability test.

steps.why: Explicit host addressing and gateways make the route usable from the endpoints. Using a router command in VPCS would not configure the intended setting.
steps.title: Configure PC2 in VPCS
steps.instruction: Right-click PC2 and choose Console. Confirm this is the VPCS window, not a router or your computer's terminal. Enter each line and press Enter. Compare the displayed address, mask and gateway with this host's table row before continuing.
steps.expectedResult: PC2 shows 192.168.2.10/24 and gateway 192.168.2.1. Record its MAC address for the later capture comparison.

show ip displays this VPCS host's address, mask, gateway and MAC address. It verifies local settings only; it does not send a reachability test.

steps.why: These displays establish configuration evidence and local interface identities. They do not show individual request TTL values or prove the full end-to-end exchange.
steps.title: Verify Router1 forwarding setup
steps.instruction: Return to Router1's console at #. Run these displays in order. Compare port addresses with the table and record each interface MAC from its hardware/address line. Require both selected ports to be up/up and the remote static route to be present before the capture experiment.
steps.expectedResult: Both selected interfaces are up/up. Router1 lists the two connected subnets and an S route to 192.168.2.0/24 via 10.0.0.2. If not, stop and resolve the port, peer or route discrepancy.
commandExplanations: show ip interface brief lists IPv4 addresses and the status and protocol state of every interface. brief requests the short summary; it does not display packet TTL.
show ip route lists known IPv4 routes. C marks connected networks, L local interface addresses on supporting releases, and S a configured static route.

show interfaces displays status, hardware MAC address and counters for the mapped GigabitEthernet0/0 port. The slash-separated numbers select one port; record that port's MAC, not a generic router MAC.
show interfaces displays the same information for the mapped GigabitEthernet0/1 port. Record its separate hardware MAC address for the outgoing or incoming frame comparison.

steps.instruction: Return to Router2's console at #. Run these displays in order. Compare port addresses with the table and record each interface MAC from its hardware/address line. Require both selected ports to be up/up and the remote static route to be present before the capture experiment.
steps.expectedResult: Both selected interfaces are up/up. Router2 lists the two connected subnets and an S route to 192.168.1.0/24 via 10.0.0.1. If not, stop and resolve the port, peer or route discrepancy.
commandExplanations: show ip interface brief lists IPv4 addresses and the status and protocol state of every interface. brief requests the short summary; it does not display packet TTL.
show ip route lists known IPv4 routes. C marks connected networks, L local interface addresses on supporting releases, and S a configured static route.

steps.why: Simultaneous captures allow comparison of one request at three places. Capturing a different request on each link would weaken the field comparison.
steps.title: Start three labelled link captures
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click the Switch–Router1 link and choose Start capture. Open Wireshark if prompted. Repeat for Router1–Router2 and Router2–PC2. Label your notes A, B and C with each link and keep all three captures running simultaneously. If Wireshark cannot open, fix its GNS3 integration before proceeding. No router command is needed.
steps.expectedResult: Three capture windows record the first LAN, the transit Ethernet segment and the final LAN. Their titles or notes identify the corresponding link.

steps.why: A peer ping exercises the routed path in both directions. Self-ping would not prove either router or the links between them work.
steps.title: Send the baseline request from PC1
steps.instruction: Open only PC1's VPCS console. Run the peer ping and let it finish. If initial requests time out while ARP resolves, repeat the same command. Obtain successful replies before adding a fault. Keep the captures running for this baseline and record the time of the test.
steps.expectedResult: PC1 receives Echo Replies from PC2 after both directions are configured. The captures contain requests and replies; missing replies require investigation before the fault test.
commandExplanations: ping sends ICMP Echo Requests to PC2 at 192.168.2.10 and waits for replies. That value is the remote endpoint, not PC1 itself or its gateway. Reply TTL describes the returning reply; it is not the outgoing request TTL.

steps.why: Matching a single request ties the field changes to forwarding. ICMP replies are different packets; comparing them to requests can produce a false conclusion about TTL or addressing.
steps.title: Compare the same captured request
steps.instruction: In each Wireshark window, click the display-filter bar, type icmp and press Enter; this word displays ICMP traffic without changing the saved capture. Select an Echo Request from 192.168.1.10 to 192.168.2.10. Match its ICMP identifier and sequence number across A, B and C, confirming direction and payload. Expand Ethernet II, Internet Protocol Version 4 and Internet Control Message Protocol in the details pane. Record MAC pairs, IP pairs, TTL and IPv4 header checksum. File packet numbers need not match.
steps.expectedResult: Endpoint IP addresses agree in A, B and C. MAC pairs follow the three interface pairs taught above. If A has TTL T, B normally has T−1 and C T−2; the IPv4 header checksum changes. Record actual values, not an assumed starting TTL.

steps.why: A controlled single change lets you relate configuration evidence to the observed failure, instead of treating every missing ping reply as a routing or TTL problem.
steps.title: Disable the Router2 PC2-facing port
steps.instruction: After recording the working baseline, open Router2 at #. Confirm GigabitEthernet0/1 is your mapped PC2-facing port and no other node uses it. Apply these lines only in the disposable lab. Do not save this temporary fault to startup configuration.
steps.expectedResult: Router2 reports its PC2-facing interface administratively down. The known baseline now differs by this one deliberate change.
commandExplanations: configure terminal enters global configuration mode, shown by (config)#, so subsequent lines can change this lab router.

interface selects the PC2 LAN port, GigabitEthernet0/1, and enters (config-if)# mode. GigabitEthernet names the port type; slash-separated numbers identify its slot and port. Use your verified mapping if different.
shutdown administratively disables only the selected Router2 PC2-facing interface. It intentionally interrupts the final Ethernet segment; it does not delete the IP address.
end returns from configuration mode to privileged EXEC, shown by #, for display commands.
show ip interface brief lists IPv4 addresses and the status and protocol state of every interface. brief requests the short summary; it does not display packet TTL.

steps.why: The known fault explains this experiment, but a real unexplained ping failure still needs port, ARP, route, filtering and endpoint checks.
steps.title: Observe the fault from PC1
steps.instruction: Return to PC1's VPCS console and run the same remote test. Record whether it times out or reports an unreachable destination. Do not change addresses or routes in response: the planned cause is Router2's administratively disabled PC2-facing port.
steps.expectedResult: PC1 no longer receives successful PC2 Echo Replies. A timeout or unreachable message is possible; neither result alone proves that TTL expired.
commandExplanations: ping again targets remote PC2 at 192.168.2.10 using ICMP Echo Requests. Keep the destination identical to the working baseline so the deliberate port shutdown is the only intended difference.

steps.why: Restoring the port removes the deliberate fault. The independent endpoint test confirms that the intended communication recovered, rather than relying on one local status display.
steps.title: Restore Router2 and verify recovery
steps.instruction: Open Router2 at #. Confirm the mapped PC2 port again, then enter these lines and check for up/up. Next switch to PC1 and repeat the exact ping from step 13 to remote PC2; its meaning is unchanged. Require successful replies again before closing the project. If replies do not return, compare all settings with the recorded working baseline.
steps.expectedResult: Router2's PC2-facing port returns to up/up and the repeated PC1-to-PC2 test receives Echo Replies again. If either check fails, recovery is not yet verified.
commandExplanations: configure terminal enters global configuration mode, shown by (config)#, so subsequent lines can change this lab router.

no shutdown removes the administrative disable from the selected lab interface. A working cable and running peer are still required for an up/up state.
end returns from configuration mode to privileged EXEC, shown by #, for display commands.

lab.title: Tracing Encapsulation Changes Hop-by-Hop in a Routed Network
cleanup: Verify the Router2 port and peer ping have recovered before stopping any node. Keep your baseline, fault and recovery notes separately.
Stop each link capture in GNS3 and use Wireshark File > Save As to save labelled capture files if needed. Close their windows after saving.

Stop all nodes in this disposable project. The exercise does not save router or VPCS startup settings. Keep the project and notes for reference, or delete only this disposable project after confirming its name; never reset shared devices.

lab.topology: Five devices, all Ethernet: PC1 Ethernet0 — Switch Ethernet0; Switch Ethernet1 — Router1 LAN; Router1 transit — Router2 transit; Router2 LAN — PC2 Ethernet0. The Switch does not add a routing hop.
verification: Confirm the addressing table against each host's show ip output and each router's show ip interface brief output, using the meanings explained in the configuration steps.
Require both connected networks and the remote S route on each router. A one-way route is insufficient for successful request/reply communication.
Require a successful PC1-to-PC2 peer ping before the fault and again after recovery; use the same destination and explained command from steps 10 and 13.
For one matched Echo Request, record identical endpoint IP addresses, three local MAC pairs, TTL changes and the IPv4 header checksum from captures A, B and C.
Keep the observations separate: router displays verify settings; packet captures demonstrate field values; successful ping demonstrates ICMP exchange only.
lab.licensingNote: GNS3 does not provide Cisco software images. Use a Cisco image only when the applicable Cisco license or entitlement legally permits that use, and do not share or redistribute Cisco image files. Cisco CML reference-platform images are licensed for use within CML unless a separate license permits outside use. Cisco Modeling Labs is the official alternative; built-in VPCS and Ethernet switch nodes do not require a Cisco image.
troubleshooting: If an interface name is rejected, stop and compare the actual inventory with your role mapping. Do not guess another port or configure a built-in Switch with IOS commands.

If a port is administratively down outside the planned fault, compare its configuration with the setup step. If it is down/down instead, check the selected cable and running peer; no shutdown cannot repair a wrong cable.

If peer ping fails, check both VPCS masks and gateways, both router addresses and both static routes. Repeat after initial ARP resolution. Do not conclude that missing replies identify a particular layer.

If a capture is empty, confirm the link label, running capture and current ping. Clear the display filter to inspect all traffic, then reapply icmp. Match requests, not replies or unrelated file packet numbers.

If a checksum is flagged unexpectedly, inspect the actual IPv4 header and matching packet before drawing a conclusion. Capture/offload presentation can affect displayed validation; an omitted Ethernet frame check sequence is not evidence of failure.

options: Ethernet destination: Router1 LAN MAC; IPv4 destination: 192.168.2.10.
Ethernet destination: PC2 MAC; IPv4 destination: 192.168.1.1.
Ethernet destination: Switch MAC; IPv4 destination: 10.0.0.2.
Ethernet destination: Router2 LAN MAC; IPv4 destination: 192.168.1.10.
quiz.question: Which destination pair does PC1 use for a request to remote PC2?
quiz.explanation: PC1 addresses the local frame to its gateway while keeping PC2 as the IP destination. PC2 and Router2 are not local Ethernet neighbors of PC1. The Switch forwards the frame; it is not the addressed gateway.

quiz.question: Capture A shows request TTL 64. What should matching captures B and C normally show?
quiz.explanation: Each of the two routers normally reduces TTL by one in this lab. It does not increase TTL or leave it unchanged. The Switch does not count as another router, and the example has no two-at-a-time decrement.

options: It must contain a TCP segment.
It contains an ICMP message directly inside IPv4.
It contains only a MAC address, with no IPv4 header.
Its final destination IP becomes each next-hop router address.
quiz.question: Which statement describes the packet inside this lab ping frame?
quiz.explanation: Ping uses ICMP over IPv4, so no TCP segment is required. The Ethernet frame still contains an IPv4 header. Ordinary forwarding in this no-NAT lab preserves the final endpoint IP address.

options: A router interface status summary alone.
Matching ICMP Echo Requests captured before and after the router.
Matching packet row numbers from unrelated capture files.
Comparing an outgoing request with any returning reply.
quiz.question: Which evidence demonstrates the TTL change of one forwarded request?
quiz.explanation: Matched captures expose the request header at both points. Interface summaries describe settings, file row numbers are local to each capture, and replies are separate packets with their own initial TTL.

options: Only typing no shutdown without checking its result.
Changing PC1 to a different destination address.
The mapped port is up/up and the original PC1-to-PC2 ping receives replies again.
quiz.question: What confirms recovery from the deliberate Router2 port shutdown?
quiz.explanation: Recovery needs both port evidence and the same peer test used for the baseline. A command alone is not a result. Changing the target weakens the comparison, and deleting routes would remove the intended path.

glossary.meaning: Adding a protocol header, and sometimes a trailer, around data for delivery at that layer.
The local Ethernet wrapper carrying an IPv4 packet, including MAC addresses and normally a frame check sequence.
A network-layer header and payload. The header contains endpoint IP addresses, TTL and a header checksum.
A TCP header and its data. TCP is a transport protocol; the ICMP ping used here does not contain a TCP segment.
A diagnostic request/reply exchange used by ping, carried directly inside IP.
Time To Live: an IPv4 field reduced during router forwarding to bound packet lifetime.
An error-checking value for the IPv4 header. Changing TTL requires updating this value.
An address identifying an Ethernet interface on a local segment; different router interfaces have their own values.
Address Resolution Protocol: a way to find the local Ethernet MAC address associated with an IPv4 next hop.
The local router interface to which a host sends traffic for a remote subnet.
A manually configured destination network and next hop used by the router to select a forwarding path.
A recorded view of traffic at a link that can be inspected in Wireshark.

sections.example: Use nested envelopes as a memory aid. The outer envelope represents delivery across one Ethernet segment; the inner label represents the endpoint IP addresses. A router replaces the outer envelope. Real network headers are fields of bits, and a router also changes selected IPv4 fields. The comparison does not mean the whole inner packet is immutable.
sections.heading: Follow one message through its wrappers
keyPoints: The lab packet carries ICMP directly inside IPv4, inside Ethernet.
TCP segments belong to TCP traffic; they are not required for ping.
A frame describes local delivery while a packet carries network-layer addressing.
sections.explanation: Encapsulation adds delivery information around a message. Ethernet uses a frame with local source and destination MAC addresses. Inside that frame, an IPv4 packet names the original sender and final receiver. Applications often use TCP, which carries data in segments, or UDP, which carries datagrams. Ping is different: its ICMP Echo message sits directly inside IPv4, without a TCP segment or UDP datagram. Do not draw a TCP segment around this lab ping. The receiver reads the outer Ethernet information, then the IPv4 information, then the ICMP message. These names describe different layers, not interchangeable names for the same header.

sections.example: Write two destination columns for PC1's outgoing request. In the Ethernet column write Router1's LAN interface MAC. In the IPv4 column write 192.168.2.10. After Router1, the Ethernet destination becomes Router2's transit-interface MAC, but the IPv4 destination is still 192.168.2.10. Never substitute the next-hop IP for the final destination in the forwarded packet.
sections.heading: Separate the endpoint from the next hop
keyPoints: The next hop is the immediate receiver on the current segment.
The final destination remains PC2 for this request throughout the lab.
The switch-to-router and PC-to-switch cables belong to the same Ethernet segment.
sections.explanation: PC1 is 192.168.1.10/24 and PC2 is 192.168.2.10/24. Their masks place them in different subnets, so PC1 sends this remote traffic to its gateway, Router1 at 192.168.1.1. PC1 uses ARP to learn that gateway interface MAC address. Its Ethernet destination is Router1, while its IPv4 destination is PC2. The built-in Switch forwards the frame within the first segment; it does not route or reduce IP TTL. Router1 selects Router2 at 10.0.0.2 as the next hop. Router2 selects its directly connected PC2 network. Replies need routes in the opposite direction as well. Successful local configuration does not by itself establish the full path.

sections.example: Build a paper table with rows for Switch-to-Router1, Router1-to-Router2, and Router2-to-PC2. Record the same endpoint IP pair in all three rows. Enter the three different local MAC pairs beside them. This predicts the capture results; it is a hypothesis until you inspect matching requests in your own captures.
sections.heading: Identify the fields that routers change
keyPoints: Routers build new Ethernet frames; an ordinary switch does not replace endpoint MAC addresses as a routing hop would.
Unchanged endpoint IP addresses are a property of this no-NAT lab, not every possible network.
The IPv4 header checksum and Ethernet frame check sequence protect different headers or frames.
sections.explanation: In this exercise there is no Network Address Translation (NAT), which would rewrite IP addresses, and no tunnelling. Router1 removes the incoming Ethernet encapsulation and creates an outgoing frame using its own transit-interface MAC as source and Router2's transit-interface MAC as destination. Router2 then uses its PC2-facing interface MAC and PC2's MAC. Interfaces on the same router can have different MAC addresses; record the actual interface value. IPv4 source 192.168.1.10 and destination 192.168.2.10 stay unchanged. The ICMP payload also remains unchanged in normal forwarding. Ethernet frame check sequences belong to each transmitted frame, but many capture paths omit them. Do not treat an absent Ethernet trailer as a broken lab.

sections.example: If your first matching request has TTL 64, expect 63 after Router1 and 62 after Router2. Those numbers illustrate the pattern, not a required starting value. Compare the same request using direction, source and destination IP, and its ICMP identifier and sequence number. A request and its reply are different packets and can start with different TTL values.
sections.heading: Read TTL and the IPv4 header checksum
keyPoints: Compare one request across capture points rather than comparing unrelated packets.
A changed TTL requires an updated IPv4 header checksum.
A single observed TTL does not reveal a hop count unless the starting TTL is known.
sections.explanation: TTL is an eight-bit IPv4 field that bounds a packet's lifetime. A forwarding router decreases it by at least one; in this small lab expect one per router. If the remaining value is insufficient to forward, the router discards the packet and normally sends an ICMP Time Exceeded message. Because TTL is in the IPv4 header, changing it requires updating that header's checksum. The checksum covers the IPv4 header, not the entire payload. Do not assume that every sender starts with TTL 64. Observe the first capture and call that value T; the next two captures should normally show T minus 1 and T minus 2. The TTL printed by PC1's ping belongs to an arriving reply, not to its outgoing request.

sections.example: If ping fails, first compare actual host addresses and gateways with the table. Then inspect router port state and the static routes in both directions. An initial lost request may occur during ARP resolution, so repeat the same test. A later successful reply demonstrates ICMP exchange at that time; it does not prove a website, TCP session, DNS lookup or Internet connection works.
sections.heading: Use the right evidence for each question
keyPoints: Interface state and routes explain configuration; captures show packet fields.
Match Echo Requests by IP pair, ICMP identifier and sequence number, then confirm direction and payload.
Keep the fault experiment separate from the successful capture baseline.
sections.explanation: Router display commands answer configuration questions. show ip interface brief summarizes addresses and interface state. show ip route displays the forwarding routes. show interfaces includes link details and counters. These displays do not show the TTL of every packet crossing the router. Use simultaneous link captures for packet fields. In Wireshark, select the same ICMP Echo Request in each capture, expand Ethernet II, Internet Protocol Version 4 and Internet Control Message Protocol, then record the addresses, TTL and IPv4 header checksum. Packet numbers in the left column are local to each capture file; they are not shared packet identities. This lab does not need packet debugging or forwarding-path changes.

content.metaTitle: CCNA Day 5: Encapsulation Changes Hop-by-Hop in Routed Networks
takeaways: In this lab, ICMP sits directly inside IPv4, which sits inside an Ethernet frame.
The Ethernet MAC pair changes at each router; an ordinary switch is not an additional routing hop.
Endpoint IPv4 addresses remain unchanged because the exercise has no NAT or tunnels.
Router forwarding reduces TTL and updates the IPv4 header checksum.
Use matched captures for packet fields, router displays for settings, and peer ping for ICMP reachability.
Verify the working baseline, observe one deliberate port fault, and confirm recovery with the original peer test.
objectives: Distinguish an Ethernet frame, an IPv4 packet, a TCP segment and an ICMP message.
Trace the same request across two routers using its addresses and ICMP identifier and sequence number.
Explain why a router replaces the Ethernet frame while preserving endpoint IP addresses in this lab.
Observe TTL and IPv4 header checksum changes without assuming that interface commands display individual packets.
Configure and verify both directions of the path, then recover from one controlled interface shutdown.
content.plainAnswer: Encapsulation wraps a message in the information needed to deliver it. In this Ethernet lab, a router removes the incoming frame and builds a new frame for its outgoing link. The IPv4 source and destination addresses stay unchanged because there is no address translation. Each forwarding router reduces Time To Live (TTL) and updates the IPv4 header checksum. Compare captures of the same ICMP Echo Request on three links to see these changes; interface status alone cannot show them.

visualStory.title: Tracing Encapsulation Changes Hop-by-Hop in a Routed Network

stages.title: PC1 sends an IP packet
stages.explanation: PC1 sends an ICMP request in IPv4: source 192.168.1.10, destination 192.168.2.10. Its Ethernet frame addresses Router1. The Switch forwards it without reducing TTL.

stages.title: Router1 updates headers
stages.explanation: Router1 reduces TTL and updates the IPv4 header checksum. Endpoint IP addresses stay unchanged. A new Ethernet frame uses Router1's outgoing MAC and Router2's incoming MAC.

stages.title: Router2 updates headers
stages.explanation: Router2 reduces TTL again and updates the IPv4 header checksum. It keeps both endpoint IP addresses and builds a new frame from its PC2-facing MAC to PC2's MAC. PC2 receives the request.

visualStory.altText: Diagram shows packet data traveling from PC1 through Router1 and Router2 to PC2 with encapsulation headers changing at each hop, including MAC address and TTL updates.
visualStory.boundary: The Switch on the first Ethernet segment is omitted for clarity. IP Packet is a data annotation, not a device or extra hop. This lab has no NAT or tunnels.
visualStory.takeaway: Routers replace Ethernet frames and update IPv4 TTL and its header checksum. Endpoint IP addresses stay unchanged in this lab.

candidates.name: Step-by-step packet journey with encapsulation layers changing
candidates.scene: Four devices form a routed path from PC1 through Router1 and Router2 to PC2. An IP Packet annotation describes the data; the first-segment switch is omitted.
candidates.limitation: Focus on a linear path may hide differences in other topologies or broadcast domains
candidates.teachingValue: Shows exactly how encapsulation headers change hop-by-hop, illustrating addresses and TTL changes in sequence

candidates.name: Before-and-after frame headers at each router hop
candidates.scene: Side-by-side comparison of frame and packet headers before and after each router, illustrating address and TTL updates
candidates.limitation: Less intuitive flow; harder to see the continuous journey through the network
candidates.teachingValue: Clear visual comparison emphasizing what fields change and what stay the same

candidates.name: Layered encapsulation exploded view with focus on TTL and MAC address
candidates.scene: Graphical exploded layers of frame, packet, segment at each hop, highlighting MAC changes and the decremented TTL in IP header
candidates.limitation: May overwhelm beginners with complexity of multiple layers and technical details
candidates.teachingValue: Shows detailed structure and fields, helping learners connect layers to contents and changes

conceptSelection.selectionReason: The step-by-step journey best matches the lesson objective of tracing encapsulation hop-by-hop, showing the gradual changes in a simple linear network topology. This approach works well to build a beginner's mental model by following the packet through each device and observing changes, without overwhelming detail.

walkthrough.why: PC2 is outside PC1's /24 subnet, so the first Ethernet receiver must be the gateway.
walkthrough.action: PC1 selects its gateway for remote PC2.
walkthrough.whatHappens: PC1 sends an ICMP request inside IPv4 and an Ethernet frame addressed to Router1; the Switch forwards that frame.

walkthrough.why: The next Ethernet segment needs a different local sender and receiver.
walkthrough.action: Router1 forwards the request toward Router2.
walkthrough.whatHappens: The router replaces the Ethernet frame, decreases TTL and updates the IPv4 header checksum without changing the endpoint IP pair.

walkthrough.why: PC2 is directly connected to Router2, so it is the final local next hop.
walkthrough.action: Router2 forwards the request to PC2.
walkthrough.whatHappens: Router2 builds the final Ethernet frame and updates TTL and checksum again. PC2 receives the ICMP Echo Request and can generate a reply.

beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: A remote destination can stay the same while each local delivery changes. Separating those facts helps you investigate the correct part of a path.

firstPractice.hint: Use interface roles instead of inventing numeric MAC addresses. Phone-only learners can do this prediction; captures still require the hands-on lab.
firstPractice.task: Before configuring devices, draw three rows for the Ethernet segments on paper. Copy the request IP pair into each row and predict each local MAC sender and receiver.
firstPractice.expected: All rows contain 192.168.1.10 to 192.168.2.10. Their MAC pairs name PC1/Router1, Router1/Router2 and Router2/PC2 interfaces.

beginnerGuide.startingPoint: An interface is a connection on a device. An IP address identifies it in an IP network; a MAC address identifies it on Ethernet. Read the short definitions above before opening the lab.

checkUnderstanding.hint: Compare the next device on one segment with the final device that should receive the request.
checkUnderstanding.answer: No. Ethernet names the next local receiver, while IPv4 still names PC2 in this no-NAT lab. Router1 therefore sends a frame to Router2 containing an IPv4 packet still addressed to 192.168.2.10.
checkUnderstanding.question: Does a changed Ethernet destination mean that the final IPv4 destination also changed?

everydayComparison.whereItStops: Routers do not drive parcels. They read binary fields and also update TTL and the IPv4 header checksum; the packet is not wholly unchanged.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: The changing local delivery represents Ethernet frames. The final destination label represents the destination IP address, which is unchanged in this lab.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: A parcel travels in several delivery vehicles. Each driver delivers to the next transfer point while the parcel keeps its final destination label.

prerequisites: Complete Day 1 or the start-here guide: open an app, create a project, click a node, and type into its console.
Recap Day 2: a switch forwards within an Ethernet segment; a router forwards between IP networks.
Recap Day 4: an interface is a device connection; a console accepts commands; ping tests ICMP reachability, not every application.
Use an isolated GNS3 desktop project with Wireshark and two entitled Cisco IOS/IOS XE router appliances with two routed Ethernet ports each.
content.learnerOutcome: Build an isolated two-router Ethernet path, explain every configuration command, and compare one ping request across three packet captures to identify unchanged IP addresses, new frame addresses, and reduced TTL.
content.metaDescription: Trace Ethernet frames and IPv4 packets across two routers, compare MAC addresses and TTL in Wireshark, and practise a guided GNS3 lab.

terms.meaning: An IPv4 address identifies an interface. A mask separates its network part from its host part. /24 means 255.255.255.0; /30 means 255.255.255.252 and gives two usable host addresses here.
A host sends traffic for another subnet to its default gateway, a local router interface. A route tells a router which next device can reach a destination network.
A MAC address identifies an Ethernet interface on its local segment. Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) discovers the MAC address associated with a local IPv4 next hop.
An Ethernet frame carries an IP packet inside a link header and trailer. A TCP segment is one possible IP payload. This ping lab instead carries an ICMP message directly inside IPv4.
Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) carries diagnostic messages. Ping sends Echo Requests and waits for Echo Replies. A missing reply alone does not identify the fault.
Time To Live (TTL) limits routed travel. A router reduces it before forwarding. The IPv4 header checksum checks the header for errors and must change when TTL changes.
A capture records traffic at one link. Wireshark opens that record and lets you expand Ethernet, IPv4 and ICMP fields to inspect what was actually sent.

teachingPrelude.explanation: Read the device name before typing. In GNS3, right-click that device and choose Console. Type one command per line and press Enter. The router prompt ends in > for basic access, # for privileged access, (config)# for general settings, or (config-if)# for one interface. Prompts are not part of the command. If a line is rejected, stop and check the selected device, spelling, mode and mapped port before continuing.
teachingPrelude.labBoundary: Use only fresh disposable lab routers, VPCS hosts and Ethernet links. Connect no Cloud, NAT or physical-network node. This exercise has no address translation, tunnels or routing protocols.

practiceQuestions.answer: An ICMP Echo message, not a TCP segment or UDP datagram.
practiceQuestions.question: What is inside the IPv4 packet used by this ping lab?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Ping uses ICMP directly over IPv4. TCP segments and UDP datagrams are other possible IP payloads, so the general layered model must be adapted to the actual traffic.

practiceQuestions.answer: Its source IPv4 address 192.168.1.10 and destination IPv4 address 192.168.2.10 remain unchanged in this no-NAT lab.
practiceQuestions.question: What stays unchanged in the request across both routers?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The Ethernet receiver changes at each routed segment. That does not replace the final IPv4 destination with a next-hop router address.

practiceQuestions.answer: It forwards the Ethernet frame within the first segment rather than routing the IPv4 packet.
practiceQuestions.question: Why does the Switch not create an extra TTL decrement?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The two cables on either side of the Switch belong to one segment in this lab. Crossing a switch is not the same operation as crossing a router.

practiceQuestions.answer: TTL changed, so the checksum over the IPv4 header must be updated.
practiceQuestions.question: Why should the IPv4 header checksum differ after forwarding?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The IPv4 header checksum covers the header, not the entire application payload. Ethernet has a separate frame check sequence that may be absent from the capture.

practiceQuestions.answer: Match the source and destination IP pair and the ICMP identifier and sequence number, confirming request direction and payload.
practiceQuestions.question: How can you compare one request across three capture files?
practiceQuestions.explanation: File packet numbers are assigned independently within each capture. A request and its reply are separate packets, even when their ICMP identifiers correspond.

practiceQuestions.answer: It displays interface addresses and status; it does not show the per-packet TTL changes that the captures demonstrate.
practiceQuestions.question: What does show ip interface brief establish, and what does it not establish?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Use the display for configuration and link-state evidence. Use matched captured requests for packet-field evidence, then verify peer reachability separately.

realWorldScenario.title: Prove what changed between two office networks
realWorldScenario.takeaway: Separate the final IPv4 destination from the next Ethernet receiver. Use captures to demonstrate header changes and configuration displays to explain why the chosen path exists.
realWorldScenario.situation: A colleague says that every router must change the destination IP because it sends to a different next device. Use the isolated lab to test that claim. In a workplace, request authorized capture evidence and inspect it read-only; do not copy the lab shutdown experiment onto a working network.
walkthrough: Identify the actual source and final destination of the request before looking at local Ethernet addresses. Here they are 192.168.1.10 and 192.168.2.10.
At capture A, record PC1 and Router1 LAN MAC addresses. The Switch forwards this same local frame and is not a TTL-decrementing hop.
At capture B, match the request using its ICMP identifier and sequence. Record Router1 transit and Router2 transit MAC addresses, the unchanged IP pair and the reduced TTL.
At capture C, find that request again. Record Router2 LAN and PC2 MAC addresses, the unchanged IP pair and the second TTL reduction.
Compare the IPv4 header checksum as well. It changes with the header; the ICMP payload is not rewritten by ordinary forwarding in this exercise.
Report only what the evidence establishes. These matched captures describe one ICMP request, not all application traffic or networks with NAT, tunnels or other transformations.

title: Copper, fiber, speed, duplex, and interface errors
moduleTitle: Network Foundations and the Packet Journey

lab.goal: Observe a working four-node path, deliberately remove its only inter-switch link, and verify recovery. Then interpret hypothetical media and interface evidence without claiming that GNS3 measured hardware faults.
setup: Finish the official GNS3 local-server setup. If VPCS is unavailable on your installation, use the official installation guidance before continuing; do not substitute an unknown image.
Create a new blank project named Day6-link-check. Do not add Cloud or NAT nodes, bridge host adapters or connect this exercise to shared networks.
From End devices add two VPCS nodes and name them PC1 and PC2. From Switches add two built-in Ethernet switches and name them Switch1 and Switch2.
Use Add a link to make exactly the three connections in the table. Turn on interface labels and verify each endpoint. Do not add a second link between the switches.
Start the VPCS nodes with the green Start button. Built-in switches do not have Cisco consoles; their port settings are available through Configure in the GUI.
Keep a plain-text notes file called Day6-baseline.txt in Notepad, TextEdit or a Linux text editor. Record device names, links and addresses before the deliberate fault.

steps.why: A recorded baseline lets you restore the exact intended path without guessing which cable belonged to which port.
steps.title: Record the isolated topology
steps.instruction: In the GNS3 workspace, check each device and cable against the addressing table. Record PC1 Ethernet0 to Switch1 Ethernet0, Switch1 Ethernet1 to Switch2 Ethernet0, and Switch2 Ethernet1 to PC2 Ethernet0. Confirm no Cloud or NAT node exists.
steps.expectedResult: Your notes show four named devices, exactly three connections and no external connection. Stop if the visible topology differs.

steps.why: Confirming the local identity prevents an address error from being confused with the deliberate link fault later.
steps.title: Configure PC1
steps.instruction: Right-click PC1 and choose Console before typing. Wait for the VPCS prompt, normally PC1>. Type only each command below, then press Enter. If a different device console opens, close it and select PC1 again.
steps.expectedResult: PC1 reports 192.168.6.10 with mask 255.255.255.0. Record it and correct any typing error before continuing.
commandExplanations: Assign PC1 the IPv4 address 192.168.6.10 with mask 255.255.255.0, placing it in network 192.168.6.0/24; no gateway is supplied.
Display PC1's current address information so you can verify the address and mask before testing the other endpoint.

steps.why: The two endpoints need matching network membership and different addresses before the connectivity test is meaningful.
steps.title: Configure PC2
steps.instruction: Right-click PC2 and choose Console before typing. Confirm that this window belongs to PC2, then enter its own address. Do not paste PC1's address into both nodes; each endpoint must be unique.
steps.expectedResult: PC2 reports 192.168.6.20 with mask 255.255.255.0. Neither endpoint needs a default gateway for this same-network exchange.
commandExplanations: Assign PC2 the IPv4 address 192.168.6.20 with mask 255.255.255.0, on the same network as PC1 but with a distinct host address.
Display PC2's address information and verify that it is the intended remote destination, 192.168.6.20.

steps.why: The fault exercise requires evidence that the same remote destination was reachable before you remove a link.
steps.title: Establish the forward baseline
steps.instruction: Right-click PC1 and choose Console before typing. Check your notes: PC1 is 192.168.6.10, so the test below targets PC2, not itself. Run the test, record replies or timeouts, and repeat if the first exchange is delayed by address discovery.
steps.expectedResult: Repeated tests should receive replies from 192.168.6.20. One initial timeout can occur during address discovery, but persistent loss is a setup problem to resolve before proceeding.
commandExplanations: Send ICMP echo requests from PC1 to PC2 at 192.168.6.20 and report whether replies return; this is not a bandwidth or cable-quality test.

steps.why: Testing both endpoints builds a clearer baseline, although neither direction establishes physical-media quality or application health.
steps.title: Establish the reverse baseline
steps.instruction: Right-click PC2 and choose Console before typing. Send the reverse test to PC1 at 192.168.6.10. Record the sender and destination explicitly so that a successful self-ping cannot be mistaken for a test of the complete path.
steps.expectedResult: PC2 receives replies from PC1 on repeated tests. If either direction repeatedly fails, inspect the recorded addresses, node state and three links before adding a fault.
commandExplanations: Send ICMP echo requests from PC2 to PC1 at 192.168.6.10 and check that replies return over the same connected topology.

steps.why: Removing one known path is a controlled connectivity fault. It does not simulate an optical-power reading or a physical duplex mismatch.
steps.title: Remove the single inter-switch link
steps.instruction: In this isolated project only, select the cable joining Switch1 Ethernet1 to Switch2 Ethernet0 and delete that link through its context menu. Do not delete a node or an endpoint cable. Keep the original port pair in your notes for restoration.
steps.expectedResult: The workspace shows PC1 attached to Switch1 and PC2 attached to Switch2, but no connection between the two switches. Both VPCS nodes remain running.

steps.why: The controlled before-and-after comparison supports this known lab fault. A failed ping on an unknown real network would not, by itself, prove a cable fault.
steps.title: Verify loss of the remote path
steps.instruction: Right-click PC1 and choose Console before typing. Repeat exactly the same destination used in the forward baseline. Leave both endpoint addresses unchanged; the only intended change is the missing link between Switch1 and Switch2.
steps.expectedResult: Expect no replies from PC2. A cached MAC address cannot carry traffic across a missing link. An unreachable message or timeout wording may vary with VPCS state.
commandExplanations: Repeat the PC1-to-PC2 echo test with the inter-switch link absent, checking whether any remote reply can traverse the now-broken path.

steps.why: Restoring the same connection preserves a fair test instead of changing several variables at once.
steps.title: Reconnect the recorded port pair
steps.instruction: Use Add a link to connect Switch1 Ethernet1 back to Switch2 Ethernet0, matching the baseline exactly. Leave the endpoint links untouched. Confirm there is only one connection between the switches and all four device names remain visible.
steps.expectedResult: The original three-link topology is restored. The addresses remain unchanged, and the complete path again ends at PC2.

steps.why: A successful repeat test supports recovery of this virtual path, with no unsupported claim about physical counters.
steps.title: Verify forward recovery
steps.instruction: Right-click PC1 and choose Console before typing. Repeat the original remote test and compare it with the recorded baseline and fault result. If repeated tests still fail, inspect the restored ports and addresses rather than changing speed or duplex.
steps.expectedResult: Replies should return on repeated tests after reconnection. Record recovery rather than claiming that a physical cable or transceiver has been tested.
commandExplanations: Retest PC2 at 192.168.6.20 from PC1 after restoring the inter-switch link, using the same sender and destination as before.

steps.why: Keeping both directions and all three phases together makes the exercise evidence useful to another learner reviewing your work.
steps.title: Verify reverse recovery
steps.instruction: Right-click PC2 and choose Console before typing. Repeat the earlier reverse test to PC1 and record the result in Day6-baseline.txt. If recovery is incomplete, keep the project isolated and compare every endpoint with the saved table.
steps.expectedResult: Repeated replies return from PC1. Your notes now contain successful baseline tests, expected loss and successful recovery with the same addresses.
commandExplanations: Retest PC1 at 192.168.6.10 from PC2 after restoration to confirm the reverse request-and-reply exchange also works.

steps.why: A paper exercise teaches selection and compatibility without fabricating hardware capabilities or asking beginners to force an unsupported gigabit half-duplex mode.
steps.title: Compare media and duplex on paper
steps.instruction: Do not type configuration commands into the built-in switches. In your notes, compare a short desk link and a longer inter-building link, listing unknown distance and port requirements. Then compare 100 Mb/s full versus 100 Mb/s half on compatible legacy hardware, and 1000 Mb/s full at both ends. Then complete the media worksheet and shared-versus-point-to-point drawings in the Media supplement section; record all three proposed media choices and their unresolved platform checks.
steps.expectedResult: Identify the legacy setting pair as a duplex disagreement and the second pair as matching. State that neither example was created or measured by GNS3 and that module and cable compatibility require actual specifications.

steps.why: Counter differences and a controlled observation interval are more informative than expecting cumulative totals to reset automatically after a repair.
steps.title: Interpret time-stamped counters on paper
steps.instruction: Use these hypothetical observations, not claimed device output: at 10:00 a port has 12 CRC errors; at 10:05 it has 27; after an approved correction, readings at 10:10 and 10:15 both show 27. Write the increase for each interval and a cautious next action. Also solve C1-C3 and F1 from the supplement sections, recording observed evidence, the next distinguishing check, correction, retest and safe rollback. Label every ticket synthetic.
steps.expectedResult: The first interval contains 15 additional errors; the final interval contains zero additional errors. Old totals remain. Investigate both ends and service behavior rather than asserting that CRC alone proves a bad cable.

steps.why: Recognizing the right command and context is useful even without hardware. It is more accurate than promising optical telemetry from a software-only node.
steps.title: Read the Cisco command plan on paper
steps.instruction: This is a read-only planning exercise, not a command block for VPCS. On authorized Cisco hardware, an operator uses enable if needed, identifies the actual interface, then uses the supported show interfaces command. An example is show interfaces GigabitEthernet1/0/1. Write what you would record: state, rate, duplex, counters and time.
steps.expectedResult: Your notes name the example command and its intended evidence, while marking the exact interface and optional transceiver telemetry as hardware-dependent. No Cisco command is run on a built-in GNS3 switch.

steps.why: Explicit cleanup prevents the practice fault from being mistaken for the intended baseline when the project is opened again.
steps.title: Preserve notes and close safely
steps.instruction: Verify the original three-link path is restored. Save Day6-baseline.txt in your notes editor; GNS3 saves the project topology as you work. Stop the nodes before closing the project. VPCS addresses may need re-entry when reopening, using the two documented address commands. Keep every test isolated.
steps.expectedResult: The project topology and notes are preserved. You have not changed a production interface, imported a Cisco image or applied a persistent physical-device configuration.

lab.title: GNS3 path recovery with separate physical-media paper tasks
cleanup: Restore exactly the three baseline links and keep the project isolated from shared or production traffic.
Save the baseline, failure and recovery notes in Day6-baseline.txt. GNS3 automatically saves the topology as you work; do not look for a separate topology Save button.
Stop the project when finished. Re-enter the documented VPCS addresses after reopening if they were not retained; never save unrelated production changes.

All switch ports remain in their default access VLAN 1. This isolated GNS3 lab tests connectivity and a missing link, not real copper, optics, speed negotiation, or duplex errors. Physical-media diagnostics are separate paper exercises.

Keep paper media choices and hypothetical counters labeled separately from actual VPCS observations.

For C1-C3 and F1, separate setting/wire-map/optical observations from inferred causes. No physical-fault diagnosis is credited as an executed GNS3 result.
lab.licensingNote: GNS3 does not provide Cisco software images. Use a Cisco image only when the applicable Cisco license or entitlement legally permits that use, and do not share or redistribute Cisco image files. Cisco CML reference-platform images are licensed for use within CML unless a separate license permits outside use. Cisco Modeling Labs is the official alternative; built-in VPCS and Ethernet switch nodes do not require a Cisco image.
troubleshooting: If a console does not open, check that the intended VPCS node is started and the GNS3 console application is configured. Built-in Ethernet switches do not expose an IOS console.

For repeated baseline loss, compare both show ip results with the table, inspect every link endpoint and confirm default access VLAN 1 on the built-in switches. Do not introduce the fault until the baseline works.

One initial timeout may reflect address discovery, but persistent loss requires investigation. On real networks, host firewalls, ICMP filtering and rate limiting can also affect ping; do not diagnose a layer from ping alone.
If recovery fails, check that Switch1 Ethernet1 reconnects to Switch2 Ethernet0. Keep the endpoint addresses and remaining links unchanged so the test stays controlled.

Physical CRC, optical power and duplex mismatch are not measured here. Use the cited platform documentation and suitably equipped, authorized hardware for those observations; never invent virtual readings.
Perform troubleshooting only inside the isolated lab. Do not bridge the project to a physical network to make a failed exercise work.

quiz.question: Which medium carries light rather than electrical signals?
quiz.explanation: Fiber carries optical signals. Choosing a working optical link still requires compatible ports, modules and fiber specifications; the material alone does not establish compatibility.

quiz.question: What does full duplex allow on a compatible link?
quiz.explanation: Full duplex describes simultaneous two-way operation. It does not promise an application's throughput, remove every source of error or replace media compatibility checks.

It produces genuine cable-induced CRC faults
It validates every Cisco duplex command

quiz.explanation: The actual exercise removes and restores one virtual link. Optical power, real cable faults and physical duplex mismatch remain outside the built-in switches' tested scope.

quiz.question: After a correction, a counter stays at 27 for two observations. What does that show?
quiz.explanation: A stable total means no additional events were recorded between those readings. It does not erase historical events or establish that every other part of the service is healthy.

quiz.explanation: PC2 uses 192.168.6.20. The first option is a self-test, loopback does not test the remote path, and show ip displays local information rather than requesting a remote echo reply.

A 100 m copper row certifies every installed cable
