glossary.meaning: An interface is a device's network connection, often called a port. The medium is what carries its signals, such as copper wire or glass fiber.
Speed is the link's signaling rate. Duplex describes whether the ends can transmit simultaneously: full duplex allows both directions at once; half duplex uses a shared transmission opportunity.
A frame is the local-link container for data. An IP packet is the network-addressed message carried inside it. A switch forwards frames; it does not repair damaged cables.
An IP address identifies an interface. The mask says which addresses share its network. A gateway is a router used to reach other networks; this same-network lab does not need one.
VPCS means Virtual PC Simulator, a small practice computer in GNS3. Its console is a text window where you type commands after a prompt such as PC1>. Do not type the prompt itself.
Ping sends an Internet Control Message Protocol echo request and waits for an echo reply. A reply confirms that exchange at that time; it does not measure cable quality or application performance.
A MAC address identifies a local-link interface. Address Resolution Protocol, or ARP, discovers the MAC address for a local IPv4 neighbor before the first unicast exchange.
A counter is a running event total. CRC means cyclic redundancy check; a failed received-frame check is an error symptom, not a diagnosis naming the defective part.
A transceiver sends and receives signals. Small Form-factor Pluggable, or SFP, is a module format; the exact module specification determines supported media and link characteristics.
A written record of the intended configuration and observed results before a change, used to compare and restore the exercise.
A supported link process by which the connected devices exchange capabilities and agree on compatible operating properties.
An authorized Cisco operational command mode, commonly indicated by #, for inspections and other privileged commands rather than a VPCS prompt.
Single-mode fiber carries one intended propagation mode; multimode fiber carries multiple modes. Their compatible modules, wavelength and cable grade determine usable reach.
A collision occurs when half-duplex transmissions overlap. A late collision occurs outside the normal window and requires investigation; it is not expected on a correctly operating full-duplex link.
A record of the conductor connections between the two cable ends. It can reveal open, shorted or incorrectly mapped conductors but does not alone certify all cable performance.

Tx is transmitted power, Rx is received power, and DOM is digital optical monitoring. dBm measures power relative to one milliwatt; compare each sensor with its own module's specifications and threshold labels.

sections.example: For a classroom planning exercise, compare a desk connection with a building-to-building link. Write the distance, available ports and required rate for each. Mark any unknown specification as unknown instead of guessing that all SFP modules, all fiber cables or all copper categories are interchangeable.
sections.heading: Choose the medium from the connection requirements
keyPoints: Choose a supported combination, not a cable based only on its appearance.
Record distance, connector, module and port requirements before selecting media.
The virtual lines in this lesson represent connectivity, not measured optical or electrical behavior.
sections.explanation: Begin with the two devices, the required distance and their supported ports. Copper carries electrical signals; fiber carries light. Neither is automatically the correct choice for every link. Check the actual module, cable and port documentation before buying or connecting anything. Connector shape alone is not compatibility evidence. For an optical link, record the module specification at both ends and the fiber type; never look into a fiber end or optical port. Treat installation, cleaning and eye safety as manufacturer-guided hardware work, not part of this software lab.

sections.example: Paper comparison: End A at 100 Mb/s full duplex and End B at 100 Mb/s half duplex disagree about duplex. In contrast, two compatible ends negotiating 1000 Mb/s full duplex agree. These are illustrative setting pairs; this GNS3 project neither changes hardware negotiation nor generates the physical mismatch.
sections.heading: Understand negotiated speed and duplex before changing them
keyPoints: Inspect both ends and the platform guide before a configuration change.
Do not present 1000 Mb/s half-duplex operation as a valid Cisco lab outcome.
A displayed link rate is not a measurement of end-to-end application throughput.
sections.explanation: Link speed is a nominal signaling rate, not a promise that an application will transfer useful files at that rate. Full duplex allows simultaneous transmission in both directions on a compatible link. A mismatch is a disagreement between the ends about duplex operation. In this lesson, a half-versus-full mismatch is a paper example for suitable legacy 10/100 equipment, not an instruction to configure Cisco Gigabit Ethernet at half duplex. Check the exact platform's capabilities. When both devices support compatible auto-negotiation, begin with the vendor's recommended automatic settings instead of forcing one end in isolation.

sections.example: A paper observation reads: port Gi1/0/1, up, full duplex, 1000 Mb/s, 12 CRC errors at 10:00. It is deliberately simplified, not copied CLI output. It does not say when those 12 errors occurred. A second reading of 12 at 10:05 suggests no additional CRC errors during that interval; it does not prove that the cable is fault-free.
sections.heading: Read interface evidence without overclaiming its meaning
keyPoints: Keep timestamps and compare counter changes, not just lifetime totals.
A built-in GNS3 Ethernet switch does not provide Cisco IOS show commands.
Hardware transceiver diagnostics and their availability depend on the platform and module.
sections.explanation: On supported Cisco hardware, show interfaces reports an interface's operational information. An interface is the connection being inspected, not the whole network. Privileged EXEC mode is the operational command level commonly shown by a prompt ending in #; enable enters it when permitted. Configuration mode, commonly shown by (config)#, changes settings and is not required for the read-only paper exercise here. Interface names vary across equipment, so GigabitEthernet1/0/1 is an example name, not a universal port. Record link state, negotiated properties, counters and observation time before deciding what to change.

sections.example: In an original paper case, a counter changes from 12 to 27 over five minutes. That is 15 additional recorded errors, not 27 new ones. After an approved correction, readings of 27 and 27 show no new errors in the second interval. You still verify service behavior, because stable counters alone do not establish that every application works.
sections.heading: Distinguish a symptom from a confirmed cause
keyPoints: Explain what was observed separately from the suspected cause.
Do not clear counters until evidence is recorded and the operation is approved.
A repeated baseline, fault and recovery test is stronger than one isolated successful ping.
sections.explanation: A missing ping reply says that this test did not complete successfully. It does not by itself identify a damaged cable or a particular network layer. Incorrect addresses, a disconnected path, host filtering, rate limiting and other conditions can cause loss. Likewise, an increasing received-frame error counter warrants investigation but does not name a defective component. Record evidence from both link ends, keep the scope narrow and change one approved factor at a time. Existing totals normally remain after a repair; look for the rate of new errors to stop rather than expecting old errors to disappear automatically.

sections.example: Record successful remote pings, remove the single inter-switch link, repeat the identical test and then reconnect the same ports. If recovery fails, compare the current links and endpoint addresses with your notes before changing anything else. For the paper tasks, label every number hypothetical and never report it as a measurement from GNS3.
sections.heading: Practice safely with a virtual path and paper diagnostics
keyPoints: Keep the project disconnected from production and from the host's physical network.
Use virtual connectivity tests for path reasoning, not claims about physical media quality.
Optional future hardware practice requires suitable equipment, authorization and platform-specific instructions.
sections.explanation: The hands-on exercise uses PC1, Switch1, Switch2 and PC2 in one straight path. Its only induced fault is removal of the link between the switches. The endpoints share one IPv4 network, so a router and default gateway are unnecessary. There are no redundant links or changes to real interfaces. Separate paper tasks cover media choice, duplex compatibility and counter interpretation. This is intentionally honest about the environment: the built-in switches do not reproduce a Catalyst 9300, physical transceiver telemetry or genuine cable-induced CRC errors.

sections.example:
Paper worksheet: DeskHost to AccessSwitch needs 1 Gb/s over 40 m; GLC-TE copper is a candidate only if the switch port/software supports it and the host has a compatible copper port. RackA to RackB needs 10 Gb/s over 250 m of OM3; the SR row is a candidate. BuildingA to BuildingB needs 10 Gb/s over 2 km of G.652; compare matching LR modules, not SR on OM3. Platform validation is still outstanding in all three.
Connection drawings: LegacyA -> HubH <- LegacyB and LegacyC -> HubH share one half-duplex medium. ModernA <-> SwitchS port1 is one point-to-point link; ModernB <-> SwitchS port2 is another. The hub drawings are paper only, not extra nodes in the live lab.
sections.heading: Media supplement: copper, single-mode and multimode
keyPoints: Select copper, MMF or SMF from the exact rate, distance, module, connector and supported host-port combination.
The listed reaches belong to those named module/media combinations; they are not all-copper or all-fiber limits.
Normal half-duplex collisions do not justify collisions on a correctly operating full-duplex link.
Paper selection and the virtual straight-line lab cannot certify installed cable or optical performance.
sections.explanation:
Multimode fiber (MMF) supports several light-propagation modes in its larger core; single-mode fiber (SMF) has a smaller core designed for one mode at the intended wavelength. OM3 is a multimode cable grade; G.652 identifies a single-mode fiber specification. A wavelength describes the light used by an optical module, in nanometers (nm). A connector fitting the socket does not prove the wavelength, fiber or Ethernet rate is compatible.

Use these source-bound rows as a planning worksheet, not universal cable limits. GLC-TE: 1000BASE-T, four-pair Category 5 copper, RJ-45, up to 100 m. SFP-10G-SR: 10GBASE-SR, 850 nm, OM3 MMF, dual LC, up to 300 m. SFP-10G-LR: 10GBASE-LR, 1310 nm, G.652 SMF, dual LC, up to 10 km. The two optical rows use PC/UPC-compatible patch connections, not APC. Check the current platform/software compatibility matrix and the complete loss/installation requirements before treating any row as an installable link.

Shared media means several stations compete for the same transmission opportunity. A legacy half-duplex hub segment is one example. A switched point-to-point full-duplex link joins exactly two ports that can transmit simultaneously. A shared collision domain is not the same thing as a VLAN's broadcast domain.

sections.example: For C1, compute 12 new late collisions at B and 8 new CRC errors at A, then distinguish the confirmed setting mismatch from possible additional cable defects. For C2, write 'no common forced rate' rather than 'duplex mismatch'. For C3, expect straight-through pin n to reach pin n on each of eight pins, but do not call a continuity pass full category certification. A capable tester can also check pair/crosstalk performance. For every ticket keep columns: observed, suspected, next check, authorized correction, retest, rollback. If a trial does not restore the baseline, restore only the recorded safe settings or known-good spare and escalate; do not generate collisions or flood traffic.
sections.heading: Copper tickets: collisions, speed and wire map
keyPoints: Compare both ends: equal speed with unequal duplex differs from incompatible forced speeds.
Late collisions are evidence to investigate, not a universal proof that the cable is damaged.
A wire-map fault and a service failure are different observations; verify both after an approved correction.
Do not run disruptive cable diagnostics or construct real faults on production equipment.
sections.explanation:
All tickets below are invented evidence for diagnosis, not measured output. A collision is overlapping transmission on a shared half-duplex medium. A late collision is detected beyond the normal collision window and calls for investigation of duplex, cable limits or hardware. A wire map records which connector pin reaches which far-end pin. An open is a broken conductor path; a short joins conductors that should be separate. Auto-MDIX can accommodate straight-through versus crossover wiring on supported equipment, but cannot repair an open conductor.

Ticket C1, legacy 10/100 ports: A is forced to 100/full; B reports 100/half. From 10:00 to 10:05, B's late-collision count rises 2 to 14 and A's CRC count rises 1 to 9. The settings prove a duplex disagreement; the counters alone would not. Inspect both-end configuration and cable requirements. On paper restore the recorded baseline, compatible automatic negotiation on both ends. Retest the same two-way service and compare new counter deltas; do not demand erased historical totals.

Ticket C2: A is forced to 100/full; B is forced to 10/full; both report link down. This is a rate disagreement, not half/full mismatch. First verify correct ports, power, settings and shared supported rates. Restore both ends to their recorded auto/auto baseline. Link-up and agreement on actual rate are necessary checks, followed by the original peer test. A missing ping alone could not identify this cause.

Ticket C3: settings agree at both ends, but the isolated copper run's tester wire map reports pin 3 open. Inspect the disconnected cable and connector pair using an appropriate tester. An approved same-specification known-good patch replacement is a narrow trial; rerun wire map and service/counter checks. Preserve the defective cable's label and results, never silently return it to service.

sections.example: Synthetic retest after a documented patch correction: A Tx=-3.0, A Rx=-6.0, B Tx=-3.2, B Rx=-6.4 dBm. B receive now fits the SR row; require stable counter deltas and the original traffic test before recording recovery. These values are not device logs. If the symptom persists, retain readings, restore the documented safe patch arrangement and investigate the next component with authorization. Do not add arbitrary attenuation, replace SR with LR, or assume stronger light is always safer. Physical diagnostics remain unperformed here; the GNS3 link-removal exercise cannot supply DOM or tester evidence.
sections.heading: Optical ticket: compare each direction with the right limits
keyPoints: A transmitter's power is compared with its own Tx specification; the remote receiver uses its own Rx limits.
Identify the affected direction before proposing a component replacement.
A reported N/A is unavailable telemetry, not zero optical power or a successful test.
No numeric reading in this ticket is a runtime measurement or a universal safe range.
sections.explanation:
Transmit (Tx) power is light leaving a module; receive (Rx) power is light arriving from its peer. dBm expresses power relative to one milliwatt on a logarithmic scale: -12 dBm is weaker than -6 dBm. Digital optical monitoring (DOM) reports supported module sensors. A vendor's operating specification is not necessarily the same value as a module's warning or alarm threshold.

Ticket F1 is synthetic. FiberA and FiberB use matching SFP-10G-SR modules and a 250 m OM3 dual-fiber path. Cisco's current SR row lists average Tx from -7.3 to -1.2 dBm and Rx from -9.9 to -1.0 dBm; these are this module's published limits, not universal optics thresholds. At 10:00, A Tx=-3.0, A Rx=-6.0, B Tx=-3.2 and B Rx=-12.0 dBm. B's receive value is below this row's minimum, while both transmit values and A's receive value fit it. Inspect the A-to-B direction first; this does not identify a particular dirty connector or failed module.

Confirm both module part numbers, host compatibility, wavelength, fiber grade/length and Tx-to-Rx mapping. Compare timestamped DOM and its own threshold labels at both ends. Under an approved isolated-hardware procedure, trained staff can inspect/clean or substitute a matching known-good patch, one factor at a time, using manufacturer laser-safety instructions. Never look into an optical port. Recheck power, link state, counter deltas and the same intended service. A DOM value within range alone is not service verification.

content.metaTitle: CCNA Day 6: Copper, Fiber, Speed and Interface Errors
takeaways: Select supported media using actual connection requirements and equipment specifications.
Inspect both link ends; do not force unsupported gigabit half-duplex operation.
Compare counter increases with recorded timestamps rather than expecting totals to reset after a correction.
A ping tests one request-and-reply exchange, not cable quality or application throughput.
Use an isolated, single-change experiment and repeat the same tests after recovery.
Keep virtual connectivity observations separate from physical-media paper examples.
objectives: Compare copper and fiber by supported port, distance, connector and module requirements.
Explain link speed, full duplex and the limited legacy context of half-duplex mismatches.
Interpret interface state and changes in error counters without claiming that one symptom proves its cause.
Build and verify a four-node GNS3 path, deliberately remove one link and demonstrate recovery.
Separate observations from the virtual lab from paper-based Cisco physical-interface diagnostics.
content.plainAnswer: Choose a cable and port combination that supports the required distance and link rate. Check both ends before changing settings, and compare new interface errors with a recorded baseline. This lesson uses an isolated GNS3 connectivity exercise plus paper examples for physical media, speed negotiation and duplex faults that its virtual switches cannot reproduce.

visualStory.title: One path: observe, disconnect, restore

stages.title: Record the working path
stages.explanation: PC1 sends a test through Switch1 and Switch2 to PC2, which replies on the same topology. The arrows summarize connectivity, not measured cable signals.

stages.title: Remove the middle link
stages.explanation: Remove only the Switch1-to-Switch2 link. PC2 remains the destination, but no complete path reaches it; the same test receives no replies.

stages.title: Restore and retest
stages.explanation: Restore the same inter-switch ports. Retest PC1 to PC2, then PC2 to PC1; record the returned replies without claiming physical-media quality.

visualStory.altText: PC1 connects through Switch1 and Switch2 to PC2. The diagram ends at PC2 and compares the intact path, a missing inter-switch link and the restored path.
visualStory.boundary: This virtual lab omits real copper, optics and duplex negotiation because built-in switches do not model physical faults. Hardware diagnostics are separate paper exercises.
visualStory.takeaway: Record the working path, change one link and verify recovery; physical-media measurements need suitable hardware.

candidates.name: Four-node recovery path
candidates.scene: Show the exact two PCs, two switches and three links used in the isolated lab, with one deliberate inter-switch disconnection.
candidates.limitation: This virtual connectivity diagram does not illustrate physical copper, optical power or duplex negotiation.
candidates.teachingValue: Every active endpoint is visible, and the changed link is traceable across baseline, failure and recovery.

candidates.name: Physical-media comparison
candidates.scene: Compare a copper cable and an optical module beside a list of compatibility questions rather than live measurements.
candidates.limitation: It would not show the exact GNS3 test path or demonstrate the controlled connection loss.
candidates.teachingValue: This could support media-selection vocabulary and emphasize hardware compatibility before purchase.

candidates.name: Counter timeline
candidates.scene: Compare time-stamped hypothetical error totals before and after a hypothetical approved correction.
candidates.limitation: It would not name the devices or illustrate where the actual virtual path was disconnected.
candidates.teachingValue: This could explain cumulative totals and error increments without expecting automatic counter resets.

conceptSelection.selectionReason: The four-node recovery path matches the reproducible hands-on exercise. Media choices and hypothetical counters remain in explicitly labeled paper tasks rather than implying that the virtual diagram measured real hardware.

walkthrough.why: One path makes the deliberate link removal easy to observe without introducing loops or alternate paths.
walkthrough.action: Draw PC1, Switch1, Switch2 and PC2 in order.
walkthrough.whatHappens: A single line between each pair creates one possible path between the endpoints. Every connection endpoint appears in both the diagram and lab table.

walkthrough.why: A baseline separates a fault that you introduce deliberately from an unrelated setup mistake.
walkthrough.action: Record addresses and establish a working baseline.
walkthrough.whatHappens: PC1 uses 192.168.6.10 and PC2 uses 192.168.6.20, both with mask 255.255.255.0. Test each computer against the other, never itself.

walkthrough.why: This controlled change illustrates a missing path, not optical damage or a measured duplex mismatch.
walkthrough.action: Remove only the connection between the two switches.
walkthrough.whatHappens: The endpoints stay configured but their only connecting path disappears. The same remote ping can no longer receive replies.

walkthrough.why: A repair is supported by a repeatable before-and-after observation, not by the fact that a command was accepted.
walkthrough.action: Reconnect the same ports and repeat the tests.
walkthrough.whatHappens: Replies should return in both directions. Keep your failure and recovery notes together so the changed link and result can be compared.

walkthrough.why: This preserves the boundary between software connectivity practice and physical measurements that require suitable hardware.
walkthrough.action: Use the paper counter and media exercises separately.
walkthrough.whatHappens: You compare hypothetical port settings and time-stamped error counts. The numbers are teaching examples, not readings generated by your virtual switches.

beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: A connection may be present but unreliable. Learning to record what changed, distinguish a symptom from a cause, and retest after one correction prevents random changes that hide the original problem.

firstPractice.hint: If either test fails repeatedly, stop and correct the basic lab before introducing a second fault. A self-ping is not a substitute.
firstPractice.task: Before removing a link, open PC1's console and verify that it is 192.168.6.10. Ping 192.168.6.20, then perform the reverse test from PC2 and record both results.
firstPractice.expected: Both remote tests should receive replies once local address discovery completes. Your notes identify the sender, destination and time for each test.

beginnerGuide.startingPoint: You do not need to remember command syntax from earlier lessons. Follow the device names exactly, open the named console, and type one line at a time. The built-in switches have no Cisco command console; their connections are managed in GNS3's graphical workspace.

checkUnderstanding.hint: Ask which device and signal were actually measured by your test, and which were only discussed on paper.
checkUnderstanding.answer: No. This ping demonstrates a particular request-and-reply exchange in the virtual topology. The lab has no physical optical receiver to measure, so it cannot establish real fiber power, connector condition or transceiver health.
checkUnderstanding.question: Does a successful virtual ping prove that a real fiber module is healthy?

everydayComparison.whereItStops: Real links follow electrical or optical specifications and supported negotiation rules. Do not infer collisions, throughput or signal quality from the conversation analogy.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: The comparison helps distinguish taking turns from simultaneous communication. It does not explain link speed: talking louder is not equivalent to a faster network, and cable material alone does not set the rate.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: As a memory aid, compare taking turns on a walkie-talkie with speaking and listening on a telephone. This is an organizational comparison, not a literal description of Ethernet signals or device behavior.

prerequisites: Read Days 1, 2 and 5 for device roles and encapsulation; console instructions and essential terms are repeated here.
Install GNS3 and complete its local-server setup before starting. Use built-in VPCS and Ethernet switch templates; no Cisco image is needed for this lab.
Create a new isolated project with no Cloud, NAT, Internet, physical adapter or production-network connection.
Use a notes editor: Notepad on Windows, TextEdit in plain-text mode on macOS, or a text editor such as Gedit on Linux.
content.learnerOutcome: Explain why a working ping does not prove a healthy physical link, choose evidence to investigate media and interface faults, and demonstrate loss and recovery of one isolated GNS3 path without inventing physical measurements.
content.metaDescription: Learn copper and fiber choices, speed, duplex and interface counters with a safe GNS3 connectivity lab and clearly labeled hardware diagnosis exercises.

terms.meaning: An interface is a device's network connection, often called a port. The medium is what carries its signals, such as copper wire or glass fiber.
Speed is the link's signaling rate. Duplex describes whether the ends can transmit simultaneously: full duplex allows both directions at once; half duplex uses a shared transmission opportunity.
A frame is the local-link container for data. An IP packet is the network-addressed message carried inside it. A switch forwards frames; it does not repair damaged cables.
An IP address identifies an interface. The mask says which addresses share its network. A gateway is a router used to reach other networks; this same-network lab does not need one.
VPCS means Virtual PC Simulator, a small practice computer in GNS3. Its console is a text window where you type commands after a prompt such as PC1>. Do not type the prompt itself.
Ping sends an Internet Control Message Protocol echo request and waits for an echo reply. A reply confirms that exchange at that time; it does not measure cable quality or application performance.
A MAC address identifies a local-link interface. Address Resolution Protocol, or ARP, discovers the MAC address for a local IPv4 neighbor before the first unicast exchange.
A counter is a running event total. CRC means cyclic redundancy check; a failed received-frame check is an error symptom, not a diagnosis naming the defective part.
A transceiver sends and receives signals. Small Form-factor Pluggable, or SFP, is a module format; the exact module specification determines supported media and link characteristics.

teachingPrelude.explanation: Start with the vocabulary below. A cable carries signals; a network interface is the device connection to that cable. We will first observe a small virtual network, then use clearly labeled paper evidence to discuss physical equipment. The two activities teach related skills but produce different evidence.
teachingPrelude.labBoundary: This isolated GNS3 lab tests connectivity and a missing link, not real copper, optics, speed negotiation, or duplex errors. Physical-media diagnostics are separate paper exercises.

practiceQuestions.answer: Record the distance, required rate, available ports, cable type and compatible module specifications.
practiceQuestions.question: What should you record before choosing copper or fiber?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A connector that fits is not enough evidence. List unknowns and check the actual device documentation before claiming that a particular media combination will work.

practiceQuestions.answer: It describes simultaneous transmission in both directions; it does not guarantee application throughput or a fault-free cable.
practiceQuestions.question: What does full duplex describe, and what does it not guarantee?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Separate a link's operating property from the result of an end-to-end application test. Two healthy full-duplex interfaces can still be part of a path with another bottleneck.

practiceQuestions.answer: That is not a supported Cisco 1000 Mb/s outcome for the cited equipment; the legacy mismatch example belongs on paper.
practiceQuestions.question: Why must this lesson not force a Cisco gigabit link to half duplex?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A configuration example must respect the platform and speed's capabilities. The built-in GNS3 switches also do not provide the physical negotiation behavior needed to measure this fault.

practiceQuestions.answer: Fifteen additional errors were recorded between the two observations.
practiceQuestions.question: A CRC total rises from 12 to 27. How many additional errors were recorded?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Subtract the earlier cumulative total from the later one. Keep the observation interval and traffic context, and investigate the cause instead of treating the total as a diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.answer: Use the platform-supported show interfaces command with the verified interface name.
practiceQuestions.question: Which Cisco command family helps inspect an identified interface?
practiceQuestions.explanation: For example, show interfaces GigabitEthernet1/0/1 inspects that particular port where it exists. Do not type IOS commands into VPCS or assume the example port exists on every device.

practiceQuestions.answer: The recorded virtual path lost connectivity when its only inter-switch link was removed and recovered after restoration.
practiceQuestions.question: What can you conclude from the link-removal experiment?
practiceQuestions.explanation: That controlled observation does not prove a real cable's category, an optical receiver's power or a duplex setting. The lesson keeps those hardware questions in separate paper exercises.

practiceQuestions.answer: GLC-TE copper, matching SFP-10G-SR on OM3, and matching SFP-10G-LR on G.652 respectively; validate both host platforms, software, ports and installation requirements.
practiceQuestions.question: Choose candidate media for 1 Gb/s at 40 m, 10 Gb/s over 250 m OM3, and 10 Gb/s over 2 km G.652. What still needs validation?
practiceQuestions.explanation: These are the supplement's specific module/media rows, not universal distances. A fitting connector and a distance within the row do not establish that a platform supports the module or that the installed path meets its requirements.

practiceQuestions.answer: Hub stations share transmission opportunities; two full-duplex ports do not. C2 instead has incompatible forced speeds, with both ends set full duplex.
practiceQuestions.question: Why can a half-duplex hub show ordinary collisions while a full-duplex point-to-point link should not? Is C2 a collision diagnosis?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Classify the connection before interpreting counters. C1 has equal speeds but a duplex disagreement; C2 has unequal speeds. Read both ends and restore their recorded compatible baseline rather than naming every failure a collision.

practiceQuestions.answer: C1: inspect both-end duplex settings and retest agreed settings with new counter deltas. C3: isolate/test the cable, try an authorized matching spare and repeat wire map and service checks.
practiceQuestions.question: C1 has rising late collisions and C3 reports pin 3 open. Which next check and retest belong to each?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The C1 settings identify a mismatch but do not exclude a second fault. C3's open is direct cable-path evidence. A continuity pass is not full cable certification, and no counter must reset to zero simply because a repair worked.

practiceQuestions.answer: B Rx=-12.0 dBm is below -9.9 dBm, so inspect A-to-B. B Rx=-6.4 dBm fits that row on retest but does not alone prove service recovery.
practiceQuestions.question: For F1, which reading is outside the SR row, which direction needs attention, and does the synthetic retest alone prove service recovery?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The receiver is at B and the sender is at A. Verify their modules, mapping and specifications before a narrow correction, then compare counters and the same traffic test. All supplied readings are synthetic, not measured hardware output.

realWorldScenario.title: Investigate an unreliable office connection with evidence
realWorldScenario.takeaway: A credible diagnosis names the affected path, the evidence, the controlled change and the repeat test. Our virtual lab practices that reasoning; it does not claim to reproduce this physical office incident.
realWorldScenario.situation: A hypothetical office reports interrupted file transfers on one desk connection. A support engineer has authorization to inspect that connection but not to change the rest of the network. The first task is to document the affected path and collect time-stamped evidence, rather than assuming that the first error counter identifies the cause.
walkthrough: Identify the endpoint and its switch port using the organization's records. Confirm the actual interface before inspecting it, and record the user-visible symptom and when it occurs.
Collect read-only interface information at both ends where available. Record speed, duplex and counter totals twice while noting traffic conditions; do not erase the initial evidence.
Compare supported settings and look for newly increasing errors. A CRC increase is evidence to investigate, while a missed ping may also involve host filtering or rate limits.
Arrange an approved, reversible test of one suspected factor, such as substituting a known-compatible cable. Do not change speed and cable simultaneously and then claim which one fixed the issue.
Repeat the same observations and the affected application's test. Existing counter values need not return to zero; the useful question is whether new errors continue under comparable conditions.
Document the confirmed result and any uncertainty. Escalate with the observations when the cause remains unknown rather than forcing unsupported settings or promising that all faults are resolved.

title: TCP and UDP through real applications
moduleTitle: Network Foundations and the Packet Journey

lab.goal: Build a local two-endpoint path, establish an ICMP baseline and identify synthetic TCP and UDP probes in a capture without claiming a full application session or performance result.
setup: Create a new GNS3 project named Day7-Transport. Use a working local or GNS3 VM server configured for your installation.
Drag two VPCS nodes from End devices and one built-in Ethernet switch from Switches. Rename them PC1, PC2 and Switch1.
Connect exactly the interfaces in the topology and start both PCs. Keep the switch's connected ports on default access VLAN 1.
Do not add Cloud, NAT, Internet or physical adapters. All probes must remain inside this disconnected lab.
Open a text editor for notes: Notepad on Windows, TextEdit in plain-text mode on macOS, or a plain-text editor on Linux. Create Day7-baseline.txt.
Confirm Wireshark is installed and configured in GNS3 before starting. If capture integration fails, fix that prerequisite before claiming any packet observations.

steps.why: Recording the real configuration prevents an address typo from being misdiagnosed as a TCP or UDP property.
steps.title: Configure PC1
steps.instruction: Right-click PC1 and choose Console before typing. Confirm a PC1> or VPCS> prompt, then enter each command separately; do not type the prompt itself. Record the returned address and mask in Day7-baseline.txt.
steps.expectedResult: PC1 displays 192.168.7.10 with mask 255.255.255.0. Stop and correct any different address before proceeding.
commandExplanations: Assign PC1 the address 192.168.7.10 and the supplied /24 local prefix. No gateway is needed for this same-subnet exercise.
Display PC1's actual address settings so you can compare them with the plan; this command does not send a connectivity test.

steps.why: Two unique local addresses are required; pinging yourself would not test the other cable or endpoint.
steps.title: Configure PC2
steps.instruction: Right-click PC2 and choose Console before typing. Check that this is PC2, not the already configured PC1 console. Enter the commands separately and add the actual result to your notes.
steps.expectedResult: PC2 displays 192.168.7.20 with mask 255.255.255.0, distinct from PC1's address.
commandExplanations: Assign PC2 its own address, 192.168.7.20, with the same /24 prefix as PC1; do not reuse PC1's address.
Display PC2's actual settings and confirm that it is the intended remote destination.

steps.why: Checking the local implementation avoids treating a simulator as a complete application host or relying on unsupported commands.
steps.title: Check installed probe help
steps.instruction: Right-click PC1 and choose Console before typing. Read the local ping help and record the VPCS version from the console banner. Confirm that -2 selects UDP, -3 selects TCP, -p sets the destination port, -f sets TCP flags and -c limits the count. If any option differs or is absent, stop those probe steps and use the paper comparison instead.
steps.expectedResult: The installed help identifies the required probe options. Unsupported options are a version or prerequisite issue, not a failed transport test.
commandExplanations: Show this VPCS installation's ping options; this is local help, not a packet sent to the other endpoint.

steps.why: A working ICMP baseline supports basic local reachability, but does not prove that a TCP or UDP application is listening.
steps.title: Establish the local baseline
steps.instruction: Right-click PC1 and choose Console before typing. Send three ordinary ping requests to PC2's address, not PC1's own address. If an initial request times out, repeat the same bounded test; persistent loss must be resolved before capture comparison.
steps.expectedResult: The repeated baseline receives echo replies from PC2. Record actual output rather than copying an expected transcript.
commandExplanations: Send three ICMP echo requests from PC1 to PC2 at 192.168.7.20; -c 3 bounds the count and does not select TCP or UDP.

steps.why: An empty filtered view before a probe is not evidence of a fault. The capture point and filter determine what you can observe.
steps.title: Start the link capture
steps.instruction: In the GNS3 workspace, right-click the PC1-to-Switch1 cable and select Start capture, then accept the offered Ethernet link capture and open it in Wireshark. Use the display-filter bar above the packet list to enter tcp || udp || icmp and apply it. This is a Wireshark filter, not a VPCS command.
steps.expectedResult: Wireshark is recording the selected virtual link. The filter may initially display no packets because no new relevant traffic has been sent yet.

steps.why: The outbound header establishes which transport was sent. A timeout or error does not establish application health or UDP delivery guarantees.
steps.title: Send a bounded UDP probe
steps.instruction: Right-click PC1 and choose Console before typing. Send three UDP probes to PC2 on destination port 5000. Return to Wireshark and select an outgoing UDP packet, then expand its IP and UDP details. Record both addresses and the observed ports.
steps.expectedResult: The capture should contain outbound UDP probes to 192.168.7.20 and destination port 5000. PC2 may return an ICMP error or no useful response; no application listener was installed.
commandExplanations: VPCS -2 selects a synthetic UDP probe, -p 5000 chooses the destination port, and -c 3 limits the count. It does not start a service on PC2.

steps.why: A chosen port and visible SYN are limited evidence. They do not prove that HTTP, a three-way handshake or reliable application delivery occurred.
steps.title: Send a bounded TCP probe
steps.instruction: Right-click PC1 and choose Console before typing. Send three SYN probes to PC2 on destination port 80. Return to Wireshark, select an outgoing TCP packet and expand TCP Flags. Record the SYN flag and the destination port, keeping any response as a separate observation.
steps.expectedResult: The capture should contain outbound TCP SYN probes to 192.168.7.20 port 80. A reset, error or timeout is possible because no TCP service was installed; do not claim a completed handshake.
commandExplanations: VPCS -3 selects TCP, -f S selects SYN, -p 80 chooses the destination port, and -c 3 limits the probe count. This is not a browser request or complete TCP session.

steps.why: Separating packets by protocol prevents a generic reply or error message from being mistaken for application success.
steps.title: Compare one packet of each kind
steps.instruction: In Wireshark, keep the same display filter and compare one UDP packet with one TCP SYN. In Day7-baseline.txt, write the addresses, transport, ports and visible flags. If ICMP errors are shown, select them separately; do not label an ICMP error as a UDP acknowledgment.
steps.expectedResult: Your table contains only observed values. TCP has its SYN flag in this test; UDP has no TCP flag field. Any ICMP response is labeled as a different protocol.

steps.why: A reverse check confirms the intended remote endpoint and makes accidental self-tests easier to detect.
steps.title: Check the reverse baseline
steps.instruction: Right-click PC2 and choose Console before typing. Use PC1's address as the remote destination and record the result. This is a separate ICMP check, not a measurement of TCP or UDP throughput.
steps.expectedResult: PC1 returns echo replies when the baseline path and settings are intact. Investigate persistent loss rather than declaring one transport broken.
commandExplanations: Send three ICMP echo requests from PC2 to PC1 at 192.168.7.10; do not use PC2's own .20 address.

steps.why: A reproducible evidence record is more useful than invented successful output and prevents the exercise being overinterpreted later.
steps.title: Save observations and stop
steps.instruction: In Wireshark, stop recording and save the capture as Day7-probes.pcapng. In GNS3, stop the cable capture as well. Add an explicit note that no application server, complete TCP transfer or performance benchmark was run, then stop the isolated project.
steps.expectedResult: You have the address plan, observed probe table and a local capture, clearly separated from the hypothetical application examples.

lab.title: Inspect ICMP, TCP and UDP probes on one isolated link
cleanup: Stop the Wireshark recording and the GNS3 link capture, then stop all nodes in the isolated project.
Keep the address plan and observations with the capture; do not publish unrelated captured data.
Keep all external connections absent. If reusing the project, verify the same baseline before the next exercise and re-enter VPCS addresses if they were not saved.
devices: PC1: GNS3 built-in VPCS endpoint
Switch1: GNS3 built-in Ethernet switch using default access VLAN 1
PC2: GNS3 built-in VPCS endpoint
Wireshark: observer opened from the virtual cable, not a fourth network node
lab.topology: PC1 Ethernet0 -- Switch1 Ethernet0; Switch1 Ethernet1 -- PC2 Ethernet0. Both PCs are on 192.168.7.0/24. There is no router, firewall, server, Cloud or NAT node. Capture the PC1-to-Switch1 link; PC2 is the destination.

addressing.purpose: Source for probes; distinct from PC2.
Destination on the same local subnet.
Joins the two local Ethernet links.

verification: Confirm PC1 and PC2 have distinct addresses and both tests target the other endpoint, not themselves.
Record ordinary ICMP replies separately from transport probes and application outcomes.
Inspect an actual outgoing UDP header and TCP SYN header at the named capture point; do not invent values if capture failed.
Confirm no router, firewall, application server or external network was added to the exercise.
State explicitly that a visible transport probe does not demonstrate a completed session, delivery guarantee or real application performance.
lab.licensingNote: This lab uses built-in VPCS and Ethernet switch nodes; no Cisco image is needed. GNS3 does not provide Cisco images. Use Cisco images only when the applicable license permits that use; do not share or redistribute image files. Cisco Modeling Labs is the official Cisco alternative.
troubleshooting: If a VPCS console will not open, start the named PC and check GNS3's console application setting. Switch1 is a built-in Ethernet switch and has no IOS console.
If the ICMP baseline repeatedly fails, inspect both addresses, masks, cable endpoints and switch VLAN settings. Do not diagnose TCP or UDP before the baseline is established.
If the installed ping help lacks a required flag, stop that probe exercise. Use the paper comparison and document the limitation instead of claiming the missing command ran.
If Wireshark appears empty, confirm the selected cable, recording state and display filter, then generate a new bounded probe. A filter changes the displayed view, not whether a service is available.

Do not treat a SYN reset, an ICMP port error or a timeout as a surprise success or definitive failure of an application: none was installed. In real networks, filtering, host state and rate limits can also affect replies.
Keep troubleshooting inside the isolated project. Never bridge it to a real network to make the example work or capture unrelated people's traffic.

options: An ordered byte stream with loss-recovery mechanisms
A guarantee that a person read the message
A fixed faster speed than UDP
Preserved boundaries for every application message
quiz.question: Which service does TCP provide to an application?
quiz.explanation: TCP presents ordered bytes and implements recovery mechanisms. It cannot guarantee application completion, preserve application message boundaries or promise a universal performance advantage.

options: The application received and saved it
No higher protocol can add reliability
UDP traffic was observed at that capture point
A full TCP connection is established
quiz.question: Which conclusion follows from a captured UDP datagram?
quiz.explanation: A capture demonstrates the observed packet at a particular point. It does not prove end-to-end application handling or establish the behavior of every protocol layered above UDP.

options: DNS can use TCP and UDP, and HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP
A port number uniquely identifies every application
quiz.question: Which statement about common services is accurate?
quiz.explanation: Transport conventions require context. DNS supports TCP as well as UDP, and HTTP/3 provides a concrete web-protocol counterexample to the idea that every web exchange uses TCP.

quiz.question: PC1 is 192.168.7.10. Which ordinary ping tests the remote PC2 in this lab?
quiz.explanation: PC2 is the distinct .20 endpoint. The .10 and loopback options are self-tests; show ip displays settings. A remote ICMP reply still does not establish that an application is running.

options: TCP guaranteed the page was delivered
The probe was observed; no complete application transaction was tested
quiz.question: The capture shows a TCP SYN to port 80 but no application was installed. What can you report?
quiz.explanation: The only supported conclusion is the observed probe and the declared test boundary. No server or router was installed, so claims about a successful page or router policy are unsupported.

options: Replace the router after one timeout
Treat ping as the complete application test
Collect the actual service context and separate reachability, transport and application evidence
Assume every UDP application is unreliable
quiz.question: What should happen before troubleshooting a failed real application?
quiz.explanation: Start with the requested service, time and endpoints, then collect evidence at the appropriate level. One timeout or one successful lower-level test cannot establish the whole application result.
