glossary.meaning: A program or service that does a useful job, such as showing a web page or looking up a website name.
Agreed rules for exchanging information, including how messages are formed and interpreted.
Rules used by endpoint software to exchange application data; TCP and UDP provide different services.
A numbered field used with an address and transport protocol to identify a communication endpoint; it is not a cable socket.
An IP packet carries network addresses. On an Ethernet link, a frame wraps that packet with local link information.
An ordered sequence of bytes, the small units that represent data; TCP does not preserve the application's separate message boundaries.
One independently handled message; UDP preserves datagram boundaries but does not itself recover missing messages.
A transport message indicating received data; a TCP acknowledgment does not prove a person read the data or that an application saved it.
A console is a text window for commands. VPCS, the Virtual PC Simulator, is a small simulated endpoint, not a full Windows or Linux computer.
A record of traffic observed at one selected link or interface; it is evidence from that observation point, not a view of every network.
ICMP carries IP control messages. Ordinary ping requests an echo reply using ICMP; it is neither a TCP test nor a UDP test.
The IP address group a host treats as directly reachable on its local network, as determined by its address and mask.
A directional traffic identifier consisting of source IP, destination IP, transport protocol, source port and destination port.
TCP flags used in establishing and acknowledging communication; SYN synchronizes sequence numbers and ACK indicates acknowledgment.
The Domain Name System, which retrieves records associated with names and supports traditional exchanges over UDP and TCP.
A transport protocol carried over UDP that provides mechanisms such as reliable streams; HTTP/3 uses it for web communication.

sections.example: A useful report says: 'PC1 received ICMP replies from PC2. A separate capture contains a TCP probe to destination port 80. No web server was installed, so web-service availability was not tested.' This is much more precise than 'TCP works.'
sections.heading: Start with the application and the evidence
keyPoints: An address identifies an endpoint in the IP plan, not an application outcome.
Record what the test observed and what remains untested.
Use the smallest isolated experiment that answers the current question.
sections.explanation: A program asks the network to help it do a job. An operator should describe that job before choosing a test. Suppose a student can ping a classroom server but cannot open its page. Record the requested page, time, client and server, then investigate the actual service. Do not report that the entire application is healthy merely because one lower-level test worked. Conversely, do not report that the entire network is down after one missing response. Our working method is to name the test, state the observation, and state the remaining uncertainty. The hands-on exercise below is deliberately narrow: it identifies transport headers in synthetic probes between two virtual endpoints. It does not install a website, simulate a live call or compare real application performance.

sections.example: Conceptual example, not captured lab output: a student transfers a document through a TCP-based application. Missing transport bytes may be retransmitted. The student should still check that the application reports completion and that the received document is usable.
sections.heading: TCP: ordered bytes, recovery and a real limit
keyPoints: TCP preserves byte order, not the application's original message boundaries.
A SYN probe is not evidence of a completed three-way handshake.
Reliability mechanisms cannot guarantee success through a permanently broken path.
sections.explanation: TCP gives applications an ordered byte stream. Sequence numbers and acknowledgments support tracking received bytes; retransmission can recover lost data. A normal new connection begins with a SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK exchange. SYN means synchronize sequence numbers; ACK means acknowledge. These are transport control flags, not application content. This service has limits: a broken path can still make the connection fail, and a transport acknowledgment does not prove the receiving application saved a file. A conceptual file-transfer example therefore needs both the transport exchange and an application-level completion check. The probe exercise later sends a SYN but deliberately does not claim to demonstrate a complete connection or file transfer.

sections.example: Conceptual example: an application sends a current position update and later receives a newer one. Its designer decides whether an old missing update should be retried or ignored. A UDP header alone does not tell the observer which policy was implemented.
sections.heading: UDP: separate messages and application responsibility
keyPoints: A datagram retains its message boundary.
No UDP reply is not proof that the outbound message never arrived.
Application behavior must be documented or observed, not guessed from the transport.
sections.explanation: UDP carries independent datagrams with source and destination port fields. UDP itself does not add acknowledgments, loss recovery or ordered delivery. This does not mean every UDP-based application is careless: software can add its own reliability, timing or security mechanisms. It also does not establish that UDP is always faster. A comparison needs a defined workload, complete protocol stack and measurements. We do not measure those properties here. For an individual update whose usefulness expires quickly, the application designer may handle lateness differently from a file-transfer program. The exact behavior belongs to that application, not to a blanket promise made by UDP.

sections.example: Paper comparison: record two possible DNS exchanges, one using UDP and one using TCP, both associated with service port 53. Add a third row for HTTP/3 over QUIC and UDP. Explain why seeing UDP does not prove that an application lacks all reliability mechanisms.
sections.heading: Real services can use more than one transport
keyPoints: DNS implementations need TCP support as well as UDP behavior.
HTTP/3 is a counterexample to the claim that every web exchange uses TCP.
The isolated VPCS exercise does not simulate these full application protocols.
sections.explanation: DNS, the Domain Name System, helps resolve names into records such as IP addresses. Traditional DNS supports UDP and TCP; TCP is not reserved exclusively for one special administrative task. HTTP/3, a version of the protocol used for web communication, runs over QUIC, which uses UDP. QUIC supplies mechanisms beyond raw UDP, including reliable streams. These examples show why 'DNS equals UDP' and 'the web equals TCP' are incomplete rules. In a troubleshooting report, identify the actual protocol version and configuration. If that information is unavailable, label the application identity as unconfirmed. These are paper comparisons in this lesson: the two VPCS nodes are not DNS, QUIC or web servers.

sections.example: Your evidence table might have columns for test, source, destination, transport, observed source port, observed destination port and conclusion. Leave a value unknown until you have read it from the capture. A destination port of 80 alone is not sufficient evidence that the payload is HTTP.
sections.heading: Read transport and port evidence without overclaiming
keyPoints: Read transport and both endpoint addresses before interpreting ports.
Distinguish an observed value from a chosen test parameter.
Do not infer application identity from a registered number alone.
sections.explanation: A network port number is a field, not a physical connector. Port registrations provide useful conventions, but a service can run on a different number and arbitrary traffic can use a familiar one. For one direction of a conversation, record the source IP, destination IP, transport, source port and destination port. Together these form a useful five-part identifier, often called a five-tuple. Check packet contents and application context before assigning a service name. In this lab, port 80 is a selected TCP probe destination and port 5000 is a selected UDP probe destination; neither selection starts a server. In Wireshark, select a packet and expand the transport details to record the actual values rather than guessing a source port.

sections.example: The expected endpoint plan is PC1 at 192.168.7.10/24 and PC2 at 192.168.7.20/24. The /24 prefix is used here as a supplied setting; Day 8 explains its mathematics. No default gateway is needed for this local exercise, and no Cloud or NAT node should be added.
sections.heading: A small lab with an explicit stopping point
keyPoints: Only the three named nodes and two named cables are active.
A switch does not require an IOS console for this built-in GNS3 setup.
Expected results are instructions for your experiment, not claims that QCS executed your local lab.
sections.explanation: Build only PC1, Switch1 and PC2. The PCs use addresses in the same local subnet and therefore exchange local traffic through the switch; there is no routing step. VPCS is intentionally limited and its network stack is not a complete substitute for a real operating system. Use its local help to check which probe options your installed version supports. If the required options are absent, stop the transport-probe part and use the clearly labeled paper comparison, rather than inventing console results. Keep a baseline note with the address plan, cable endpoints, installed VPCS version and what was actually observed. Stop if the ordinary ICMP baseline is not working. That prevents an unrelated setup problem from contaminating the transport comparison.

content.metaTitle: TCP vs UDP: Applications and a Beginner GNS3 Lab | QCS
takeaways: Choose and test transport behavior in the context of the actual application.
TCP provides ordered bytes and recovery mechanisms, not an unconditional promise of application success.
UDP datagrams do not include built-in ordered delivery, but higher protocols can add their own mechanisms.
Record addresses, protocol and ports rather than naming an application from its port alone.
A synthetic probe, ICMP reply and successful application transaction are different observations.
Keep the lab isolated and clearly label conceptual examples and unmeasured properties.
objectives: Compare TCP's byte-stream service with UDP's datagram service without assuming one is always faster.
Explain why application names and port numbers do not uniquely determine the transport in use.
Generate bounded synthetic probes and inspect their transport fields on an isolated virtual link.
Separate successful network reachability from a listening service, complete session and successful application transaction.
content.plainAnswer: TCP offers an ordered byte stream with loss recovery; UDP sends separate datagrams without built-in delivery or ordering guarantees. Choose by application needs, then inspect actual traffic. A port number or successful ping alone cannot identify or prove a working application.

visualStory.title: One local path, two transport probes

stages.title: Establish the local path
stages.explanation: Configure PC1 and PC2 on the same subnet and check ICMP replies through Switch1. Both cable endpoints are shown; no router forwards this local exchange.

stages.title: Observe the UDP probe
stages.explanation: PC1 sends a synthetic UDP probe through Switch1 toward PC2. Inspect the UDP header at the PC1 link; no application server or delivery guarantee is demonstrated.

stages.title: Observe the TCP probe
stages.explanation: PC1 sends a synthetic TCP SYN through Switch1 toward PC2. Inspect its flags and port; a SYN alone does not show a completed handshake or a successful web request.

visualStory.altText: PC1 sends probes through Switch1 to PC2. The diagram ends at PC2 and compares outgoing UDP and TCP probes, not completed application sessions.
visualStory.boundary: This isolated wired path omits routers, firewalls and application servers. VPCS probes reveal transport fields; they do not demonstrate full sessions, application delivery or performance.
visualStory.takeaway: Identify what PC1 sends to PC2; a captured probe is not proof that an application completed its work.

candidates.name: One path, two probes
candidates.scene: The exact two VPCS endpoints and switch, with the two cables and three observation stages visible.
candidates.limitation: The diagram does not simulate a full transport session or a real application.
candidates.teachingValue: Connects actual probe observations to the precise local path without inventing router or application behavior.

candidates.name: Application comparison
candidates.scene: A separate paper table contrasts file transfer, DNS and HTTP/3 requirements with their transport context.
candidates.limitation: A conceptual table would not show which virtual cables the learner must connect.
candidates.teachingValue: Shows why a familiar application category can involve more than one transport.

candidates.name: Header comparison
candidates.scene: TCP and UDP header fields are shown side by side with ports and TCP flags emphasized.
candidates.limitation: A header-only visual would omit the destination and physical lab boundary.
candidates.teachingValue: Helps distinguish field evidence from assumptions about a running service.

conceptSelection.selectionReason: Use the exact reproducible local path for the visual, and keep protocol-header details and real-application comparisons in the text and captured observations.

walkthrough.why: The required behavior is a better starting point than a memorized slogan about TCP being slow or UDP being fast.
walkthrough.action: Name the task before choosing a protocol.
walkthrough.whatHappens: Write whether the application needs a complete ordered result, timely individual updates, or its own reliability rules. Do not start by assuming that every video or web service uses the same transport.

walkthrough.why: Knowing the path prevents you from inspecting an unrelated router and mistaking its local sockets for all transit sessions.
walkthrough.action: Name the evidence you can actually collect.
walkthrough.whatHappens: A capture can show addresses, the transport and ports at the selected link. In our lab, PC1 sends to PC2 through Switch1; no router forwards this same-subnet exchange.

walkthrough.why: This keeps your conclusion proportional to the evidence and avoids treating a missing reply as proof of a particular fault.
walkthrough.action: Compare the test with the real application.
walkthrough.whatHappens: A synthetic TCP probe is not a browser fetching a page. A UDP probe is not a phone call. Keep the real-application explanation separate from what the simulator actually ran.

beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: A website can fail even when ping works. A transport can be visible even when no application is listening. Learning to separate those observations prevents unnecessary router changes and makes troubleshooting reports more useful.

firstPractice.hint: Ask what produced each observation and whether an application actually completed its requested job.
firstPractice.task: On paper, make three columns: ICMP reachability, TCP or UDP traffic, and successful application work. Place 'a ping reply', 'a captured UDP datagram' and 'a completed web request' into the appropriate columns.
firstPractice.expected: The three observations answer different questions; none should be silently substituted for another.

beginnerGuide.startingPoint: You do not need to know router commands. Imagine two programs exchanging data, then ask what help they need from the transport. Use the definitions first. When a lab instruction says Console, right-click the named GNS3 device and choose Console; its prompt shows where commands belong.

checkUnderstanding.hint: Compare the ICMP definition with the transport and application definitions.
checkUnderstanding.answer: No. An ICMP echo reply supports reachability for that test at that time. A web service needs its own transport exchange and successful application response; it may be unavailable even while ping works.
checkUnderstanding.question: Does a reply to ordinary ping prove that a TCP web service is running?

everydayComparison.whereItStops: Real protocols use headers, state and timers, not paper or people. The analogy cannot predict speed, establish security or demonstrate how an actual application handles missing data.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: TCP provides ordered bytes and mechanisms to recover loss. UDP provides independent messages; an application can implement additional checking when needed. The application decides what successful work means.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: For a memory aid, compare a numbered set of notes checked for missing pages with separate announcements sent without that check. This is an organizational metaphor, not a literal description of devices or a promise that every message arrives.

prerequisites: Review the earlier lessons on endpoints, Ethernet frames and IP packets; the key terms are reintroduced here.
Install GNS3 with its included VPCS and Ethernet switch nodes, plus a working Wireshark capture integration.
Use a new isolated project with no Cloud, NAT, physical adapter or connection to shared networks.
No Cisco image, Linux container, web server or previous router configuration is needed for this lab.
content.learnerOutcome: Explain the transport behavior an application needs, distinguish TCP, UDP and ICMP in a capture, and document what a small GNS3 probe exercise proves and does not prove.
content.metaDescription: Learn TCP and UDP with clear application examples, packet evidence, an isolated GNS3 lab, explained commands, practice questions and a beginner quiz.

terms.meaning: A program or service that does a useful job, such as showing a web page or looking up a website name.
Agreed rules for exchanging information, including how messages are formed and interpreted.
Rules used by endpoint software to exchange application data; TCP and UDP provide different services.
A numbered field used with an address and transport protocol to identify a communication endpoint; it is not a cable socket.
An IP packet carries network addresses. On an Ethernet link, a frame wraps that packet with local link information.
An ordered sequence of bytes, the small units that represent data; TCP does not preserve the application's separate message boundaries.
One independently handled message; UDP preserves datagram boundaries but does not itself recover missing messages.
A transport message indicating received data; a TCP acknowledgment does not prove a person read the data or that an application saved it.
A console is a text window for commands. VPCS, the Virtual PC Simulator, is a small simulated endpoint, not a full Windows or Linux computer.
A record of traffic observed at one selected link or interface; it is evidence from that observation point, not a view of every network.
ICMP carries IP control messages. Ordinary ping requests an echo reply using ICMP; it is neither a TCP test nor a UDP test.
The IP address group a host treats as directly reachable on its local network, as determined by its address and mask.

teachingPrelude.explanation: Read these definitions before the comparison. This lesson separates three questions: can the other endpoint be reached, which transport is present, and did an actual application complete its job? Each question needs different evidence. Our practical exercise answers the first two only; the application examples are conceptual comparisons.
teachingPrelude.labBoundary: PC1, Switch1 and PC2 form one isolated wired subnet. No router or firewall is in this path. VPCS probes show transport fields, not full applications, throughput or reliable delivery under load.

practiceQuestions.answer: Both PCs are in the same supplied /24 local subnet and connect through Switch1.
practiceQuestions.question: Why does the PC1-to-PC2 path not need a router in this lab?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The local exchange uses the two shown Ethernet links. Introducing an unseen router into the explanation would contradict the actual topology and send the learner to the wrong place for evidence.

practiceQuestions.answer: It shows that the observed probe used TCP with SYN set; it does not prove a completed handshake or working web service.
practiceQuestions.question: What useful fact does the outgoing TCP SYN prove, and what does it not prove?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The lab does not install a listener on PC2. Read the outgoing fields and any response separately, and retain uncertainty about the application instead of claiming a successful transaction.

practiceQuestions.answer: Performance depends on the full application and network conditions, not just the transport name.
practiceQuestions.question: Why is 'UDP is always faster' an unsafe general conclusion?
practiceQuestions.explanation: This exercise does not run an application benchmark. A fair comparison needs a workload, metrics and the full protocol behavior, including any mechanisms the application adds above UDP.

practiceQuestions.answer: Yes; UDP's own service and the behavior of a protocol built above it are different things.
practiceQuestions.question: Can an application using UDP add reliability above it?
practiceQuestions.explanation: HTTP/3 over QUIC is a useful counterexample to simple slogans. Do not use the presence of a UDP header to conclude that every higher-level exchange lacks reliable delivery mechanisms.

practiceQuestions.answer: Stop that optional probe portion, record the version limitation and use the labeled paper comparison.
practiceQuestions.question: What should you do if a required VPCS probe option is missing?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Unsupported commands do not establish a network failure. Do not make up expected output or change the topology to a real network just to force a demonstration.

practiceQuestions.answer: The actual application protocol and service context have not been verified.
practiceQuestions.question: What is missing from the claim 'destination port 80 proves this is HTTP'?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A number is a useful convention but not an identity guarantee. This lab deliberately sends a synthetic probe to port 80 without running a web server, making that distinction visible.

realWorldScenario.title: A classroom page fails although ping replies
realWorldScenario.takeaway: Write conclusions in layers: what was reachable, which transport was seen, and whether the requested application work completed. Keep untested explanations as hypotheses, not facts.
realWorldScenario.situation: A hypothetical training room reports that a classroom page will not open. One learner has a ping reply and concludes that the application must be fine. Another sees a missing response to a probe and wants to replace the router. Both conclusions go beyond the evidence. Before making changes, the operator separates local reachability, the actual service transport and the requested application result. This is a conceptual scenario, not an additional server installed in the lab.
walkthrough: Record the affected client, requested service and time. Ask which protocol version and service address are intended rather than assuming a port from the application name.
Record ping as an ICMP observation only. In real networks, missed replies can reflect filtering, rate limits, host behavior or link problems; they do not isolate one fault.
Capture only authorized test traffic at a known observation point. Check direction, addresses, transport and ports; avoid collecting unrelated users' data.
Check whether the actual service is listening and whether its application request succeeds using its own approved diagnostic method. A synthetic probe cannot substitute for that transaction.
Compare observations with the known working baseline. Change one authorized setting only after the evidence supports it, then repeat the same application check and record the outcome.

title: IPv4 addresses, masks, networks, and broadcasts

lab.goal: Compare a calculated address plan with actual VPCS settings and remote ICMP results, then restore one deliberate wrong-subnet fault without changing shared or production networks.
setup: Create a fresh GNS3 project; use a configured local server or GNS3 VM appropriate to your installation.
Drag two built-in VPCS nodes from End devices and a built-in Ethernet switch from Switches. Rename them PC1, PC2 and Switch1.
Connect the exact interfaces in the topology. Start both PCs and leave the switch ports on their default access VLAN 1.
Do not add a Cloud, NAT or physical network adapter. Perform these tests only in the isolated lab, never on production or shared traffic.
Open Notepad on Windows, TextEdit in plain-text mode on macOS, or a plain-text editor on Linux. Save your baseline and observations as Day8-address-plan.txt.

steps.why: The arithmetic and the device configuration are separate checks. Establishing the expected plan first makes later discrepancies visible instead of silently accepting a typo.
steps.title: Calculate before typing
steps.instruction: On paper, record both endpoint addresses, the /24 prefix and mask 255.255.255.0. Calculate the full network and broadcast addresses before assigning anything. The /24 prefix leaves eight host bits, so the block contains 256 addresses; the ordinary usable range is 192.168.8.1 through 192.168.8.254. These are calculations, not commands to type in a console.
steps.expectedResult: Your written plan identifies network 192.168.8.0/24 and broadcast 192.168.8.255, and places both proposed host addresses strictly between them.

steps.why: A configured value and a planned value can differ. Inspecting the actual endpoint first prevents a typo from being interpreted as a failure of the subnet calculation.
steps.title: Configure and inspect PC1
steps.instruction: Right-click PC1 and choose Console before typing. Confirm the PC1> or VPCS> prompt, then enter the commands separately without typing the prompt itself. Copy the displayed settings into your baseline note.
steps.expectedResult: PC1 shows 192.168.8.10 with mask 255.255.255.0. Stop if it differs from the written baseline.
commandExplanations: Assign PC1 address 192.168.8.10 and prefix /24; no gateway is needed for this isolated local path.
Display the actual settings rather than assuming the previous input was correct; compare address and mask with the plan.

steps.why: Matching only one side is not enough. Both endpoints must agree with the intended addressing plan, and they must not use the same host address.
steps.title: Configure and inspect PC2
steps.instruction: Right-click PC2 and choose Console before typing. Check that the window belongs to PC2 rather than PC1. Assign its distinct address, inspect the result and copy the actual values into the same baseline note.
steps.expectedResult: PC2 shows 192.168.8.20 with mask 255.255.255.0. Both endpoints are inside 192.168.8.0/24.
commandExplanations: Assign PC2 its unique address 192.168.8.20 using the same /24 prefix as PC1.
Read PC2's actual address and mask so the remote end is verified independently.

steps.why: A working baseline is necessary for a meaningful fault comparison. Initial address discovery can delay a reply; persistent loss needs investigation before the experiment continues.
steps.title: Test the remote baseline
steps.instruction: Right-click PC1 and choose Console before typing. Test PC2's address, not PC1's own address. Repeat the bounded command if an initial request times out; do not introduce the fault until repeated baseline requests receive replies.
steps.expectedResult: The remote endpoint replies during the working baseline. Record actual results, including any initial missing replies, rather than copying a sample transcript.
commandExplanations: Send three ICMP echo requests to PC2 at 192.168.8.20; -c 3 limits the count. This is a remote reachability test, not an application test.

steps.why: Changing one documented value isolates the experiment. The switch still has the same cables; an IP subnet mismatch is not the same as a missing physical link.
steps.title: Introduce one wrong address
steps.instruction: Right-click PC2 and choose Console before typing. Change only PC2 to 192.168.9.20/24; keep the cables, mask and PC1 unchanged. Inspect the new settings and mark this clearly as an intentional fault, not the final configuration.
steps.expectedResult: PC2 now shows 192.168.9.20/24. The original PC2 address is no longer the correct target during this fault step.
commandExplanations: Move PC2 to 192.168.9.20, outside PC1's /24 subnet, without adding a gateway or router.
Confirm that the wrong address was actually applied so the next observation has a known cause in this controlled lab.

steps.why: The observation demonstrates the boundary of this configured local path. It does not prove that every real-world ping failure is caused by a wrong IP address.
steps.title: Test the changed destination
steps.instruction: Right-click PC1 and choose Console before typing. Test PC2's current wrong address, 192.168.9.20. There is no default gateway or router in this project, so PC1 has no configured path to that different subnet.
steps.expectedResult: Expect no successful remote echo replies; VPCS may report a missing gateway, unreachable destination or timeouts. Record its exact wording. Do not claim a successful cross-subnet exchange.
commandExplanations: Try three ICMP requests to the deliberately changed PC2 address 192.168.9.20; the expected failure concerns this exact isolated address plan.

steps.why: Rollback is an exact restoration, not an unrelated workaround. Inspecting the restored value catches a second typing error before you judge recovery.
steps.title: Restore the recorded address
steps.instruction: Right-click PC2 and choose Console before typing. Read the original baseline first, restore the exact planned PC2 address and inspect it again. Do not change PC1 or add a router to make the test succeed.
steps.expectedResult: PC2 again shows 192.168.8.20 with mask 255.255.255.0. The planned local subnet is restored.
commandExplanations: Restore PC2 to its baseline address 192.168.8.20/24.
Confirm the address and mask match the original baseline before the recovery test.

steps.why: Repeating the original check closes the experiment and distinguishes a restored configuration from an observed recovery.
steps.title: Verify forward recovery
steps.instruction: Right-click PC1 and choose Console before typing. Repeat the same remote test used for the working baseline, now aimed at the restored PC2 address. Record the result beside the baseline and deliberate-fault observations.
steps.expectedResult: Expect remote replies after restoration. If they remain absent, inspect both settings and exact cable endpoints instead of claiming the lab has recovered.
commandExplanations: Repeat three ICMP requests to the restored peer 192.168.8.20, using the same test as the baseline.

steps.why: Two named remote checks make the test direction clear. A successful ping does not prove that every application or future route will work.
steps.title: Check the reverse direction
steps.instruction: Right-click PC2 and choose Console before typing. Test PC1's address and record the result. This explicitly tests the other endpoint rather than PC2's own address, preventing a misleading self-test.
steps.expectedResult: Expect replies from PC1 in the restored isolated topology. Keep this result separate from any claim about websites, throughput or Internet access.
commandExplanations: Send three ICMP echo requests from PC2 to the remote PC1 address 192.168.8.10.

lab.title: Day 8: calculate, configure, change and restore one subnet
cleanup: Restore the baseline PC2 address and verify the final remote results before stopping nodes.
Save the topology and your text notes. VPCS address settings can be lost after a restart unless saved; re-enter and inspect the documented addresses when reopening.
Stop the isolated project when finished. Never use these fault tests or rollback instructions on production or shared networks.
devices: PC1: built-in VPCS endpoint
Switch1: built-in GNS3 Ethernet switch
PC2: built-in VPCS endpoint
lab.topology: PC1 Ethernet0 -- Switch1 Ethernet0; Switch1 Ethernet1 -- PC2 Ethernet0. Only these three nodes and two cables are active. No router, firewall, Cloud or NAT connection is present; the switch uses default access VLAN 1.

addressing.purpose: First host in the planned local test.
Joins the two isolated local links.

verification: Verify the arithmetic: network 192.168.8.0/24, mask 255.255.255.0, broadcast 192.168.8.255; neither PC uses a reserved boundary address.
Inspect both show ip outputs and compare them to the saved baseline rather than relying on visual cable status alone.
Record working baseline, deliberate wrong-subnet failure and restored remote replies as three separate observations.
Confirm every ping targets the other PC's address appropriate to that step, not the sender's own address.
Do not claim application health, VLAN security or routed connectivity from this local exercise.
lab.licensingNote: Built-in VPCS and Ethernet switch nodes require no Cisco image. GNS3 does not provide Cisco images. Use Cisco images only when the applicable license permits the intended use; do not share or redistribute image files. Cisco Modeling Labs is the official Cisco alternative.
troubleshooting: If a console does not open, start the intended VPCS node and check GNS3's configured console application. The built-in Ethernet switch does not provide an IOS command console.

If the baseline repeatedly fails, compare both addresses and masks, inspect the two exact cable endpoints and confirm the switch ports use default access VLAN 1. Do not introduce the wrong address until baseline connectivity works.

An initial timeout can accompany address discovery. In real networks, persistent loss may also involve filtering, host behavior, rate limits or link problems; ping alone does not identify a faulty layer.
If the deliberate wrong-subnet test unexpectedly replies, stop and inspect the actual masks, routes and topology. Do not change the expected conclusion to fit an unexplained result.
If recovery fails, restore the exact saved address and mask on PC2, inspect PC1 without changing it, and retest the baseline destination. Keep the project isolated throughout.

quiz.question: Which mask corresponds to /26?
quiz.explanation: Twenty-four ones fill the first three octets; two more ones contribute 128 plus 64 in the last octet, producing 192.

quiz.question: What is the network of 192.168.8.70/26?
quiz.explanation: The 64-address block containing 70 begins at 64 and ends at 127. The .70 address is a host and .127 is this block's broadcast.

quiz.question: How many ordinary usable host addresses are in a /24 LAN?
quiz.explanation: Eight host bits give 256 total addresses. Exclude the network and broadcast addresses for this ordinary /24 LAN, leaving 254.

options: No guarantee that every host accepts or replies
All routers forward it to the Internet
quiz.question: What does a broadcast destination guarantee?
quiz.explanation: The destination has broadcast semantics, but receiving and replying depend on host state and network controls. Do not use broadcast ping as a complete inventory or success test.

quiz.question: PC1 is 192.168.8.10. Which baseline target tests the other PC?
quiz.explanation: PC2 uses .20 in the supplied baseline. The first two options are self-tests; the broadcast is not the explicitly named individual peer.

glossary.meaning: A bit is one binary digit, 0 or 1. An octet contains eight bits and can represent a decimal value from 0 to 255.
A 32-bit network address, commonly written as four decimal octets, assigned to an interface; one device can have several interfaces and addresses.
An interface is a network connection on a device. A host is an endpoint that sends or receives data, such as a computer.
The prefix length counts the leading network bits. A contiguous mask represents those bits as ones followed by host-bit zeros.
An IP address block defined by a network address and prefix length. The host uses its mask to decide whether a destination belongs to its local subnet.
For an ordinary IPv4 LAN subnet, all-zero host bits identify the network and all-one host bits identify its directed broadcast, not ordinary host assignments.
The addresses between network and broadcast in the ordinary LAN examples here. Special /31 point-to-point and /32 cases use different rules.
A router's local address used for destinations without a more specific route. No gateway is configured in this isolated same-subnet lab.
VPCS is GNS3's lightweight Virtual PC Simulator. Its console is a text window opened by right-clicking the named PC and choosing Console.
ICMP is an IP control-message protocol. Ordinary ping sends echo requests and reports replies or missing replies; it does not prove application health.
A baseline records the intended settings and working observations. Rollback restores those exact settings after a controlled test.

sections.example: Write 192.168.8.10/24 as an address-plus-prefix pair. The /24 means 24 leading network bits, not 24 hosts and not a number to append to the last octet.
sections.heading: Four numbers represent thirty-two bits
keyPoints: An IPv4 octet is an eight-bit value from 0 through 255.
Always record the configured prefix along with the address.
One device can have more than one addressed interface.
sections.explanation: An IPv4 address such as 192.168.8.10 is written as four decimal octets. Each octet represents eight binary bits, so the full address has 32 bits. An octet's decimal value is between 0 and 255. An address belongs to a network interface, not permanently to a person or an entire device; a router can have several interfaces and addresses. The mask must be considered with the address. Do not conclude that an address beginning with 192 always uses /24, or that one beginning with 10 always uses /8. Modern classless addressing uses the supplied prefix. In our lab the addresses are private examples confined to a disconnected project, not instructions to change a home or office adapter.

sections.example: Compare 192.168.8.10/24 with the same address at /26. The first block spans .0 through .255; the second spans .0 through .63. Both calculations use the address and mask, not the address alone.
sections.heading: A mask marks the network bits
keyPoints: /24 corresponds to 255.255.255.0.
/26 corresponds to 255.255.255.192 and leaves six host bits.
A prefix boundary need not line up with a printed dot.
sections.explanation: A contiguous subnet mask consists of leading ones followed by zeros in binary. The ones select the network portion; the zeros leave the host portion. For /24, three whole octets contain ones and the final octet contains zeros, giving 255.255.255.0. This whole-octet example is easy to see, but the division can occur inside an octet. In /26, the last mask octet is 11000000 in binary: 128 plus 64 equals 192. The full mask is 255.255.255.192 and six host bits remain. That is why the first three printed numbers alone are not a universal test for whether two addresses share a subnet. Read the actual prefix before using a shortcut.

sections.example: For 192.168.8.10/24: network 192.168.8.0, broadcast 192.168.8.255, usable hosts 192.168.8.1 through 192.168.8.254. Eight host bits give 256 total addresses and 254 ordinary usable hosts.
sections.heading: Find network, broadcast and usable hosts
keyPoints: Network and broadcast are full addresses, not just final-octet numbers.
Do not confuse total address count with usable host count.
Special /31 and /32 cases require their own context.
sections.explanation: For an ordinary IPv4 LAN subnet, keep the network bits and set every host bit to zero to obtain the network address. Set every host bit to one to obtain the broadcast address. Do not assign those two boundary addresses as ordinary hosts in the LAN examples here. With h host bits, a block has 2^h total addresses and these ordinary examples have 2^h minus 2 usable addresses. The notation 2^h means multiply two by itself h times. This subtract-two formula is not universal: /31 point-to-point links have a defined exception and a /32 identifies one address. We acknowledge those boundaries now; do not apply their rules to the /24 lab or assume that every /31 is suitable for an ordinary multi-host LAN.

sections.example: Paper exercise: identify 192.168.8.255 as the broadcast of 192.168.8.0/24. Do not run a broadcast ping. Test only the explicitly named remote host, 192.168.8.20, in the isolated lab.
sections.heading: Broadcast is a destination, not a response guarantee
keyPoints: Identify broadcast boundaries without scanning or broadcasting to real networks.
Never assume every host responds to a broadcast ping.
Address planning and security-policy enforcement are different tasks.
sections.explanation: A subnet-directed broadcast address identifies the hosts in the target IPv4 subnet. It does not guarantee that every machine is powered on, accepts a particular message or replies to a ping. Host software and network controls affect behavior. Directed broadcasts arriving from other networks are commonly restricted for security reasons; this beginner exercise does not enable them. Calculate the broadcast address on paper instead of probing a whole real network. The built-in GNS3 switch and two VPCS nodes are used only for individual peer checks. A broadcast calculation is not evidence that an application reached all intended recipients, and changing a mask alone does not create a firewall or reliable security separation.

sections.example: Check 192.168.8.70/26 by asking whether 64 <= 70 <= 127. Then exclude .64 and .127 as ordinary hosts in this example. Compare the 62 usable /26 addresses with the 254 usable /24 addresses.
sections.heading: Check a non-octet boundary before the lab
keyPoints: The containing block must include the given host address.
Reserve network and broadcast in the ordinary LAN example.
Changing the mask changes the boundary, not just its written label.
sections.explanation: For 192.168.8.70/26, six host bits give blocks of 64 addresses. The fourth-octet blocks begin at 0, 64, 128 and 192. Seventy lies in the block starting at 64, so the network is 192.168.8.64 and the broadcast is 192.168.8.127. Ordinary usable hosts are .65 through .126. This is a paper comparison; the hands-on lab below deliberately stays with /24 so you can first connect the calculation to inspected settings and a controlled fault. Day 9 develops the broader four-step method. During any real change, confirm the existing address plan and permission first; do not replace a production mask just because a classroom example uses a different one.

Use a defined method and check that the result contains the original host.
Separate total addresses, ordinary usable hosts and special-prefix cases.
A broadcast address is not a promise that every device will respond.
Subnet arithmetic alone does not configure routing or enforce security.
Inspect both endpoints, change one lab value and restore the recorded baseline.

Calculate network, broadcast and usable host boundaries for the supplied /24 and /26 examples.
Explain that a broadcast destination does not guarantee every device responds.
Compare a written address plan with a reversible isolated two-PC GNS3 test.
content.plainAnswer: An IPv4 address has 32 bits. Its prefix or mask identifies which bits describe the network. In the ordinary LAN examples here, all-zero host bits identify the network and all-one host bits identify the broadcast. Host addresses lie between those boundaries; special /31 and /32 cases differ.

visualStory.title: One address, three boundary roles

stages.title: Read address and prefix
stages.explanation: 192.168.8.10/24 uses mask 255.255.255.0. Twenty-four network bits leave eight host bits, giving 256 total addresses in the containing block.

stages.title: Find the containing block
stages.explanation: Set the eight host bits to zero for network 192.168.8.0 and to one for broadcast 192.168.8.255. The input address lies between these boundaries.

stages.title: Check ordinary host space
stages.explanation: Ordinary hosts run from 192.168.8.1 through 192.168.8.254. The lab uses .10 and .20. Do not apply this ordinary-LAN rule unchanged to /31 or /32 cases.

visualStory.altText: The address 192.168.8.10/24 leads to network .0, usable hosts .1 through .254 and broadcast .255 within 192.168.8.0/24. This is a calculation, not a packet path.
visualStory.boundary: This conceptual calculation omits physical devices and traffic because it explains address boundaries. The separate lab names PC1, Switch1 and PC2; this is not their wiring diagram.

beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: The IPv4 endpoints in this lab need distinct addresses and compatible local subnet settings to exchange IP traffic. Switch1 forwards their Ethernet frames without needing its own IP address. Knowing which address bits identify the network helps you configure the endpoints and troubleshoot their connection.

firstPractice.hint: For this /24 only, keep the first three octets and vary the final eight host bits.

practiceQuestions.answer: It counts 24 leading network bits out of the 32 IPv4 address bits.
practiceQuestions.question: What does /24 count?
practiceQuestions.explanation: It is not a host count. The remaining eight bits give 256 total addresses, of which 254 are ordinary usable host addresses in the /24 LAN example.

practiceQuestions.answer: Network 192.168.8.0 and broadcast 192.168.8.255; ordinary hosts .1 through .254.
practiceQuestions.question: What are the boundaries of 192.168.8.10/24?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Keep the first 24 bits and set the final eight host bits to zero or one. Both .10 and .20 lie inside the ordinary usable interval.

practiceQuestions.question: What subnet contains 192.168.8.70/26?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A /26 has 64-address blocks in this fourth octet. Seventy lies between 64 and 127; ordinary host assignments range from .65 through .126.

practiceQuestions.answer: In this ordinary LAN example it names the subnet-directed broadcast rather than one ordinary host.
practiceQuestions.question: Why should you avoid assigning the broadcast address to PC2?

practiceQuestions.answer: Not by itself; compare the actual settings, path and test context.

practiceQuestions.answer: The two planned endpoints share a local subnet and the same switch path.

title: Subnetting in a reliable four-step method

lab.goal: Compare a calculated address plan with actual VPCS settings and remote ICMP results, then restore one deliberate wrong-subnet fault without changing shared or production networks.
setup: Create a fresh GNS3 project; use a configured local server or GNS3 VM appropriate to your installation.
Drag two built-in VPCS nodes from End devices and a built-in Ethernet switch from Switches. Rename them PC1, PC2 and Switch1.
Connect the exact interfaces in the topology. Start both PCs and leave the switch ports on their default access VLAN 1.
Do not add a Cloud, NAT or physical network adapter. Perform these tests only in the isolated lab, never on production or shared traffic.
Open Notepad on Windows, TextEdit in plain-text mode on macOS, or a plain-text editor on Linux. Save your baseline and observations as Day9-address-plan.txt.

steps.why: The arithmetic and the device configuration are separate checks. Establishing the expected plan first makes later discrepancies visible instead of silently accepting a typo.
steps.title: Calculate before typing
steps.instruction: On paper, record both endpoint addresses, the /28 prefix and mask 255.255.255.240. Calculate the full network and broadcast addresses before assigning anything. The increment is 16 in the fourth octet; .33 and .34 belong to the block .32 through .47, whose ordinary usable hosts are .33 through .46. These are calculations, not commands to type in a console.
steps.expectedResult: Your written plan identifies network 192.168.9.32/28 and broadcast 192.168.9.47, and places both proposed host addresses strictly between them.

steps.why: A configured value and a planned value can differ. Inspecting the actual endpoint first prevents a typo from being interpreted as a failure of the subnet calculation.
steps.title: Configure and inspect PC1
steps.instruction: Right-click PC1 and choose Console before typing. Confirm the PC1> or VPCS> prompt, then enter the commands separately without typing the prompt itself. Copy the displayed settings into your baseline note.
steps.expectedResult: PC1 shows 192.168.9.33 with mask 255.255.255.240. Stop if it differs from the written baseline.
commandExplanations: Assign PC1 address 192.168.9.33 and prefix /28; no gateway is needed for this isolated local path.
Display the actual settings rather than assuming the previous input was correct; compare address and mask with the plan.

steps.why: Matching only one side is not enough. Both endpoints must agree with the intended addressing plan, and they must not use the same host address.
steps.title: Configure and inspect PC2
steps.instruction: Right-click PC2 and choose Console before typing. Check that the window belongs to PC2 rather than PC1. Assign its distinct address, inspect the result and copy the actual values into the same baseline note.
steps.expectedResult: PC2 shows 192.168.9.34 with mask 255.255.255.240. Both endpoints are inside 192.168.9.32/28.
commandExplanations: Assign PC2 its unique address 192.168.9.34 using the same /28 prefix as PC1.
Read PC2's actual address and mask so the remote end is verified independently.

steps.why: A working baseline is necessary for a meaningful fault comparison. Initial address discovery can delay a reply; persistent loss needs investigation before the experiment continues.
steps.title: Test the remote baseline
steps.instruction: Right-click PC1 and choose Console before typing. Test PC2's address, not PC1's own address. Repeat the bounded command if an initial request times out; do not introduce the fault until repeated baseline requests receive replies.
steps.expectedResult: The remote endpoint replies during the working baseline. Record actual results, including any initial missing replies, rather than copying a sample transcript.
commandExplanations: Send three ICMP echo requests to PC2 at 192.168.9.34; -c 3 limits the count. This is a remote reachability test, not an application test.

steps.why: Changing one documented value isolates the experiment. The switch still has the same cables; an IP subnet mismatch is not the same as a missing physical link.
steps.title: Introduce one wrong address
steps.instruction: Right-click PC2 and choose Console before typing. Change only PC2 to 192.168.9.50/28; keep the cables, mask and PC1 unchanged. Inspect the new settings and mark this clearly as an intentional fault, not the final configuration.
steps.expectedResult: PC2 now shows 192.168.9.50/28. The original PC2 address is no longer the correct target during this fault step.
commandExplanations: Move PC2 to 192.168.9.50, outside PC1's /28 subnet, without adding a gateway or router.
Confirm that the wrong address was actually applied so the next observation has a known cause in this controlled lab.

steps.why: The observation demonstrates the boundary of this configured local path. It does not prove that every real-world ping failure is caused by a wrong IP address.
steps.title: Test the changed destination
steps.instruction: Right-click PC1 and choose Console before typing. Test PC2's current wrong address, 192.168.9.50. There is no default gateway or router in this project, so PC1 has no configured path to that different subnet.
steps.expectedResult: Expect no successful remote echo replies; VPCS may report a missing gateway, unreachable destination or timeouts. Record its exact wording. Do not claim a successful cross-subnet exchange.
commandExplanations: Try three ICMP requests to the deliberately changed PC2 address 192.168.9.50; the expected failure concerns this exact isolated address plan.

steps.why: Rollback is an exact restoration, not an unrelated workaround. Inspecting the restored value catches a second typing error before you judge recovery.
steps.title: Restore the recorded address
steps.instruction: Right-click PC2 and choose Console before typing. Read the original baseline first, restore the exact planned PC2 address and inspect it again. Do not change PC1 or add a router to make the test succeed.
steps.expectedResult: PC2 again shows 192.168.9.34 with mask 255.255.255.240. The planned local subnet is restored.
commandExplanations: Restore PC2 to its baseline address 192.168.9.34/28.
Confirm the address and mask match the original baseline before the recovery test.

steps.why: Repeating the original check closes the experiment and distinguishes a restored configuration from an observed recovery.
steps.title: Verify forward recovery
steps.instruction: Right-click PC1 and choose Console before typing. Repeat the same remote test used for the working baseline, now aimed at the restored PC2 address. Record the result beside the baseline and deliberate-fault observations.
steps.expectedResult: Expect remote replies after restoration. If they remain absent, inspect both settings and exact cable endpoints instead of claiming the lab has recovered.
commandExplanations: Repeat three ICMP requests to the restored peer 192.168.9.34, using the same test as the baseline.

steps.why: Two named remote checks make the test direction clear. A successful ping does not prove that every application or future route will work.
steps.title: Check the reverse direction
steps.instruction: Right-click PC2 and choose Console before typing. Test PC1's address and record the result. This explicitly tests the other endpoint rather than PC2's own address, preventing a misleading self-test.
steps.expectedResult: Expect replies from PC1 in the restored isolated topology. Keep this result separate from any claim about websites, throughput or Internet access.
commandExplanations: Send three ICMP echo requests from PC2 to the remote PC1 address 192.168.9.33.

lab.title: Day 9: calculate, configure, change and restore one subnet
cleanup: Restore the baseline PC2 address and verify the final remote results before stopping nodes.
Save the topology and your text notes. VPCS address settings can be lost after a restart unless saved; re-enter and inspect the documented addresses when reopening.
Stop the isolated project when finished. Never use these fault tests or rollback instructions on production or shared networks.

Switch1: built-in GNS3 Ethernet switch
PC2: built-in VPCS endpoint
lab.topology: PC1 Ethernet0 -- Switch1 Ethernet0; Switch1 Ethernet1 -- PC2 Ethernet0. Only these three nodes and two cables are active. No router, firewall, Cloud or NAT connection is present; the switch uses default access VLAN 1.

addressing.purpose: First host in the planned local test.
Joins the two isolated local links.

verification: Verify the arithmetic: network 192.168.9.32/28, mask 255.255.255.240, broadcast 192.168.9.47; neither PC uses a reserved boundary address.
Inspect both show ip outputs and compare them to the saved baseline rather than relying on visual cable status alone.
Record working baseline, deliberate wrong-subnet failure and restored remote replies as three separate observations.
Confirm every ping targets the other PC's address appropriate to that step, not the sender's own address.
Do not claim application health, VLAN security or routed connectivity from this local exercise.
lab.licensingNote: Built-in VPCS and Ethernet switch nodes require no Cisco image. GNS3 does not provide Cisco images. Use Cisco images only when the applicable license permits the intended use; do not share or redistribute image files. Cisco Modeling Labs is the official Cisco alternative.
troubleshooting: If a console does not open, start the intended VPCS node and check GNS3's configured console application. The built-in Ethernet switch does not provide an IOS command console.

If the baseline repeatedly fails, compare both addresses and masks, inspect the two exact cable endpoints and confirm the switch ports use default access VLAN 1. Do not introduce the wrong address until baseline connectivity works.

An initial timeout can accompany address discovery. In real networks, persistent loss may also involve filtering, host behavior, rate limits or link problems; ping alone does not identify a faulty layer.
If the deliberate wrong-subnet test unexpectedly replies, stop and inspect the actual masks, routes and topology. Do not change the expected conclusion to fit an unexplained result.
If recovery fails, restore the exact saved address and mask on PC2, inspect PC1 without changing it, and retest the baseline destination. Keep the project isolated throughout.

quiz.question: What is the /28 block increment in the final octet?
quiz.explanation: The mask ends in 240, so 256 minus 240 gives a 16-address increment. Fourteen is the ordinary usable host count, not the block size.

quiz.question: Which network contains 192.168.9.33/28?
quiz.explanation: Thirty-three lies in the block from 32 through 47. The next aligned start, 48, is greater than the host and cannot be its containing network.

quiz.question: Which is the broadcast for 172.16.18.77/20?
quiz.explanation: The /20 boundary lies in the third octet, with the containing block from 16 through 31. All remaining host bits set to one produce 172.16.31.255.

options: For the ordinary /28 and /20 LAN examples
quiz.question: When is the ordinary total-addresses-minus-two rule appropriate here?
quiz.explanation: The examples reserve network and broadcast addresses. /31 point-to-point use and /32 single-address prefixes have different semantics and must not be forced into this rule.

options: Guessing the mask from the first octet

Assuming a green node proves the application
quiz.question: Which step confirms actual configuration rather than arithmetic alone?
quiz.explanation: Inspecting both endpoints and a specific remote exchange connects the written plan to observed settings and reachability. It still does not prove application health or security policy.

sections.example: For a memory aid, imagine grouping numbered lockers into labeled ranges. This is not a literal device action or a promise of security; real hosts use binary masks and routes, not locker labels.
sections.heading: What the four-step method solves
keyPoints: Start from the given prefix, not an assumed address class.
Subnet calculations do not configure routing or security controls.
The final result must contain the original address.
sections.explanation: Subnetting divides a parent address block into smaller aligned blocks. It helps organize an address plan, but arithmetic alone does not enforce a firewall policy, configure a VLAN or guarantee improved performance. Our task is precise: given an address and prefix, find its containing network, broadcast and ordinary host interval. Use four steps in the same order each time: read the prefix and mask, find the block size at the changing octet, locate the containing block, and check the boundaries. A changing octet is the mask octet that contains both network ones and host zeros. For whole-octet boundaries such as /24, use the boundary directly rather than forcing the partial-octet shortcut.

sections.example: Given 192.168.9.33/28, write mask 255.255.255.240, host bits 4, total addresses 16 and ordinary usable hosts 14. Do not confuse /28 with 28 usable devices.
sections.heading: Step one: identify the mask and host bits
keyPoints: Host bits equal 32 minus prefix length.
Borrowed bits require an explicitly identified parent prefix.
Ordinary /28 LAN capacity is 14 usable hosts.
sections.explanation: An IPv4 address has 32 bits. For /28, 28 are network bits and four remain for hosts. The corresponding mask is 255.255.255.240 because the final octet 11110000 has decimal value 128 + 64 + 32 + 16 = 240. Four host bits give 2^4, or 16, total addresses. If a stated /24 parent is divided into /28 children, four additional network bits are used and the parent contains 16 equal child subnets. Without a stated parent prefix, do not call those four bits 'borrowed from a class C network'; the original block must be known. Separate the number of child subnets from the number of addresses in each child, even when those numbers happen to match.

sections.example: For 192.168.9.33/28, floor(33 / 16) times 16 equals 32. Here floor means discard the fractional part. The network is 192.168.9.32 and the next block begins at 192.168.9.48.
sections.heading: Steps two and three: locate the containing block
keyPoints: Find the changing octet before calculating its increment.
Round down to an aligned start, never up past the host.
Keep earlier network octets and zero later host octets.
sections.explanation: At a partial mask octet, subtract that octet from 256 to find its block increment. For /28, the changing octet is the fourth and 256 - 240 = 16. The blocks start at 0, 16, 32, 48 and so on. Choose the largest aligned start no greater than the address's changing octet. For a final octet of 33, choose 32, not 48. Preserve the earlier network octets and set any later octets to zero for the network address. This produces 192.168.9.32/28. The phrase 'subtract the last octet' is only correct when the boundary is actually in that last octet. Always identify where the network-host division occurs before using the decimal shortcut.

sections.example: Write two self-checks: .33 lies between .32 and .47 for the /28, and 172.16.18.77 lies between 172.16.16.0 and 172.16.31.255 for the /20. Check alignment as well as inclusion.
sections.heading: Step four: boundaries and an earlier-octet example
keyPoints: Broadcast is the last address of the containing block.
For /20, the relevant increment is in the third octet.
Do not apply ordinary LAN host rules to every /31 or /32.
sections.explanation: The broadcast is the address immediately before the next subnet. For 192.168.9.32/28 it is .47; ordinary usable hosts run from .33 to .46. Now test a wider block: 172.16.18.77/20 has mask 255.255.240.0, so the changing octet is the third. Its increment is 16. The third octet 18 belongs to the block 16 through 31, yielding network 172.16.16.0 and broadcast 172.16.31.255. Ordinary usable hosts range from 172.16.16.1 to 172.16.31.254. There are 12 host bits, 4096 total addresses and 4094 ordinary usable hosts. This example shows why repeatedly subtracting the final zero mask octet gives the wrong reasoning. Special /31 point-to-point links and /32 single-address prefixes are outside the ordinary subtract-two LAN rule.

sections.example: The lab baseline uses PC1 192.168.9.33/28 and PC2 192.168.9.34/28. The wrong value is PC2 192.168.9.50/28, and the rollback restores .34/28 without changing PC1, cables or switch settings.
sections.heading: Use the calculation without inventing connectivity
keyPoints: Validate actual settings separately from arithmetic.
Test the named remote endpoint, never your own address.
Restore the exact baseline and repeat the same check.
sections.explanation: A correct paper answer does not install device settings. In the isolated lab, assign PC1 and PC2 separate addresses inside 192.168.9.32/28, inspect both masks and test the remote peer. The built-in switch does not route between subnets and requires no IOS commands. A deliberate change of PC2 to .50/28 puts it in a different block, .48 through .63. Because no gateway or router exists, the planned cross-subnet request should fail. Restore .34/28 and repeat the original test. Keep the failure claim specific to this controlled experiment: in real networks, missing replies can also result from filtering, host state, rate limits or link trouble. Do not promise every mismatched mask produces the same visible behavior.

walkthrough.action: Calculate boundaries before assigning a host.
walkthrough.whatHappens: Find the network, last address and ordinary usable host range. Check that the example host lies inside the intended block, not on a reserved LAN boundary.

beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Subnetting organizes IP address blocks and helps you identify which destinations belong to a local subnet. It does not itself guarantee faster communication or prevent transmission errors. Calculating boundaries correctly helps avoid invalid host assignments and mismatched subnet settings.

firstPractice.hint: Choose the largest multiple of 16 that does not exceed 33, then use the next block start to locate the broadcast.
firstPractice.task: Apply all four steps to 192.168.9.33/28 on paper. Write the mask, changing octet, block increment, network, broadcast and usable range, then check that .33 is included.
firstPractice.expected: Mask 255.255.255.240; fourth-octet increment 16; network .32, broadcast .47, ordinary hosts .33 through .46.

beginnerGuide.startingPoint: No router command knowledge is assumed. Read the definitions first and write the address plan on paper. A console is the text window opened by right-clicking the named GNS3 PC and choosing Console; do not type commands into the switch or your computer's operating-system terminal.

checkUnderstanding.hint: Compare /28 with /20 and identify the octet that contains both ones and zeros.
checkUnderstanding.answer: The boundary can be in an earlier octet. For /20, use the third mask octet 240 and increment 16; the last mask octet is zero and does not identify the containing third-octet block.
checkUnderstanding.question: Why is subtracting the last mask octet unsafe as a universal rule?

everydayComparison.whereItStops: This is a memory aid, not a literal delivery process. Devices compare binary address bits and routing information; they do not understand streets, buildings or floors. The analogy cannot prove connectivity or security.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: Subnet mask divides network and host parts to segment devices into subnets.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: Dividing a building address into floors and apartments to find a place easily.

terms.meaning: A bit is one binary digit, 0 or 1. An octet contains eight bits and can represent a decimal value from 0 to 255.
A 32-bit network address, commonly written as four decimal octets, assigned to an interface; one device can have several interfaces and addresses.
An interface is a network connection on a device. A host is an endpoint that sends or receives data, such as a computer.
The prefix length counts the leading network bits. A contiguous mask represents those bits as ones followed by host-bit zeros.
An IP address block defined by a network address and prefix length. The host uses its mask to decide whether a destination belongs to its local subnet.
For an ordinary IPv4 LAN subnet, all-zero host bits identify the network and all-one host bits identify its directed broadcast, not ordinary host assignments.
The addresses between network and broadcast in the ordinary LAN examples here. Special /31 point-to-point and /32 cases use different rules.
A router's local address used for destinations without a more specific route. No gateway is configured in this isolated same-subnet lab.
VPCS is GNS3's lightweight Virtual PC Simulator. Its console is a text window opened by right-clicking the named PC and choosing Console.
ICMP is an IP control-message protocol. Ordinary ping sends echo requests and reports replies or missing replies; it does not prove application health.
A baseline records the intended settings and working observations. Rollback restores those exact settings after a controlled test.

teachingPrelude.explanation: A layered explanation is useful only when the basic words are clear. Start with the definitions below, then separate the paper calculation from the actual device test. practiceQuestions.question: What is the ordinary host range for 192.168.9.33/28?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The containing network is .32 and broadcast is .47. Exclude those two boundaries for this ordinary LAN, leaving 14 usable host addresses.

practiceQuestions.answer: The third octet; the mask is 255.255.240.0.
practiceQuestions.question: Which octet changes for 172.16.18.77/20?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Twenty network bits include 16 bits in the first two octets and four more in the third. The increment is 16 in that third octet, not 256 in the last.

practiceQuestions.answer: Network 172.16.16.0 and broadcast 172.16.31.255.
practiceQuestions.question: What are the /20 network and broadcast for 172.16.18.77?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The third octet 18 belongs to the 16-through-31 block. Set the remaining host bits to zero for the network and one for the broadcast.

practiceQuestions.answer: Sixteen equal /28 child blocks.
practiceQuestions.question: How many /28 children fit inside an explicitly given /24 parent?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The prefix increases by four bits, giving 2^4 child blocks. Each child also happens to have 16 total addresses, but that is a different calculation using its four host bits.

practiceQuestions.answer: No; address allocation and security enforcement are different tasks.
practiceQuestions.question: Does subnetting alone enforce a firewall policy?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A network design may combine subnets, VLANs, routing and policy controls, but writing a prefix does not automatically create those configurations or prove isolation.

practiceQuestions.answer: It is outside PC1's .32/28 block and no gateway or router provides a path.
practiceQuestions.question: Why does the .50/28 fault fail in this specific lab?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The conclusion depends on the documented two-PC topology and unchanged masks. It is not a claim that every failed ping in a real network has the same cause.

quiz.question: Which is a valid ordinary Management host in 192.168.10.96/28?
quiz.explanation: The ordinary usable range is .97 through .110. The .96 and .111 addresses are boundaries, and .112 begins the next block.

quiz.question: How many ordinary usable addresses does /27 provide?
quiz.explanation: Five host bits give 32 total addresses. This ordinary LAN reserves network and broadcast, leaving 30 usable addresses including any gateway assignment.

quiz.question: Which proposed range overlaps both Engineering and Management?
quiz.explanation: The .64/26 range covers .64 through .127. It intersects the existing .64-.95 and .96-.111 allocations; the other listed ranges do not.

options: Any free address anywhere permits in-place expansion
Growth needs capacity and adjacent aligned space or a revised plan
A /26 can expand to any 100-address subnet
quiz.question: Which statement describes growth accurately?
quiz.explanation: A larger prefix block must remain aligned and non-overlapping. Capacity somewhere else in the parent is not sufficient to expand an existing allocation in place.

options: Both PCs have the Engineering /27 settings
quiz.question: Before the Engineering phase ping, what must be true?
quiz.explanation: Both PCs must use the current phase's planned addresses and prefix. The test targets the other endpoint inside the isolated local path, not an Internet or self-test destination.

sections.example: Sales: 50 required, 62 available, 12 spare. Engineering: 20 required, 30 available, 10 spare. Management: 10 required, 14 available, 4 spare. Record what each requirement includes before calling the plan sufficient.
sections.heading: Count the actual address requirement
keyPoints: State the parent prefix explicitly.
Count infrastructure and growth requirements consistently.
Do not confuse total block size with usable host capacity.
sections.explanation: Start with a written parent allocation and the number of usable addresses each group needs. Include user endpoints, any planned gateway and other infrastructure; do not silently count a gateway twice or forget it. In this worked example the parent is 192.168.10.0/24. Sales needs 50 usable addresses in total, Engineering 20 and Management 10; those totals already include one future gateway reservation per group. Choose ordinary LAN blocks whose usable capacity is large enough. A /26 has 64 total addresses and 62 ordinary usable hosts, a /27 has 32 and 30, and a /28 has 16 and 14. There are therefore 12, 10 and 4 spare usable addresses within these allocations. These are planning numbers, not claims that every possible real deployment has the same reserved-address rules.

sections.example: Write the full rows: Sales network .0, hosts .1-.62, broadcast .63; Engineering network .64, hosts .65-.94, broadcast .95; Management network .96, hosts .97-.110, broadcast .111. All addresses use the 192.168.10 prefix.
sections.heading: Allocate aligned blocks from largest to smallest
keyPoints: Use aligned network starts, not arbitrary host addresses.
The Management network .96/28 is not a host assignment.
Check the whole block through its broadcast, not only the first usable host.
sections.explanation: In an initially empty parent, placing larger requirements first is a useful planning heuristic because they need larger aligned spaces. It is not a universal optimization guarantee for an already fragmented plan. Allocate Sales to 192.168.10.0/26, which spans .0 through .63. Next allocate Engineering to 192.168.10.64/27, spanning .64 through .95. Allocate Management to 192.168.10.96/28, spanning .96 through .111. The starts are aligned to increments of 64, 32 and 16 respectively. A subnet cannot begin at any convenient next host number: for example, .97 is a valid Management host but not the /28 network boundary. The first and last addresses of each block remain reserved as network and broadcast in these ordinary LAN examples.

sections.example: For each pair, ask whether the larger starting address is no greater than the smaller ending address. If yes, the intervals intersect. Also verify that every child start and end remains within the parent range.
sections.heading: Check overlap and parent containment
keyPoints: Check full intervals, including reserved boundary addresses.
Two different prefixes can still overlap.
A device command's acceptance is not an organization-wide allocation audit.
sections.explanation: Two different written network names can still describe overlapping ranges. Compare the complete first and last address of each allocation. Our three blocks are adjacent and disjoint: .0-.63, .64-.95 and .96-.111. All lie inside the parent .0-.255. Now reject a proposed 192.168.10.64/26 addition: it spans .64-.127 and overlaps both Engineering and Management. Similarly, 192.168.10.30/27 belongs to .0-.31 and overlaps Sales, not Engineering. These are paper checks; do not deliberately install an invalid address on an unfamiliar router to see whether it rejects it. Router validation varies by context, and a device accepting a command does not prove that the overall organization's allocation is correct.

sections.example: Reserve .112/28 for a future small segment and .128/25 for a future larger requirement. Do not assign either range until the plan is reviewed. Keep the Sales in-place expansion limitation visible in the same document.
sections.heading: Reserve growth where it can actually be used
keyPoints: Unallocated address count and immediately expandable capacity are different.
Document reservation ownership and intended purpose.
Recheck alignment and overlap before enlarging any existing prefix.
sections.explanation: After the three allocations, .112 through .255 remains unallocated: 144 total addresses. Represent that remainder as two aligned blocks, 192.168.10.112/28 and 192.168.10.128/25. They are separate reservations, not one automatically assignable subnet. Label their intended use and owner in the plan. Spare hosts inside Sales allow growth up to its present usable capacity, but increasing Sales from /26 to /25 would consume .0-.127 and overlap the other allocated blocks. Expansion may require renumbering, relocation or an earlier design that reserves adjacent aligned space. There is no promise of automatic growth merely because VLSM is used. A useful review asks which group is expected to expand, by how much and whether its specific adjacent space is still free.

sections.example: Use PC1/PC2 .2/.3 at /26, then .66/.67 at /27, then .98/.99 at /28. Every pair sits inside its ordinary host range and avoids the reserved future gateway, network and broadcast addresses.
sections.heading: Test the plan without inventing three routed networks
keyPoints: Only one subnet is active on the two-PC path at a time.
Inspect both endpoints after every readdressing phase.
A local ICMP reply does not prove routed connectivity or policy isolation.
sections.explanation: This beginner lab uses two VPCS nodes and one built-in Ethernet switch. Reuse that exact isolated path for three sequential phases: first Sales, then Engineering, then Management. Readdress both endpoints before testing each phase and record the result; do not mix old and new endpoint settings. The future gateway addresses .1, .65 and .97 are reservations on paper only, not active routers. The lab observes local reachability inside each selected block. It does not demonstrate simultaneous departments, communication between the blocks, VLAN separation, routing protocols, firewall behavior or growth under load. Those need a different topology and later lessons. If an application or security result was not tested, state that limitation instead of implying it from a successful ping.
