glossary.meaning: An IPv6 address is a 128-bit identifier written in hexadecimal groups. A prefix identifies leading bits shared by an address block. Day 12 explains how to expand :: and read a /64.

An interface is a device's network connection. A link is the local network over which neighboring interfaces communicate without an intervening IP router. Our lab link is one cable between two routers.
Unicast identifies one interface as the destination. Global, unique-local and link-local are unicast categories; link-local is not a fourth delivery type alongside unicast, multicast and anycast.
Scope limits where an address has meaning. A zone is a particular region of that scope, such as your selected local link. An interface selection tells a tool which local link you mean.

Global unicast supports addressing beyond one link, subject to allocation and routing. Unique-local addresses support private routing within and between cooperating networks, not normal global Internet routing. Neither label is a security policy.

Multicast identifies a group of receiving interfaces. A group address is different from the individual unicast address of each member. Group membership and permitted scope determine the intended audience.

Anycast uses a shared address at multiple service locations. Routing chooses a destination for a packet. A routing metric is a protocol's measure of path preference, not necessarily geographical distance or server load.

IPv6 neighbor discovery exchanges local control messages to learn about nearby interfaces and other link information. It uses multicast for some tasks. Its detailed message exchanges and automatic assignment belong to Day 14.

ICMPv6 carries IPv6 control messages. Ping sends echo requests and waits for echo replies. Receiving replies tests that exchange with that address, not every address, service or security setting on the device.

Console is a virtual device's text window in GNS3. Right-click the named router and choose Console before typing. Cisco prompts ending >, #, (config)# and (config-if)# mark user, privileged, global and interface modes.

A baseline records the original configuration and actual observations. Rollback restores the intended settings after a controlled change. Repeat the original tests rather than assuming that an accepted command fixed the problem.

The special value ::1 is loopback: the local device talking to itself. The special value :: is unspecified: no address has been selected in a permitted protocol situation. Neither is an ordinary remote peer target to assign in this lab.
The special address ::1 refers to the local node. A reply tests a local function and does not demonstrate that another device or cable is reachable.
The special value :: indicates the absence of an address in defined protocol situations. It is not an address to assign to a host or use as an ordinary destination.
An address from example space such as 2001:db8::/32. It supports documentation and disconnected exercises, not a public production allocation.

sections.example: Make a two-column worksheet headed recipient behavior and scope or use. Put fe80::13:2 in unicast and local link. Put ff02::1 in multicast and local link. For an ordinary service address with unknown deployment, write unicast-format, anycast not established. Do not guess its routing design from its spelling.
sections.heading: Separate recipient type from address scope
keyPoints: Address appearance can identify several categories, but it cannot reveal every deployment property.
Several valid addresses on one interface do not automatically mean duplicate addressing.
sections.explanation: Unicast, multicast and anycast answer a recipient question: one interface, a group, or one routing-selected recipient of a shared address. Scope answers where an address is meaningful. Link-local belongs under unicast, so the chapter title does not describe four mutually exclusive delivery modes. IPv6 does not use broadcast addresses. An interface can have multiple addresses and group memberships; count and classify them before deciding that extra entries are errors.

sections.example: The paper example fd7a:115c:a1e0:13::2 contains the local prefix fd7a:115c:a1e0::/48 and a /64 subnet with group 13. Use it only for classification here. If two businesses connect their networks, they still need an address plan, route policy and security controls. The word local does not encrypt traffic or grant permission to merge networks.
sections.heading: Global and unique-local are not security settings
keyPoints: Do not equate unique-local with link-local, a firewall rule or automatic privacy.
A successful documentation-address ping in this isolated lab does not test public IPv6 routing.
sections.explanation: Global unicast is used for communication beyond one link, but a plausible-looking address does not prove a legitimate allocation, route or Internet access. Our 2001:db8::/32 examples are reserved for documentation and must stay in the disconnected exercise. Unique-local addresses occupy fc00::/7; the locally assigned form uses fd00::/8. A production ULA plan uses a pseudo-random 40-bit Global ID to reduce collision risk, not a familiar number copied from a tutorial. ULAs can be routed across cooperating private networks; they are not confined to one cable.

sections.example: A computer may display an address such as fe80::13:2%7. The %7 suffix is local zone information, not part of the 128-bit address and not a globally meaningful router number. Do not copy that suffix into another operating system. Our Cisco Console exercise instead answers the Output Interface prompt using the local cable port recorded from the topology.
sections.heading: Link-local needs the correct link context
keyPoints: A link-local address need not be derived from a hardware address; this lab assigns it manually.
Selecting the correct interface is part of the test, not an optional cosmetic detail.
sections.explanation: Link-local unicast is identified by fe80::/10. The standard format sets the following 54 bits to zero before the 64-bit interface identifier, which explains the familiar fe80:: addresses in this lab. Routers do not carry link-local-addressed packets across to another link. The same numerical link-local address can exist on separate links, but it must not be duplicated on one link. An output interface or local zone identifier resolves which link a diagnostic tool means.

sections.example: On Router1, inspect the Joined group address(es) part of show ipv6 interface. Record the actual entries and identify ff02::1 if present. Do not configure ff02::1 as the router's individual address. A class exercise can send a paper token to two marked group members while leaving a nonmember unmarked; this represents intended group delivery, not measured packet delivery.
sections.heading: Multicast identifies a group, not a device port
keyPoints: Scope matters for multicast too; do not assume every multicast address is limited to one link.
This lab observes memberships and makes no claim to simulate a multicast application or multicast routing.
sections.explanation: IPv6 multicast uses ff00::/8, with additional fields describing properties including scope. ff02::1 identifies all IPv6 nodes on the local link, while ff02::2 identifies local IPv6 routers. Interfaces also join solicited-node multicast groups associated with their addresses. Their detailed derivation and neighbor-discovery exchanges are reserved for Day 14. Seeing a joined group in a display proves local membership state; it does not prove an application stream arrived or every member replied to a ping.

sections.example: Paper exercise: draw Client, RouteChoice, ServiceA and ServiceB. Connect Client to RouteChoice and that decision point to both services. Give both services the same documentation service address and fictional comparable path costs 10 and 30. Under the exercise's rule, choose ServiceA. Remove its route and choose ServiceB if still available. State that these invented costs are a teaching rule, not a measured protocol result or proof of application failover.
sections.heading: Anycast depends on routing and service readiness
keyPoints: Anycast delivery selects a recipient; it does not replicate the same request to every service instance.
Route reachability and service health are separate facts that an operational deployment must coordinate.
sections.explanation: An anycast service makes one address available at multiple locations. Routing chooses a destination based on the routes and policies available from a particular source. Nearest is a routing concept, not a promise of the geographically closest or least-loaded server. The address comes from unicast space, so no universal leading hex pattern identifies anycast. Operating the service requires appropriate routing and application readiness; entering the same ordinary address on two adjacent lab devices is not a sound anycast deployment.

sections.example: Suppose a report says IPv6 works because ping ::1 succeeded, but the intended service was Router2 at 2001:db8:13:1::2. The tests name different recipients. Correct the evidence record before drawing conclusions. In our controlled fault, a reply from fe80::13:2 is useful local evidence, but it cannot replace the failed test to the removed documentation address.
sections.heading: Special values prevent misleading tests
keyPoints: Test the peer's address, not the sender's own address or the loopback special value.
Missed replies can also reflect filtering, rate limits or interface problems; do not diagnose by a single ping alone.
sections.explanation: The loopback address ::1 refers to the local node. A reply from it does not test a cable, neighboring router or remote service. The unspecified address :: represents the absence of an address in permitted protocol contexts and is not an ordinary address to assign to an interface. Do not confuse a shortened address containing :: with the complete special value ::. A technical note should include the source device, full target, selected output interface, time and observed result.

sections.example: Without a permitted image, draw the two-router lab and create baseline, removed-address and restored-address rows on paper. Predict which target should respond and explain why the second address is retained. Mark every result as predicted. For the multicast and anycast paper comparisons, state the omitted membership protocol, route implementation and application health checks instead of claiming they were configured.
sections.heading: Turn address classification into an operator checklist
keyPoints: GNS3 does not supply Cisco images; use them only where the applicable entitlement permits.
A paper result, a command accepted by a device and an observed reply are different kinds of evidence.
sections.explanation: Use a five-part record: planned address, category, meaningful scope, local interface and actual observation. Start with a known-good isolated baseline, change one assignment, compare the same targets, then restore and retest. Do not expand a limited local success into a claim about routing or applications. The lab uses documented IOS-style commands, but exact port names and software support depend on the authorized image. QCS has source-reviewed these steps; it has not executed this lesson on a Cisco image.

content.metaTitle: CCNA Day 13: IPv6 Address Types and Link-Local Scope
takeaways: Ask who the recipient is and where the address is meaningful before selecting a test.
Link-local is unicast limited to one link; unique-local can be routed within a cooperating private network.
Multicast membership describes a group relationship, not measured application delivery.
Anycast uses unicast-format addresses and routing choice; it is not identified by a magic prefix or automatically by geography.
A retained link-local reply cannot prove that a removed unicast target or dependent application works.
Keep baseline, controlled fault and restoration evidence separate, and never report paper predictions or static review as device execution.
objectives: Separate unicast, multicast and anycast delivery behavior from the scope of an address.
Recognize global, unique-local and link-local unicast and the loopback and unspecified special cases.
Explain why anycast needs routing and service context rather than a distinctive hexadecimal prefix.
Configure unique link-local and documentation addresses, then inspect the interface's multicast memberships.
Remove one peer address safely, compare two exact tests, restore the address and retest both directions.
content.plainAnswer: Unicast targets one interface, multicast targets a group, and anycast lets routing select a destination using a shared address. Link-local is unicast limited to one link, not a separate delivery type. Identify the address category and scope, then verify the exact interface and destination; a successful local test does not establish Internet or application connectivity.

visualStory.title: IPv6: who should receive it?

stages.title: One interface
stages.explanation: Unicast names one interface. Global, unique-local and link-local are unicast categories; a link-local test must identify the intended local link.

stages.title: A group of members
stages.explanation: Multicast identifies a group within a defined scope. A joined-group entry is membership evidence, not proof that every receiver got an application packet.

stages.title: One routed recipient
stages.explanation: Anycast shares an address across service instances. Routing selects a destination; a special prefix, physical distance or automatic load check does not identify that choice.

visualStory.altText: Three concept panels compare unicast to one interface, multicast to group members, and anycast to one routing-selected recipient. These are address roles, not a wired topology.
visualStory.boundary: This compares intended recipients, not measured delivery or physical wiring. It omits routing and membership protocols; the separate lab scene shows the two actual endpoints.
visualStory.takeaway: One interface, a member group, or one routing-selected recipient. Scope is a separate question.

comparisons.title: One peer. Two different address tests.

stages.title: Verify both targets
stages.explanation: Router1 tests Router2 at 2001:db8:13:1::2 and fe80::13:2. Both requests end at Router2; select Router1's cable interface for the link-local target.

stages.title: Remove one assignment
stages.explanation: Remove only Router2's documentation address. The original target should stop replying; a request to retained fe80::13:2 still ends at Router2 on this link.

stages.title: Restore and retest
stages.explanation: Restore 2001:db8:13:1::2/64 on Router2. Repeat both peer tests and the reverse checks; a completed reply returns to the router that sent the request.

comparisons.altText: Router1 connects directly to Router2 on one isolated link. Requests end at Router2 and replies return to Router1; the tests use two different addresses on that same peer.
comparisons.boundary: Only Router1, Router2 and one cable are simulated. Internet access, anycast services and multicast applications are omitted; the arrows describe expected peer tests, not captured traffic.
comparisons.takeaway: A local-link reply does not prove that the peer's other address or an application is working.

candidates.name: Same peer, two targets
candidates.scene: Router1 and Router2 share one isolated cable, with stages comparing two assigned targets before and after removing one address.
candidates.limitation: The two endpoints do not simulate an anycast service or multicast application.
candidates.teachingValue: Connect address classification to a precise observed test and complete request and reply endpoints.

candidates.name: A cloud of global clients
candidates.scene: Several clients reach servers across many networks.
candidates.limitation: Those devices are not in the hands-on lab and would make the tested boundary ambiguous.
candidates.teachingValue: Suggest broader scope beyond a local link.

candidates.name: A table without devices
candidates.scene: A before-and-after table records two target addresses and expected outcomes.
candidates.limitation: The table alone hides which two nodes and cable the learner must build.
candidates.teachingValue: Compare expected test states clearly.

conceptSelection.selectionReason: Show every actual lab endpoint and the single link; use the stages for the different targets rather than inventing extra paths or devices.

candidates.name: Who should receive it?
candidates.scene: Three labeled address-role panels distinguish one interface, a member group and one routing-selected service instance.
candidates.limitation: Concept panels are not physical devices, cables or measured traffic.
candidates.teachingValue: Teach recipient behavior without pretending the address prefix alone reveals anycast.

candidates.name: A wall of address prefixes
candidates.scene: Several long IPv6 address examples appear as classification rows.
candidates.limitation: Prefix recognition alone cannot identify an anycast deployment.
candidates.teachingValue: Practice recognizing address families from text.

candidates.name: A global service map
candidates.scene: Multiple distant servers share an address and receive routes from a worldwide network.
candidates.limitation: A geographic map could wrongly imply that physical distance always decides the recipient.
candidates.teachingValue: Introduce distributed services and routing choice.

conceptSelection.selectionReason: The lesson separates recipient behavior from scope. Three explicit roles make that distinction before the separate two-router scene demonstrates the limited hands-on test.

walkthrough.why: Avoid treating every address on a screen as an interchangeable device destination.
walkthrough.action: Classify the address before planning a test.
walkthrough.whatHappens: A target beginning fe80 is a link-local unicast example. ff02::1 is a link-scoped multicast group. An ordinary-looking unicast address might be used by anycast, but its text alone cannot prove that deployment.

walkthrough.why: Link-local addresses are meaningful on a selected link; the tool needs that scope context.
walkthrough.action: Choose the actual local link for link-local traffic.
walkthrough.whatHappens: Router1's Console may ask for an output interface when you ping Router2's link-local address. Enter Router1's recorded cable port, not Router2's port or an interface on your physical laptop.

walkthrough.why: One remaining working address does not prove that a removed address or dependent application still works.
walkthrough.action: Compare two targets on the same peer.
walkthrough.whatHappens: The lab first verifies Router2 at 2001:db8:13:1::2 and fe80::13:2. Removing only the first assignment should stop replies to that target while the separately configured link-local address remains available on the same link.

walkthrough.why: A before-change-after comparison supports a precise conclusion without blaming an entire protocol.
walkthrough.action: Restore the assignment and repeat identical tests.
walkthrough.whatHappens: Restore Router2's original /64 address, inspect it, and repeat both target tests. Record actual results; do not copy expected success symbols into your evidence table.

beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: An operator may see one successful ping and assume that every service is healthy. This lesson shows why that conclusion is too broad. A device can retain local communication while losing the particular address an application expects. The exact source, destination and interface must accompany the result.

firstPractice.hint: Read the beginning and special complete values, then check the intended use. Do not configure the paper-only unique-local example on a real network.
firstPractice.task: On paper, place fe80::13:2, fd7a:115c:a1e0:13::2, ff02::1, ::1 and :: into categories. Write whether each example is a normal remote peer target, needs link context, refers to the local device or indicates no assigned source address.
firstPractice.expected: The first is link-local; the second is unique-local unicast; the third is a multicast group; ::1 is loopback; :: is unspecified and must not be assigned as a host destination.

beginnerGuide.startingPoint: You do not need a running network to begin. Read the definitions, classify the paper examples, then use the lab if you have an authorized router image. Commands go in the named GNS3 router's Console, not in your computer's terminal. An address category is a clue to the test you need, not proof that the device is reachable.

checkUnderstanding.hint: Name the exact address that replied, the selected link and the address that was removed.
checkUnderstanding.answer: No. The result supports only the local exchange with the retained link-local address. Retest the removed address after restoring it, and use separate tests for any application. Our lab has no Internet connection or application server.
checkUnderstanding.question: Router1 can ping Router2's link-local address after Router2 loses its documentation address. Is all IPv6 service therefore healthy?

everydayComparison.whereItStops: Anycast does not automatically choose the least busy server or physically closest office. Multicast is not a promise of reliable delivery to every member. Reachability and application health still need appropriate evidence.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: Use the three ideas to remember one interface, a group of interfaces and one routing-selected instance. Then add a separate scope question. The memory aid does not tell you the actual address prefix, which interface to use or how a router chooses a path.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: As a memory aid, compare a named person, a subscribed group and one available branch of a service. These are organizational metaphors, not literal forwarding rules; real devices do not understand people, subscriptions or business opening hours.

prerequisites: Complete Day 12's IPv6 notation exercise; be able to expand an address and identify its /64 prefix.
Use a fresh disconnected GNS3 project with two authorized Cisco IOS or IOS XE routers and one routed Ethernet port each.
Have legal permission to run the selected images in GNS3, or use an authorized Cisco Modeling Labs environment or the labeled paper alternative.
Prepare a text notes file using Notepad on Windows, TextEdit on macOS or a plain-text editor on Linux.
content.learnerOutcome: You will classify IPv6 destinations, distinguish unique-local from link-local, interpret multicast membership, and verify why a link-local peer test can still work after another address is removed from that peer.
content.metaDescription: Understand IPv6 unicast, multicast, anycast and scope, then compare link-local and documentation-address reachability in an isolated lab.

terms.meaning: An IPv6 address is a 128-bit identifier written in hexadecimal groups. A prefix identifies leading bits shared by an address block. Day 12 explains how to expand :: and read a /64.

An interface is a device's network connection. A link is the local network over which neighboring interfaces communicate without an intervening IP router. Our lab link is one cable between two routers.
Unicast identifies one interface as the destination. Global, unique-local and link-local are unicast categories; link-local is not a fourth delivery type alongside unicast, multicast and anycast.
Scope limits where an address has meaning. A zone is a particular region of that scope, such as your selected local link. An interface selection tells a tool which local link you mean.

Global unicast supports addressing beyond one link, subject to allocation and routing. Unique-local addresses support private routing within and between cooperating networks, not normal global Internet routing. Neither label is a security policy.

Multicast identifies a group of receiving interfaces. A group address is different from the individual unicast address of each member. Group membership and permitted scope determine the intended audience.

Anycast uses a shared address at multiple service locations. Routing chooses a destination for a packet. A routing metric is a protocol's measure of path preference, not necessarily geographical distance or server load.

IPv6 neighbor discovery exchanges local control messages to learn about nearby interfaces and other link information. It uses multicast for some tasks. Its detailed message exchanges and automatic assignment belong to Day 14.

ICMPv6 carries IPv6 control messages. Ping sends echo requests and waits for echo replies. Receiving replies tests that exchange with that address, not every address, service or security setting on the device.

Console is a virtual device's text window in GNS3. Right-click the named router and choose Console before typing. Cisco prompts ending >, #, (config)# and (config-if)# mark user, privileged, global and interface modes.

A baseline records the original configuration and actual observations. Rollback restores the intended settings after a controlled change. Repeat the original tests rather than assuming that an accepted command fixed the problem.

The special value ::1 is loopback: the local device talking to itself. The special value :: is unspecified: no address has been selected in a permitted protocol situation. Neither is an ordinary remote peer target to assign in this lab.

teachingPrelude.explanation: Start by asking two questions: who is the intended recipient, and where is this address meaningful? Those questions are related but different. A router can show a link-local address, another unicast address and several joined multicast groups on the same interface without having a fault.
teachingPrelude.labBoundary: Only Router1, Router2 and one disconnected Ethernet link are simulated. The lab tests unicast peer addresses and observes multicast membership; Internet routing, anycast services, multicast applications and automatic address assignment are not simulated.

practiceQuestions.answer: No. Link-local is a unicast category with local-link scope.
practiceQuestions.question: Is link-local a fourth alternative to unicast, multicast and anycast?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Recipient behavior and scope are separate questions. Classifying fe80::13:2 as unicast and local-link avoids treating two compatible properties as competing answers.

practiceQuestions.answer: The tool needs to identify the particular local link on which the address has meaning.
practiceQuestions.question: Why can a link-local ping require the sending interface?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A link-local numerical value can appear on separate links. The local interface selection resolves that ambiguity; it is not part of a globally unique address and is not the remote interface name.

practiceQuestions.answer: A production ULA plan needs an appropriately generated Global ID and coordination, not a copied familiar prefix.
practiceQuestions.question: What is wrong with using fd00::1 everywhere because ULA means private?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The locally assigned fd00::/8 form includes a pseudo-random 40-bit Global ID to reduce collision risk. Private routing still needs route and security policy, especially when networks merge.

practiceQuestions.answer: No. Address shape alone does not establish allocation, routing or reachability.
practiceQuestions.question: Does an address beginning with 2001 prove public Internet reachability?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The lesson deliberately uses 2001:db8::/32 documentation space in a disconnected project. Successful peer replies there show only the local test, not a public allocation or Internet connection.

practiceQuestions.answer: No. The shared-address deployment and routing behavior must be known.
practiceQuestions.question: Can the text of an ordinary unicast-format address prove that a service uses anycast?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Anycast does not have a universal distinctive prefix. Under the paper example's stated routing rule one available service is selected; the rule does not claim geographical proximity or automatic health checking.

practiceQuestions.answer: It shows that the interface is a member of that group, not that an application stream arrived.
practiceQuestions.question: What does a joined multicast group entry establish?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The membership display is useful local state. Application delivery, forwarding policy and group scope need their own evidence. This exercise does not deploy a multicast application.

practiceQuestions.answer: Only the documentation assignment was removed; the separate link-local assignment and cable remain.
practiceQuestions.question: During the controlled fault, why may link-local work while the original target fails?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The two tests name different targets on one peer. A retained local reply cannot substitute for restoring and retesting the removed address, and a cached neighbor entry does not reassign that address.

practiceQuestions.answer: Loopback tests the local node rather than the intended remote peer.
practiceQuestions.question: Why is a reply from ::1 insufficient to close a remote connectivity incident?
practiceQuestions.explanation: An evidence record must match the actual requirement. Use the named peer target, source and local interface, then record results; self-tests and paper predictions cannot replace those observations.

realWorldScenario.title: The local check passes, but the intended target is missing
realWorldScenario.takeaway: A useful handover says exactly what worked and what remains untested. Address type tells you which test is meaningful; it does not replace the evidence of the test or establish application health.
realWorldScenario.situation: A trainee validates a maintenance change using a link-local ping and writes that IPv6 is fully restored. The intended monitoring address was removed, however, and the trainee never retested that target. This fictional incident shows an evidence problem rather than proving a particular production outage. The correct response is to compare the assigned addresses and test the actual requirement, not to disable IPv6 or assume that every failure has the same cause.
walkthrough: Write the original requirement as a complete test: source Router1, destination 2001:db8:13:1::2, and the isolated cable interface.
Read Router2's actual assignments and distinguish the missing documentation address from the retained fe80::13:2 link-local address.
Compare both target results using the correct output interface for link-local. Keep the local success and missing-target failure as separate observations.
Restore only the authorized missing address in the disconnected lab and repeat the original target test, then verify the reverse direction.
In a real network, obtain approval and check other causes such as firewalls, source selection, link state or rate limiting. This controlled example is not a universal diagnosis.

title: SLAAC, modified EUI-64, and IPv6 neighbor discovery

lab.goal: Configure a controlled advertisement and a Cisco autoconfig client, record address, route and neighbor evidence, then remove and restore the client setting. The commands are source-reviewed instructions, not a claim that QCS executed these router images.
setup: Create a new GNS3 project named Day14-SLAAC. Import or select your authorized router template according to its platform instructions; do not download unofficial Cisco images.

Use the same supported IOS/IOS XE family on both nodes and record the exact show version output. These commands target classic IOS syntax, not IOS XR, NX-OS or VPCS. Unsupported commands require a compatible authorized platform, not guessed replacements.
Drag two router instances into the workspace, rename them Router1 and Router2, and use Add a link to connect one Ethernet port on each. Record both exact port names, then start both nodes.

If a fresh router asks to enter the initial configuration dialog, answer no, then press Enter for its prompt. Save a clean project snapshot before the experiment. Do not reuse a router with other addresses or services.
Write port mappings in notes: for example Router1 cable = GigabitEthernet0/0/0, Router2 cable = GigabitEthernet0/1. Substitute each independently wherever the sample uses GigabitEthernet0/0.
Keep the project disconnected. GNS3 does not provide Cisco images; legal entitlement must permit their use in GNS3. CML reference-platform ownership alone does not grant that permission.

Without authorized images, use the paper worksheet: draw the two nodes and cable, calculate the IID, and predict the three verification states. Label predictions clearly; do not fabricate command output.

steps.why: Port names differ by image. Mapping the real port prevents configuring an unrelated or nonexistent interface.
steps.title: Record Router1 platform and port
steps.instruction: In the isolated project, right-click Router1 and choose Console before typing. Run these read-only commands. Save output in Day14-baseline.txt using your operating system text editor; check that the cabled port exists. If absent, stop and inspect the template and cable selection.
steps.expectedResult: Your notes identify Router1 software and its exact cable port. An administratively down fresh port will be enabled in the next configuration step.
commandExplanations: Enter privileged mode from >; skip this line if already at #. Do not type the prompt itself.
Record the exact software release and platform without sharing serial numbers or credentials.
Identify the actual Ethernet port selected in GNS3; IPv4 inspection here is for interface names and state.
Record the clean configuration and confirm no unrelated production settings are present.

steps.why: The later removal command can remove all IPv6 addresses on this interface, so a clean disposable client is mandatory.
steps.title: Record Router2 platform and port
steps.instruction: In the isolated project, right-click Router2 and choose Console before typing. Save the same baseline for this node. Use its own port mapping, not Router1 output. The lab requires a clean client interface with no other IPv6 address assignments.
steps.expectedResult: Both nodes have distinct recorded baselines and a verified cable mapping; no shared or production configuration is involved.
commandExplanations: Enter privileged mode from >; skip this line if already at #. Do not type the prompt itself.
Record Router2 exact release; it must support the specified autoconfig and RA-suppression syntax.
Match the cabled port to Router2 actual interface list.
Confirm no other address assignments exist before using the removal experiment.

steps.why: The router must have the intended advertised prefix; merely writing a client address would not demonstrate automatic formation.
steps.title: Configure Router1 advertisement
steps.instruction: In the isolated project, right-click Router1 and choose Console before typing. Use its mapped cable port. Type one line at a time. Stop on any rejected command; do not continue with a partial baseline. This router advertises only the disconnected documentation /64.
steps.expectedResult: Router1 shows the assigned /64 and fe80::14:1. After the peer is enabled, the link should be up/up; RAs are not deliberately suppressed.
commandExplanations: Enter global configuration mode on this fresh disposable lab router.
Enable IPv6 forwarding and router advertisement behavior on this dedicated lab router.
Select the recorded cable port; substitute its exact name for GigabitEthernet0/0.
Set Router1 unique link-local address for a recognizable gateway reference.
Assign the documentation /64, which the default Ethernet RA policy advertises.
Enable the mapped interface administratively; a working peer and cable are still needed.
Return to the # prompt to inspect or test the resulting state.
Inspect port state, link-local address, /64 assignment and RA information; substitute the mapped port.

steps.why: The default keyword makes route learning explicit. Suppressing client advertisements does not suppress incoming Router1 messages.
steps.title: Enable Router2 automatic assignment
steps.instruction: In the isolated project, right-click Router2 and choose Console before typing. Use its mapped cable port. Router2 remains Cisco software but acts as the receiving endpoint. Suppress its own advertisements so Router1 is the only advertiser. Do not manually enter a documentation address on Router2.
steps.expectedResult: Router2 is enabled for autoconfiguration and default-router learning. Allow discovery and DAD to complete before treating an address as ready.
commandExplanations: Enter global configuration mode on this fresh disposable lab router.
Enable IPv6 routing support for observing the learned route on this Cisco instance.
Select the recorded cable port; substitute its exact name for GigabitEthernet0/0.
Stop Router2 from advertising itself on this one-link exercise.
Learn an address from eligible advertised prefixes and install a selected default-router route.
Enable the client cable port so discovery exchanges can take place.
Return to the # prompt to inspect or test the resulting state.

steps.why: The local peer ping does not exercise the default route. Its presence is verified by the routing display, not inferred from the ping.
steps.title: Verify Router2 address and route
steps.instruction: In the isolated project, right-click Router2 and choose Console before typing. Run the displays separately after discovery settles. Record the actual /64 address and its IID, the default route and neighbor information. If no advertisement has arrived yet, allow up to four minutes before troubleshooting rather than declaring immediate failure.
steps.expectedResult: Expect a usable 2001:db8:14:1::/64 address, a default route via Router1 and peer echo replies. Record actual outcomes and any initial loss.
commandExplanations: Inspect the mapped client port and copy its actual learned address, not the fictional worksheet result.
Find ::/0 and record its next hop and cable interface; it should refer to Router1 fe80::14:1.
Request echo replies from Router1 documentation address, not Router2 own address.
Record the peer mapping and current state after the test; a non-REACH state is not automatically a fault.

steps.why: The fictional MAC worksheet teaches the arithmetic; your router output establishes which identifier this particular instance actually uses.
steps.title: Compare the IID with the actual MAC
steps.instruction: In the isolated project, right-click Router2 and choose Console before typing. Read the mapped port MAC and the generated IPv6 address. On paper, apply the modified EUI-64 calculation to that actual MAC and compare the IID. Do not edit the MAC or privacy controls to force a match.
steps.expectedResult: For the documented Cisco autoconfig behavior, the generated IID should match the modified EUI-64 calculation. A mismatch calls for checking the actual source interface and platform documentation.
commandExplanations: Record the actual Ethernet hardware address; dotted MAC notation can be regrouped into six byte pairs.
Compare the generated low 64 bits with your calculation and record platform-specific differences.

steps.why: This controlled local removal avoids the misleading claim that suppressing new RAs immediately expires an already-valid SLAAC address.
steps.title: Remove only the disposable client setting
steps.instruction: In the isolated project, right-click Router2 and choose Console before typing. Confirm the mapped interface and clean baseline again. This command can remove all IPv6 addresses on that interface; use it only on this isolated client with no other assignments. Do not alter Router1 or its advertisement timers.
steps.expectedResult: The automatically formed documentation address is no longer assigned. Do not assume a remaining cached route or neighbor entry means the address still exists.
commandExplanations: Enter global configuration mode on this fresh disposable lab router.
Select the recorded cable port; substitute its exact name for GigabitEthernet0/0.
Remove the client autoconfiguration and its interface addresses on this disposable node only.
Return to the # prompt to inspect or test the resulting state.
Verify the learned documentation address is absent before interpreting a traffic test.
Confirm the autoconfig setting is absent and no unrelated lines were changed.

steps.why: Never interpret residual control-plane entries as proof that the removed address remains usable. This change is client configuration, not a measured upstream outage.
steps.title: Record the changed Router2 test
steps.instruction: In the isolated project, right-click Router2 and choose Console before typing. Repeat the same peer target and the routing display. Record any error message or missing-source condition. If the old address is still assigned, stop and reconcile the command result before drawing a conclusion.
steps.expectedResult: The original learned-address test is no longer a valid successful baseline. Expect failure or inability to select the former source in this clean setup; record the actual result.
commandExplanations: Repeat the baseline destination after the automatic assignment was removed.
Record remaining or removed routes without treating cached information as a local address.
Record current neighbor state; an old mapping does not restore the removed assignment.

steps.why: The recovered state must match the intended network and router, not simply contain any IPv6-looking value.
steps.title: Restore Router2 automatic assignment
steps.instruction: In the isolated project, right-click Router2 and choose Console before typing. Return only the setting removed in this experiment. Keep Router1 configuration and both cable mappings unchanged. Wait for discovery and DAD again; compare with the baseline rather than assuming an accepted command completed recovery.
steps.expectedResult: Router2 again has a usable learned address and the expected route after discovery. Preserve any timing observations rather than inventing a fixed recovery duration.
commandExplanations: Enter global configuration mode on this fresh disposable lab router.
Select the recorded cable port; substitute its exact name for GigabitEthernet0/0.
Restore automatic address formation and selected default-route installation.
Return to the # prompt to inspect or test the resulting state.
Check that a usable documentation /64 address reappears on the mapped interface.
Verify the default route again and record the Router1 link-local next hop.

steps.why: Restoration plus the same successful test demonstrates recovery of this limited exercise. All changes and snapshot operations remain confined to the isolated lab.
steps.title: Retest and save the final comparison
steps.instruction: In the isolated project, right-click Router2 and choose Console before typing. Repeat the original peer test after the address is usable. Save before, changed and restored observations. Then stop both nodes through GNS3; preserve notes and return this disposable project to its clean snapshot only after saving your evidence.
steps.expectedResult: Expect peer replies again. Your three-state worksheet separates address and route evidence from ping evidence, without claiming Internet or application access.
commandExplanations: Request replies from the same Router1 destination used before the fault.
Record the actual peer mapping and state after recovery.

steps.why: A controlled sizing question must not be mistaken for the earlier removal of the client's autoconfig setting.
steps.title: Read the separate prefix-sizing ticket
steps.instruction: After completing and restoring the original router lab, open your plain-text worksheet. This supplementary step is paper-only: do not type its hypothetical RA fields into either router Console. Copy the good and bad PIOs from the supplement, label them synthetic and write the fixed 64-bit IID length. Router1 Gi0/0 and Router2 Gi0/0 retain the original mapped cable; no third node, route or alternate advertiser is added.
steps.expectedResult: Your worksheet isolates one changed field: prefix length /64 versus /80. The prefix bits, A/L flags and lifetimes are identical.

steps.why: SLAAC eligibility, on-link determination and default-router selection are independent checks; a default route does not supply a missing source address.
steps.title: Predict address and next-hop consequences
steps.instruction: Stay in the worksheet, not a device Console. Compute 80+64 and compare it with 128. Record three separate predictions: global SLAAC address formation, on-link prefix information and default-router learning. Then classify 2001:db8:14:1:1::20 against the /80 and /64. Do not run a ping from an invented global address or mark the predicted route as observed output.
steps.expectedResult: The /80 cannot form the 64-bit-IID SLAAC address. Its L flag can still advertise the narrower on-link range, and the RA's nonzero router lifetime can still supply a default router.

steps.why: The exact inverse repairs the prefix-sizing error; a manual address, disabled duplicate-address detection or a changed destination would evade it.
steps.title: Correct the PIO and specify the retest
steps.instruction: In the worksheet, cross out only /80 and restore /64 in the PIO. Keep the other fields and client settings unchanged. Write a verification plan: inspect a newly received /64 RA, allow duplicate-address detection, inspect the learned address and routes, then repeat the original ping to Router1. If you inspect the real baseline, right-click Router2 and choose Console; use the existing verification step, not an invented fault command. No new runtime result is asserted.
steps.expectedResult: The corrected prediction is a usable address after successful duplicate-address detection, intended /64 on-link information and the same Router1 destination. The real lab remains at its already restored baseline.

lab.title: Observe, remove and restore automatic IPv6 assignment
cleanup: Restore Router2 autoconfig default and confirm the final checks before stopping the experiment.
Save the evidence, stop Router1 and Router2, and use the recorded clean snapshot for a complete disposable-project reset if required.
Do not erase real routers, change shared interfaces or export Cisco images. Perform these tests only in the isolated lab, never on production or shared-use networks.

The prefix-sizing ticket changes only worksheet fields. Leave the restored two-router configuration untouched, and label all ticket predictions as synthetic rather than as captures or observed CLI output.
devices: Router1: fresh authorized Cisco IOS 15.x or IOS XE 16/17.x router, one Ethernet port.
Router2: second fresh authorized Cisco router supporting ipv6 address autoconfig default; not VPCS.
lab.topology: Router1 GigabitEthernet0/0 connects directly to Router2 GigabitEthernet0/0. Substitute the actual mapped port names. These are the only two nodes and the only cable; do not attach a Cloud, NAT, bridge, physical adapter or production network.

addressing.purpose: Advertises the documentation prefix and provides the local test destination.
Record the actual generated IID and learned default router; do not hard-code the worksheet IID.

verification: Record both exact software releases and the two cable-port mappings before configuration.
Verify the actual learned /64 address rather than copying the fictional EUI-64 worksheet result.
Record ::/0 next hop independently; the same-link ping does not prove default-route forwarding.
Compare the same target before removal, while the learned assignment is absent, and after restoration.
Keep DAD enabled; do not treat a tentative or duplicate address as ready for normal use.
No router emulator was executed during authoring. These are source-reviewed instructions; learners must record actual runtime observations.

For the synthetic /80 ticket, require 80+64=144, a separate L-flag/default-router explanation, the exact /64 correction and a plan to inspect the new RA plus address/route state before repeating the original peer test.
lab.licensingNote: GNS3 does not provide Cisco images. Use them only when the applicable license or entitlement permits your selected environment. Do not share or redistribute image files. Cisco Modeling Labs is the official alternative; its reference images are not licensed for export into GNS3 merely because you have CML. Without an authorized image, use the labeled paper exercise and do not claim device execution.
troubleshooting: If the expected port is missing, stop and match the GNS3 template and cable to show ip interface brief. If administratively down, recheck the mapped interface and its no shutdown step; if up/down, inspect peer state and cabling before changing addressing.

If no learned address appears, check Router1 prefix, Router2 autoconfig setting, and RA configuration. An unsuitable prefix length or A flag policy can prevent formation. Do not disable DAD, privacy or security controls as a shortcut.

If an address exists but ::/0 is missing, inspect the default keyword and router-lifetime policy separately. A local peer reply does not exercise that route; there is deliberately no off-link destination in this lab.

If a ping misses replies, check the precise destination and actual source/address state. Initial discovery, filtering, rate limits and platform behavior can also affect replies. One lost probe does not diagnose an entire network layer.

If a removal leaves unexpected addresses or a test still succeeds, stop. Recheck the fresh-client prerequisite, selected interface and actual source instead of forcing the expected answer. Restore the baseline only in this isolated project.

A surviving link-local address or learned default router does not refute the /80 SLAAC-sizing fault. Old valid global addresses can conceal it; the paper ticket deliberately starts without one and does not authorize clearing unrelated live addresses.

quiz.question: Which field permits autonomous formation from a Prefix Information option?
quiz.explanation: The A flag concerns autonomous address formation. Prefix length and lifetimes also matter; it does not by itself establish default-router eligibility.

quiz.question: Which message pair advertises and solicits router information?
quiz.explanation: Router Solicitation requests router information and Router Advertisement supplies it. Neighbor Solicitation and Advertisement have different local-neighbor functions.

quiz.question: What is the modified EUI-64 IID for 00:11:22:33:44:55?
quiz.explanation: Insert ff:fe and invert the U/L bit of the first byte, giving 02 from 00. The result is four 16-bit groups, not an entire IPv6 address by itself.

options: Every existing address is instantly deleted
Address and default-router state need separate checks
quiz.question: An address exists but the advertising router lifetime is zero. What follows?
quiz.explanation: Router lifetime governs default-router eligibility. Prefix information and address validity have their own rules; an address screenshot cannot prove a usable default route.

options: An echo exchange with that local target
quiz.question: What does the successful Router2-to-Router1 peer ping establish here?
quiz.explanation: It supports only the local echo exchange. Default-route installation is inspected separately, and this lab has no Internet connection or application server.

options: Stop, inspect the actual interface and source, and reconcile the baseline
quiz.question: What is the safe response to an unexpected result during the removal test?
quiz.explanation: Only the fresh isolated client is authorized for this experiment. Preserve actual evidence, restore the intended settings and retest; never turn a prediction into a claimed observation.

options: Change the PIO to /64 and recheck RA, learned address, route scope and original peer
Leave /80 and change only the last address digit
Treat a default route as proof of a global address
quiz.question: In the synthetic /80 ticket, what fixes the sizing error without changing the test?
quiz.explanation: The intended 64-bit prefix plus the fixed 64-bit IID fits 128 bits. The other choices change another variable or confuse routing evidence with assignment.

quiz.question: Which destination lies inside 2001:db8:14:1::/64 but outside 2001:db8:14:1::/80?
quiz.explanation: The fifth hextet is part of the /80 prefix. Its value 1 differs from the /80's zero, but the first four hextets still match the /64. This is a prefix-length distinction, not compression.

glossary.meaning: An interface is a network connection. A link joins neighbors without an intervening router. A MAC address is an Ethernet interface identifier used for local frame delivery. Our lab has one link and two interfaces.

An IPv6 packet carries source and destination IPv6 addresses. An Ethernet frame wraps a packet for local delivery using MAC addresses. Finding the next neighbor is not the same task as choosing an IP route.
A prefix supplies the leading address bits. An interface identifier, or IID, supplies the remaining interface-specific bits in this /64 exercise. A /64 leaves 64 of the 128 bits for the IID.

A host originates or receives traffic. Its default gateway is a local router used when no more specific route matches. Router2 acts as the address-learning endpoint here; it is Cisco software, not a model of every desktop operating system.

Stateless Address Autoconfiguration, or SLAAC, lets an interface form an address using advertised information. Modified EUI-64 is one way to derive a 64-bit IID from a 48-bit MAC address; it is not synonymous with SLAAC.

ICMPv6 carries control messages for IPv6. Neighbor Discovery, or ND, uses several of these messages to discover routers, learn local neighbors and check reachability. IPv6 does not use IPv4 ARP for these jobs.

Router Solicitation asks routers for information; Router Advertisement supplies it. Neighbor Solicitation asks about a particular neighbor or checks an address; Neighbor Advertisement responds in defined situations. These are different messages, not four names for a ping.

Duplicate Address Detection, or DAD, checks a tentative address before normal use. Tentative means not yet ready for ordinary traffic. A successful check is not proof that no later configuration mistake can create a conflict.

A flag is a yes/no field. The prefix A flag permits autonomous address formation; L concerns whether a prefix is on-link. Lifetimes are timers. Address validity and default-router eligibility have separate timers.

Console is a device text window. In GNS3, right-click the named node and choose Console before typing. Cisco prompts ending >, #, (config)# and (config-if)# indicate user, privileged, global and interface modes.

A baseline records the original settings and observations. Rollback restores the intended settings after a controlled change. A retest repeats the original test and records real results rather than copied example output.

Ping requests an ICMPv6 echo reply. A neighbor cache records local IPv6-to-link-layer information and reachability state. A cached entry is not an address assignment, a default route or proof that an application works.

sections.example: Make an evidence row with four empty cells: address, default route, neighbor and tested destination. Fill only what you observed. For example, a local-link reply cannot fill the default-route cell because the neighbor may be reachable without using that route.
sections.heading: One interface needs several different kinds of evidence
keyPoints: Address formation is not the same operation as discovering a default router.
The lab has no Internet path; even a learned default route is only configuration evidence here.
sections.explanation: Stateless does not mean that a host has no state. The interface still keeps addresses and timers. The useful distinction is that SLAAC does not require a DHCPv6 server to allocate and track each address. Start with the local interface, then ask which prefix was learned, how the IID was formed, whether the address is usable and which router can carry nonlocal traffic. Do not collapse these questions into the phrase IPv6 works.

sections.example: Paper diagnosis: an RA advertises our /64 with A set but router lifetime zero. The host may still form an address, yet must not select that advertisement as a default-router offer. A second worksheet with A clear is different: that prefix is not offered for autonomous address formation. Neither observation alone proves a cable fault.
sections.heading: Read the advertisement before blaming the host
keyPoints: Keep the A flag, prefix length and prefix lifetimes together when checking address creation.
Do not treat a router lifetime as the expiration timer for every address.
sections.explanation: A host can solicit router information, and routers also send advertisements periodically. A usable Prefix Information option with autonomous configuration enabled supplies input to SLAAC. In this Ethernet exercise the prefix is /64. The A and L flags have different jobs: autonomous address formation and on-link determination. The RA source is link-local; its router lifetime governs default-router eligibility, independently of the prefix address lifetimes. The M and O flags describe DHCPv6-related information, not a command to erase all SLAAC addresses.

sections.example: Join 2001:db8:14:1::/64 to that IID to obtain 2001:db8:14:1:211:22ff:fe33:4455. This is a fictional documentation example, not the address to expect from your router. Modern stable-address guidance favors methods that avoid embedding a stable link-layer identifier; temporary addresses may coexist. Do not disable privacy settings to make a real laptop match the worksheet.
sections.heading: Modified EUI-64 is a method, not all of SLAAC
keyPoints: The Cisco autoconfig command in this lab documents EUI-64-based behavior; other operating systems can differ.
Recognizing ff:fe in an address is a clue, not universal proof of its complete configuration history.
sections.explanation: For the worked 48-bit Ethernet MAC example, divide 00:11:22:33:44:55 into 00:11:22 and 33:44:55. Insert ff:fe, then invert the universal/local bit of the first byte: 00 XOR 02 becomes 02. The resulting IID is 0211:22ff:fe33:4455. This is a reversible bit manipulation, not encryption, and does not hide the original hardware identifier. If the first byte were 02, the inversion would produce 00 rather than 04.

sections.example: For a target ending 33:4455, take its low 24 bits, 33:44:55, to construct the example solicited-node group ff02::1:ff33:4455. Multiple IPv6 addresses can map to the same group, so the full target in the NS still matters. A STALE neighbor-cache state means reachability needs confirmation when used; it is not by itself proof of a broken cable.
sections.heading: Neighbor Discovery is more than IPv6 ARP
keyPoints: Do not describe IPv6 neighbor resolution as sending an IPv4 ARP broadcast.
Keep DAD enabled and resolve duplicate configuration rather than bypassing the check.
sections.explanation: RS and RA concern router information. NS and NA support local-neighbor functions, including address resolution and reachability checks; NS is also used during DAD. For ordinary Ethernet address resolution, a sender asks about the target using its solicited-node multicast group, and learns appropriate link-layer information from the response. DAD probes a tentative address before normal use, with an unspecified source in that process. Its purpose and source rules differ from an ordinary peer ping.

sections.example: If Router2 has only a link-local address, check Router1 advertises the intended /64, verify the A flag policy and inspect Router2 autoconfig configuration. If an address appears but no default route does, check the default keyword and router information separately. Do not conclude that all RA traffic is absent just because one address is missing.
sections.heading: Troubleshoot the missing fact, not a familiar-looking address
keyPoints: SLAAC addresses can remain valid for a time after advertisements stop; absence of a new RA is not immediate revocation.
A ping failure can involve filtering or source selection as well as addressing; record the actual failure.
sections.explanation: Follow an ordered checklist: confirm the mapped interface and link state; inspect router advertising configuration; inspect the client assignment and tentative or duplicate state; inspect the learned default route; then compare the exact target and neighbor information. A missing address can reflect an unsuitable prefix or disabled autoconfiguration. A missing route can reflect router-lifetime or client-policy differences. Neither symptom licenses disabling security controls across a real network.

sections.example: Without licensed images, draw both routers and complete a baseline/fault/restored worksheet. Predict which records should change and explain why an old neighbor entry cannot reassign a removed local address. Label the entire worksheet predicted, not executed. A later real lab must still collect command output; the paper alternative does not establish hands-on competence.
sections.heading: Know what this exercise can and cannot demonstrate
keyPoints: No DNS service, DHCPv6 deployment, Internet forwarding or application performance is measured.
This chapter adds IPv6 configuration and assignment diagnosis; it does not alone prove every exam objective.
sections.explanation: The hands-on task uses two Cisco instances on one isolated cable. Router1 advertises, and Router2 explicitly learns an address and default route. This makes the state visible without importing your physical laptop into the lab. The planned fault removes the client automatic-address configuration, not an advertisement timer. It avoids pretending that simply suppressing RAs instantly removes a previously valid address.

sections.example: Correction worksheet: replace the erroneous PIO 2001:db8:14:1::/80 with 2001:db8:14:1::/64, retaining A=1 and L=1. The same 64-bit IID now fits: 64+64=128. The /80 covers addresses whose fifth hextet is zero; 2001:db8:14:1:1::20 is outside it but inside the intended /64. An L=1 /80 would therefore provide narrower on-link information even though its A=1 setting is unusable for this SLAAC client. A default-route entry is not evidence that global address formation succeeded.
sections.heading: Supplement: a valid-looking prefix that cannot form this SLAAC address
keyPoints: Inspect the advertised prefix length, A/L flags and client IID length separately; address spelling alone cannot diagnose this ticket.
Verify a corrected RA, a non-tentative learned global address, the intended on-link scope and the original peer test. Predictions are not observations.
The /64 requirement here is for this Ethernet SLAAC mechanism, not a claim that every IPv6 route or every manually addressed link must use /64.
sections.explanation:
A Prefix Information Option (PIO) is the part of a Router Advertisement (RA) that describes one prefix. Its A flag permits autonomous address formation; its L flag supplies on-link information. On-link means the destination can be reached directly on this link instead of through a router. These are separate decisions. For this Ethernet ticket the interface identifier (IID) is 64 bits, so an autonomous /80 plus that IID would require 144 bits. IPv6 has only 128 bits. RFC 4862 therefore rejects this PIO for SLAAC address formation; it does not repair the prefix by silently shortening it.

This is a synthetic diagnostic ticket, not a router capture or an instruction to force unsupported IOS behavior. Router1 and Router2 are the same two endpoints as the original lab. Router2 starts each ticket with no saved global address, no static route and no other advertiser. Good ticket: Router1 fe80::14:1 sends prefix 2001:db8:14:1::/64, A=1, L=1, valid lifetime 3600 seconds, preferred lifetime 1800 seconds and router lifetime 1800 seconds. Bad ticket: change only the PIO prefix length to /80. Keep its prefix bits, flags, lifetimes, cable and 64-bit IID unchanged. This isolates sizing; changing ::1 to ::2 or deleting autoconfig would test something else.

The bad /80 can still supply on-link information under RFC 4861, and the nonzero RA router lifetime can still identify a default router. Neither fact creates a usable global SLAAC source address. A client may retain a working link-local address while this global assignment fails. On a previously configured client, old addresses and prefix lifetimes could conceal the failure; that is why the ticket specifies a fresh client.

content.metaTitle: CCNA Day 14: SLAAC, EUI-64 and Neighbor Discovery
takeaways: Keep address, default-route and neighbor evidence separate.
SLAAC is not synonymous with MAC-derived modified EUI-64.
RA prefix flags and address lifetimes differ from default-router lifetime.
RS/RA and NS/NA support different Neighbor Discovery jobs.
A same-link ping cannot prove default-route forwarding or application health.
Restore the isolated baseline and record actual results; never claim a paper worksheet or static review is device execution.
objectives: Separate prefix discovery, IID formation, default-router discovery and neighbor resolution.
Calculate a modified EUI-64 IID and explain why modern hosts may use a different method.
Distinguish RS/RA from NS/NA and explain DAD without disabling it.
Configure and verify an advertised /64, an automatically formed address and a learned default route.
Remove automatic assignment on the disposable client, restore it and repeat the same evidence checks.
content.plainAnswer: SLAAC uses an advertised prefix and a locally formed interface identifier to create an IPv6 address. Neighbor Discovery also supplies router information and resolves local neighbors, but those are separate jobs. Modified EUI-64 is one IID method, not a requirement for every modern host. Verify the address, selected gateway and neighbor state separately before testing traffic.

visualStory.title: An address is not a gateway

stages.title: Read the prefix
stages.explanation: Router1 advertises an eligible /64. The prefix A flag concerns address formation; it is not the same as the default-router lifetime.

stages.title: Form and check an address
stages.explanation: The receiving interface combines the prefix with its IID and performs duplicate-address checks. Modified EUI-64 is one IID method, not every modern host method.

stages.title: Verify the router too
stages.explanation: Check the selected default router independently. A usable address, a neighbor entry and a peer ping cannot substitute for route evidence.

comparisons.title: Router1 advertises. Router2 learns.

stages.title: Advertise to Router2

stages.title: Inspect Router2

walkthrough.why: The worksheet separates facts that a single successful ping cannot independently establish.
walkthrough.action: Write three evidence headings before configuring.
walkthrough.whatHappens: Create columns for interface address, default router and neighbor entry. Add time and device-name columns so a later screenshot cannot be mistaken for the other router.

walkthrough.why: The calculation makes the method visible while avoiding a false promise that every host uses MAC-derived addressing.
walkthrough.action: Read a prefix and calculate an example IID.
walkthrough.whatHappens: On paper, combine 2001:db8:14:1::/64 with the worked IID 0211:22ff:fe33:4455. Do not configure that fictional MAC address on a real adapter.

walkthrough.why: An actual baseline gives you something precise to compare with the deliberately changed state.
walkthrough.action: Observe the Cisco client before making a fault.
walkthrough.whatHappens: Router2 should learn the advertised prefix, form its own address and learn a default route when configured with the default keyword. Record the actual IID rather than copying the paper example.

walkthrough.why: Recovery requires both configuration and observed state; entering an accepted command alone is not evidence of success.
walkthrough.action: Restore automatic assignment and compare again.
walkthrough.whatHappens: After the isolated removal test, restore autoconfig default on Router2, wait for the advertised information and DAD, and inspect the address and route before repeating the peer ping.

beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: A device can display an IPv6 address while lacking a usable default router. It can also have a neighbor entry without the address an application expects. Checking these facts individually prevents random configuration changes and makes your explanation useful to another engineer.

firstPractice.hint: Inverting that bit is XOR with hexadecimal 02. For first byte 00 the result is 02; it is not a rule to add two to every possible first byte.
firstPractice.task: On paper, start with MAC 00:11:22:33:44:55. Insert ff:fe between its two three-byte halves and invert the universal/local bit in the first byte. Group the resulting eight bytes into four hexadecimal groups, then attach the /64 prefix.
firstPractice.expected: The IID is 0211:22ff:fe33:4455. The example address is 2001:db8:14:1:211:22ff:fe33:4455; leading zeros within a group may be omitted.

beginnerGuide.startingPoint: Read the definitions first. You can complete the address worksheet without installing anything. For the lab, commands go in the named GNS3 device Console, not your laptop terminal. Check the device name and prompt before every block. The expected results below are predictions for you to verify, not output recorded by QCS.

checkUnderstanding.hint: Separate the prefix A flag and address lifetimes from the RA router lifetime and default-router selection.
checkUnderstanding.answer: No. Address formation and default-router discovery are distinct. Check each independently. A zero router lifetime can exclude an advertising router as a default while its prefix information remains useful. A local address also does not prove Internet access.
checkUnderstanding.question: A host has an address but no default route. Has SLAAC necessarily failed completely?

everydayComparison.whereItStops: Real IPv6 has flags, timers and duplicate checks; a neighborhood story has none of those rules. Use the actual protocol fields and measured device state rather than deriving behavior from the analogy.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: The advertised prefix contributes network bits, the interface forms the IID, and router discovery identifies a possible next hop. Keep these as separate lines in a worksheet. The address and gateway need not share a similar-looking ending.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: As a memory aid, imagine receiving a neighborhood name, choosing your own door label, and separately learning the exit road. This is an organizational metaphor, not a literal postal system or a description of how devices think.

prerequisites: Complete Days 12 and 13 on IPv6 notation, /64 prefixes and address scope.
Use GNS3 with two fresh authorized Cisco IOS 15.x or IOS XE 16/17.x router instances supporting the listed commands.
Confirm image entitlement and command support before configuration; CML or the paper alternative may be used instead.
Prepare notes in Notepad on Windows, TextEdit on macOS or a plain-text editor on Linux.
