content.learnerOutcome: Configure and compare Layer 2 and Layer 3 LACP in separate isolated pairs, identify consistency failures from operational evidence, and verify recovery from a single-member outage in each design.
content.metaDescription: Build separate Layer 2 and routed LACP bundles, verify member consistency and partner state, and test one-link failures without claiming doubled flow speed.

terms.meaning: EtherChannel groups compatible physical links into one logical interface called a port-channel. A member is one physical link in that group; a configured member is not necessarily successfully bundled.

Link Aggregation Control Protocol negotiates compatible aggregation with a peer. Active initiates negotiation; passive responds. Active/active or active/passive can form; passive/passive does not initiate.

A Layer 2 port-channel carries Ethernet VLAN traffic as access or trunk. A Layer 3 port-channel uses no switchport and has an IP address on the logical interface, not separate addresses on its members.
Member attributes must be compatible, including speed, duplex and Layer 2/Layer 3 mode. Layer 2 members must also agree on access VLAN or trunk/native/allowed settings.

A hash selects a member from packet-header fields using a platform's distribution method. Traffic with the same relevant fields commonly stays on one member; one conversation does not automatically use the sum of link speeds.

Bundled means participating in the logical channel. Suspended or standalone states mean the port is not contributing as intended. Read the command's own legend rather than equating every physical up state with a healthy bundle.

A remaining eligible member can preserve logical connectivity after one member fails, subject to configuration such as minimum links. It does not protect against failure of both peer switches or every shared dependency.
Console directly manages a named lab node. The baseline must include member participation, LACP partner evidence and the same traffic test before a controlled member shutdown.

A network interface card (NIC) is a physical Ethernet attachment. A Linux bond groups NICs under one logical interface. The Linux term slave means member here; bonding mode 802.3ad negotiates LACP rather than merely providing an active-backup pair.

An aggregator is the compatible set of links selected to act together. The partner is the LACP system at the other cable ends. Two links being electrically up does not prove they have the same intended partner or participate in one aggregator.

miimon is the Linux interval, in milliseconds, for checking member link state. A minimum-links policy sets how many usable members are needed for the logical interface to report carrier. Neither setting measures end-to-end application health.

A VLAN subinterface is a logical attachment that adds/removes one specified 802.1Q VLAN tag over a parent interface. A hypervisor runs virtual machines; its guest switching and security policies must also agree with the physical uplink profile.

teachingPrelude.explanation: Think of a port-channel as one logical interface backed by several compatible links. First prove those links are actually participating, then test the service it carries. The two lab pairs deliberately separate VLAN carriage from routed addressing.
teachingPrelude.labBoundary: SW1/SW2 form an access VLAN 10 bundle; RSW1/RSW2 form a separate routed /30 bundle. There is no connection between pairs, no host teaming, no multichassis system and no hardware bandwidth measurement. The separate physical host supplement below has its own topology.

realWorldScenario.takeaway: Service through one member is not proof that a multi-member design is healthy. Verification must include the intended member count and consistent negotiated state.
realWorldScenario.situation: A hypothetical uplink passes a basic ping, yet one physical member shows suspended state after a configuration change. The operator is tempted to ignore it because users still have some connectivity. The missing member means the intended redundancy and aggregate capacity are not established.

lab.title: Predict and recover a three-switch VLAN tree
cleanup: Leave SW3 Gi0/0 enabled and verify the restored role table before stopping the lab.
Preserve desired root intent in the isolated lab only; no production timer, guard or mode changes are authorized.
devices: SW1 and SW2: CML 2.10 bundled IOSvL2 nodes, intended primary and secondary root.
SW3: a third fresh IOSvL2 node; record all exact IOS 15.2 image builds with show version.
lab.topology: SW1 Gi0/0--SW2 Gi0/0; SW1 Gi0/1--SW3 Gi0/0; SW2 Gi0/1--SW3 Gi0/1. All six ports are access VLAN 10 with cost 10. Vlan10 SVIs on the switches are the only endpoints.
verification: Match all six stable baseline roles to the actual three cables.
Verify SW1's root ID on SW2 and SW3, and SW2's configured successor priority.
Compare explicit direct cost 10 with indirect cost 20.
During the fault, confirm SW1 remains root while SW3's root port changes.
After restoration, require original roles and the original destination test to recover.
Preserve real logs and note absent messages or unsynchronized clock information.
lab.licensingNote: Use an existing Cisco Modeling Labs 2.10 entitlement and its bundled reference images inside CML only. GNS3 does not provide Cisco images; use images there only when a separate applicable license permits that environment. Do not share or redistribute image files. A CML subscription alone does not authorize exporting its Cisco images to GNS3. Without entitlement, use the explicitly labeled paper exercises; they do not establish hands-on competence.
troubleshooting: If the wrong switch wins, compare full bridge IDs and actual configured priorities rather than hostnames or IP addresses.
If the predicted alternate differs, inspect cable mapping, VLAN membership and per-port costs before considering tie-breakers.
If a port is physically down, fix its actual connectivity; that is different from an up alternate/discarding port.
If traffic does not recover, verify the surviving VLAN path and both endpoint SVIs. Do not disable STP to force forwarding.
If the image lacks the documented mode or syntax, stop and label that branch unsupported; paper predictions are not runtime.

quiz.question: Which switch has no root port for VLAN 10?
quiz.explanation: The root is the reference point, while non-root switches select their best path toward it.

quiz.question: What is the stable baseline role of SW3 Gi0/1?
quiz.explanation: SW3 prefers its direct root path; SW2 wins designated status on their equal-root-cost segment by bridge ID.

quiz.question: What changes after SW3 Gi0/0 is shut?

quiz.question: Which state learns MAC addresses but does not forward user frames?
quiz.explanation: Learning is a state; root is a role. Separating the two avoids misreading operational output.

quiz.explanation: Convergence timing and loss require actual observations, and no runtime measurement is claimed here.

glossary.meaning: Cisco's rapid per-VLAN spanning tree runs a separate loop-free tree for each VLAN using rapid spanning-tree behavior. A physical link can have different roles in different VLANs.
A bridge protocol data unit carries spanning-tree information between switches. Receiving these control messages is compatible with discarding ordinary user frames.
The root bridge is the reference point for one tree, not automatically the default gateway. The lowest bridge ID wins: compare priority including the VLAN system-ID extension, then the MAC address.
A non-root switch chooses one root port offering its best path toward the root. A designated port offers the best information onto its attached segment. These are roles, not physical cable types.

An alternate port offers another path toward the root through a different bridge. A backup port backs up a designated port on the same shared segment. This point-to-point triangle demonstrates alternate, not backup.

Discarding does not learn source MAC addresses or forward ordinary frames. Learning learns source addresses but does not forward ordinary frames. Forwarding does both. IOS may display BLK for discarding.

A numeric preference accumulated along a path to the root; lower is preferred. It is not a hop count or a measured delay. Explicit costs in this lab remove dependence on default speed-to-cost methods.

Convergence establishes consistent roles after a change. A rapid topology change can cause MAC relearning. Exact packet loss and convergence time require measurement, not an assumption from the word rapid.

sections.example: In this fresh lab, root primary on SW1 normally selects base priority 24576; root secondary on SW2 sets 28672, while SW3 remains 32768. These are configuration effects, not a permanent primary/standby protocol. A later switch with a still lower bridge ID can change the election.
sections.heading: A root is elected separately for each VLAN
keyPoints: Verify the actual root ID on every switch after configuration.
The root bridge is not necessarily an IP gateway or the busiest device.
sections.explanation: Rapid PVST+ runs per VLAN, so always name the VLAN when reading root output. Bridge priority is considered before the MAC-address tie-breaker. The displayed priority commonly includes the VLAN system-ID extension: configured 24576 with VLAN 10 appears as 24586. An IP address does not decide the election.

sections.example: Each direct link to SW1 costs 10. SW3's path through SW2 costs 10 plus 10, so SW3 Gi0/0 wins initially. On the SW2-to-SW3 segment both switches advertise cost 10; SW2's lower bridge ID makes its Gi0/1 designated. No MAC-address guess is needed because their configured priorities differ.
sections.heading: Cost selects a path; later tie-breakers resolve equality
keyPoints: Cost is a preference, not a measured latency or traffic load.
Explicit per-VLAN cost makes this example independent of short versus long default cost tables.
sections.explanation: A non-root switch compares received root information and cumulative root path cost. When candidates tie, sender bridge ID, sender port ID and finally local port ID can distinguish them. Do not jump straight to the lowest local interface number. The designated-port comparison also considers advertised root-path information.

sections.example: SW3 Gi0/1 is expected to appear as Altn BLK on common IOS output. Here BLK represents the rapid discarding behavior. It can be physically up and still intentionally not carry user frames. A backup role requires a different shared-segment situation and is not manufactured by adding decorative nodes.
sections.heading: A role answers why; a state answers what happens
keyPoints: Do not confuse an alternate port with an administratively shut interface.
Learning learns source MAC addresses without forwarding user frames.
sections.explanation: Root, designated, alternate and backup describe a port's function in the tree. Discarding, learning and forwarding describe data behavior. A designated port can temporarily be discarding during convergence. In a stable ordinary point-to-point tree, root and designated ports forward and alternate ports discard.

sections.example: After SW3 Gi0/0 is shut, Gi0/1 should become the root port and the SVI peer test should recover through SW2. The author has not run this event, so no millisecond figure or zero-packet-loss claim is attached. A learner records actual observations and any transient loss.
sections.heading: Rapid transition is conditional, not a stopwatch promise
keyPoints: Do not apply PortFast to these inter-switch links to force quick forwarding.
Rapid PVST+ changes convergence behavior, not the need for a loop-free final tree.
sections.explanation: Rapid spanning tree can coordinate safe transitions using proposal/agreement on suitable point-to-point links and can promote an alternate when the root path fails. Legacy neighbors and shared links can change behavior. Keep default timers in this lesson and verify the actual protocol and link type rather than tuning timers to chase a promised number.

sections.example: A hypothetical LINEPROTO message naming Gi0/0 going down supports a link-state event, but does not by itself identify the alternate port or prove forwarding recovery. The actual role table and the repeated SVI ping supply those missing observations. Do not fabricate a log line when the image's buffer is empty.
sections.heading: Use logs as corroboration, not as the whole diagnosis
keyPoints: Read the actual log buffer and note clock accuracy or missing history.
Root-primary/secondary configuration is directly practiced; whole-root-device failover remains a paper prediction.
sections.explanation: Capture show spanning-tree vlan 10 and its detail output before and after the controlled event. Compare root identity, root cost, port role and topology-change information. Read show logging for relevant interface events and preserve the time context; absence of a retained message does not prove absence of a change.

content.metaTitle: CCNA Day 23: Rapid PVST+ Roots, Roles and Recovery
takeaways: Name the VLAN before identifying its root and port roles.
A lower bridge ID wins the root election.
Path cost is cumulative and does not measure delay.
An alternate/discarding link can be healthy and useful.
Verify primary and secondary intent against actual priorities.
Correlate roles, traffic and retained logs through fault and rollback.
objectives: Distinguish root election from root-port selection.
Separate rapid spanning-tree roles from forwarding states.
Configure and verify primary and secondary root priorities.
Predict the alternate port using path cost and bridge-ID comparisons.
Correlate role changes, traffic tests and actual logs during a safe fault.
content.plainAnswer: Rapid PVST+ keeps a separate loop-free tree for each VLAN. The lowest bridge ID becomes root; other switches select root ports using their best path toward it. Designated ports serve segments, while alternate ports can discard user frames yet remain useful recovery paths. Configure root intent explicitly, then verify actual root IDs, costs, roles and states. A blocked alternate is not automatically a broken cable.

visualStory.title: One VLAN, three links, one alternate

stages.title: Baseline tree
stages.explanation: SW1 is root. SW2 and SW3 use their direct cost-10 root links. SW3 Gi0/1 discards on the third physical segment.

stages.title: Direct link fails
stages.explanation: Shut SW3 Gi0/0 only. SW3 Gi0/1 becomes its root port, reaching SW1 through SW2 with cumulative cost 20.

beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: A redundant physical design needs one loop-free forwarding topology. Removing a healthy alternate link to make every port appear forwarding throws away the recovery path you deliberately installed.

firstPractice.task: Use the explicit costs and priorities to mark both SW1 ports, SW2 Gi0/0 and Gi0/1, and SW3 Gi0/0 and Gi0/1. Then erase only the SW1-to-SW3 link and predict SW3's new root port.

checkUnderstanding.hint: How would the port know that its alternate path still exists?
checkUnderstanding.answer: No. A functioning alternate must process spanning-tree information. Discarding describes ordinary forwarding and MAC learning behavior; it does not mean the control protocol is deaf.
checkUnderstanding.question: Does an alternate port discard BPDUs as well as ordinary data?

everydayComparison.whereItStops: Spanning tree exchanges protocol messages and compares numeric information. It does not understand people, emergency signage or the shortest walking distance.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: The selected corridors resemble forwarding ports and the retained alternate resembles a discarding alternate port. A route change can use that previously idle path.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: A building has several exits, but a temporary route plan directs normal movement through selected corridors while retaining a usable alternate.

teachingPrelude.explanation: First choose the root of one VLAN, then work outward to choose each switch's best path and each segment's designated port. Finally ask what each port currently does with data. Keeping election, role and state separate makes a blocked-but-healthy link understandable.
teachingPrelude.labBoundary: Three IOSvL2 switches form one access-VLAN triangle. Their SVIs are the only traffic endpoints. No trunks, hosts, backup shared segment, routing, PortFast or protection features are added. All runtime results remain unmeasured.

practiceQuestions.answer: The lowest bridge ID, with priority considered before MAC address.
practiceQuestions.question: Which bridge wins when priority values differ?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The root election is not based on a switch's IP address, hostname or traffic volume.

practiceQuestions.answer: It can include base priority 24576 plus the VLAN-ID extension 10.
practiceQuestions.question: Why can VLAN 10 priority show 24586?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Compare like-for-like bridge IDs and distinguish the configured base priority from the displayed extended value.

practiceQuestions.answer: Ten through the direct SW1 link.
practiceQuestions.question: What is SW3's baseline root cost in this lab?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The indirect path adds SW3's receiving-port cost ten to SW2's advertised root cost ten.

practiceQuestions.answer: A healthy alternate role discarding ordinary traffic in the stable tree.
practiceQuestions.question: What does Altn BLK imply here?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The port can remain up and process BPDUs; an administrative shutdown is a different condition.

practiceQuestions.answer: No; the resulting priority must be compared with all other bridge IDs.
practiceQuestions.question: Does root secondary guarantee the next root in every network?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Another bridge with a better ID can win, so the macro is not a reservation or a dynamic standby election.

practiceQuestions.answer: Original root/port roles and successful repeated traffic tests.
practiceQuestions.question: What evidence completes rollback?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Merely entering no shutdown does not establish that the desired loop-free forwarding topology recovered.

realWorldScenario.title: The healthy link that looks blocked
realWorldScenario.takeaway: A blocked role is evidence to interpret, not an error to remove. The useful question is whether the actual tree matches the intended loop-free and recoverable design.
realWorldScenario.situation: A hypothetical technician sees a physically up campus link marked Altn BLK and plans to disable spanning tree to make it forward. The topology contains a redundant triangle. The port may be performing exactly the loop-prevention role required by the design.
walkthrough: Name the affected VLAN and trace all three physical segments before changing state.

title: PortFast, BPDU guard, root guard, and loop guard

lab.goal: Establish an ordinary switching baseline, demonstrate a deliberately wrong edge profile, restore a legitimate bridge boundary, and test Root Guard with a reversible priority change. No runtime execution is claimed.
setup: Use an existing CML entitlement and exactly one cable between these fresh nodes. Never connect this experiment to a production or external network.
On each node open Console, enter enable, show version and show running-config. Record build and confirm no automatic errdisable recovery, prior guard/filter configuration or extra links.
Preserve a starting copy. Stop if the image rejects the documented guard syntax; a paper comparison remains useful but cannot establish a successful guard event.
The intentional edge misclassification is a negative test only. No actual endpoint PortFast startup timing or missing-BPDU Loop Guard failure is tested.

After the original guard recovery, use the final Loop Guard extension only on fresh SW2 Gi0/0 with no pre-existing guard/filter/PortFast and global Loop Guard default disabled. Record before/during/after state; normal BPDUs continue throughout. Stop for unsupported syntax or a wrong root/point-to-point role.

Recover the physical port under the corrected policy.
Return to privileged EXEC without saving or reversing the configuration.
Verify no root inconsistency at the original peer priority.
Confirm SW1 remains root and the link forwards.
Require the original peer test to succeed again.

steps.why: This tests Root Guard's specific trigger separately from any-BPDU guarding.
steps.title: Introduce superior root information
steps.instruction: In CML, select SW2, open its Console tab and connect before typing. Proceed only after the corrected Root Guard baseline works. Change the peer priority alone, leaving cabling, VLANs and all guards unchanged.
steps.expectedResult: The peer now advertises superior information toward the protected boundary.
commandExplanations: Enter global configuration mode from privileged EXEC; changes apply as accepted.
Temporarily offer a better bridge ID than SW1's 8192.
Return to privileged EXEC without saving or reversing the configuration.

steps.why: The intended root region is protected even though normal downstream service is temporarily blocked.
steps.title: Read root inconsistency
steps.instruction: In CML, select SW1, open its Console tab and connect before typing. Inspect the protected boundary without disabling Root Guard. An affected SVI may also lose line protocol because this is its sole active physical link.
steps.expectedResult: Expect root-inconsistent blocking and loss of the sole data path.
commandExplanations: Identify VLAN 10's root-inconsistent condition if triggered.
Read the actual protected tree state.
Preserve real root-guard messages if retained.
Retest the original destination during the blocking condition.

steps.why: Rollback corrects the offending information rather than weakening the boundary. Automatic inconsistency recovery differs from the earlier manual error-disable/profile correction.
steps.title: Withdraw the superior root claim; Verify automatic recovery
steps.instruction: Commands 1-4 use the first named console. In CML, select SW2, open its Console tab and connect before typing. Restore the exact original base priority. Do not cycle SW1's port or remove Root Guard to hide the trigger. Then stop typing, switch consoles, and run commands 5-9 on the second node. In CML, select SW1, open its Console tab and connect before typing. Wait for actual stable state and repeat the same checks. Preserve the Root Guard configuration for the legitimate downstream-switch design.
steps.expectedResult: The superior advertisement ceases; Root Guard can recover automatically. Expect normal forwarding and reachability without manually reopening the Root Guard port.
commandExplanations: Enter global configuration mode from privileged EXEC; changes apply as accepted.
Return the peer to its recorded initial priority.
Return to privileged EXEC without saving or reversing the configuration.
Observe convergence back toward the intended SW1 root.
Require the root-inconsistent entry to clear.
Verify SW1 root identity and designated forwarding.
Confirm Root Guard remains and the temporary edge profile is absent.
Repeat the original successful peer test.
Record actual recovery evidence if the buffer contains it.

steps.why: This adds real configuration and verification actions without manufacturing selective BPDU loss. A working ordinary path checks that the correctly placed protection has not disrupted the baseline.
steps.title: Configure and read back Loop Guard on SW2
steps.instruction: In CML, select SW2, open its Console tab and connect before typing; require privileged EXEC (#), using enable if needed. Run the first four read-only checks, then STOP unless the supplement's fresh-baseline prerequisites hold: SW1 root, SW2 Gi0/0 root/forwarding and point-to-point, no prior interface protections, global Loop Guard default disabled, peer replies. Only then run commands 5-12. Keep ordinary BPDUs flowing; do not inject a fault.
steps.expectedResult: With the prerequisites met, expect the explicit Loop Guard line, continued root/forwarding operation, no inconsistency and replies from 192.0.2.1. These are acceptance criteria, not executed results.
commandExplanations: Record SW2's exact interface baseline; stop for any prior guard, PortFast or filtering configuration.
Confirm the global Loop Guard default is disabled; do not change a pre-existing global policy to fit this exercise.
Require VLAN 10 root/forwarding, point-to-point operation and received BPDUs on this eligible port.
Record the pre-change test from SW2 to SW1's original SVI, 192.0.2.1.
Enter global configuration only after all four baseline checks satisfy the stated prerequisites.
Select SW2's sole root-facing cable port; do not configure SW1's Root Guard port.
Enable the interface-scoped Loop Guard setting; preserve an unsupported-command error and stop if rejected.
Return to privileged EXEC without saving to startup configuration.
Require the added interface setting to appear in the active configuration.
Read actual guard detail and confirm the root/forwarding role remains; a command's acceptance alone is not enough.
Require no unexpected inconsistent port while normal BPDUs continue; preserve discrepancies and stop.
Repeat the identical SW2-to-SW1 peer test and record actual results, not the predicted result.

steps.why: Exact rollback proves the added setting can be removed without disturbing the earlier legitimate Root Guard boundary. An unsuccessful rollback remains a recorded failure, not an assumed pass.
steps.title: Remove only the added Loop Guard and retest
steps.instruction: In CML, select SW2, open its Console tab and connect before typing; require privileged EXEC (#), using enable if needed. Remove only the setting introduced by the previous step, even if verification failed after it was accepted. Do not change SW1, priorities, VLANs or cabling. Compare the final interface configuration with the recorded clean baseline. Save evidence, not an unverified startup configuration.
steps.expectedResult: Expect the original SW2 interface settings and global default, ordinary root/forwarding state, no inconsistency and the original peer replies. SW1 Root Guard remains configured. No missing-BPDU recovery or timing is measured.
commandExplanations: Enter global configuration on the same SW2 instance used for the added setting.
Select the same SW2 root-facing interface; keep SW1's downstream Root Guard unchanged.
Remove this exercise's explicit Loop Guard setting, restoring the recorded initially unguarded SW2 port.
Return to privileged EXEC without writing a startup configuration.
Confirm the added line is absent and other interface settings match the captured baseline.
Verify that the original disabled global Loop Guard default remains unchanged.
Confirm SW2 still has the ordinary VLAN 10 root/forwarding path toward SW1.
Require no unexplained inconsistency after rollback; preserve and investigate any remaining condition.
Repeat the same destination and compare with both pre-change and configured-state observations.

lab.title: Two guard triggers on one isolated cable
cleanup: Leave SW2 at priority 32768, SW1 at 8192 and both physical ports enabled with the legitimate Root Guard boundary restored.
Do not enable automatic errdisable recovery or BPDU filtering merely to suppress evidence; retain private observations and stop the isolated lab.

Remove only the extension's SW2 Gi0/0 Loop Guard setting and confirm its original clean interface/global baseline. Keep SW1 Root Guard and both original bridge priorities; retain any unsupported/error evidence.
devices: SW1: fresh CML 2.10 bundled IOSvL2 switch; initial bridge priority 8192.
SW2: fresh IOSvL2 peer; initial priority 32768. Record each exact IOS 15.2 build.
lab.topology: SW1 Gi0/0--SW2 Gi0/0 only, access VLAN 10. SW1 Vlan10 192.0.2.1/24 and SW2 Vlan10 192.0.2.2/24 are the only traffic endpoints. Every other physical port stays unconnected.
verification: Require a successful ordinary-link baseline before the first guard test.
Separate actual error-disabled state from root-inconsistent state.
Confirm BPDU Guard triggers without lowering SW2's original priority.
Establish a new successful Root Guard baseline before the priority fault.
Restore SW2 priority 32768 and verify inconsistency clears with the guard retained.
Label Loop Guard failure and filtering comparisons as conceptual, not performed tests.
For the extension, require SW2's explicit Loop Guard readback, unchanged root/forwarding and peer replies, then exact removal and the same retest. A missing-BPDU trigger remains unperformed.
lab.licensingNote: Use an existing Cisco Modeling Labs 2.10 entitlement and its bundled reference images inside CML only. GNS3 does not provide Cisco images; use images there only when a separate applicable license permits that environment. Do not share or redistribute image files. A CML subscription alone does not authorize exporting its Cisco images to GNS3. Without entitlement, use the explicitly labeled paper exercises; they do not establish hands-on competence.
troubleshooting: If BPDU Guard does not trigger, inspect explicit interface configuration and verify the peer actually participates in VLAN 10 STP; do not fabricate a BPDU receipt.
If the port repeatedly error-disables, correct the peer role before another recovery attempt.
If Root Guard blocks at baseline, compare actual bridge IDs and confirm the intended root is on the permitted side.
If the peer remains unreachable after priorities recover, inspect SVI line protocol, VLAN membership and actual port state.
If a command is unsupported, preserve the error and stop that branch; do not substitute filtering or a loop as a workaround.

glossary.meaning: A port's intended neighbor behavior: a single nonbridging endpoint, an allowed downstream bridge, or a path toward the legitimate root. The correct protection follows that role, not just the label access or trunk.
A bridge protocol data unit carries spanning-tree information. A superior BPDU offers a better tree path or root claim; not every BPDU is superior.
An edge-port feature that permits rapid entry into forwarding for an intended end station. It does not disable spanning tree and is not permission to connect arbitrary bridges.

A protection that error-disables a guarded port when it receives a BPDU. Explicit interface-level enable does not depend on PortFast; the global PortFast default applies through edge-operational behavior.
A protection on a designated boundary where a better root path must not appear. Superior information causes root-inconsistent blocking; ordinary inferior BPDUs can still be allowed.

A protection for eligible root or alternate paths that rely on received BPDUs. Loss of expected BPDUs can cause loop-inconsistent blocking instead of an unsafe transition toward designated forwarding.

Error-disabled is a disabled-port condition requiring cause correction and recovery. Root-inconsistent and loop-inconsistent are spanning-tree protection conditions that can recover automatically when their specific trigger clears.

Suppression of spanning-tree messages, not a synonym for BPDU Guard. Interface-level filtering can effectively remove STP protection on that port. Global PortFast-default filtering has different receipt and fallback behavior.

sections.example: The lab intentionally assigns an edge profile to a known switch-facing port only while its peer is administratively silent, then enables that peer to demonstrate a violation. This is a controlled negative test on one isolated cable, not a recommended production configuration.
sections.heading: PortFast changes entry behavior, not the neighbor contract
keyPoints: An access port can connect to a switch, so access mode alone does not justify PortFast.
The lab's SVIs are test endpoints; no imaginary workstation is added to the diagram.
sections.explanation: Use PortFast for an intended end station that is not bridging another network. It accelerates entry into forwarding but does not remove STP. A received BPDU can remove edge-operational status. A laptop running a bridge or a downstream switch does not fit the simple endpoint assumption merely because it connects to an access VLAN.

sections.example: SW2 initially has priority 32768, worse than SW1's 8192. Its BPDU still triggers the explicit guard on SW1. The demonstration therefore separates 'a BPDU arrived' from 'a superior root appeared'. Read actual error-disabled status and retained logging rather than expecting a particular hard-coded message.
sections.heading: BPDU Guard reacts to participation, not superiority
keyPoints: Do not lower the peer's priority merely to make BPDU Guard work.
An empty log buffer does not prove a guard was never triggered.
sections.explanation: An interface explicitly configured with spanning-tree bpduguard enable can error-disable on a received BPDU whether or not PortFast is active. Global default configuration has a PortFast-operational scope. Correct the cause before manual shutdown/no shutdown recovery; automatic timers are policy choices, not a cure for a still-connected offender.

sections.example: After removing the lab's false edge profile, SW1 Gi0/0 receives Root Guard. The baseline is SW1 priority 8192 and SW2 priority 32768. Changing only SW2 to 4096 tests the superior-information trigger; restoring 32768 removes it without disabling the guard.
sections.heading: Root Guard allows a bridge but constrains root placement
keyPoints: Do not place Root Guard on an uplink that is supposed to lead toward the legitimate root.
A downstream priority rollback restores the intended policy instead of bypassing protection.
sections.explanation: Root Guard belongs on a designated boundary that must not become a path to the root. Inferior downstream information can coexist with normal forwarding. Superior information can place the affected VLAN in root-inconsistent state. When superior advertisements cease, normal STP recovery is automatic; this is different from manual error-disable recovery.

sections.example: Missing-BPDU prediction remains paper-only: on eligible root-facing SW2 Gi0/0, predict loop-inconsistent blocking if expected BPDUs vanish while the link remains up, and recovery when they return. The final two lab steps now configure, read back and remove Loop Guard with ordinary BPDUs still flowing. They do not induce missing BPDUs, create a loop, or claim a runtime result.
sections.heading: Loop Guard watches for information that disappears
keyPoints: Root Guard and Loop Guard must not be combined on the same interface.
Loop Guard does not replace every physical unidirectional-link detection function.
sections.explanation: An eligible root or alternate port relies on received BPDUs. If they stop while conditions might otherwise allow an unsafe transition, Loop Guard can hold the VLAN in loop-inconsistent state. Normal BPDU reception permits automatic recovery. A physical shutdown is not the same failure as losing BPDUs on an otherwise active path.

sections.example: Do not apply interface BPDU filtering to quiet the demonstration. That would remove the evidence BPDU Guard is meant to detect. This lesson explains filtering because v1.1 names it; it does not claim filtering is a separately named v2.0 objective or ask the learner to deploy it.
sections.heading: Filtering and guarding have different consequences
keyPoints: BPDU Guard is not a filter that silently drops control packets.
The lab never disables STP or creates a second physical path to provoke a storm.
sections.explanation: BPDU filtering suppresses messages instead of reacting with a protective guard state. Explicit interface filtering can effectively disable STP on that link and make a loop possible. The global PortFast-default form behaves differently: initial messages and received BPDUs can cause fallback from filtering/edge operation. Scope and platform matter.

sections.example: In this authored exercise SW2 is a legitimate switch and the edge profile is intentionally wrong. The approved correction is to shut SW1's port, remove that temporary edge/guard profile, apply the correct Root Guard boundary, and re-enable it. In a real host-only port incident, remove the unexpected bridge instead and keep the edge guard.
sections.heading: Recovery restores the intended boundary
keyPoints: Retest the exact original peer destination after each correction.
No independent runtime, measured recovery delay or production suitability is asserted.
sections.explanation: Read running interface configuration, current role/state, inconsistent-port output and actual logs together. Identify whether an edge profile was applied to a legitimate bridge or an unexpected bridge appeared at a true edge. The authorized response differs. Do not automatically remove a guard whenever it blocks traffic.

sections.example: Expected comparison, not a captured transcript: before, SW2 Gi0/0 is root/forwarding toward SW1 with no explicit guard; during, the running interface includes spanning-tree guard loop and ordinary forwarding continues; after no spanning-tree guard loop, the added line is absent and the original role and peer test remain. No loop-inconsistent state is expected without a missing-BPDU fault. If one appears unexpectedly, preserve the evidence and stop; do not use BPDU filtering, a unidirectional cable, STP disablement or an added link to manufacture or hide the event.
sections.heading: Loop Guard supplement: configure, inspect and restore safely
keyPoints: The added practical scope is configuration, readback, same-peer verification and exact rollback, not a Loop Guard trigger test.
SW1's Root Guard and SW2's Loop Guard are on different interfaces with different roles.
A disabled global default is required so removing the explicit setting returns this fresh lab to its recorded baseline.
No runtime, convergence time or missing-BPDU recovery result has been measured by the author.
sections.explanation:
Complete both original guard exercises and their recovery first. Keep exactly the existing SW1 Gi0/0--SW2 Gi0/0 cable, access VLAN 10 and the two SVI addresses. SW1 stays root at base priority 8192 with Root Guard on its designated Gi0/0. SW2 stays at 32768, with its Gi0/0 as the root-facing port. The original diagram illustrates the two earlier trigger tests; this extension uses those same endpoints and does not add a hidden node.

Use the same entitled CML 2.10 IOSvL2 instances and record their exact IOS 15.2 builds. Require SW2's port to show root, forwarding and point-to-point operation, with ordinary received BPDUs. Require no PortFast, BPDU Guard, BPDU filter, Root Guard or existing Loop Guard on that interface, and no global Loop Guard default. Stop on any discrepancy instead of stripping unknown protection. The configuration below enables Loop Guard only on SW2's eligible port; it never combines Root Guard and Loop Guard on one interface.

Read the active interface configuration and spanning-tree detail before and after the change, then repeat the same peer ping. An accepted command alone is insufficient: record its presence, the port's actual role/state and the successful unchanged traffic test. Remove just the added interface setting and repeat those checks. If the image rejects syntax or cannot expose the required state, stop and label this branch unperformed. CML's generic STP support is not an author's runtime test of every guard feature.

content.metaTitle: CCNA Day 24: Choose the Right Spanning-Tree Guard
takeaways: Choose protection from the intended neighbor and root boundary.
PortFast is edge behavior, not a replacement for spanning tree.
BPDU Guard and Root Guard react to different information.
Error-disabled and inconsistent states have different recovery paths.
Loop Guard depends on expected BPDU reception.
BPDU filtering is not BPDU Guard and can create loop risk.
objectives: Explain the distinct trigger and recovery of each guard.
Configure explicit interface-level PortFast and BPDU Guard in a bounded violation experiment.
Configure Root Guard on a designated downstream boundary and test superior information.
Interpret Loop Guard and BPDU filtering without claiming an unperformed failure simulation.
Restore the legitimate neighbor policy and verify both state and traffic.
content.plainAnswer: Choose spanning-tree protection from expected neighbor behavior. PortFast suits a nonbridging endpoint; BPDU Guard reacts to a received BPDU. Root Guard permits a downstream bridge but rejects a superior root path. Loop Guard protects a path that unexpectedly stops receiving needed BPDUs. Their triggers and recovery differ. BPDU filtering suppresses protocol messages and can create loops; it is not a safer spelling of BPDU Guard.

visualStory.title: The same cable, two different guard tests

stages.title: Ordinary baseline
stages.explanation: The single access-VLAN cable joins two legitimate switches. SW1 priority 8192 beats SW2 priority 32768.

stages.title: Wrong edge profile
stages.explanation: Temporarily classify SW1 Gi0/0 as an edge with explicit BPDU Guard. SW2's ordinary BPDU should error-disable the port.

stages.title: Correct bridge boundary

visualStory.takeaway: Any BPDU triggers BPDU Guard. Superior root information triggers Root Guard. The correct choice depends on the intended neighbor.

walkthrough.why: The presence of a BPDU has different meaning at different boundaries.
walkthrough.action: Classify the intended neighbor.
walkthrough.whatHappens: A nonbridging endpoint should not send BPDUs; an authorized downstream switch should.

walkthrough.why: One generic blocked-port diagnosis hides the cause and the correct recovery.
walkthrough.action: Match the actual trigger.

beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: An overbroad guard can shut a legitimate uplink; removing a working guard can allow an unauthorized topology change. Diagnose the violated assumption before changing the protection.

firstPractice.hint: Ask whether the problem is any BPDU, a better BPDU or a missing BPDU.
firstPractice.task: For a single workstation, an authorized downstream switch that must never lead to the root, and a root-facing link that must keep receiving BPDUs, choose PortFast/BPDU Guard, Root Guard or Loop Guard. Explain why the other guards are not substitutes.
firstPractice.expected: The workstation uses edge treatment with BPDU Guard; the downstream boundary uses Root Guard; the eligible root-facing path can use Loop Guard.

beginnerGuide.startingPoint: Write the intended neighbor role before writing a command. A workstation without bridging, an authorized downstream switch and an uplink toward the root have different expectations.

checkUnderstanding.hint: Consider whether root and loop protection expect the same port role.
checkUnderstanding.answer: No. Root Guard and Loop Guard are mutually exclusive on the same interface and protect different assumptions. BPDU Guard on an ordinary switch uplink can disable the expected connection as soon as a BPDU arrives.
checkUnderstanding.question: Does enabling every protection on one uplink provide maximum safety?

everydayComparison.whereItStops: Switches evaluate protocol information rather than human identities. These guards are not user authentication, encryption or a complete security perimeter.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: A port's intended role determines which messages are normal. BPDU Guard rejects bridge participation, while Root Guard allows participation within a root-placement boundary.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: Different doors can admit staff, accept deliveries or serve as emergency exits. The rule depends on the doorway's purpose, not merely its physical size.

prerequisites: Understand root, designated and alternate roles from Day 23.
Use two fresh IOSvL2 nodes under an existing CML 2.10 entitlement.
Know that PortFast is intended for nonbridging endpoints, not ordinary switch uplinks.
content.learnerOutcome: Select the correct protection for a stated port role, distinguish error-disabled from inconsistent state, and safely test and recover BPDU Guard and Root Guard in a single-link isolated pair.
content.metaDescription: Match PortFast, BPDU Guard, Root Guard and Loop Guard to their boundaries, test two safe protection events, and distinguish BPDU filtering from guarding.

teachingPrelude.explanation: Ask three different questions: should this port receive any BPDUs, may it lead toward a better root, and must it continue receiving BPDUs to remain safe? The answer determines the guard. These protections are not interchangeable switches to turn on everywhere.
teachingPrelude.labBoundary: SW1 and SW2 have one cable only. A deliberately misclassified edge profile demonstrates BPDU Guard, then the same link returns to a legitimate downstream-bridge profile for Root Guard. No host is simulated, no loop is created and no missing-BPDU failure is executed.

practiceQuestions.answer: No; it changes edge forwarding behavior.
practiceQuestions.question: Does PortFast disable STP?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A port can lose operational edge status on BPDU receipt, and the intended endpoint role still matters.

practiceQuestions.answer: No; a received BPDU is sufficient.
practiceQuestions.question: Must a BPDU be superior to trigger explicit BPDU Guard?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The lab intentionally keeps the peer's worse priority during the first test to separate this trigger from Root Guard.

practiceQuestions.answer: The superior information must cease, followed by normal STP recovery.
practiceQuestions.question: What clears root-inconsistent state?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Restoring the peer's legitimate priority removes the trigger while leaving Root Guard in place.

practiceQuestions.answer: Loss of expected BPDUs on an eligible non-designated path.
practiceQuestions.question: What failure does Loop Guard address?
practiceQuestions.explanation: It prevents an unsafe transition based merely on missing information, and is not equivalent to physical-link shutdown.

practiceQuestions.answer: No; they are mutually exclusive protections for different roles.
practiceQuestions.question: Can Root Guard and Loop Guard protect the same interface together?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Choose according to whether the boundary must remain designated or must continue hearing a valid upstream path.

practiceQuestions.answer: Filtering suppresses messages and can remove the information STP needs to prevent loops.
practiceQuestions.question: Why not replace BPDU Guard with filtering?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Global-default and explicit interface filtering also behave differently, so neither is a generic guard substitute.

practiceQuestions.answer: SW2 Gi0/0, after SW1 is restored as root; it must be an ordinary root/forwarding point-to-point port receiving BPDUs, with the documented clean interface and disabled global default.
practiceQuestions.question: Which exact port receives the Loop Guard extension, and what must be true before configuration?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The role differs from SW1's designated Root Guard boundary. A prior protection or global default invalidates this fresh-lab rollback assumption, so stop rather than removing unknown policy.

practiceQuestions.answer: Configuration practice records the explicit setting, role/state and unchanged peer test, then removal and retest. A failure test would need actual missing-BPDU and loop-inconsistent evidence, which this lab does not create.
practiceQuestions.question: What evidence distinguishes successful Loop Guard configuration practice from a measured Loop Guard failure test?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The supplement preserves normal BPDU exchange. Its paper prediction explains the trigger but cannot be relabeled as a measured event. Unsupported syntax or a failed retest must remain in the record.

realWorldScenario.title: A small switch appears behind a desk
realWorldScenario.takeaway: A guard event is a clue about a broken design assumption. Restore that assumption; do not make the warning disappear by weakening the boundary.
realWorldScenario.situation: A hypothetical desk port is error-disabled after someone adds a switch. The support request asks only to reopen the port. The port was intentionally a guarded endpoint boundary, so reopening it without investigating the new neighbor would ignore the reason for the protection.
walkthrough: Read the exact interface status and retained message rather than assuming a cable fault.
Verify the intended endpoint-only policy and physically or administratively identify the new bridge.
Remove the unauthorized bridge according to local policy before recovering the port.
Retain the edge protection and perform the authorized manual recovery.
Repeat the workstation's original connectivity test and verify the port does not immediately retrigger.

title: Troubleshooting a switched campus path

lab.goal: Build five named nodes, capture a working flow, introduce one router-facing VLAN error, and restore the original path. All observations below are expected conditions for the learner to measure, not executed author evidence.
setup: Create exactly five fresh entitled CML nodes and the five stated cables, isolated from all external connectors.
On every node open Console, enter enable, show version and show running-config. Record builds and verify there are no existing routes, guards, channel groups or endpoint addresses that conflict.
Keep one learner-owned baseline/fault/restored capture each; captures can contain sensitive data, so use only this synthetic isolated traffic and do not publish raw files.
If IOSvL2 or capture support is unavailable, use the clearly labeled paper inference exercise. It does not establish packet delivery or measured recovery.

steps.why: The chosen source and return path stay constant across the later comparison.
steps.title: Establish controlled-source probes
steps.instruction: In CML, select H1, open its Console tab and connect before typing. For ping prompts enter protocol ip, target 198.51.100.10, count 5, size 100, timeout 2, extended commands y, source 192.0.2.10; accept defaults for remaining options, including no sweep. For traceroute enter protocol ip, target 198.51.100.10, source 192.0.2.10, numeric y, timeout 1, probes 1, minimum TTL 1, maximum TTL 4, port 33434 and no IP options. Read prompts individually; do not paste answers blindly.
steps.expectedResult: Require gateway and remote success before continuing; record actual routed-hop responses.
commandExplanations: First test the declared local gateway.
Run the interactive extended ping using the stated source and parameters.
Run the interactive bounded trace using the stated prompts.

steps.why: CML link capture observes this access cable in both directions; it is not unsupported IOSvL2 SPAN.
steps.title: Capture the working access-side flow
steps.instruction: In CML, select H1, open its Console tab and connect before typing. Keep H1's Console connected. In Workbench right-click H1 Gi0/0--SW1 Gi0/0, choose Packet Capture, Settings, Max Packets 100 and Max Time 20, leave BPF empty, Save, Start. Return to H1 Console and run the ping below. Stop if needed, select actual request/reply rows, inspect Ethernet and IP fields, then Download before starting another capture.
steps.expectedResult: Look for matching request/reply IP endpoints and compare Ethernet addresses with the recorded H1/R1 interfaces.
commandExplanations: Generate a small baseline ICMP exchange from H1's sole interface.

steps.why: A VLAN classification error need not produce a cable-down event.
steps.title: Move only the router-facing access VLAN
steps.instruction: In CML, select SW2, open its Console tab and connect before typing. Proceed only after the baseline works. Gi0/0 is outside Po1; do not touch the bundle members or R1's addresses. This is the sole deliberate fault.
steps.expectedResult: Expect the physical link and LACP bundle to stay up while the intended gateway path fails.
commandExplanations: Enter global configuration mode from privileged EXEC; changes apply as accepted.
Select only the access cable to R1.
Temporarily classify R1's untagged traffic into the wrong VLAN.
Return to privileged EXEC without saving or reversing the configuration.
Observe the actual VLAN 20 assignment.
Confirm both VLANs exist and Gi0/0 is misplaced.
Verify the separate Po1 bundle can remain healthy.
Check the still-valid logical root path for VLAN 10.
Note actual messages, including an absence of physical-link change.

steps.why: The capture's local request does not prove delivery across SW2, and stale ARP is not live reachability.
steps.title: Correlate the failed probe and capture
steps.instruction: In CML, select H1, open its Console tab and connect before typing. Download the baseline first. Start a new 100-packet/20-second capture on the same access cable, then use the probes below. Download this fault capture. Compare actual rows: cached ARP can yield unanswered echo requests; expired ARP can yield unanswered gateway requests. No single transcript is guaranteed.
steps.expectedResult: Expect failed gateway and remote tests with evidence consistent with the broken VLAN boundary.
commandExplanations: Test whether even the local gateway is reachable.
Repeat the exact extended-ping parameters from the baseline step.
Repeat the bounded trace parameters, without treating timeout as a unique diagnosis.
Read actual gateway resolution state, including any still-cached entry.

steps.why: A narrow correction preserves the evidence supporting the root cause.
steps.title: Restore the one proven mismatch
steps.instruction: In CML, select SW2, open its Console tab and connect before typing. Return the router-facing access port to VLAN 10. Leave the functioning channel, root priority and router addresses unchanged.
steps.expectedResult: The intended VLAN path is restored without unrelated configuration changes.
commandExplanations: Enter global configuration mode from privileged EXEC; changes apply as accepted.
Select the same port altered by the fault.
Restore the recorded working broadcast-domain assignment.
Return to privileged EXEC without saving or reversing the configuration.
Verify the restored access VLAN.
Confirm VLAN 10 still traverses the trunk.
Verify both members remain bundled.
Confirm the original root and logical forwarding roles.
Inspect relearning after the following fresh probes.

steps.why: Rollback is complete only when the original full test works, not just when a configuration line changes.
steps.title: Repeat the complete original test
steps.instruction: In CML, select H1, open its Console tab and connect before typing. Download the fault capture, start a fresh bounded capture at the same link, and repeat the exact baseline extended-ping and trace parameters. Download the restored capture before stopping the lab. Finally revisit SW2 Console to reread its VLAN 10 MAC table after this traffic.
steps.expectedResult: Expect gateway/remote recovery with matching capture evidence; record any actual exceptions.
commandExplanations: Require the local gateway test to recover.
Repeat the same selected source, destination, count, size and timeout.
Compare actual routed-hop responses using the same bounded settings.
Confirm the current gateway mapping against the recorded R1 MAC.

lab.title: Correlate a campus path before repairing one VLAN
cleanup: Restore SW2 Gi0/0 to VLAN 10 and verify the original path before stopping the lab.
Download each required capture before replacing it or stopping its link; keep it private and remove any unwanted learner-owned capture using normal local policy.
Leave no production, external connector or social state involved; the exercise is an isolated author candidate.
devices: SW1 and SW2: CML 2.10 bundled IOSvL2, IOS 15.2 family; record exact builds.
R1, H1 and H2: bundled IOSv, IOS 15.x family; H1/H2 each use one interface as a test endpoint.
lab.topology: H1 Gi0/0--SW1 Gi0/0; SW1 Gi0/1--SW2 Gi0/1 and SW1 Gi0/2--SW2 Gi0/2 form LACP Po1 trunk VLAN 10; SW2 Gi0/0--R1 Gi0/0; R1 Gi0/1--H2 Gi0/0. No other links.
verification: Require baseline gateway and remote success before creating the VLAN fault.
Verify actual MAC addresses, VLAN IDs and port names instead of using invented transcript values.
Require both Po1 members and correct LACP neighbors throughout the intended experiment.
Check actual VLAN 10 root identity and SW2's logical root port.
Interpret R1's routed interfaces separately from SW2's Layer 2 access port.
Preserve baseline/fault/restored captures with observation point and probe parameters.
Repeat all source-controlled tests after restoring Gi0/0 to VLAN 10.
lab.licensingNote: Use an existing Cisco Modeling Labs 2.10 entitlement and its bundled reference images inside CML only. GNS3 does not provide Cisco images; use images there only when a separate applicable license permits that environment. Do not share or redistribute image files. A CML subscription alone does not authorize exporting its Cisco images to GNS3. Without entitlement, use the explicitly labeled paper exercises; they do not establish hands-on competence.
troubleshooting: If baseline fails, stop before introducing a fault; inspect endpoint masks/default routes and R1 connected interfaces first.
If only one bundle member participates, resolve that actual mismatch before proceeding; a partial bundle is not the required baseline.
If a capture is empty, verify the running link, capture timing and limits before diagnosing packet loss.
If no ARP appears, inspect cached ARP; fresh ICMP may use the cached gateway MAC without a new broadcast.
If a traceroute prints stars, correlate with gateway ping, source/return routes and ICMP behavior rather than declaring the last responding router faulty.
If virtual features are unsupported, record the exact limitation and use paper interpretation without claiming a practical pass.

glossary.meaning: A sequence of observations connecting a named source, local VLAN, forwarding path, gateway and destination. A conclusion should explain all observations, including facts that remain healthy during a failure.
A Layer 2 switchport carries frames within an access VLAN or trunk. A routed Layer 3 port owns an IP attachment. Here SW2 Gi0/0 is Layer 2 while the connected R1 Gi0/0 is a routed interface.
Address Resolution Protocol maps a local IPv4 next hop to its MAC address. A switch MAC table maps learned source MAC addresses to VLANs and ports. The two tables answer different questions.
Link Aggregation Control Protocol negotiates physical members of one logical interface. Both physical members must participate; spanning tree treats the channel as one logical link.
A ping with controlled parameters such as a selected local source, count and size. A successful test needs an echo request and its reply path; it does not prove every application works.
Traceroute probes with increasing Time To Live values to expose responding routed hops. Layer 2 switches do not consume IP TTL merely while switching, so they do not appear as ordinary routed hops.
A capture records traffic visible on one selected link during a bounded interval. Missing packets can reflect the wrong point, timing or filter, not just a forwarding failure.
The baseline records a working test with its exact source and destination. Rollback restores the changed setting, then repeats those same checks rather than replacing them with an easier test.

sections.example: H1 192.0.2.10 sends traffic for H2 198.51.100.10 through gateway 192.0.2.1. R1 has a directly connected interface on each /24. H2's default route points back to 198.51.100.1, so reply traffic has an explicit return path.
sections.heading: Start with a flow and an exact physical map
keyPoints: The lab's source-side capture should be interpreted against actual H1 and R1 MAC addresses.
Both endpoint default routes are part of the baseline, not an optional afterthought.
sections.explanation: Name both endpoint addresses, masks, gateways and interface MAC addresses. On the source-side LAN the remote packet is addressed in Ethernet to the gateway's MAC, not to the remote endpoint's MAC. Across the routed boundary, Ethernet headers change while the original IP source and destination remain, absent translation.

sections.example: The deliberate fault moves SW2 Gi0/0, which is not a bundle member, into VLAN 20. Both Gi0/1 and Gi0/2 can remain correctly bundled in Po1, and Po1 can continue carrying VLAN 10. Rebuilding the healthy channel would not repair the wrong access boundary.
sections.heading: Separate wire health from VLAN and channel health
keyPoints: Check both ends of each actual link and read the command's flag legend.
A single successful flow can hide a missing bundle member, so verify both members explicitly.
sections.explanation: show interfaces reports physical state and counters, while show interfaces switchport and show vlan brief explain access classification. show interfaces trunk exposes VLAN carriage, and show etherchannel summary with show lacp neighbor proves participating members. A configured channel is not necessarily a complete operational bundle.

sections.example: SW1 is the intended VLAN 10 root. SW2 should use Po1 toward that root, with its router-facing Gi0/0 designated in the working baseline. A stale gateway MAC in VLAN 10 can persist after a fault, so correlate it with current interface membership and fresh packet observations rather than treating a cached row as a live test.
sections.heading: Use MAC and spanning-tree evidence in the same VLAN
keyPoints: Record MAC addresses from actual interfaces instead of inventing them.
Do not disable STP or clear every table just to make evidence easier to read.
sections.explanation: MAC entries include a VLAN and interface, so a matching address in the wrong VLAN is not proof of the intended path. Dynamic entries may remain until aging or may be relearned after changes. Check the actual root ID and port roles for VLAN 10; the LACP bundle is one logical STP link.

sections.example: The baseline uses source 192.0.2.10 and destination 198.51.100.10. R1 should be the transit hop, followed by the destination if expected ICMP behavior is allowed. The two Layer 2 switches are not separate IP hops. Retest these same parameters after repair rather than pinging only a local interface.
sections.heading: Control the source and understand traceroute limits
keyPoints: A source address cannot be borrowed from another node to create a meaningful endpoint test.
A working ICMP probe does not establish TCP, DNS or application health.
sections.explanation: Extended ping lets the learner choose an address actually owned by the source device and keep count, size and timeout stable. Cisco IOS traceroute commonly uses UDP probes and ICMP responses with increasing TTL. Asterisks mean no response within the interval; they do not uniquely identify a dead router.

sections.example: A baseline can contain an echo request from 192.0.2.10 to 198.51.100.10 and the matching reply. During the fault, the capture may show unanswered requests with a cached gateway MAC or unanswered ARP if resolution is needed. Those are conditional predictions, not a fabricated packet transcript.
sections.heading: A capture must have a stated observation point
keyPoints: Capture timing and cached ARP change what is visible.
Seeing a request leave H1 proves only that observation point, not arrival at H2.
sections.explanation: Use CML's running-link capture on H1 Gi0/0--SW1 Gi0/0. Bound it by 100 packets or 20 seconds, preserve it before starting another capture, and inspect actual Ethernet/IP/ICMP fields. IOSvL2 does not support SPAN, so do not invent a monitor-session result. The access-side observation does not include trunk tags.

sections.example: Restore SW2 Gi0/0 from VLAN 20 to VLAN 10. Confirm membership, MAC learning, Po1 participation and root roles, then repeat the source-controlled probes and a fresh bounded capture. State exactly what was restored and leave unsupported features or unperformed runtime explicitly unverified.
sections.heading: Repair only the contradiction and retain honest evidence
keyPoints: The supplied lesson is an authored procedure; no author runtime or performance result is claimed.
This integrates selected switching objectives rather than claiming all campus troubleshooting cases.
sections.explanation: Compare the current state to the recorded design, change one proven mismatch and repeat all affected checks. Read actual logs, but a VLAN reassignment need not produce a physical link-down message. A quiet buffer does not establish an unchanged data path. Keep the channel, root and router settings stable during the controlled fault.

content.metaTitle: CCNA Day 25: Troubleshoot a Complete Campus Path
takeaways: Start with a named flow and a complete physical map.
A healthy channel does not prove every access VLAN is correct.
Correlate MAC and STP evidence within the same VLAN.
Treat source-controlled probes and captures as bounded evidence.
Router interfaces and switchports can meet on one cable with different roles.
Repair the proven mismatch and repeat the original end-to-end test.
objectives: Document every physical link and both IP endpoints.
Correlate access, trunk, MAC, LACP and STP state on the same VLAN.
Distinguish a switchport from the routed port on the other end of its cable.
Use extended ping, traceroute and actual capture fields without overclaiming their meaning.
Repair one deliberate VLAN mismatch and repeat the full baseline.
content.plainAnswer: Troubleshoot a named flow by correlating evidence at each boundary. Confirm physical and logical interface state, access VLAN, trunk carriage, MAC learning, LACP participation and the VLAN's spanning tree before blaming routing. Use a controlled-source ping and traceroute, then a capture at a stated link. A healthy trunk does not prove the router-facing access port belongs to the correct VLAN. Restore one proven mismatch and repeat the original test.

visualStory.title: Trace the whole path, then fix one boundary

stages.title: Working complete flow
stages.explanation: H1 reaches H2 through VLAN 10, the two-member Po1 trunk and R1. H2 returns through 198.51.100.1.

stages.title: Wrong access VLAN
stages.explanation: Only SW2 Gi0/0 moves to VLAN 20. Po1 remains healthy, but the intended source VLAN no longer reaches its gateway.

stages.title: Repair and retest
stages.explanation: Restore SW2 Gi0/0 to VLAN 10. Repeat the same source-controlled probes and access-link capture to verify the complete path.

visualStory.altText: H1 connects through SW1, two Po1 member cables, SW2 and router R1 to H2. The tested fault is SW2 Gi0/0's VLAN assignment, not the trunk bundle.
visualStory.boundary: All five nodes and five cables are shown. H1 and H2 are IOSv endpoint models. Both member edges show the bundle, not a claim that each single flow uses both.
visualStory.takeaway: The trunk bundle can remain healthy while SW2's router-facing access port breaks the VLAN 10 path.

walkthrough.why: A known working baseline identifies what the deliberate fault actually changes.
walkthrough.action: Establish working service and local forwarding facts.
walkthrough.whatHappens: The endpoint reaches its gateway and remote peer while both LACP members and VLAN 10's tree are healthy.

beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Without a fixed source and destination, a different successful ping can accidentally test another VLAN or return path. A consistent test makes before-and-after evidence comparable.

firstPractice.hint: IP addresses do not override a switch's VLAN classification.
firstPractice.task: On paper, assume both LACP members are bundled and VLAN 10 is allowed on Po1, but SW2 Gi0/0 reports access VLAN 20. Explain why H1 cannot reach R1's 192.0.2.1 address despite both devices using a /24 mask.
firstPractice.expected: The address plan expects one VLAN 10 segment, but the access-port assignment places R1 in a different Layer 2 domain.

beginnerGuide.startingPoint: Write the test as 192.0.2.10 to 198.51.100.10, then trace its local next hop 192.0.2.1. Label each cable before reading any command output.

checkUnderstanding.hint: Ask which devices decrement the probe's IP TTL.
checkUnderstanding.answer: No. These two switches forward at Layer 2 in this design. R1 is the transit router; a missing switch name in traceroute does not mean the frame bypassed that switch.
checkUnderstanding.question: Should a normal IP traceroute list SW1 and SW2 as routed hops?

everydayComparison.whereItStops: Packets can take asymmetric paths and control messages can be filtered. The analogy does not make one observation proof of the entire route.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: The source address, gateway, switching path and remote endpoint provide checkpoints. A verified healthy checkpoint narrows the remaining possibilities.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: To find a misdelivered parcel, check the sender, local collection point, transfer route and final address instead of replacing every vehicle on the route.

Traceroute probes with increasing Time To Live values to expose responding routed hops. Layer 2 switches do not consume IP TTL merely while switching, so they do not appear as ordinary routed hops.
A capture records traffic visible on one selected link during a bounded interval. Missing packets can reflect the wrong point, timing or filter, not just a forwarding failure.
The baseline records a working test with its exact source and destination. Rollback restores the changed setting, then repeats those same checks rather than replacing them with an easier test.

teachingPrelude.explanation: A packet crosses several boundaries, and each tool exposes only part of that journey. The exercise keeps the bundle healthy while moving one access port into the wrong VLAN. That lets you learn why a green uplink and a failed remote ping are not contradictory.
teachingPrelude.labBoundary: H1--SW1==SW2--R1--H2 is complete. The double link is a two-member Layer 2 trunk bundle, not two routed hops. H1 and H2 are single-interface IOSv test endpoints. No DNS, firewall, NAT, Internet, wireless or hidden server is present.

practiceQuestions.answer: Yes; the router-facing access port can be in the wrong VLAN.

practiceQuestions.explanation: Po1 participation verifies only the aggregated link, not every edge classification in the path.

practiceQuestions.answer: The local next-hop gateway R1, after ARP resolves it.

practiceQuestions.explanation: The IP destination remains H2, but the source LAN's Ethernet delivery is to the gateway.

practiceQuestions.answer: It can remain after the path changes.

practiceQuestions.answer: They switch frames without decrementing IP TTL in this design.

realWorldScenario.title: The gateway cable is up, but the VLAN is wrong
realWorldScenario.takeaway: Healthy components can surround a failed boundary. A narrow diagnosis explains both the successful control-plane checks and the failed end-to-end service.

The endpoint loses remote connectivity, while the uplink bundle and router interfaces still look physically healthy. An engineer proposes rebuilding EtherChannel before checking where the router's untagged frames are classified.

title: RF, bands, channels, interference, and coverage

lab.goal: Use a complete declared network context to compare channel plans and calculate a one-variable SNR degradation. This is an offline reasoning lab, not a wireless emulator, captured output or a claim of hands-on RF validation.
setup: Label the worksheet SYNTHETIC INPUTS - NOT MEASURED. Do not start CML, GNS3, a radio transmitter or a paid service for this activity.
Use the declared 2.4 GHz 20 MHz example: AP-A channel 1 and AP-B channel 6, with C1 associated to AP-A. This is a teaching plan, not authorization to use a channel in an unchecked regulatory domain.
Prepare three columns: baseline, changed-input case and restored case. Record signal, noise, computed SNR and what remains unmeasured.

For a real-hardware follow-on, obtain owner authorization and record exact AP model/firmware, client adapter/driver, country setting, band/width, location and local service endpoint first. That separate measurement is not completed by this paper lab.

steps.why: A complete context avoids drawing a wireless path with an unexplained destination or an invented controller.
steps.title: Declare the full paper scope
steps.instruction: Draw all five declared entities and the three wired links plus C1's association to AP-A. Name AP-B as a neighboring radio. Label every value as a paper assumption and state that no command console exists in this exercise.
steps.expectedResult: The model has one named client-to-server path and an explicit neighboring radio.

steps.why: A reasoning exercise can use constructed inputs without pretending they came from hardware or a capture.
steps.title: Record the baseline inputs
steps.instruction: Record AP-A channel 1, AP-B channel 6, both 20 MHz. For the C1 receiver, assign synthetic signal -60 dBm and noise -90 dBm. Leave retry rate, ping result and throughput unmeasured; do not fill them with plausible numbers.
steps.expectedResult: The only numeric performance-related inputs are two explicitly invented power levels.

steps.why: This establishes a repeatable calculation before changing one variable.
steps.title: Calculate the baseline margin
steps.instruction: Calculate -60 - (-90) and write the result with dB units. Check the sign by asking whether the signal is stronger than the noise. Do not call the result a data rate.
steps.expectedResult: The arithmetic result is 30 dB SNR, not 30 dBm or 30 Mbps.

steps.why: This comparison does not invent a causal conversion from a channel number to an exact noise reading.
steps.title: Compare channel alternatives separately
steps.instruction: Keep the power-input calculation unchanged. In a separate channel-plan note, compare AP-B on channel 6, then 1, then 3 while AP-A stays on 1. Classify separated channels, co-channel sharing and partial overlap. Restore AP-B to 6 on paper.
steps.expectedResult: Channel 6 is separated in this stated plan; 1 shares the channel; 3 overlaps it.

steps.why: A one-variable change exposes the margin relationship without causing real interference.
steps.title: Introduce one synthetic degradation
steps.instruction: In the changed-input column, keep signal at -60 dBm and change only the receiver noise floor from -90 to -70 dBm. Do not change channels, locations, antennas, IP addresses or widths. This is the safe paper fault.
steps.expectedResult: The new noise is stronger because -70 dBm is less negative than -90 dBm.

steps.why: A correct calculation does not authorize a fabricated runtime result.
steps.title: Retest the calculation and its limits
steps.instruction: Recalculate SNR and compare it with the baseline. Write one supported conclusion and two unmeasured outcomes. For example, distinguish a calculated reduction from any claim about exact packet loss or application throughput.
steps.expectedResult: The new SNR is 10 dB, a 20 dB reduction; exact service outcomes remain unmeasured.

steps.why: Separating hypotheses prevents combining several uncontrolled changes into one claimed diagnosis.
steps.title: Test a different coverage hypothesis
steps.instruction: On a separate scratch line, keep noise at -90 dBm but change signal to -75 dBm. Calculate that case, then discard the scratch change. Explain why weaker signal and stronger noise are different hypotheses even though both can lower SNR.
steps.expectedResult: This separate example gives 15 dB SNR; it is not evidence that a particular wall or distance caused it.

steps.why: Rollback is exact restoration of the stated assumptions, not a claim that a real radio recovered.
steps.title: Restore the exact baseline
steps.instruction: Return the changed-input column to signal -60 dBm and noise -90 dBm, with AP-A channel 1 and AP-B channel 6 at 20 MHz. Recalculate and compare every field with the first column.
steps.expectedResult: The restored calculation is again 30 dB and the recorded channel plan matches the original.

steps.why: Movement may affect signal or service, but the result must be recorded rather than assumed.
steps.title: Define an honest physical follow-on
steps.instruction: Write a measurement plan for an already authorized AP/client pair: record a stationary baseline, move only the client to a safe marked point, then return. Keep the same BSSID and test when possible; if association changes, note that confound. Mark absent noise fields unavailable.
steps.expectedResult: The plan identifies equipment, location, time and controlled variables before any real observation.

steps.why: A learner should finish with useful reasoning and an honest path to future measurement, not false operational confidence.
steps.title: Close the evidence boundary
steps.instruction: Summarize the completed work as channel classification and SNR arithmetic. List physical coverage, noise-source identity, retry counts, packet delivery and throughput as unmeasured. Do not issue a site-survey or practical-runtime pass.
steps.expectedResult: The conclusion accurately states what the paper exercise established and what it did not.

Keep the channel-plan comparison separate from the noise-floor calculation.
Identify channel 1/1 sharing and channel 1/3 overlap without assigning an invented throughput.

If an actual client exposes signal percent but not noise, do not invent an RSSI conversion or a noise floor to complete the table.
