glossary.meaning: Radio frequency is electromagnetic energy used to carry wireless signals. A band is a frequency range, such as the Wi-Fi ranges called 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz and 6 GHz; GHz means billions of cycles per second.

A channel selects an operating part of a band. Channel width, measured in MHz, describes how much spectrum the transmission uses. Nearby channel numbers need not mean separate, nonoverlapping spectrum.

The service set identifier is the wireless network name. The basic service set identifier identifies a particular radio service, commonly by a MAC address. A shared SSID does not identify one physical AP or one channel.

dBm expresses absolute power relative to one milliwatt. A received level of -60 dBm is stronger than -75 dBm. A signal-strength indicator or percentage may be vendor-specific; bars are not calibrated universal measurements.

The noise floor is the background power level at the receiver. Signal-to-noise ratio is the signal margin over that floor: when both levels are in dBm, subtract noise from signal to obtain SNR in dB, not dBm.

Wi-Fi devices that can hear one another on the same channel share airtime. This is often called co-channel interference, but coordinated contention is different from arbitrary overlapping-channel corruption.

Partially overlapping transmissions can interfere without useful coordination. Other radio sources can also consume or disrupt spectrum; a Wi-Fi network-name scan does not identify every non-Wi-Fi interferer.

Attenuation reduces signal power as it travels. Walls and materials affect loss; reflections create multiple arrival paths. Their effects depend on location, frequency, antennas and radio capabilities, not just distance.

Coverage means the intended client can sustain the required service at a location. Capacity means the network can support its actual traffic load. A strong signal can coexist with insufficient shared airtime.
An antenna shapes where energy is sent and received; gain is not free creation of power. Increasing AP transmit power alone may not improve the weaker client's return transmission.

Dynamic Frequency Selection is used on applicable channels to avoid protected radar operation. Country rules and approved hardware determine permitted channels, widths and power; a channel plan is not universally legal.

sections.example: A 2.4-only sensor cannot join a 6 GHz radio merely because both advertise the same network name. A country may permit only part of a band, so do not copy a complete channel list or power limit from a deployment in another region. Here 6 GHz is conceptual context, not a configured lab service.
sections.heading: Band choice includes clients, spectrum and location
keyPoints: GHz names a frequency range, not a guaranteed data rate.
Actual range depends on power limits, antennas, materials and receiver behavior as well as frequency.
sections.explanation: The 2.4 GHz band often reaches farther under comparable conditions but offers limited channel reuse and shares spectrum with many other devices. The 5 GHz band offers more planning choices, with some channels subject to DFS. The 6 GHz band adds spectrum where permitted and requires compatible AP and client radios. Wi-Fi 6 does not automatically mean 6 GHz; 6E and compatible later products add that capability.

sections.example: Paper comparison: AP-A on channel 1 and AP-B on 6 is a separated pair in the stated plan. Moving AP-B to 1 creates co-channel sharing; moving it to 3 creates partial overlap. Neither edit yields a numeric throughput prediction. Do not apply this channel-number rule unchanged to other bands or bonded widths.
sections.heading: Channel width consumes spectrum, not just a larger number
keyPoints: A channel number must be interpreted together with its band and width.
Do not widen channels merely because a speed test is disappointing.
sections.explanation: A wider channel can offer higher possible rates in suitable conditions, but consumes more spectrum and reduces independent reuse choices. For this beginner 2.4 GHz example, use 20 MHz and the common 1/6/11 plan where permitted. Channel centers are closer together than the occupied width, so several different channel numbers overlap.

sections.example: Two APs using channel 1 do not automatically destroy every packet. Their load, visibility and client placement matter. A nearby channel-3 transmission can overlap channel 1, while an intermittent non-Wi-Fi source might not appear in a list of SSIDs at all. A spectrum-capable observation is needed to identify that kind of source.
sections.heading: Separate contention from other interference
keyPoints: Do not equate a count of visible SSIDs with measured airtime utilization.
Never generate jamming or disturb another network to demonstrate interference.
sections.explanation: Nearby decodable Wi-Fi transmissions on the same channel usually contend for the shared medium; more airtime demand can reduce each client's opportunity to send. Partially overlapping channels can produce interference without equivalent coordination. Non-Wi-Fi sources can also affect the band, and their activity may be intermittent.

sections.example: Constructed example, not measured output: baseline signal -60 dBm and noise -90 dBm produce 30 dB SNR. Keeping signal unchanged and raising noise to -70 dBm produces 10 dB. The margin fell by 20 dB; this does not mean throughput fell by 20 Mbps or that the client moved 20 meters.
sections.heading: Calculate margin with consistent units
keyPoints: SNR is signal minus noise when both powers use dBm.
No universal signal or SNR threshold guarantees every application.
sections.explanation: Use dBm for an absolute signal or noise power level and dB for their ratio expressed as a difference. Less-negative received power is stronger. RSSI implementations and percentage bars vary, so use a documented unit and matching receiver/time context. Do not combine a client signal reading with an unrelated AP noise reading.

sections.example: A client near a doorway can have different conditions after it moves behind a wall. Do not assign a universal loss to every wall or assume one exact cell radius. The paper model deliberately contains no wall-loss or distance equation, so it cannot certify a floor plan or prove a hardware placement.
sections.heading: Coverage is a two-way and environment-dependent result
keyPoints: Antenna gain redistributes energy; it is not unlimited power.
Test with representative client hardware and the actual application needs.
sections.explanation: A client and AP must hear one another sufficiently for the intended service. Walls attenuate, surfaces reflect and antenna orientation affects reception. Higher AP power may improve what the client hears without fixing what the AP hears from the client. Additional APs can help coverage or capacity only when placement and channel reuse are planned.

sections.example: An authorized real-hardware follow-on can record a stationary baseline, move the same client to one safe marked location, and return to the original position while leaving radio settings unchanged. Record actual values each time. It is observational practice, not permission to reconfigure neighbors, claim a site survey from one sample or infer noise from bars.
sections.heading: Observe service before choosing a remedy
keyPoints: Virtual packet forwarding and software wireless simulation are not measurements of a physical room.
WLAN security configuration and controller architecture are reserved for later lessons.
sections.explanation: Collect band, channel width, BSSID, received signal, available noise/SNR, retries and channel utilization with time and location. Compare local application or gateway behavior with the wired side so an upstream fault is not mislabeled as RF. Mark unavailable fields unmeasured, especially if a client exposes only percentage signal.

content.metaTitle: CCNA Day 26: Wi-Fi Signal, Channels and Interference
takeaways: Strong signal alone does not prove a healthy radio service.
Read band, channel and width together.
Co-channel sharing differs from partial overlap and non-Wi-Fi interference.
Use dBm for absolute power and dB for SNR.
Coverage and capacity are separate, two-way service questions.
Treat paper and virtual exercises as models, not physical site measurements.
Verify compatibility and local regulatory settings before any real RF change.
objectives: Compare 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz without claiming universal range or availability.
Explain channel width and the common 2.4 GHz 1/6/11 plan.
Compute SNR and distinguish dB from dBm.
Separate interference, coverage and capacity hypotheses.
Complete a labeled paper baseline, one-variable degradation, retest and rollback.
Specify the observations needed before making a real RF change.
content.plainAnswer: Wi-Fi quality depends on useful signal, background noise, shared airtime and both ends of the radio link. Channel number, width and regulatory domain matter together. A strong -60 dBm signal has 30 dB SNR over -90 dBm noise, but only 10 dB over -70 dBm noise. The same signal bars can therefore hide a much worse radio environment. A paper calculation explains the relationship; only real observations establish site performance.

visualStory.title: Same signal, smaller signal-to-noise margin

stages.title: Calculate the baseline
stages.explanation: Synthetic signal -60 dBm minus noise -90 dBm gives 30 dB SNR. These are worksheet inputs, not radio measurements.

stages.title: Change noise only
stages.explanation: The signal stays -60 dBm. Raising the synthetic noise floor to -70 dBm leaves only 10 dB of calculated margin.

stages.title: Restore and compare
stages.explanation: Restore the noise input to -90 dBm and recalculate 30 dB. No exact throughput or packet-loss outcome follows from these values alone.

visualStory.altText: Two calculations compare identical -60 dBm signal with -90 and -70 dBm noise. The resulting SNR values are 30 and 10 dB. Every value is synthetic.
visualStory.boundary: This is a calculation comparison, not a topology, spectrum trace or measured site survey. Arrows connect inputs to arithmetic results; no packet path is implied.
visualStory.takeaway: Keeping signal at -60 dBm while noise rises from -90 to -70 dBm reduces calculated SNR from 30 to 10 dB.

beginnerGuide.startingPoint: Write -60 dBm for useful signal and -90 dBm for background noise. Subtract carefully: -60 minus -90 equals positive 30 dB. Do not subtract the magnitudes in the wrong order.

checkUnderstanding.hint: Compare occupied spectrum, not merely whether the channel numbers differ.
checkUnderstanding.answer: No. At the ordinary widths discussed here, those channels overlap. Different numbers are not sufficient separation. A compatible nonoverlapping plan and an actual site assessment are needed.
checkUnderstanding.question: Does choosing channel 3 avoid an AP using channel 1 in the 2.4 GHz band?

everydayComparison.networkMeaning: The unchanged voice represents the same received signal, while the raised background represents a higher noise floor and reduced signal margin.

realWorldScenario.title: Full signal bars during a slow meeting
realWorldScenario.takeaway: The useful diagnosis explains when and where service degrades. Maximum power and maximum width are changes with tradeoffs, not universal repairs.
realWorldScenario.situation: A hypothetical meeting room reports strong Wi-Fi signal but poor service when many participants arrive. The first proposal is to set every AP to maximum power and the widest channel. Strong received signal alone does not show whether airtime, interference, the client return path or a wired service is the limitation.
walkthrough: Record the affected client, BSSID, band, channel and width at the time of the complaint.
Check local signal quality and any available utilization/retry evidence rather than relying on bars.

title: Access points, controllers, CAPWAP, and roaming

lab.goal: Construct central and local switching models, predict one wrong-VLAN failure, restore the intended mapping and explain which operational checks a real rack would require. All results below are predictions, not measured wireless behavior.
setup: Use paper or a diagram editor; create two copies labeled CENTRAL and LOCAL, and mark all observations predicted.
Optional physical observation requires an authorized AireOS 8.10.190.0 WLC 3504, compatible AP1832i, PoE switch and owned client; use vendor-supported software and regulatory settings.
A physical instructor must prepare isolated VLANs, AP join, WLAN security and the static controller LAG before observation. This chapter does not supply a from-factory wireless build.

steps.why: The final recipient matters: reaching a controller is not the same as delivering a client's payload.
steps.title: Establish the central baseline

steps.why: This prevents an apparently healthy management path from being mistaken for proof of user-data delivery.
steps.title: Separate the control exchange

steps.why: Local switching changes the wired exit dependency without removing the controller's management role.
steps.title: Create the local-switching baseline
steps.instruction: On LOCAL, map the WLAN to VLAN 20 and AP1's trunk to native VLAN 10 with VLANs 10 and 20 allowed. Trace Client1, AP1, SW1 and Server1, retaining the separate AP-controller control annotation.

steps.why: One changed variable allows an explanation tied to VLAN membership rather than a vague claim that Wi-Fi is down.
steps.title: Inject one worksheet VLAN fault

steps.why: A paper retest checks reasoning and documentation; it cannot substitute for an actual client exchange.
steps.title: Restore and retrace both directions

steps.why: Aggregation configuration belongs to the exact controller family and release rather than to the generic word WLC.
steps.title: Audit the controller bundle
steps.instruction: Inspect the AireOS WLC1 ports 1/2 to SW1 Gi1/0/23-24 annotation. Write static mode on, consistent trunk policy and platform-specific reboot planning. Beside it, note that supported 9800 LACP is a different platform case.
steps.expectedResult: The bundle design does not incorrectly require AireOS to negotiate LACP, nor prohibit LACP universally.

steps.why: Clear limits make the exercise reusable without converting drawings into invented test results.
steps.title: Close with a practical evidence plan
steps.instruction: List the physical checks an instructor would collect: AP join and mode, WLAN switching policy, switch VLAN settings, client association and addresses, and same-server reachability. Add a second AP only on a separate future roaming plan.
steps.expectedResult: The report labels RF, PoE, roaming latency and LAG member failure as unmeasured, with a specific path to later observation.

glossary.meaning: An access point (AP) provides an 802.11 radio connection. A wireless LAN controller (WLC) manages participating APs and policies; it is not automatically the client's IP gateway.

A service set identifier (SSID) is a wireless network name. A wireless LAN (WLAN) configuration combines that name with security and forwarding policy. Identical names do not guarantee identical policies.
Control traffic coordinates operation, such as AP configuration. Data traffic carries client payloads. The two can take different paths in the same wireless design.
Control And Provisioning of Wireless Access Points (CAPWAP) carries AP-controller messages. A tunnel encapsulates one packet inside another; the outer addresses identify tunnel endpoints.

A virtual LAN (VLAN) is a Layer 2 broadcast domain. An access port normally carries one untagged VLAN; an 802.1Q trunk can carry several identified VLANs, with a defined native VLAN for untagged traffic.
A link aggregation group (LAG) combines compatible links into one logical connection. Link Aggregation Control Protocol (LACP) negotiates membership where supported; LAG is not a synonym for LACP.
FlexConnect is an AP deployment mode. A locally switched WLAN exits through the AP's wired connection, while centrally switched traffic is tunneled to the controller.
Roaming changes a client's AP association. A basic service set identifier (BSSID) identifies a particular radio service, unlike the shared SSID name.
Power over Ethernet (PoE) supplies power over suitable Ethernet cabling. Radio frequency (RF) describes wireless electromagnetic signals; virtual cables do not emulate coverage or interference.
Datagram Transport Layer Security protects datagram exchanges. CAPWAP discovery is initially unprotected; established control protection is distinct from optional data-channel protection.

sections.example: In our drawing, WLC1 manages AP1 through VLAN 10. Client1 belongs to VLAN 20 and Server1 is another VLAN 20 endpoint. WLC1's management address 192.0.2.2 is not the client's gateway. This same-subnet exercise needs no router, and its absence is intentional rather than an omitted Internet path.
sections.heading: Three architectures, different places to inspect
keyPoints: An AP name in an inventory is not evidence that a client has authenticated.
A cloud-management label alone does not specify a client forwarding path.
sections.explanation: A standalone AP holds its wireless configuration locally and bridges clients onto its attached network. A controller-based AP receives policy from a WLC, but the client-data exit depends on switching policy. Cloud management names the location of management services; it does not by itself mean every user packet passes through a cloud server. Keep device management, wireless association and IP forwarding as separate jobs. A client may pass one stage and fail the next, so an inventory of APs is not a connectivity test.

sections.example: A worksheet packet from AP1 192.0.2.11 to WLC1 192.0.2.2 is an outer tunnel exchange. Client1 198.51.100.10 sending to Server1 198.51.100.20 describes the inner service exchange in the central-switching model. A successful outer exchange does not show that Server1 answered the inner packet.
sections.heading: CAPWAP carries coordination and, when selected, payloads
keyPoints: Control health and end-to-end client health are different observations.
CAPWAP is context for wireless architecture in v1.1, not a separately named v2.0 objective.
sections.explanation: CAPWAP separates control and data exchanges between an AP and controller. The standard controller UDP ports are 5246 for control and 5247 for data. Encapsulation adds an outer transport path; the inner client addresses retain their own meaning. Discovery precedes the protected control relationship. Do not describe all CAPWAP packets as encrypted: discovery is clear, and data protection is a separate consideration. Reachability, discovery, certificates and software compatibility can each affect AP join.

sections.example: Changing a serving AP into dedicated monitor mode can remove client service even when the AP remains managed. This is why the required fault is on paper, not a mode change on an office AP. On Catalyst 9800, site tags participate in Local/FlexConnect selection; an AireOS menu recipe is not automatically a 9800 recipe.
sections.heading: AP modes are operational roles, not signal-strength levels
keyPoints: Check AP model, radio role and software before promising a mode.
FlexConnect local switching and local authentication are separate decisions.
sections.explanation: Local mode normally serves clients with centrally switched traffic in the conventional controller design. FlexConnect supports branch operation and per-WLAN switching choices. Monitor mode dedicates an AP to observing the wireless environment rather than normal client service. Sniffer mode sends selected captured radio traffic to an analyzer. Bridge or mesh roles interconnect supported wireless infrastructure; supported radio roles and combinations depend on model and release. Legacy modes such as rogue detector are platform-specific, not a required capability of every modern AP.

sections.example: For the paper local-switching variant, SW1 Gi1/0/1 to AP1 Ethernet0 uses native VLAN 10 and allows VLANs 10 and 20. For the central variant, it is access VLAN 10; SW1 Gi1/0/23 and Gi1/0/24 to WLC1 ports 1 and 2 form the service trunk LAG carrying VLANs 10 and 20. Server1 stays on access VLAN 20.
sections.heading: Choose the physical port from the real VLAN exit
keyPoints: Do not add client VLANs to every AP link without examining switching policy.
A diagram can specify PoE intent but cannot measure delivered power.
sections.explanation: An AP carrying only untagged management and centrally tunneled client traffic can use an access port in the management VLAN in this design. A locally switched AP carrying management plus multiple client VLANs needs an appropriate trunk. The AP's native VLAN and the switch's treatment of untagged frames must agree. The controller service uplink must carry centrally switched client VLANs. PoE requirements also depend on AP model and feature set; a link LED alone does not prove adequate power.

sections.example: Our paper WLC1 is AireOS, with ports 1 and 2 connecting to one SW1 logical bundle. A worksheet showing switch-side LACP active against this static controller is inconsistent. Correct the design annotation rather than pasting a command into production. One surviving member can preserve connectivity, but that does not establish twice the throughput for one flow.
sections.heading: Controller LAG needs a platform-specific agreement
keyPoints: Match aggregation mode and VLAN policy on every member.
LAG is link redundancy, not a second controller or guaranteed seamless failover.
sections.explanation: A LAG is a logical link made from physical member ports. Both ends need compatible VLAN and aggregation settings. In the cited AireOS implementation, configure the neighboring switch's EtherChannel statically in mode on; LACP and PAgP negotiation are not supported by that controller LAG. Catalyst 9800 releases document LACP support with platform restrictions. Therefore, neither 'all WLCs use LACP' nor 'no WLC supports LACP' is safe. Enabling AireOS LAG can require a reboot and alter interface mappings, so do not casually toggle it for discovery.

sections.example: A future physical exercise could record Client1's BSSID, address and continuous application test before and after moving between two authorized APs. Our required single-AP paper topology cannot produce that evidence. For v2.0, AP edge-port attributes are a partial link to 2.2.b; CAPWAP, AP modes and controller LAG remain supporting context rather than a claim that this lesson covers the whole objective.
sections.heading: Roaming changes association; evidence defines the result
keyPoints: A stable IP address does not prove that no packets were lost during a roam.
Keep physical RF and timing observations separate from architectural predictions.
sections.explanation: A client generally decides when to roam, with infrastructure features able to assist or influence it. Moving between APs with a compatible WLAN requires more than matching SSID text: security and network policy must remain appropriate. A BSSID change identifies a changed radio association; application continuity needs its own measurements. Layer 2 versus more complex mobility designs affect where traffic is anchored. This chapter explains those dependencies without measuring a roam or configuring a mobility domain.

content.plainAnswer: An AP provides radio access, while a controller coordinates the participating APs. In central switching, client data crosses the AP-controller tunnel; with FlexConnect local switching, it leaves at the AP's wired VLAN. Identify the actual switching policy and controller platform before deciding which uplink must carry a client VLAN or which aggregation protocol to use.

firstPractice.hint: Follow the payload, not the line labeled management. An AP's operational mode and its WLAN switching policy are related but are not interchangeable labels.
firstPractice.task: On the worksheet, circle the point where a VLAN 20 client frame reaches the wired network for central switching and then for FlexConnect local switching. Keep the management VLAN 10 annotations unchanged.
firstPractice.expected: Central switching exits at WLC1's service side; local switching exits at AP1's Ethernet side. The control relationship still ends at WLC1.

beginnerGuide.startingPoint: Start with a blank sheet and the five named roles below. Mark the AP's management address separately from the client's address. A source-reviewed prediction is not a captured packet; write predicted beside every result in this exercise.

checkUnderstanding.hint: Ask which evidence describes the management path and which describes the client's wired exit.
checkUnderstanding.answer: No. AP join supports management-path operation, not correct carriage of VLAN 20. Inspect the WLAN-to-VLAN mapping and the AP-facing trunk's allowed and native VLAN settings before treating controller health as client success.
checkUnderstanding.question: AP1 is joined, but its locally switched VLAN 20 client cannot reach Server1. Does a healthy CAPWAP session clear the AP trunk?

everydayComparison.whereItStops: This is only a memory aid. People and parcels do not model authentication, frame encapsulation, VLAN tags or RF behavior, and office geography cannot predict packet delay.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: The instructions resemble controller management, while the local delivery resembles FlexConnect local switching. A centrally processed job instead resembles data sent through the controller before entering the wired service network.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: Think of a branch office receiving instructions from headquarters while delivering some local work directly to a nearby customer. The instructions and the delivered work need not travel through the same building.

practiceQuestions.answer: Join tests the management relationship, not correct carriage of the client's local VLAN.
practiceQuestions.question: Why can AP join succeed while a locally switched client fails?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The AP can communicate in VLAN 10 while its WLAN is mapped to the wrong client VLAN or that VLAN is absent from the AP-facing trunk.

practiceQuestions.answer: At the controller service-side connection, before SW1 forwards to Server1.
practiceQuestions.question: Where does our central-switching client enter wired VLAN 20?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The AP uplink carries the encapsulated exchange in the management network; the configured controller service mapping provides the central data exit.

practiceQuestions.answer: No; cited AireOS LAG is static, while supported 9800 platforms can use LACP.
practiceQuestions.question: Must every WLC LAG use LACP?
practiceQuestions.explanation: LAG describes the bundle. Negotiation capabilities and configuration restrictions are properties of the particular controller platform and release.

practiceQuestions.answer: No; it changes the AP's role to monitoring rather than ordinary client service.
practiceQuestions.question: Does dedicated monitor mode improve normal client service?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The model and radio role matter, so never change a serving AP simply to see what a diagnostic mode looks like.

practiceQuestions.answer: Record old and new BSSID association evidence, then separately test service continuity.
practiceQuestions.question: What would you record to establish that a client roamed?
practiceQuestions.explanation: SSID names can stay the same across a roam. A BSSID change establishes association movement, but loss and application behavior need separate observations.

practiceQuestions.answer: SW1 Gi1/0/1, carrying AP1's native management VLAN 10 and tagged client VLAN 20.
practiceQuestions.question: Which AP port needs the client VLAN in our local variant?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The local client data leaves AP1 rather than WLC1. The switch port must therefore carry the VLAN where Server1 resides.

realWorldScenario.title: A healthy AP with a broken local client VLAN
realWorldScenario.takeaway: A controller's healthy AP list answers a management question. Trace the particular WLAN's payload exit before diagnosing a client path, and retain distinct evidence for association, addressing, wired VLANs and the final destination.
realWorldScenario.situation: In this hypothetical branch, AP1 is visible to its controller and Client1 authenticates, but the client cannot reach a same-subnet test server. The branch WLAN uses FlexConnect local switching. An operator who checks only controller uptime can miss the point where VLAN 20 leaves AP1 and enters the switch.
walkthrough: Confirm the WLAN is locally switched before choosing the uplink to inspect. Record the management and client addresses as separate evidence.
Compare the WLAN-to-VLAN assignment with the AP trunk's allowed VLANs. Do not infer the client VLAN from the SSID spelling.
Check Server1's access VLAN and address as well as the AP side. Both endpoints must belong to the intended service segment.
Correct only the documented local VLAN mismatch, then repeat the same client-to-server exchange and record the actual result.
Retain any remaining authentication or RF symptoms as separate hypotheses; one repaired VLAN does not prove roaming or application performance.

title: WLANs, SSIDs, VLANs, WPA2, and authentication

lab.goal: Create one isolated AireOS WLAN, verify a local client exchange, introduce a wrong credential only on the owned client, restore it and retest. The practical track requires the prepared dependencies; no runtime was executed during authoring.
setup: Instructor must prebuild the exact ports/VLANs, management and lab20 interfaces, legal radio country/channel/power, AP join and Router1 responder before this task. No DHCP or RADIUS is provided.
Confirm WLAN ID8, profile QCS28 and SSID QCS-LAB28 are unused, AP1 uses default-group, and this is a dedicated rack with no other clients. Stop if any prerequisite differs.
AdminPC opens https://192.0.2.2 using the instructor-verified certificate and authorized account. Do not bypass an unexplained certificate identity warning.
Set Client1's Wi-Fi IPv4 settings through Windows Settings to the address plan, recording previous settings privately. Instructor verifies a known-good test WLAN can reach Router1 first.
Paper alternative: draw the named AireOS pages and fill every specified field. Label association, ping and fault results predicted; no hardware or RF claim is allowed.

steps.why: A new WLAN cannot compensate for a missing AP join, VLAN or prepared local destination.
steps.title: Record the prepared baseline
steps.instruction: On AdminPC's authenticated WLC GUI, inspect Controller > Interfaces for management and lab20 and Wireless > All APs for AP1. Record versions, addresses, AP group and Local mode. Stop if the instructor's baseline client cannot reach Router1.
steps.expectedResult: The required service interface and joined AP are present before a new WLAN is created.

steps.why: Identity and forwarding decisions are reviewed before making the service available to a client.
steps.title: Create an inactive service identity
steps.instruction: In the same AdminPC browser, open WLANs, choose Create New and Go. Select WLAN, profile QCS28, SSID QCS-LAB28 and ID8, then Apply. On General keep Status disabled and select Interface lab20; keep SSID broadcast enabled.
steps.expectedResult: The controller has a distinct disabled WLAN mapped to VLAN20 through lab20.

steps.why: The menu family and enabled policy are distinct; reading both avoids accidentally enabling legacy compatibility.
steps.title: Configure WPA2 Personal securely
steps.instruction: On WLAN ID8, open Security > Layer 2. Choose WPA+WPA2, Personal where shown, WPA2 Policy and AES/CCMP128. Clear WPA Policy, choose PSK authentication and ASCII format, and enter the private generated lab passphrase. Leave MAC filtering and iPSK off; Apply.
steps.expectedResult: The intended security is WPA2-PSK with AES, without WPA1, TKIP or Enterprise authentication.

steps.why: This checks the advanced policy against an actual requirement rather than treating every checkbox as a performance improvement.
steps.title: Inspect traffic treatment and advanced options
steps.instruction: Still on WLAN ID8, choose QoS, select Silver and WMM Allowed, and Apply. On Advanced leave AAA Override off, peer-to-peer blocking disabled and DHCP Address Assignment Required off. Record session timeout and exclusion defaults; do not alter global QoS profiles.
steps.expectedResult: The data WLAN uses best-effort policy and allows the specified static client addressing.

steps.why: A visible SSID or Apply confirmation alone does not demonstrate that the client completed authentication.
steps.title: Enable and associate the test client
steps.instruction: Review ID8 once more, enable Status on General and Apply. On Client1 select QCS-LAB28 in Windows Wi-Fi settings and enter the private correct passphrase. Confirm WPA2-Personal/AES and the expected AP association in the WLC client details.
steps.expectedResult: The expected result is successful association on the intended WLAN; record the actual state before proceeding.

steps.why: This adds forwarding evidence to the association evidence and establishes the exact test to repeat after the fault.
steps.title: Measure the local baseline
steps.instruction: On Client1, open Start > Command Prompt before typing. Confirm this is the owned laptop, its only active data adapter is Wi-Fi, and the static settings match the plan. Record actual output without exposing the credential.
steps.expectedResult: Expect Wi-Fi 198.51.100.10/24, gateway 198.51.100.1 and replies if all prepared dependencies work.
commandExplanations: Display Windows adapter addresses, mask, gateway and configuration details; inspect the Wi-Fi adapter rather than an unrelated virtual adapter.
Send ICMP echo probes from Client1 to Router1's local VLAN20 address; replies support this exchange, not Internet or application health.

steps.why: A single client-side fault isolates credential agreement without exposing an open WLAN or disrupting another user's service.
steps.title: Introduce only a client credential fault
steps.instruction: On Client1 forget only QCS-LAB28, then reconnect using a deliberately wrong lab passphrase. Do not modify the WLC or weaken its policy. Record the connection failure and controller client state; cached IP information is not proof of association.
steps.expectedResult: The expected result is failed secure connection; controller configuration and other prepared dependencies remain unchanged.

steps.why: Restoring the exact profile preserves the original security design instead of hiding the symptom with a weaker policy.
steps.title: Restore the authorized client profile
steps.instruction: Forget the incorrect QCS-LAB28 profile and reconnect with the original correct private passphrase. Recheck the Wi-Fi static address and controller client details. If exclusion temporarily blocks retries, wait for the recorded timeout rather than changing global security settings.
steps.expectedResult: The client should regain the same authorized association and addressing; record any unexpected state.

steps.why: The retest closes the experiment; removal and credential disposal restore the isolated rack without preserving a temporary service.
steps.title: Retest and close the temporary WLAN
steps.instruction: On Client1 open Start > Command Prompt before typing and repeat the same destination. After recording the result, use AdminPC's GUI to disable and remove only WLAN ID8, then restore Client1's previous adapter settings and forget the test profile.
steps.expectedResult: Recovery should match the baseline before cleanup. After WLAN removal, the test SSID is no longer offered by this rack.
commandExplanations: Recheck the active Wi-Fi address and gateway after reconnecting; compare them with the baseline record.
Repeat the original local ICMP test to Router1 so failure and recovery are compared on the same path.

Static address; gateway 198.51.100.1; no DNS needed

Record WPA2-only AES and PSK selection without recording the key.

Compare baseline, wrong-key failure and restored same-target result; mark paper predictions explicitly.

glossary.meaning: The SSID is the name clients select. An AireOS profile name identifies a controller configuration, and the WLAN ID is its numeric identifier. These three values can differ.
Authentication checks the credential or identity allowed to join. Encryption protects data using keys. A successful password exchange does not establish correct addressing or application access.
A preshared key (PSK) is a shared credential for a Personal WLAN. Every holder can use that credential; it does not identify an individual employee.
Enterprise WLANs normally use 802.1X access control and an authentication service such as RADIUS. RADIUS carries authentication policy exchanges; this lab has no RADIUS server.
Wi-Fi Protected Access names security generations. Legacy WPA commonly used TKIP; this lesson configures WPA2 with AES-CCMP. WPA3-Personal uses SAE, a different password-authentication exchange.

Simultaneous Authentication of Equals (SAE) is WPA3-Personal's password-based key establishment. Protected Management Frames (PMF) protect specified management traffic; WPA3 requires appropriate PMF support.
A VLAN is a Layer 2 broadcast domain. An AireOS dynamic interface maps a service to a wired VLAN; its IP address is not automatically the clients' default gateway.
Quality of Service (QoS) controls traffic treatment under contention. Wi-Fi Multimedia (WMM) defines wireless access categories. A priority label does not create radio capacity.
DHCP leases IP settings to clients. Static addressing is entered manually. This lab uses static client addresses and leaves DHCP Address Assignment Required disabled.
A graphical user interface (GUI) presents configuration pages. Apply changes the active settings; Save Configuration preserves them for restart. Neither button is a connectivity test.

sections.example: This lab uses WLAN ID 8, profile QCS28, SSID QCS-LAB28 and dynamic interface lab20 in VLAN 20. WLC1 management is 192.0.2.2, while its lab20 interface is 198.51.100.2. Client1's gateway is Router1 at 198.51.100.1, not either WLC address.
sections.heading: Give every GUI field a specific job
keyPoints: Do not infer the VLAN from the WLAN ID or SSID spelling.
Check the complete profile-to-interface mapping before client testing.
sections.explanation: AireOS WLAN creation asks for a profile name, SSID and WLAN ID. The ID selects the configuration entry; it is not a VLAN assignment. An interface mapping associates centrally switched traffic with a wired service network. The management interface has a different purpose from a client dynamic interface. Keep a table of these relationships before enabling the WLAN, especially when several profiles have similar names.

sections.example: The configured service is WPA2-Personal, AES, with one private lab-only passphrase. No authentication-server address is needed. A WPA3-only service would require compatible client and AP support and the correct SAE/PMF settings; simply selecting a different cipher in a WPA2 profile does not create WPA3.
sections.heading: Compare security generations without enabling a weak fallback
keyPoints: A shared key is not a unique user account.
Do not enable WPA1 or TKIP as a shortcut for an unexplained join failure.
sections.explanation: WPA, WPA2 and WPA3 describe different security capabilities. Legacy WPA/TKIP is comparison material, not the target configuration. WPA2-Personal with AES-CCMP uses a shared credential; WPA2-Enterprise uses an identity-authentication framework and normally RADIUS. WPA3-Personal uses SAE rather than the WPA2 PSK exchange and adds required management-frame protection. Device and release compatibility matters. A transition mode intentionally permits more than one security method and is not identical to WPA3-only operation.

sections.example: The passphrase must meet the documented format: 8-63 ASCII characters, or the separate 64-hexadecimal-key format. Generate a strong disposable ASCII value privately rather than publishing a reusable password in a lesson. Record the selected format, but redact the value from screenshots and handover notes.
sections.heading: Follow creation, security and activation in order
keyPoints: Check WPA Policy is off and WPA2 Policy with AES is on.
A hidden or set-only PSK field should not be interpreted as proof that a saved key is missing.
sections.explanation: Build the WLAN disabled so its identity, wired mapping and security can be inspected first. In AireOS, WLANs leads to the ID-specific edit page. General identifies the SSID, status and interface. Security > Layer 2 controls the policy and authentication key management. For this exercise select WPA+WPA2 as the menu family, enable only WPA2 with AES, choose PSK and enter the authorized ASCII passphrase. The family label does not mean WPA1 must also be enabled.

sections.example: Use Silver and WMM Allowed for the basic data exercise. Leave Allow AAA Override off, peer-to-peer blocking disabled, and DHCP Address Assignment Required off because Client1 is manually addressed. Record the default session timeout and exclusion behavior without changing global profiles. A DHCP-required policy could reject the static-address plan even after the password is correct.
sections.heading: Read QoS and advanced settings as policy, not magic repairs
keyPoints: A QoS selection cannot repair a mismatched credential or VLAN.
Interpret a setting against this lab's requirements before copying it to another WLAN.
sections.explanation: AireOS offers Platinum for voice, Gold for video, Silver for best effort and Bronze for background treatment. These are profiles, not promises of bandwidth or latency. WMM must be considered with client capabilities and the wireless design. Advanced settings such as session timeout, client exclusion, AAA override and DHCP-required behavior change specific admission or service rules. AAA override permits an authentication policy to replace certain configured choices; this PSK lab does not need it.

sections.example: Our fault is one wrong character in Client1's saved QCS-LAB28 credential. WLC1 remains unchanged. After forgetting the test profile and reconnecting with the correct private passphrase, repeat the same Router1 ping. A successful result supports this local exchange, not Internet access, roaming quality or application throughput.
sections.heading: Use checkpoints to locate the failing stage
keyPoints: Record actual timestamps and state rather than pasting predicted results.
Test the same source and destination before the fault and after restoration.
sections.explanation: First confirm the intended SSID and negotiated security on the client, then its assigned or configured address, mask and gateway. Next test the local intended IP destination. If association fails after changing only the client password, investigate that profile before changing controller VLANs. If association works but IP communication fails, compare the service interface, wired VLAN, client IP settings and any filters. A cached address may remain visible after disconnect, so an IP display alone does not establish current association.

sections.example: A student without a controller can complete all GUI decision fields on paper and predict the wrong-key result. That preparation is useful, but must be recorded as 'worksheet completed; hardware verification pending'. Do not treat a virtual router or a screenshot of an unrelated controller as evidence that a radio client joined this WLAN.
sections.heading: Keep the exam mapping and platform boundary honest
keyPoints: v1.1 remains current through 2 February 2027; v2.0 starts 3 February 2027.
Controller setup, RF design and Enterprise authentication require separate practical work.
sections.explanation: The current v1.1 blueprint explicitly includes WLAN GUI interpretation, WPA-family descriptions and WPA2-PSK GUI configuration. This lesson provides those tasks on a specified prepared platform; completing the worksheet alone is conceptual practice. The announced v2.0 wireless-security principles are a partial mapping, while AP-facing wired connectivity is supporting context. AireOS is used to make one coherent GUI path; Catalyst 9800 uses profiles and tags and needs its own instructions.

content.metaTitle: CCNA Day 28: Configure and Verify a WPA2 WLAN
takeaways: Treat SSID, WLAN ID, profile and VLAN as separate fields.
Authenticate securely before interpreting a client IP test.
Use WPA2-AES for this bounded lab; legacy security remains comparison material.
Read QoS and advanced settings against the actual client requirements.
Change only the client key for the controlled fault.
Record hardware limitations and never equate a worksheet with radio execution.
objectives: Map the visible SSID to WLAN ID, profile and VLAN.
Compare WPA, WPA2 and WPA3 without enabling legacy security.
Configure WPA2-PSK with AES in a supported controller GUI.
Interpret QoS and advanced settings without assuming they repair authentication.
Observe a single wrong-client-key fault and repeat the original reachability test.
content.plainAnswer: A WLAN needs a matching SSID, authentication method, encryption settings and wired VLAN mapping. Configure those fields deliberately, then test a client from association to its intended destination. A visible SSID, accepted GUI change or successful password entry does not prove the client has a usable IP path.

visualStory.title: One SSID, four independent decisions

stages.title: Name the service
stages.explanation: The client selects QCS-LAB28; the controller uses profile QCS28 and ID8.

stages.title: Protect and map
stages.explanation: Match WPA2-AES credentials, then check that lab20 carries the intended VLAN20 service.

stages.title: Interpret policy
stages.explanation: Silver controls treatment, not authentication. Verify client state and a real destination separately.

visualStory.altText: Four records show the SSID identity, WPA2 security, VLAN20 exit and Silver QoS policy. Each must match the intended lab service.
visualStory.boundary: Configuration comparison, not a packet capture. The drawing does not prove client association, radio coverage, encryption strength or measured traffic performance.
visualStory.takeaway: A matching password is only one part of a usable wireless service.

walkthrough.action: Record identity before security.

beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: A common error is to weaken wireless security when the real fault is the wrong service VLAN. Separating authentication from forwarding makes the next test useful and avoids exposing unrelated clients.

firstPractice.hint: Do not treat the number 8 as the VLAN number. The lab intentionally uses different identifiers.
firstPractice.task: On paper, write QCS-LAB28, QCS28, 8 and VLAN 20 in four labeled columns. Add WPA2-Personal, AES and the statement 'credential stored privately', then identify which fields a client normally sees.
firstPractice.expected: The client normally selects the SSID and compatible security settings; the profile name, WLAN ID and wired VLAN remain controller-side identifiers.

beginnerGuide.startingPoint: Begin with the SSID-to-VLAN worksheet before opening any settings page. The same SSID spelling can exist in different profiles or environments, so record the controller and numeric WLAN ID as well as the name.

checkUnderstanding.hint: Ask whether priority treatment checks the shared credential.
checkUnderstanding.answer: No. QoS controls traffic treatment, not credential agreement. Correct the client profile to the authorized WPA2-PSK settings, then verify association and IP reachability without changing the priority policy.
checkUnderstanding.question: Would switching from Silver to Platinum QoS repair an incorrect PSK?

everydayComparison.whereItStops: A WLAN is not literally a ticket desk. Wireless key establishment and encryption have technical rules; a familiar analogy cannot show that authentication or data protection succeeded.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: SSID resembles the public name, WLAN ID resembles the internal reference, and VLAN mapping resembles the assigned room. The credential check is separate from all three.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: A venue's public event name, internal booking reference and room number are separate labels. Matching the event name does not prove that a visitor has the right ticket or reached the right room.

prerequisites: Read Day 27's central-switching and AP/controller roles.
The practical track requires the exact prepared, isolated rack below and permission to create only WLAN ID 8.
Without that rack, complete the clearly labeled GUI worksheet; do not claim hands-on configuration.
Use a dedicated test credential generated locally; never use an employer or personal account password.
content.learnerOutcome: You will interpret an AireOS WLAN's identity, VLAN, security, QoS and advanced settings; configure WPA2-PSK on an isolated prepared rack; and distinguish a wrong client credential from a forwarding problem.
content.metaDescription: Build a bounded WPA2-PSK WLAN in the AireOS GUI, inspect VLAN, QoS and advanced settings, and diagnose a wrong client key without weakening security.

teachingPrelude.explanation: Read the WLAN as a set of independent decisions: which name is advertised, who may join, how frames are protected, where client traffic exits and how it is treated. Use the prepared rack only after every dependency is checked. Expected results below are predictions; authoring did not execute a controller.
teachingPrelude.labBoundary: Physical prepared-rack exercise or labeled paper GUI alternative. No production WLAN, RADIUS, DHCP, Internet, RF survey or WPA3 runtime is included. GNS3 cannot substitute virtual AP radios for this hardware test.

practiceQuestions.answer: No; the ID identifies the WLAN, while VLAN20 identifies its wired service domain.
practiceQuestions.question: Are WLAN ID8 and VLAN20 contradictory?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Different namespaces serve different purposes. The interface mapping connects them; there is no rule requiring their numbers to match.

practiceQuestions.answer: The client uses an intentionally static address rather than a DHCP lease.
practiceQuestions.question: Why leave DHCP Address Assignment Required off here?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A policy requiring observed DHCP assignment conflicts with this lab's static-address design, even when authentication succeeds.

practiceQuestions.answer: It selects a configuration family; the policy checkboxes determine enabled versions.
practiceQuestions.question: Why does the WPA+WPA2 dropdown not require enabling WPA1?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The exercise explicitly enables WPA2 with AES and leaves WPA Policy off. The family label must not be mistaken for the final active policy.

practiceQuestions.answer: WPA3-Personal uses SAE and requires appropriate protected management-frame support.
practiceQuestions.question: What makes WPA3-Personal different from WPA2-PSK?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Changing an SSID label or enabling a stronger-looking QoS profile does not change the authentication exchange or establish WPA3 compatibility.

practiceQuestions.answer: It uses best-effort treatment without claiming a special voice or video service.
practiceQuestions.question: Why is Silver appropriate for this basic exercise?
practiceQuestions.explanation: QoS is separate from authentication and addressing. No congestion workload is measured, so the lesson cannot claim throughput or latency improvement.

practiceQuestions.answer: Only that the operating system still displays an address value, not a current wireless connection.
practiceQuestions.question: What does a retained address after failed authentication prove?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Static or cached settings can persist while association is absent. Correlate the adapter's connection state, controller record and actual destination test.

realWorldScenario.title: The correct password did not put the client in the correct VLAN
realWorldScenario.takeaway: Security success and forwarding success answer different questions. A complete WLAN check preserves the credential boundary while comparing identity, policy, addressing and the exact service destination.
realWorldScenario.situation: In a hypothetical training room, QCS-LAB28 is visible and a learner can associate, but the endpoint cannot reach Router1. The profile was accidentally mapped to management instead of lab20. The useful response is to compare the mapping and address plan, not enable open authentication or change every QoS setting.
walkthrough: Identify WLAN ID 8 and compare its profile, SSID and interface with the worksheet before editing.
Keep a screenshot of the relevant non-secret settings and record Client1's association and address state.
Check whether the traffic is centrally switched and whether VLAN 20 reaches Router1 through the WLC service port.
Restore only the lab20 interface selection while following the platform's disable/apply/enable procedure, then reconnect the test client.
Repeat the same local reachability check and keep remaining symptoms separate from the corrected mapping.

title: Wired and wireless client troubleshooting

lab.goal: Collect equivalent Windows, macOS and Linux observations on an instructor-prepared isolated network. Run only on available owned clients, label missing tracks untested, and compare baseline, client Wi-Fi-off fault and restoration on Windows.
setup: Instructor recreates Day28's WPA2-AES QCS-LAB28 service, confirms local reachability and privately supplies its disposable credential. No DHCP, DNS or Internet is present.
Record previous client settings. Set the listed static parameters using each OS Network settings GUI. Leave unrelated managed clients untouched; a single test adapter must carry each observation.

Windows command references: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/ipconfig and https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/netsh-wlan. Never export profiles with plaintext keys.
macOS inspection reference: https://support.apple.com/en-gb/guide/mac-help/mh11395/mac. Use System Settings > Network > selected service > Details, TCP/IP and DNS.

Linux reference: https://networkmanager.pages.freedesktop.org/NetworkManager/NetworkManager/nmcli.html. Confirm NetworkManager manages the chosen adapter; do not install or reconfigure network services during this exercise.
If any OS or radio is unavailable, use a labeled worksheet for that track. A VM can inspect virtual IP settings but does not establish physical wireless behavior.

steps.why: A clear service boundary keeps a generic 'no Internet' indicator from overriding the actual local test requirement.
steps.title: Identify links and the test boundary
steps.instruction: On the rack worksheet, mark every port above and record whether each OS track is real or paper-only. Verify only owned clients join the test SSID. Record the absence of DHCP, DNS and Internet so later errors are not mistaken for new faults.
steps.expectedResult: The evidence ledger identifies the actual clients, available platforms and exact local test target.

steps.why: This correlates current radio association with addressing and one specific service path.
steps.title: Inspect Windows adapter and wireless state
steps.instruction: On Win1, open Start > Command Prompt before typing. Use the Wi-Fi adapter's output, not a disconnected virtual adapter. If wireless details are permission-restricted, use the authorized Windows Wi-Fi properties view and record the limitation.
steps.expectedResult: Expect the planned static settings, QCS-LAB28 association and local replies when the prepared rack is working.
commandExplanations: Display full adapter addressing, mask, gateway, DNS and assignment information; inspect the active Wi-Fi entry.
Display detected wireless interfaces and available current association/security details without revealing a stored key.
Test the planned local router from Win1 using ICMP; preserve the actual bounded result.

steps.why: The graphical view provides platform-appropriate inspection without relying on retired private wireless command paths.
steps.title: Inspect macOS parameters and security
steps.instruction: On Mac1 open System Settings > Network, select Wi-Fi and open Details. Record TCP/IP address, mask and Router plus DNS entries; inspect Wi-Fi's current network/security details. Option-click the Wi-Fi menu and open Wireless Diagnostics if authorized; do not change the service.
steps.expectedResult: Expect 198.51.100.11/24, Router 198.51.100.1 and the prepared WPA2 service; DNS is intentionally absent.

steps.why: The same destination makes the Mac evidence comparable with the Windows baseline despite different command syntax.
steps.title: Test the macOS local exchange
steps.instruction: On Mac1 open Applications > Utilities > Terminal before typing. Confirm the selected Wi-Fi service is active and other data paths are not carrying the test. Do not treat a local self-ping as a substitute for this router destination.
steps.expectedResult: Record the actual four-probe result; replies support only this local IP exchange.
commandExplanations: Send four ICMP probes to Router1 from Mac1; -c limits the count so the test ends without a manual interruption.

steps.why: This collects the same categories as the other OS tracks while respecting Linux's installed network manager.
steps.title: Inspect the Linux NetworkManager state
steps.instruction: On Linux1 open its desktop Terminal before typing. Confirm NetworkManager is installed and manages the test adapter; otherwise stop this CLI track. Read the adapter name from device status and correlate it with the IP information.
steps.expectedResult: Expect the Linux test adapter at 198.51.100.12/24 and the intended profile, then local replies if the path works.
commandExplanations: List interface names, types and connection state so the actual Wi-Fi adapter can be identified.
Display per-device properties including addresses, gateway and DNS; inspect the identified test adapter.
List active connection profiles; a saved inactive profile is not the active network.
List visible Wi-Fi service information and the active marker; this does not reveal the private PSK or prove service health.
Send four ICMP probes to the same local Router1 target and retain the observed result.

steps.why: A wired comparison can narrow an RF-specific hypothesis, but a different VLAN or address would make the comparison misleading.
steps.title: Compare a wired observation
steps.instruction: For one owned client only, record its Wi-Fi baseline, turn Wi-Fi off, and connect its Ethernet port to SW1 Gi1/0/4 access VLAN20. Apply that client's same planned static address to Ethernet only. Inspect the selected OS network settings, then restore the original Wi-Fi arrangement.
steps.expectedResult: The wired interface has a physical link and its own configuration; wireless SSID and BSSID are not wired parameters.

steps.why: This intentionally changes association availability without injecting RF interference or disrupting infrastructure shared by other clients.
steps.title: Create the controlled Windows disconnect
steps.instruction: After restoring Win1's original Wi-Fi baseline, use Windows Quick Settings to turn Wi-Fi off on Win1 only. Keep its Ethernet unplugged. Observe adapter state; do not change WLC, AP, client credentials or gateway configuration.
steps.expectedResult: Win1 loses its wireless data path; a retained static address does not establish connection.

steps.why: The observation links the controlled access fault to the same destination used in the working baseline.
steps.title: Record the failed same-target test
steps.instruction: On Win1 open Start > Command Prompt before typing. Confirm Wi-Fi is off and no alternative data adapter is active. Record both the adapter display and the router test; error wording may vary with OS state.
steps.expectedResult: Expect no successful Router1 exchange from Win1, with actual output retained rather than invented wording.
commandExplanations: Observe the adapter's disconnected state and any retained configuration instead of assuming the address disappeared.
Repeat the original Router1 test during the controlled disconnect; no successful exchange is expected over the disabled path.

steps.why: Restoration is complete only when the original scoped checks are repeated, not merely when the Wi-Fi toggle is on.
steps.title: Restore and verify the original connection
steps.instruction: On Win1 turn Wi-Fi on, select QCS-LAB28 and verify the planned static settings. Then open Start > Command Prompt before typing. Keep the same local destination and compare timestamps with the baseline and fault.
steps.expectedResult: Expected recovery is the original association, address plan and local replies, not a claim of Internet or DNS access.

glossary.meaning: An adapter connects a host to a network. A host may have Ethernet, Wi-Fi, VPN and virtual interfaces at once; inspect the one actually carrying the test traffic.
Association connects a wireless station to an AP's radio service. WPA authentication and key establishment must also complete before protected user traffic can flow.
SSID is the wireless service name. BSSID identifies the particular radio service. Record both where permitted, because the same SSID may be offered by several APs.
The address identifies an interface and its prefix defines the local subnet. The default gateway is the local router used for destinations without a more specific route.
DHCP provides a timed address assignment and related options. A lease is not proof that today's wireless association or application is healthy; cached information can remain.
Windows APIPA is automatic IPv4 link-local addressing in 169.254.0.0/16. Such addresses are for local-link use, not ordinary routed reachability.
DNS translates names into records such as IP addresses. A resolver performs lookups. An IP test and a name lookup answer different questions.
Ping uses ICMP echo exchanges to test one IP destination. No reply can reflect filters, rate limits or either path direction; it is not a complete diagnosis.
RSSI is received signal-strength indication. Signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) compares signal with noise. Interference, contention and client behavior can affect service even with strong signal.
A baseline records known settings and actual tests before a change. Rollback restores the specific changed setting and repeats the original test, rather than resetting unrelated network state.

sections.example: A laptop can have Ethernet connected while Wi-Fi is disconnected. A successful ping might therefore be using the wired path. In this lab each client has only the chosen data adapter active during its test. Record any VPN or additional route before interpreting a result; do not silently disable an employer-managed agent.
sections.heading: Start with link and association evidence
keyPoints: A signal-strength indicator is not an application-health measurement.
Inspect only authorized devices and do not inject interference to create a fault.
sections.explanation: For a wired client, record cable connection, adapter state, negotiated speed and errors available from the OS or switch. For a wireless client, record SSID, BSSID where permitted, connection state and negotiated security. Do not treat the saved Wi-Fi profile as the current association. Physical distance, obstacles, channel use and noise require physical observations; no virtual cable in GNS3 or CML can reproduce those conditions.

sections.example: Windows may show mask 255.255.255.0 where Linux shows /24. These describe the same prefix length. A Mac's Router field is the gateway field, not the AP's radio address. Linux interface names such as wlp2s0 are discovered on that machine; the example is not a universal adapter name.
sections.heading: Compare client parameters across Windows, macOS and Linux
keyPoints: Do not copy another operating system's syntax into a client console.
Record unavailable fields and permissions rather than trying to bypass them.
sections.explanation: The evidence columns are the same across systems even when their displays differ: interface, address, prefix or mask, gateway, DNS and assignment method. Windows ipconfig /all displays adapter details; netsh wlan show interfaces adds current wireless information. macOS exposes the selected service through System Settings > Network and Wi-Fi Details, including TCP/IP and DNS. Linux with NetworkManager provides device and connection inspection through nmcli. Official OS links in the setup notes support the exact client procedure; Cisco's source supports the troubleshooting method.

sections.example: Our prepared WLAN uses static addresses, so the absence of a DHCP lease is expected. Client1 is 198.51.100.10/24 with gateway 198.51.100.1. Changing a static client to DHCP in this rack would not repair anything: the rack deliberately contains no DHCP server. A 169.254 address would contradict the specified baseline.
sections.heading: An address must match the intended service
keyPoints: A client without a DHCP lease is not necessarily faulty when static addressing was intended.
IPv4 link-local addresses are not a substitute for a planned routed address.
sections.explanation: Check whether the client should use static addressing or DHCP. A DHCP-enabled client with a link-local address warrants investigation of assignment, but one observation does not identify the failed server or relay. A correct-looking address can be stale, duplicated or assigned to an inactive interface. A wrong mask can make a remote destination appear local; a wrong gateway can break remote paths while same-subnet peers still work. IPv6 must be assessed separately rather than assumed broken because IPv4 is wrong.

sections.example: The lab destination is Router1 198.51.100.1. Windows sends the default bounded ping; macOS and Linux use four probes. No public address is used. If the gateway replies while a later remote test fails, the next question concerns routing or the remote service, not whether the local Wi-Fi password must be changed.
sections.heading: Use reachability tests with narrow conclusions
keyPoints: Keep the source interface and destination fixed when comparing a fault and repair.
Do not declare every protocol healthy from one successful ICMP exchange.
sections.explanation: Test a documented local destination before an approved remote destination, and compare replies with interface and route evidence. A self-ping tests local stack behavior, not a physical cable or AP path. A gateway reply confirms that particular exchange but not the gateway's upstream route. Missing replies can reflect filters, host settings, load or the return path. Preserve outputs and timestamps so the next operator can distinguish persistent failure from transient neighbor discovery.

sections.example: This isolated rack intentionally has no DNS server and no Internet route. A browser's 'no Internet' indicator is therefore not evidence that the local WLAN failed. On paper, compare 'ping 198.51.100.1 replies' with 'a name lookup has no configured resolver'. The correct conclusion is a limited successful local exchange and an unprovided name service.
sections.heading: Separate DNS and wireless security from IP routing
keyPoints: An unavailable service is different from a misconfigured service.
Keep passwords, private keys and full client identifiers out of shared diagnostic notes.
sections.explanation: A name lookup asks a resolver for records. If an IP endpoint works but its name fails, inspect the configured resolver, suffix and returned record before flushing caches. A correct DNS answer can still point to a service that is unreachable or unavailable. Wireless security failures occur earlier: mismatched WPA mode, unsupported cipher, wrong PSK or Enterprise certificate validation can prevent data service. Do not disable certificate checking, authentication or endpoint firewalls simply to obtain a green test.

sections.example: A useful report says which OS tracks ran, which interfaces were inspected, what failed during the controlled disconnect and what recovered. It also says that DNS, Internet access and physical RF survey were not supplied. This directly supports current v1.1 client-parameter verification and partially practices the wider v2.0 troubleshooting objective.
sections.heading: Restore one change and report the remaining uncertainty
keyPoints: A paper interpretation must be labeled predicted rather than observed.
Record one platform as unavailable rather than marking all three client tracks complete.
sections.explanation: The deliberate fault is turning Wi-Fi off on the owned Windows test laptop after a working baseline. The AP, VLAN and credentials remain unchanged. Restore Wi-Fi, select the same test network and repeat the original destination. This demonstrates a local access dependency when actually executed; it does not measure roaming, interference or throughput. For macOS and Linux, collect equivalent inspection evidence without requiring a second fault.

content.metaTitle: CCNA Day 29: Diagnose Wired and Wireless Clients
takeaways: Inspect the interface actually carrying the traffic.
Keep association, IP configuration and name resolution as separate checks.
Compare equivalent evidence across operating systems, not identical syntax.
A local reply does not prove upstream forwarding or application health.
Use only a bounded owned-client fault with a recorded restoration.
Treat physical RF and unavailable OS tracks as explicitly unmeasured.
objectives: Inspect address, prefix, gateway and resolver information on all three client OS families.
Identify active wired versus wireless interface evidence and security parameters.
Separate RF, authentication, DHCP, DNS and routing hypotheses.
Perform one client-only disconnect and restore the original association.
State what remains unmeasured when a platform or physical radio is unavailable.
content.plainAnswer: Troubleshoot the active client interface in stages: physical link or wireless association, security, IP settings, local gateway, remote destination and name resolution. Record what each check proves. A strong Wi-Fi signal or an address displayed by the OS does not establish current authentication, correct routing or a healthy application.

firstPractice.task: Given a client at 198.51.100.10/24, gateway 198.51.100.1 and destination 198.51.100.20, write whether the destination is local. Then explain why reaching it would not test the default gateway's remote forwarding.
firstPractice.expected: The destination is in the same /24 subnet. Its local exchange does not establish the router's ability to forward toward a remote network.

beginnerGuide.startingPoint: Start by writing the client's interface name, current connection state and intended destination. Leave blank any field you cannot actually observe. A missing OS or Wi-Fi adapter is a limitation to record, not an invitation to invent output.

checkUnderstanding.hint: Separate association from the source and scope of the IPv4 address.
checkUnderstanding.answer: No. Association does not prove that DHCP succeeded, and IPv4 link-local addressing does not provide ordinary routed access. Check whether DHCP was intended, then inspect the lease path and service VLAN without blaming radio strength alone.
checkUnderstanding.question: Wi-Fi shows connected and ipconfig displays 169.254.8.9. Is an ordinary routed IPv4 service established?

everydayComparison.whereItStops: The postal comparison cannot explain wireless authentication, IP routing or DNS behavior. A network can filter replies, and failed ping is not proof that a destination is powered off.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: The address plan resembles the labels, the gateway resembles the next delivery point, and a destination test checks a particular exchange. Each observation narrows the question.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: When a letter does not arrive, checking the sender's address, local collection point and recipient address answers different questions. A correctly written envelope alone does not show delivery.

teachingPrelude.explanation: Choose one client, one interface and one destination before running a command. Compare the observation with the address plan, then ask the next narrow question. The lab's three OS tracks collect equivalent facts using different interfaces; unavailable platforms remain explicitly untested.
teachingPrelude.labBoundary: Only an isolated prepared rack and owned clients are in scope. No Internet, DNS server, RF interference injection, password extraction or packet capture of other users. Emulator links cannot measure radio coverage.

practiceQuestions.answer: Local destinations do not normally need the default gateway.
practiceQuestions.question: Why can a same-subnet test work with the wrong gateway?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The host uses its prefix to decide whether a destination is local. A wrong gateway becomes relevant to routed destinations, so choose tests that exercise the suspected dependency.

practiceQuestions.answer: No; it indicates link-local addressing, not the exact cause of missing intended assignment.
practiceQuestions.question: Does 169.254.8.9 prove that the DHCP server is down?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The client may not reach DHCP because of association, VLAN, relay or server problems. First establish whether DHCP was intended at all.

practiceQuestions.answer: Interface state, address/prefix, gateway, DNS, assignment method and applicable wireless security.
practiceQuestions.question: What fields should the three OS tracks have in common?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Different tools format the information differently. A comparable ledger records the meaning of each field instead of requiring identical command output.

practiceQuestions.answer: It changes evidence before confirming whether name resolution is the failing stage.
practiceQuestions.question: Why avoid a blanket DNS cache flush first?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A numeric IP test and a lookup through the configured resolver can isolate the problem. No resolver is supplied in this lab, so flushing a cache cannot create one.

practiceQuestions.answer: No; physical radio, antenna and environmental behavior are outside that virtual interface.
practiceQuestions.question: Does a VM with a virtual Ethernet adapter test RF coverage?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A VM can provide useful IP configuration practice, but its Ethernet link does not measure channel contention, signal strength or wireless roaming.

practiceQuestions.answer: Confirm the intended association and static settings, then repeat the original Router1 test.
practiceQuestions.question: What should follow restoring Wi-Fi on Win1?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The toggle only enables the adapter. The client must reconnect to the correct service and successfully exchange traffic on the original path.

realWorldScenario.title: The no-Internet icon was not the local fault
realWorldScenario.takeaway: Diagnostic tools become useful when tied to an expected service and an actual interface. A client can be locally healthy without Internet access, and a displayed address can belong to the wrong adapter.
realWorldScenario.situation: In this hypothetical training rack, a Windows learner sees 'No Internet' and assumes the WLAN password is wrong. The rack has no Internet connection by design, while the real local test is a ping to Router1. Meanwhile a Linux client uses a different interface than expected. Both cases require a scoped evidence ledger rather than a blanket network reset.
walkthrough: Confirm the test requirement is local Router1 reachability, not public web access or DNS resolution.
Identify the active adapter and collect its address, prefix, gateway and assignment method on the actual OS.
Record wireless association and negotiated security independently of any browser connectivity icon.
Run the same intended destination test and compare with a known-working client on the same service.
Correct only an evidenced setting, then repeat the original test and state which services were never in scope.

title: Reading the routing table and choosing a route

lab.goal: Build two routers, establish reachability to R2's loopback, add one host route to Null0 on R1, observe the predicted lookup change, remove that route and retest. No router runtime or timing is claimed during authoring.
setup: Use Cisco Modeling Labs 2.10 with its legally entitled bundled IOSv 15.9M reference image. Record the complete show version release; do not export that image to GNS3. No paid API is involved.
Create fresh nodes and only the listed links. No External Connector, NAT node, bridge, public uplink or production network is permitted. Leave console access independent of the test data links.

IOSv examples use GigabitEthernet0/0 and GigabitEthernet0/1. Confirm those exact ports in the workbench and show ip interface brief before configuring; if your image differs, document an explicit port substitution first.

Decline the initial configuration dialog on a new authorized node, press Enter to reach the prompt, then use enable. Do not bypass unknown credentials. All displayed expected results are predictions, not author runtime.
Without an entitled compatible image, complete the address and route-selection worksheet only. Mark command execution, packet forwarding and recovery unmeasured.

steps.why: Mapping the real interface prevents a correct command from being sent to the wrong port.

List interface names and state; confirm the mapped Gi0/0 cable endpoint.

steps.instruction: In the isolated CML workbench, select R1, open its Console tab and connect before typing. Start at > or #; use end first if a prior task left configuration mode. Only configure the single listed port; this lab contains no existing production configuration.

Enter global configuration mode on this named router; accepted changes affect its running state.
Route the destination /24 through neighboring R2; default static AD is 1.
Return to privileged EXEC; this neither saves nor reverses accepted configuration changes.

steps.why: This records what worked and why before adding a more-specific route.
steps.title: Record the destination baseline
steps.instruction: In the isolated CML workbench, select R1, open its Console tab and connect before typing. Start at > or #; use end first if a prior task left configuration mode. Do not add the deliberate fault until the destination lookup and ping have a working baseline.
steps.expectedResult: Expect the /24 through 192.0.2.2 and replies, subject to actual interface and neighbor state.
commandExplanations: Enter authorized privileged EXEC mode to inspect this named router.
Inspect C, L and S entries, prefixes and bracketed values.
Ask which installed route matches the exact loopback destination.
Send a bounded ICMP exchange to R2's loopback using the outgoing transit source by default.
