glossary.meaning: A route describes a destination IP range and a way to reach it. A prefix combines a network value with a length such as 198.51.100.0/24.
The routing table contains selected routing information. A forwarding table is derived for packet lookup. A configured route may not qualify for installation.
Among installed routes matching the destination, forwarding selects the most specific prefix: the greatest matching prefix length.
Administrative distance (AD) is Cisco's local preference for a route source when sources compete for the same prefix. Lower is preferred; AD is not path length or a security guarantee.
A metric ranks paths within a routing protocol's rules. Values from unrelated protocols are not generally comparable.
The next hop is the immediate router to receive a forwarded packet. The exit interface is the local port used to reach it; neither must be the final destination.
A connected route covers an enabled interface's network. A local host route identifies the router's own interface address for local delivery.
A default route is /0 and matches any destination not covered more specifically. A host route identifies one address: /32 in IPv4 and /128 in IPv6.
Null0 is a logical discard interface. A selected route to Null0 intentionally drops matching traffic; it is not an unplugged Ethernet port.
A loopback is a software interface used here as a stable test address. A console is the router's direct text-management window, independent of its data link.

sections.example: The invented teaching entry 'S 198.51.100.0/24 [1/0] via 192.0.2.2' says static route, destination /24, AD1, metric0 and next hop 192.0.2.2. It is not a captured router output. Nothing in that row alone says that a server responded or that an application is available.
sections.heading: Read an entry as several separate facts
keyPoints: Decode fields before comparing values.
A route-table row is forwarding information, not an end-to-end service receipt.
sections.explanation: An IOS route code identifies its source: C for connected, L for local, S for static and O for OSPF. The prefix and mask describe destinations, not the source host. A via field identifies the next hop; an interface identifies the local exit. Bracketed values commonly show administrative distance followed by metric. Output may also include an age, which is time-related information rather than path quality. Read the displayed legend because additional codes depend on platform and route type.

sections.example: R1 Gi0/0 is 192.0.2.1/30 and R2 Gi0/0 is 192.0.2.2/30. R1 should show the transit network 192.0.2.0/30 as connected and its own .1 address as local. R2 Loopback0 at 198.51.100.20/24 is our final responder; the lab does not contain a separate server.
sections.heading: Connected networks and local addresses are not duplicates
keyPoints: Up/up and the intended address are prerequisites for the connected route.
Keep a diagram's loopback destination explicit rather than drawing an imaginary endpoint.
sections.explanation: An enabled addressed interface creates a connected network route when its state qualifies, and IOS also represents the router's own address as a local route. A connected /30 says the transit subnet is attached. A local /32 says a packet for the router's precise interface address is delivered locally rather than forwarded to a neighbor. A loopback can provide a software destination without pretending there is a physical host behind it.

sections.example: Two candidates for 198.51.100.0/24, one static AD1 and one OSPF AD110, compete for the same prefix. A candidate 198.51.100.20/32 is different: it can coexist with the /24. The lab uses static routes only; the OSPF comparison is a labeled interpretation example, not an executed routing protocol.
sections.heading: Installation compares sources for the same prefix
keyPoints: Compare AD only in the correct identical-prefix context.
A protocol's metric is not interchangeable with another protocol's metric.
sections.explanation: A routing protocol first uses its own rules to select paths. The routing table then considers eligible candidates for a given prefix, including source preference through AD and next-hop resolution. A lower distance generally wins among competing sources for the identical prefix. Common defaults include connected 0, static 1 and OSPF 110. Changing distance is a local policy decision, not an advertisement of a better path to other routers, and should never be used to hide missing reachability.

sections.example: Our baseline /24 sends 198.51.100.20 through R2. The deliberate fault adds 198.51.100.20/32 to Null0 with AD200. Both prefixes may appear in the table, but .20 selects the discard. An address such as .21 still selects the /24; that lookup alone does not mean a .21 endpoint actually exists.
sections.heading: Forwarding selects the most specific installed match
keyPoints: A matching route is necessary for forwarding, not proof that every address in its range is in use.
A default route is not automatically an Internet route.
sections.explanation: Once usable routes are installed, an ordinary destination-based lookup chooses the longest matching prefix. A /32 can override a /24 for one IPv4 address even with a larger AD. A default /0 is the least specific match and is used when no more-specific installed route matches. Without a matching route, ordinary forwarding cannot proceed. This lesson does not add policy-based routing, source routing or other mechanisms that can alter the simple destination-based model.

sections.example: R1's network route points to 192.0.2.2, not to the final 198.51.100.20 destination as a neighbor. If R1's transit port is down, checking only the configured static line can be misleading. Conversely, after adding the Null0 /32, the transit link can remain healthy while the destination-specific test fails.
sections.heading: Resolve the next hop and examine the return path
keyPoints: Keep configured intent separate from the installed route and actual exchange.
Do not add a broad default route merely to mask an unresolved next hop.
sections.explanation: A next-hop address must lead to an appropriate local forwarding adjacency. The routing entry, interface state and neighbor resolution describe different dependencies. On Ethernet, IPv4 ARP resolves the immediate neighbor's MAC address. A ping response also needs a reverse path to the chosen source. The lab uses R1's connected transit address as the ping source, so R2 already knows how to return through the connected /30.

sections.example: This chapter directly teaches current v1.1 route components and default route selection, and announced v2.0 routing-table interpretation. Static commands create the controlled example; complete network, default, host and floating route practice is assigned to Days31-33. A structural content score is not evidence that any router ran.
sections.heading: Use a lookup and a test to close the explanation
keyPoints: Document the lookup result and same-target test as separate observations.
Rollback removes the exact host discard, leaving the known-working /24 intact.
sections.explanation: A destination-specific show command explains which route the router selects. A packet test asks whether the exchange completes. Pair them before the fault, during the discard and after exact removal. If the predicted behavior is not observed, retain the actual output and inspect overlapping routes or an unintended source. Do not claim the routing table is wrong merely because a ping failed; the table may correctly select a configured discard.

content.metaTitle: CCNA Day 30: Read Routes and Apply Longest Prefix Match
takeaways: Decode codes and fields before selecting a route.
Separate installation preference from forwarding specificity.
Different prefix lengths can coexist in the routing table.
A host discard can override an otherwise working network route.
Next-hop reachability and return paths still need verification.
A successful lookup is not the same as a successful application exchange.
objectives: Identify route code, prefix, mask, next hop, AD, metric and default-route meaning.
Separate routing-table construction from longest-prefix forwarding.
Explain connected and local entries without confusing them.
Predict how a /32 discard route overrides an installed /24.
Restore only the intentional route change and repeat the same lookup and ping.
content.plainAnswer: Forwarding uses the longest matching prefix among installed routes. Administrative distance helps choose a route source for the same prefix; protocol metrics rank paths within their own rules. Do not compare a /32 and a /24 by distance and call the lower distance the winner: they can coexist, and the matching /32 is more specific.

visualStory.title: Specificity wins this packet lookup

stages.title: Find the matches
stages.explanation: 198.51.100.20 matches the installed /24 and its exact /32.

stages.title: Choose specificity
stages.explanation: The matching /32 is longer, so its Null0 action wins despite AD200.

stages.title: Remove and recheck

beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: A route can have a less-preferred administrative distance and still win a packet lookup because it describes a more specific destination. Confusing installation and forwarding can make a deliberate discard look like a mysterious network outage.

firstPractice.hint: The prefix length is the number after the slash. Match the address first; different prefix lengths are not identical-route competitors.
firstPractice.task: On paper, compare installed 198.51.100.0/24 via 192.0.2.2 with AD1 and 198.51.100.20/32 to Null0 with AD200. Select the forwarding action for 198.51.100.20 and for 198.51.100.21.
firstPractice.expected: The .20 destination selects the /32 discard. The .21 destination does not match that host route and selects the /24 next hop.

beginnerGuide.startingPoint: Write the destination 198.51.100.20 at the top of your notes. Under it list every route whose range contains that address. Only then choose the most specific prefix; do not start by circling the smallest number anywhere in the output.

checkUnderstanding.hint: Decide whether the two entries describe the same destination prefix or overlapping ranges.
checkUnderstanding.answer: They are different prefixes and can both be installed. During forwarding, .20 matches both, and /32 is longer than /24. AD does not make a broader route override a more-specific installed route.
checkUnderstanding.question: Why does the AD200 host route beat the AD1 network route for .20?

everydayComparison.whereItStops: The directory metaphor does not model routing protocol metrics, next-hop resolution or packet loss. Only the actual installed entries determine this lookup.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: The /24 resembles the wider office entry, while the /32 resembles one exact destination. Both records can exist without competing to describe the same-sized range.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: A directory may have a general office address and a special instruction for one named room. The room-specific entry provides more detail than the building-wide entry.

teachingPrelude.explanation: Read the table in two stages. First ask why an entry qualified for installation. Then, for one packet destination, compare only the installed matching prefixes. Use the worked addresses to make that distinction concrete before entering the lab's commands.

practiceQuestions.answer: Administrative distance 110 and OSPF metric 20, not delay or hop count.
practiceQuestions.question: What does [110/20] mean in a normal OSPF route row?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The bracket order is distance then metric. A metric's meaning depends on its protocol; it is not directly comparable to an unrelated protocol's value.

practiceQuestions.answer: They describe different prefixes, even though one range lies inside the other.
practiceQuestions.question: Why can /24 and /32 routes both appear?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Installation can retain both. Forwarding then selects the longest matching prefix for the actual destination address.

practiceQuestions.answer: C describes the connected network; L identifies the router's own local address.
practiceQuestions.question: What is the distinction between C and L?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A local host route supports delivery to the router itself. The connected prefix describes the attached subnet used to reach neighbors.

practiceQuestions.answer: The .20/32 host route matches only .20, not .21.
practiceQuestions.question: Why does .21 still select the /24 during the fault?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The lookup chooses from matching prefixes only. Selection of the /24 does not assert that any endpoint currently owns .21.

practiceQuestions.answer: No; it is local route-source preference, not security validation or measured performance.
practiceQuestions.question: Does AD1 prove the route is secure or fast?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A static route can point to an unusable or undesirable path. Operational verification and security policy require independent evidence.

practiceQuestions.answer: R2 owns that local address and can terminate the ICMP exchange itself.
practiceQuestions.question: Why is R2's loopback a complete destination here?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The lesson does not claim a server exists behind R2. Its address plan and diagram explicitly end at the software interface.

realWorldScenario.title: A specific discard hidden beneath a working summary
realWorldScenario.takeaway: A working broad route can coexist with a more-specific black hole. Destination-specific evidence and a precise rollback explain the result more reliably than comparing every AD value in the table.
realWorldScenario.situation: In a hypothetical maintenance lab, the network route to 198.51.100.0/24 remains installed and R2's transit address replies. Yet one destination, .20, fails after a change. The responsible operator asks for a destination-specific lookup rather than arguing that the route with the smallest administrative distance must always carry the packet.
walkthrough: Record the failing destination and source, then verify that the original transit link and next hop still exist.
List every installed route matching .20, including host routes that a brief table scan might miss.
Compare prefix lengths before considering same-prefix source preference. Identify whether the selected exit is Null0.
Remove only the documented temporary /32 discard, not the broader network route or unrelated policy.
Repeat the exact destination lookup and ping; retain any remaining failure as a separate question.

IOSv examples use GigabitEthernet0/0 and GigabitEthernet0/1. Confirm those exact ports in the workbench and show ip interface brief before configuring; if your image differs, document an explicit port substitution first.

Decline the initial configuration dialog on a new authorized node, press Enter to reach the prompt, then use enable. Do not bypass unknown credentials. All displayed expected results are predictions, not author runtime.

If a route appears but traffic fails, examine neighbor and reply-path evidence rather than assuming installation proves reachability.

glossary.meaning: A manually configured route for a destination subnet. It supplies a local forwarding instruction, not a route automatically installed on every other router.
A static route naming the next router's IP address. IOS must resolve that address to a usable output interface.
A static route naming the local output interface without a next-hop address. On Ethernet this can cause ARP for individual destinations and reliance on proxy ARP.
A static route containing both the local output interface and the adjacent next-hop address. It makes the intended Ethernet forwarding relationship explicit.
ARP finds an IPv4 neighbor's Ethernet address. Proxy ARP is a router answering on behalf of another destination; it can hide an inappropriate interface-only route.
A routing lookup used to determine how to reach a configured next hop. A route line alone does not establish that the intended neighbor or service is alive.
The source is the address from which a packet is sent. A reply needs a route back to that source; choosing a different ping source can expose a missing reverse route.
A software interface with an address that the router owns. Here loopbacks are explicit source and destination endpoints, not networks full of unseen PCs.
A mask defines the destination range of a route. A /24 network route differs from a /32 host route, a /0 default or a higher-distance floating backup.
Running configuration records intended commands. The routing table records selected entries. ARP and traffic tests add further evidence about actual forwarding.

sections.example: R1 uses destination 203.0.113.0 with mask 255.255.255.0 and next hop 192.0.2.2. The destination is R2's loopback network, while the next hop is R2's transit interface. Swapping those addresses would describe a different and likely unusable instruction.
sections.heading: A static route is a local destination instruction
keyPoints: Write destination, mask and next hop in separate worksheet columns.
An accepted command still needs installed-route and traffic verification.
sections.explanation: The IOS command ip route takes a destination network, mask and forwarding information. It is entered in global configuration mode and affects only that router. The destination must be a valid prefix for the chosen mask, not a host address incorrectly paired with a network mask. A static route does not assign an interface address, create a remote network or tell another router how to return traffic.

sections.example: For the same /24, compare 'ip route 203.0.113.0 255.255.255.0 192.0.2.2' and the fully specified form adding GigabitEthernet0/0 before 192.0.2.2. The paper-only serial form uses Serial0/0 without an IP next hop. Do not type a Serial0/0 command into IOSv, which has no such lab interface.
sections.heading: Compare three forms before choosing one
keyPoints: Use the local exit interface name, not the peer's port name.
Do not depend on proxy ARP to make an unsuitable Ethernet recipe appear correct.
sections.explanation: Next-hop-only syntax names the neighbor address and lets the router resolve the output interface. A fully specified route adds the local output interface, which is useful on Ethernet and makes the intended adjacency clear. An exit-interface-only route identifies no neighbor. That form is appropriate on a true point-to-point serial interface in the comparison example, but can cause Ethernet to resolve many remote destinations as though they were attached. A cable directly between two routers does not change Ethernet's multiaccess forwarding semantics.

sections.example: The .2 transit neighbor should be reachable from R1 before the remote loopback test. The ARP entry should correspond to the immediate transit neighbor rather than each address in 203.0.113.0/24. A fully specified route binds that forwarding intent to Gi0/0, but cannot make an unplugged or stopped R2 answer.
sections.heading: Verify route eligibility and neighbor resolution separately
keyPoints: Configured, installed and reachable are three different claims.
A next-hop-only route can resolve unexpectedly through another route in more complex designs.
sections.explanation: A route may remain in running configuration while its intended next hop is unresolved or its interface is unavailable. Conversely, an installed route can point to a next hop whose Ethernet neighbor cannot actually be reached. Check interface state, the connected transit prefix, the destination-specific route and ARP evidence. Avoid clearing all ARP or routing state as a first response; doing so destroys useful context and can affect unrelated traffic.

sections.example: R1 sends to 203.0.113.1 with source 198.51.100.1. R2's reply needs 198.51.100.0/24 through 192.0.2.1. During the fault, R1 still has its forward route and can still reach 192.0.2.2. That surviving transit reachability is useful evidence rather than a contradiction.
sections.heading: The reply follows its own routing lookup
keyPoints: Inspect the reply destination explicitly.
Do not replace a missing exact route with an unexamined default just to make one test pass.
sections.explanation: Each direction is routed independently. A request to R2's loopback can arrive successfully even when R2 has no path to the source loopback. Ping's failure then does not prove the forward route is wrong. A source-qualified ping is useful because it holds the return destination constant. The lab's two routes are exact network routes, not broad defaults, so deleting the reverse /24 has a visible and explainable effect.

sections.example: The current v1.1 static-routing objective includes both IP families and all four route types. The v2.0 objective emphasizes troubleshooting them. Completing only today's IPv4 network-route lab is therefore partial coverage, even though its configuration and source-aware diagnosis are necessary skills.
sections.heading: Scope the route types across the sequence
keyPoints: Do not mark both-stack static routing complete from one IPv4 exercise.
A floating backup is an installation preference, not automatic detection of every remote outage.
sections.explanation: A network route covers a subnet, a host route covers one address, and a default covers otherwise unmatched destinations. A floating static uses a higher AD than a preferred route for the same prefix and becomes eligible when that preferred route is absent. This chapter configures network routes and diagnoses their bidirectional dependency. Day 32 performs default, host and floating exercises, and Day 33 supplies the IPv6 route-type counterpart.

sections.example: The expected lesson result is recovery of the two loopback exchanges after replacing the reverse /24. Record actual accepted commands and outputs rather than formatting a predicted success as a transcript. CML is suitable for supported configuration reasoning, but this exercise does not measure hardware throughput or a production change window.
sections.heading: Choose an exact inverse and a meaningful retest
keyPoints: Rollback restores the known state; it is not a broad cleanup guess.
No independent review, image QA or runtime success is implied by static content validation.
sections.explanation: Before introducing the fault, copy the working R2 route into the private worksheet and write its exact restoration command. Remove only that route after baseline success. Preserve the forward lookup, transit test and failed fixed-source exchange. Restore the same reverse route and repeat both loopback-to-loopback tests. Do not erase configurations, reload nodes or reset the entire interface to recover a one-line change.

content.plainAnswer: An IPv4 static route tells one router how to forward toward a destination prefix. On Ethernet, specifying the neighbor address, and often the exit interface too, avoids treating every remote destination as directly attached. Verify the installed route, the immediate neighbor and the route back to the packet's actual source.

visualStory.title: The request and reply need different routes

stages.title: Send the request
stages.explanation: R1 routes the request through R2 to its local 203.0.113.1 loopback.

stages.title: Route the reply
stages.explanation: R2 needs 198.51.100.0/24 to return to the explicit source loopback.

visualStory.altText: R1's source loopback sends through the transit to R2's loopback. The reply targets R1's loopback network and needs R2's separate reverse route.

beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: A successful ping from a router's transit address can give false confidence that all remote networks work. Specifying the source tests the actual reverse-route requirement instead of whichever source the router happens to choose.

firstPractice.hint: Reverse the packet addresses, not the static command's mask. Each router evaluates the reply destination independently.
firstPractice.task: On paper, a ping leaves R1 with source 198.51.100.1 and destination 203.0.113.1. Write the reply's source and destination, then identify the remote prefix R2 needs.
firstPractice.expected: The reply originates at 203.0.113.1 and targets 198.51.100.1, so R2 needs a route covering 198.51.100.0/24 in this lab.

beginnerGuide.startingPoint: Write R1 Loopback0 198.51.100.1 and R2 Loopback0 203.0.113.1 at opposite sides of the page. Between them place only the 192.0.2.0/30 transit. Mark the address that each router must reach to return a reply.

checkUnderstanding.hint: The outgoing interface address is in the transit subnet both routers already know.
checkUnderstanding.answer: R1 may source that ping from 192.0.2.1. R2 has a directly connected route to the transit /30, so it can reply without a route to 198.51.100.0/24. The loopback-sourced test exercises the missing remote return path.
checkUnderstanding.question: Why might a default-source ping still work after R2's reverse /24 is removed?

everydayComparison.whereItStops: Routing is not postal delivery: ARP, interface state and prefix selection still determine forwarding. This analogy cannot promise delivery or diagnose a filter.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: Each static route is a local instruction for one direction. The source written on the request determines the destination that the return route must cover.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: Two offices can each know how to send a parcel to the other. Giving directions to only one office does not guarantee that a reply can find its way back.

teachingPrelude.explanation: Draw the request and the reply before configuring either route. A router-generated ping often uses its outgoing interface as the source by default; that can hide a missing route to another source subnet. This lesson names the loopback source explicitly so the test exercises both planned routes.
teachingPrelude.labBoundary: Two virtual routers, one transit Ethernet link and two loopback endpoints. No public network, dynamic protocol or proxy-ARP-dependent lab. Interface-only serial syntax is a paper comparison because this topology has no serial link.

practiceQuestions.answer: The destination network or host prefix, not the local interface address.
practiceQuestions.question: What does the first address in ip route identify?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The subsequent mask defines that destination range. The next-hop field names a forwarding neighbor, so swapping these meanings changes the route.

practiceQuestions.answer: It avoids treating every remote destination as if it were directly attached.
practiceQuestions.question: Why prefer an explicit neighbor on Ethernet?
practiceQuestions.explanation: An interface-only Ethernet route may trigger ARP for individual remote destinations and rely on proxy ARP. This is not the same as a true point-to-point serial link.

practiceQuestions.answer: No; each static route is configured locally on its own router.
practiceQuestions.question: Does adding R1's route create R2's return route?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Replies are new packets whose destination is the request's source. R2 independently needs a route covering that source.

practiceQuestions.answer: They give explicit source and destination addresses without adding unconfigured host devices.
practiceQuestions.question: Why are loopbacks used as endpoints?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Their networks are remote across the transit, so a source-qualified exchange requires both network routes. They do not represent a hidden LAN of clients.

practiceQuestions.answer: A static route naming the destination, mask, local exit interface and next-hop IP.
practiceQuestions.question: What is a fully specified route?
practiceQuestions.explanation: It makes the intended Ethernet adjacency explicit but does not independently confirm the neighbor's liveness or the final service.

practiceQuestions.answer: Default, host and floating routes plus the IPv6 counterpart are completed in the following lessons.
practiceQuestions.question: What part of the exam static-routing objective remains?
practiceQuestions.explanation: This chapter's IPv4 network-route exercise is deliberately scoped. One successful test cannot establish mastery of every route type in both stacks.

realWorldScenario.title: The router ping passed, but the source subnet could not return
realWorldScenario.takeaway: Source selection changes the return-path requirement. A useful test matches the intended traffic, and a complete static design accounts for both independently selected directions.
realWorldScenario.situation: In a hypothetical branch, an operator tests a remote loopback from the router and gets replies, then concludes the remote route is complete. A later test using the branch loopback as source fails. The first test used the transit interface source, which the far router already knew as connected; the branch loopback network lacked a reverse route.
walkthrough: Record the source and destination of both tests instead of comparing only the word ping.
Verify the outgoing route to the remote loopback still selects the intended transit neighbor.
On the far router, look up the branch loopback source prefix and identify its missing reverse route.
Restore the authorized exact reverse network route and leave the forward route unchanged.
Retest with the fixed source in both directions, then explain why the earlier transit-sourced success was narrower evidence.

title: Default, host, and floating static routes

lab.goal: Establish a fixed-source baseline, withdraw both primary endpoints, test the backup, restore the link and diagnose a temporary host discard. Predicted outcomes below are not fabricated router transcripts.
setup: Use Cisco Modeling Labs 2.10 with its legally entitled bundled IOSv 15.9M reference image. Record the complete show version release; do not export that image to GNS3. No paid API is involved.
Create fresh nodes and only the listed links. No External Connector, NAT node, bridge, public uplink or production network is permitted. Leave console access independent of the test data links.

IOSv examples use GigabitEthernet0/0 and GigabitEthernet0/1. Confirm those exact ports in the workbench and show ip interface brief before configuring; if your image differs, document an explicit port substitution first.

Decline the initial configuration dialog on a new authorized node, press Enter to reach the prompt, then use enable. Do not bypass unknown credentials. All displayed expected results are predictions, not author runtime.
Without an entitled compatible image, complete the address and route-selection worksheet only. Mark command execution, packet forwarding and recovery unmeasured.

glossary.meaning: The IPv4 prefix 0.0.0.0/0, matching every destination but selected only when no installed, more-specific matching route applies.
A /32 IPv4 route covering exactly one address. It can override a matching network or default route regardless of their lower administrative distance.
A local preference between eligible route sources for the same prefix; lower values are preferred. It is not a latency measurement or a comparison across different prefix lengths.
A configured static route with higher distance than its intended same-prefix primary. It can become selected when that primary is no longer eligible.
A logical discard interface. A selected route to Null0 intentionally drops matching traffic rather than forwarding it to another device.
Failover moves work to an available alternative after the preferred choice is lost. Failback restores the preferred choice; neither term promises zero packet loss.
A static route naming both the local exit interface and adjacent next-hop address, making the intended Ethernet adjacency explicit.
A software interface belonging to a router. Its address can be the actual source or destination of this lab's ping without a hidden host or LAN.

sections.example: R1 has defaults via 192.0.2.2 and 192.0.2.6. Its connected /30 transit networks and local addresses remain more specific. A ping to R2's 203.0.113.10 uses the default because R1 has no remote /24 until a deliberate host route changes that lookup.
sections.heading: A default is a fallback destination range
keyPoints: A /0 can be selected without any Internet attachment.
Do not use ip default-gateway as a substitute on an IP-routing router.
sections.explanation: The command ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 supplies a next hop for destinations without a more-specific installed match. A default does not provide Internet service by itself, distribute routes to peers or repair a missing return path. In this lab it reaches only R2's explicit loopback endpoint. R2 has no onward provider and needs no default of its own.

sections.example: R1's two defaults have identical destination and mask, but different interfaces, neighbors and distances. R2 similarly has two 198.51.100.0/24 return routes. A /32 marked 200 would not be an alternative to /0 because their destination scopes differ.
sections.heading: A floating route must compete for the same prefix
keyPoints: Inspect running configuration as well as the selected table.
Equal-distance eligible alternatives are not the intended floating-primary design.
sections.explanation: A normal static route has default distance 1. Here distance 200 makes another /0 less preferred while both links are usable. Use a value greater than the intended primary and less than 255; distance 255 does not install. Raising distance does not reduce bandwidth or delay a packet. The same idea applies to a static backup for a dynamic route, but this lab uses two statics so no protocol is hidden.

sections.example: We administratively shut Gi0/0 on R1 and R2. This models a complete primary-link withdrawal without assuming CML's virtual cable signals down identically on every release. The backup can still fail if its addresses or R2's return route are wrong; distance alone cannot repair those faults.
sections.heading: Interface failure is not every possible service failure
keyPoints: Test both forwarding directions after withdrawing the primary.
Never infer end-service health solely from route installation.
sections.explanation: Both interface and next-hop information are specified to tie each route to its intended Ethernet link. Removing that local interface dependency makes the primary ineligible in this exercise. A remote server failure with the local interface still up may leave the route installed. More advanced tracking can address some cases, but no tracking object or probe is configured here.

sections.example: The instruction ip route 203.0.113.10 255.255.255.255 Null0 200 affects one destination. The healthy /0 does not rescue packets that selected this /32. Removing the /32 restores default-based forwarding without altering either default.
sections.heading: A host exception can defeat the default
keyPoints: A higher-distance more-specific route is not automatically a backup.
Check the exact failed destination, not just the default route display.
sections.explanation: An IPv4 host route uses mask 255.255.255.255. Longest-prefix lookup selects it for exactly that address even if a matching default has a lower distance. Null0 is a deliberate discard, not a router with an unresolved address. After the backup test, the lab temporarily adds a host discard and verifies that the route lookup explains the failed exchange.

sections.example: A report saying 'failover works' is incomplete if it contains only a backup configuration line. A useful report shows the primary absent, backup selected and the same endpoint exchange restored. It also labels any packet loss or elapsed time unmeasured when no real run occurred.
sections.heading: Keep evidence and exam scope explicit
keyPoints: No runtime, pixel QA or independent review is claimed here.
The complete static objective requires both address families and all reserved route types.
sections.explanation: Use the same loopback source and destination at baseline, on the backup, during the host fault and after restoration. Preserve selected prefix, exit interface and next hop with each observation. The current v1.1 window ends February 2, 2027; the announced v2.0 starts February 3. This lesson supplies the IPv4 default, host and floating portion, while Day 33 provides the IPv6 counterpart.

content.metaTitle: CCNA Day 32: Default, Host and Floating Static Routes
takeaways: Defaults cover otherwise unmatched destinations, not guaranteed Internet service.
Floating routes compete with primaries for the same prefix.
Explicit interfaces constrain the intended Ethernet adjacency.
Both directions need a usable backup route.
A host discard can override a healthy default.
No loss or convergence duration is claimed without a real measurement.
objectives: Distinguish default, host and floating route purposes.
Configure identical-prefix alternatives with distances 1 and 200.
Verify failover and return-path behavior separately.
Explain why a /32 discard beats a /0 default.
Restore both interfaces and remove only the deliberate host fault.
content.plainAnswer: A default route handles otherwise unmatched destinations. A host route matches one address more specifically. A floating static is a higher-distance alternative to the same prefix, not a universal outage detector. Check which prefix matches first, which same-prefix route is installed, and whether both request and reply can actually traverse the chosen links.

everydayComparison.whereItStops: Signs do not model neighbor resolution, independent return paths or router failure detection. This comparison explains scope, not measured convergence time.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: The specific room resembles a host prefix; the general sign resembles a default. The two alternative exits resemble routes for the same prefix with different local preferences.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: A building can have a general exit sign and a specific instruction for one room. The room-specific instruction takes precedence for that room, while another exit can replace a closed general exit.

teachingPrelude.explanation: Keep two decisions separate. Route installation chooses among candidates for an identical prefix, while packet forwarding chooses the longest matching installed prefix. A high-distance /32 is not a backup for a low-distance /0. This lesson deliberately creates both situations so the distinction is visible.
teachingPrelude.labBoundary: Two isolated routers and two direct Ethernet links only. Both loopbacks terminate on the routers. No provider, Internet destination or service-liveness tracking is present; all results are predictions until executed.

practiceQuestions.answer: No; it is a destination fallback toward a next hop.
practiceQuestions.question: Does a default route prove Internet access?
practiceQuestions.explanation: This isolated topology ends at R2's loopback and contains no provider. Route syntax cannot create an external service.

practiceQuestions.answer: It is higher than the primary's 1 and lower than 255.
practiceQuestions.question: Why is distance 200 used on the second default?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The same-prefix primary wins while eligible. A distance of 255 would not be a usable fallback.

practiceQuestions.answer: It explicitly withdraws each direction's local interface dependency.
practiceQuestions.question: Why disable both primary ports?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Virtual carrier signaling is not assumed. The test states precisely what failed and keeps the backup links untouched.

practiceQuestions.question: Why does the /32 beat the /0?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Distance chooses among equal-prefix candidates; it does not let a default override an installed host route.

practiceQuestions.question: Will a failed remote service always activate the backup?
practiceQuestions.explanation: This lab detects an interface dependency withdrawal, not application health. No tracking probe is configured.

realWorldScenario.title: The backup activated, but one address still failed
realWorldScenario.takeaway: Route availability and destination specificity are independent questions. Diagnose the chosen prefix before changing backup preferences.
realWorldScenario.situation: In a hypothetical isolated branch test, an operator sees the backup default installed and assumes every destination is covered. One diagnostic address still fails because a forgotten host discard is more specific. Repeatedly changing the default's distance cannot override that /32.
walkthrough: Identify the exact failing destination and the packet's source.
Inspect its longest matching prefix instead of only the gateway-of-last-resort line.
Confirm whether the selected action is a next hop or Null0.
Remove only the authorized mistaken host entry, leaving both default preferences unchanged.
Repeat the same exchange and retain both lookup states as the explanation.

title: IPv6 static routes

lab.goal: Configure both links, verify a network route, withdraw its primary candidate, exercise the default, demonstrate a host discard and restore the baseline. No IOSv runtime was executed during authoring.
setup: Use Cisco Modeling Labs 2.10 with its legally entitled bundled IOSv 15.9M reference image. Record the complete show version release; do not export that image to GNS3. No paid API is involved.
Create fresh nodes and only the listed links. No External Connector, NAT node, bridge, public uplink or production network is permitted. Leave console access independent of the test data links.

IOSv examples use GigabitEthernet0/0 and GigabitEthernet0/1. Confirm those exact ports in the workbench and show ip interface brief before configuring; if your image differs, document an explicit port substitution first.

Decline the initial configuration dialog on a new authorized node, press Enter to reach the prompt, then use enable. Do not bypass unknown credentials. All displayed expected results are predictions, not author runtime.
Without an entitled compatible image, complete the address and route-selection worksheet only. Mark command execution, packet forwarding and recovery unmeasured.

glossary.meaning: An IPv6 address range written with a slash and count of fixed leading bits, such as 2001:db8:20::/64. IPv6 addresses contain 128 bits.
A network route covers a prefix such as /64. The default ::/0 covers otherwise unmatched destinations. A host /128 identifies one exact IPv6 address.
A link-local address such as fe80::2 identifies an interface on its own link and is not forwarded between links. The output interface disambiguates its scope.
IPv6's ICMPv6-based mechanisms for discovering local neighbors and their link-layer addresses. IPv6 does not use IPv4 ARP.
A higher-distance candidate for the same prefix. Here the /64 at distance 200 becomes selected after the preferred /64 at distance 1 is removed.
A route containing the destination prefix, local exit interface and next-hop address. A link-local next hop needs the interface because its scope is local to a link.
A ping whose source address is explicitly selected. It tests the reverse route to that source rather than relying on the router's default source choice.
Null0 intentionally discards selected traffic. A /128 discard is more specific than matching /64 and /0 routes, even when its distance is higher.

sections.example: R1 Loopback0 is 2001:db8:10::10/64. R2 Loopback0 is 2001:db8:20::10/64. These are two distinct software endpoints on different routers, not the universal ::1 loopback address and not unnamed client networks.
sections.heading: Start with forwarding and exact address scope
keyPoints: Documentation prefixes are safe examples, not external reachable services.
Record the source address with every end-to-end test.
sections.explanation: An IPv6 interface address does not by itself state that the router should forward IPv6 between interfaces. This lab enables ipv6 unicast-routing, assigns addresses and checks the relevant interface states. The special address ::1 means the local node itself; it is not the same thing as the router's named Loopback0 interface carrying a documentation-prefix address. Avoid using ::1 as a remote lab target.

sections.example: The primary instruction names GigabitEthernet0/0 and fe80::2. The backup names GigabitEthernet0/1 and fe80::22. The destination remains 2001:db8:20::/64 in both commands. A typographical next hop can leave configured intent that never produces a working exchange.
sections.heading: A link-local next hop needs an interface
keyPoints: Use show ipv6 neighbors for the local neighbor evidence.
Do not forward link-local source or destination packets to a different link.
sections.explanation: Link-local addresses are valid only on their local link. The address may appear on separate links without identifying a single global location, so an IPv6 static route using such a next hop must also state the outgoing interface. Neighbor Discovery resolves the neighbor's link-layer address on that interface. Do not diagnose this using show ip arp, which displays IPv4 information.

sections.example: When only ::/0 remains for the remote destination, a successful probe establishes the route to this particular R2 endpoint. It does not establish reachability to arbitrary documentation addresses. No third endpoint is invented merely to demonstrate a default lookup.
sections.heading: Exercise network, default and host scopes
keyPoints: Keep the final endpoint constant while changing route scope.
A /128 Null0 route is an intentional drop, not failed neighbor discovery.
sections.explanation: A /64 route covers the entire named destination network. The default ::/0 covers any destination lacking a more-specific installed match. A /128 matches one address. The commands in the lab deliberately test these scopes with the same final endpoint: the network route normally wins, the default carries that exchange when both network candidates are removed, and the temporary host discard overrides both.

sections.example: The backup test proves selection after an administrative route withdrawal, not link failure detection. R2's configured backup return route is retained but not exercised by this one-sided withdrawal. Day 32's two-sided interface test provides the corresponding IPv4 failure experiment; do not relabel this test as a measured two-sided IPv6 outage.
sections.heading: Floating selection does not require a broken cable
keyPoints: Asymmetric routing is not automatically a fault.
Describe the actual withdrawn dependency instead of overstating failover coverage.
sections.explanation: This exercise removes R1's preferred /64 configuration line while leaving both cables up. The higher-distance /64 should then install through the backup link. The lower-distance default does not override it because /64 is more specific. R2's replies still prefer its primary /64 return route, producing an explicitly asymmetric exchange. That is permitted here because no stateful firewall or policy is present.

sections.example: The final retest should show the preferred remote /64, the correct scoped neighbor and the same loopback-source exchange. Current v1.1 static-route coverage is completed across Days 31-33, not by this IPv6 lesson alone; v2.0 troubleshooting coverage likewise spans the two stacks and remains unmeasured until performed.
sections.heading: Read three independent kinds of evidence
keyPoints: Do not paste predicted success markers into a runtime report.
Unexpected behavior should retain its original output for review.
sections.explanation: The configuration shows what was requested, the selected routing table shows usable route choices, and neighbor plus traffic tests show more about forwarding. A route can exist while the neighbor cannot answer. A neighbor can answer while the source lacks a return route. Compare these observations at each stage and preserve real output only after execution.

content.plainAnswer: IPv6 static routing uses ipv6 route with a prefix length rather than an IPv4 mask. Enable IPv6 forwarding, identify the next hop and specify an interface for a link-local neighbor. Verify /64 network, ::/0 default, /128 host and higher-distance floating behavior separately, keeping the packet's source and return route explicit.

checkUnderstanding.hint: Link-local addresses cannot be forwarded beyond their link.
checkUnderstanding.answer: No. It can name an adjacent next hop only with the correct link scope. The remote destination uses its own routable prefix, and the router needs an output interface for a link-local static next hop.

everydayComparison.whereItStops: An interface is a network scope, not a physical floor. The comparison does not model Neighbor Discovery, prefix lookup or actual packet timing.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: The floor resembles interface scope for a link-local next hop. The final office resembles the remote destination prefix, which is not replaced by the local neighbor's address.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: A building can have the same room number on different floors. A local room reference needs the floor as well as the number, while a full delivery destination names the final office.

teachingPrelude.explanation: An IPv6 destination and its next hop have different jobs. The packet remains addressed to the remote loopback; fe80::2 identifies only the adjacent router receiving its next Ethernet frame. Writing the correct interface is part of the next-hop identity, not optional decoration.
teachingPrelude.labBoundary: Two CML IOSv routers with two direct links and local software loopbacks. Addresses in 2001:db8::/32 are documentation examples, not public services. No SLAAC clients, DHCPv6, DNS or Internet path is implied.

practiceQuestions.answer: It is ::/0, not the loopback address ::1.
practiceQuestions.question: What is the IPv6 default prefix?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A zero-length prefix is a fallback for otherwise unmatched destinations. The address ::1 identifies only the local node.

practiceQuestions.answer: The next hop has link-local scope and needs a specific output link.
practiceQuestions.question: Why include an interface with fe80::2?
practiceQuestions.explanation: An address alone does not identify which local link contains that neighbor. The route must include the intended interface.

practiceQuestions.answer: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery evidence from show ipv6 neighbors.
practiceQuestions.question: What replaces IPv4 ARP evidence here?
practiceQuestions.explanation: IPv6 uses ICMPv6-based neighbor mechanisms. An IPv4 ARP table cannot verify the IPv6 next-hop mapping.

practiceQuestions.answer: The /64 is a longer matching prefix than ::/0.
practiceQuestions.question: Why can the AD 200 /64 beat an AD 1 default?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Distance compares eligible routes for an identical prefix, while forwarding uses the longest matching installed prefix.

practiceQuestions.answer: Only R1's preferred /64 configuration line, not either physical link.
practiceQuestions.question: What does the backup test actually withdraw?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The result demonstrates route selection after an administrative withdrawal. It does not measure link-down detection or two-sided convergence.

practiceQuestions.answer: No; it matches only its one exact IPv6 destination.
practiceQuestions.question: Does a /128 Null0 exception affect the whole /64?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Other addresses may continue to match the network route, though this lab supplies only one real destination endpoint.

realWorldScenario.title: The neighbor address was right on the wrong link
realWorldScenario.takeaway: For a link-local next hop, the address and interface form one scoped forwarding choice. Correct address text on the wrong port is still wrong.
realWorldScenario.situation: In a hypothetical training network, a learner copies a link-local next hop but pairs it with the backup port instead of the primary. The router has IPv6 enabled and the destination prefix looks correct, yet the frame cannot reach the intended neighbor on that interface.
walkthrough: Separate destination prefix from next-hop address in the route command.

title: Single-area OSPFv2 neighbors and router IDs

lab.goal: Build a complete OSPFv2 point-to-point exchange between two named loopbacks, remove only the Hello capability on one transit, and restore it. No router output or runtime is claimed by the authored lesson.
setup: Use Cisco Modeling Labs 2.10 with its legally entitled bundled IOSv 15.9M reference image. Record the complete show version release; do not export that image to GNS3. No paid API is involved.
Create fresh nodes and only the listed links. No External Connector, NAT node, bridge, public uplink or production network is permitted. Leave console access independent of the test data links.

IOSv examples use GigabitEthernet0/0 and GigabitEthernet0/1. Confirm those exact ports in the workbench and show ip interface brief before configuring; if your image differs, document an explicit port substitution first.

Decline the initial configuration dialog on a new authorized node, press Enter to reach the prompt, then use enable. Do not bypass unknown credentials. All displayed expected results are predictions, not author runtime.
Without an entitled compatible image, complete the address and route-selection worksheet only. Mark command execution, packet forwarding and recovery unmeasured.

glossary.meaning: Open Shortest Path First version 2 is a link-state routing protocol used here to learn IPv4 routes within one administrative routing domain.
An area is an OSPF topology database scope. Area 0 is the backbone; this beginner exercise uses only area 0 and has no area-border router.
A unique 32-bit OSPF identity displayed in dotted-decimal form. It is not necessarily an assigned interface address or a reachable ping target.
A Cisco local number selecting an OSPF process on one router. Neighboring routers can use different process numbers.
Hellos discover and maintain neighbors. The dead interval bounds how long the local router waits without an accepted Hello before declaring that neighbor lost.
A neighbor is discovered through OSPF communication. An adjacency is a selected neighbor relationship that synchronizes topology information; Full indicates completed synchronization.
A link-state advertisement describes topology information; the link-state database stores it. Shortest Path First calculates routes from that database using OSPF costs.
An OSPF interface that does not form neighbor relationships by sending Hellos. Its enabled connected prefix can still be advertised through other active adjacencies.
An OSPF interface setting for a link with two routers. It forms a full adjacency without a designated-router election; the underlying medium can still be Ethernet.

sections.example: R1 learns R2's 203.0.113.34/32 through OSPF, while its own 198.51.100.34/32 remains local. The transit 192.0.2.0/30 is already connected. A transit ping would therefore not prove that the remote loopback advertisement was learned.
sections.heading: OSPF learns topology before calculating routes
keyPoints: Inspect the remote prefix, not just any successful ping.
An area 0-only lab requires no area-border or redistribution configuration.
sections.explanation: OSPF is a link-state protocol: routers exchange descriptions of their local links and prefixes so each can calculate paths. A neighbor table, topology database and routing table answer different questions. Seeing a remote router ID in one output does not establish that every intended prefix was enabled, that a better route did not override OSPF, or that a final host answered.

sections.example: R1's identity 1.1.1.1 is distinct from its loopback 198.51.100.34. R2's identity 2.2.2.2 is distinct from 203.0.113.34. The local process numbers 10 and 20 select configuration containers; unlike area 0, they are not required to match across the cable.
sections.heading: Choose the router ID before enabling the links
keyPoints: Router IDs must be unique within the relevant OSPF domain.
A router ID is neither automatically a gateway nor an assigned host address.
sections.explanation: An explicit router-id command removes ambiguity. Without it, traditional IOS selection prefers the highest eligible loopback IPv4 address, then an eligible interface address when the process starts. The selected value does not continuously follow whichever address later becomes highest. Changing an established identity can require process restart and disrupt adjacencies, so this lesson sets it on fresh processes and does not issue a broad clear command.

sections.example: A stuck Init observation suggests one-way Hello processing, not proof of a missing remote static route. Persistent ExStart or Exchange warrants checks such as duplicate IDs, MTU agreement and packet delivery. Record evidence before applying broad resets or disabling MTU checks.
sections.heading: Know what a neighbor state actually says
keyPoints: Full is a control-plane result, not an application health certificate.
Do not require every transient state to appear in a captured manual transcript.
sections.explanation: Down means no recent accepted conversation; Init means a Hello was seen without confirmed two-way recognition. Two-Way means both sides recognize each other. ExStart and Exchange negotiate and exchange database summaries; Loading requests missing information; Full indicates synchronization is complete. Some transitions are too brief to observe in manual polling. On our point-to-point link, expect Full with no DR/BDR role. On broadcast segments, Two-Way can be normal between two non-designated routers.

sections.example: R1's Gi0/0 address is 192.0.2.1/30; R2's is 192.0.2.2/30. Both interfaces are enabled in area 0, while each Loopback0 is enabled but passive. Marking the transit passive removes the Hello relationship even though the Ethernet address remains configured and a connected ping can still work.
sections.heading: Enable the correct interface in the correct area
keyPoints: Passive is suitable for this loopback, not the required neighbor-facing transit.
OSPF network type is configured separately from the physical cable type.
sections.explanation: The interface command ip ospf process-id area 0 makes membership explicit. The older router-process network command selects local interfaces by address and wildcard; it does not create a route to an arbitrary remote network. On this two-router Ethernet cable, both ends deliberately use point-to-point OSPF type. Compare area, timers, network type, addressing and authentication policy when diagnosing a neighbor. No authentication is configured in this isolated exercise.

sections.example: For current v1.1, this chapter directly supports neighbor adjacency, point-to-point and router-ID tasks. Broadcast behavior continues in 35. Announced v2.0 expands the sequence to OSPFv3 in 36; this IPv4 lab alone is not complete two-version coverage.
sections.heading: Diagnose the intended fault without masking it
keyPoints: Do not infer precise convergence time from a default timer or a simulation.
Keep predictions distinct from actual terminal output and independent review.
sections.explanation: The controlled change makes R1's transit passive after a working baseline. After neighbor expiry and recalculation, the remote loopback route should disappear and its fixed-source exchange should fail. The connected transit can remain reachable. Restore only the passive setting, allow adjacency to reform, and repeat neighbor, route and traffic checks. Adding a static default would obscure the OSPF dependency instead of repairing it.

content.metaTitle: CCNA Day 34: OSPFv2 Neighbors and Router IDs
takeaways: OSPF exchanges topology information before calculating routes.
Router IDs are unique identities; process IDs are local numbers.
Area and compatible interface parameters matter to neighbors.
Full does not replace a destination-route or traffic check.
Passive endpoints differ from passive neighbor-facing transits.
Restore the exact fault and preserve runtime uncertainty.
objectives: Distinguish local process ID, router ID and area ID.
Configure single-area OSPFv2 on an explicit point-to-point link.
Interpret basic neighbor states without equating them with application health.
Verify learned loopback routes in both directions.
Diagnose and reverse one passive-transit mistake.
content.plainAnswer: OSPFv2 discovers compatible IPv4 neighbors, synchronizes topology information and calculates routes. Use unique router IDs and matching area and interface parameters; local process IDs need not match. A Full neighbor is useful evidence, but verify the learned destination route and an end-to-end exchange before declaring the intended network reachable.

beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Treating every number as a value that must match leads to unnecessary changes. Unique identities prevent confusion; shared link parameters let the actual neighboring interfaces communicate.

firstPractice.hint: Ask whether a value is local bookkeeping, shared link configuration or unique protocol identity.
firstPractice.task: Predict whether process 10 on R1 can become adjacent to process 20 on R2 when both transit interfaces use area 0 and compatible point-to-point settings.
firstPractice.expected: Yes. The local process IDs may differ; the router IDs must be unique and the neighbor-facing area and relevant parameters must agree.

beginnerGuide.startingPoint: Make three columns: process number, router ID and area. Fill R1 with 10,1.1.1.1,0 and R2 with 20,2.2.2.2,0. Put their transit IP addresses in a separate fourth column.

checkUnderstanding.hint: The command sets an identity, not an interface address.
checkUnderstanding.answer: No. Router ID is a 32-bit protocol identifier. A ping requires an actual assigned destination and valid forwarding; this lab instead tests R2 Loopback0 at 203.0.113.34.
checkUnderstanding.question: Does router-id 2.2.2.2 make that address pingable?

everydayComparison.whereItStops: OSPF does not copy an entire forwarding table like a book list. It exchanges topology information and each router independently calculates its own routes.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: The local catalog numbers resemble process IDs, the names resemble router IDs, and the shared collection resembles the area's topology information.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: Two librarians can keep different internal catalog numbers while agreeing on a shared collection and using distinct names when exchanging updates.

teachingPrelude.explanation: Separate identity, scope and local bookkeeping. R1's process 10 and R2's process 20 can participate in the same area 0 while identifying themselves as 1.1.1.1 and 2.2.2.2. None of these labels replaces the transit addresses used to deliver packets.
teachingPrelude.labBoundary: Two routers, one transit and two /32 loopbacks only. No redistribution, authentication, multi-area design, Internet default or performance measurement. Broadcast DR/BDR is reserved for Day 35; OSPFv3 is Day 36.

practiceQuestions.answer: No; they identify local processes on each Cisco router.
practiceQuestions.question: Must OSPF process numbers match across the cable?
practiceQuestions.explanation: R1 uses 10 and R2 uses 20 in this working design. Shared area and compatible neighbor-facing parameters are different requirements.

practiceQuestions.answer: No; each router needs a unique protocol identity.
practiceQuestions.question: Must router IDs match?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Duplicate router IDs can corrupt the intended topology identity. They are not shared area labels or default gateways.

practiceQuestions.answer: The selected neighbor relationship has completed database synchronization.
practiceQuestions.question: What does Full establish?
practiceQuestions.explanation: It does not prove every prefix is advertised or every destination application works. Route and traffic checks remain necessary.

practiceQuestions.answer: Its prefix can be advertised without seeking neighbors on a software endpoint.
practiceQuestions.question: Why leave Loopback0 passive?
practiceQuestions.explanation: No second router is attached to that loopback. Passive prevents unnecessary Hello behavior without removing its OSPF-enabled prefix.

practiceQuestions.answer: It uses the connected /30 and does not require the lost OSPF adjacency.
practiceQuestions.question: Why can the transit ping survive the fault?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The fault changes Hello participation, not the Ethernet address. Remote loopbacks depend on learned routes and expose the difference.

practiceQuestions.answer: The exact inverse is to remove passive status from the transit.
practiceQuestions.question: Why avoid a process reset to repair this fault?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A broad reset adds disruption and obscures attribution. The configured router IDs are already correct and need no restart.

realWorldScenario.title: The cable answered, but the routing conversation stopped
realWorldScenario.takeaway: A working Ethernet exchange does not establish an active routing-protocol relationship. Fix the intended adjacency dependency and verify the remote prefix.
realWorldScenario.situation: A hypothetical learner makes all interfaces passive to reduce unwanted OSPF Hellos. The intended transit is included accidentally. The connected neighbor still answers ping, yet remote loopbacks disappear because the only OSPF adjacency is lost.

title: OSPF broadcast networks, DR/BDR, and path cost

lab.goal: Build the complete shared VLAN, establish known roles, verify the direct R3-to-R2 route and restore an intentionally wrong R3 cost. No runtime output is fabricated and no alternate physical path is assumed.
setup: Use Cisco Modeling Labs 2.10 with its legally entitled bundled IOSv 15.9M reference image. Record the complete show version release; do not export that image to GNS3. No paid API is involved.
Create fresh nodes and only the listed links. No External Connector, NAT node, bridge, public uplink or production network is permitted. Leave console access independent of the test data links.

IOSv examples use GigabitEthernet0/0 and GigabitEthernet0/1. Confirm those exact ports in the workbench and show ip interface brief before configuring; if your image differs, document an explicit port substitution first.

Decline the initial configuration dialog on a new authorized node, press Enter to reach the prompt, then use enable. Do not bypass unknown credentials. All displayed expected results are predictions, not author runtime.
Without an entitled compatible image, complete the address and route-selection worksheet only. Mark command execution, packet forwarding and recovery unmeasured.
Add SW1 using the bundled IOSvL2 image. Map the three exact ports above; no uplinks, SVI or external bridge. Read show version on every node before configuration.
Follow R1, then R2, then R3 startup in order. Wait for the documented interface role before proceeding; a fresh lab has no prior election state.

lab.licensingNote: GNS3 does not provide Cisco images. Use software only when the applicable license or entitlement permits that environment. Do not share or redistribute image files. Cisco Modeling Labs is the official alternative; its reference images are licensed for use within CML unless separately licensed. A paper exercise needs no image, but does not establish hands-on competence. Virtual routers do not reproduce physical radios, PoE delivery, hardware forwarding rates or failover timing.

quiz.question: Which parameter influences DR election?
quiz.explanation: Eligible election candidates are compared using priority and then router ID, not packet latency.

quiz.question: Which parameter contributes to path calculation?
quiz.explanation: OSPF cost is directional and cumulative along the relevant path toward the destination.

quiz.question: What is R3's expected next hop to R2 Loopback0?
quiz.explanation: R2 owns the target and is directly reachable across the shared LAN; the DR is not a mandatory forwarding waypoint.

options: An OSPF cost sum of 100 plus 1.
quiz.question: What does metric 101 mean here?
quiz.explanation: The metric is an abstract path cost, not an observed delay, utilization or hop count.

quiz.question: What should rollback change?
quiz.explanation: Restoring the exact cost deviation preserves the known roles, addresses and working broadcast segment.

glossary.meaning: An OSPF mode for a shared multiaccess segment such as this Ethernet VLAN. It elects a DR and BDR to organize topology exchange.
The designated router and backup designated router coordinate adjacency and flooding on one broadcast segment. They are not automatically every packet's next hop.
A router that is neither DR nor BDR on the segment. It becomes fully adjacent to those two roles, not necessarily to every other DROTHER.
An election value from 0 through 255. Higher eligible priority is preferred during election; zero makes the interface ineligible for DR or BDR.
An established DR is not displaced merely because a new router arrives with a higher priority. Existing roles and startup history matter.
A directional routing metric assigned to an outgoing interface. OSPF selects lower total-cost paths within the applicable route class; cost is not milliseconds.
The numerator used with interface bandwidth to derive a default OSPF cost. Consistent reference settings are needed across a domain; an explicit interface cost overrides the calculation.
The control plane learns and calculates routes. The forwarding plane sends data using selected next hops; a DR control role does not require a data detour.

sections.example: R1, R2 and R3 attach to VLAN 35 with addresses 192.0.2.1, .2 and .3. Their OSPF area is 0. SW1 switches Ethernet frames but does not participate in OSPF, receive a router ID or need an IP address in this exercise.
sections.heading: A broadcast segment has local elected roles
keyPoints: DR and BDR are per-segment roles, not an area-wide king and deputy.
Do not label every Two-Way observation as a failed adjacency.
sections.explanation: A broadcast network type can contain several OSPF routers. DR and BDR roles reduce the need for every pair to maintain full database adjacencies. Each DROTHER becomes fully adjacent to the DR and BDR. Two DROTHERs can remain Two-Way normally. Our three-router lab has only one DROTHER, so it cannot demonstrate a DROTHER-to-DROTHER Two-Way pair; that remains an explicitly explained comparison.

sections.example: R1 uses priority 200, R2 uses 100 and R3 uses 0. R3 cannot become DR even though its router ID 3.3.3.3 is numerically highest. If you reuse a running lab with an existing DR, the expected roles may differ; use the fresh-project prerequisite rather than resetting a production process.
sections.heading: Election uses priority and history, not cost
keyPoints: Higher priority helps an eligible election candidate, not an already completed election.
A router ID breaks a tie; it does not override priority 0.
sections.explanation: Eligible candidates are compared using interface priority, with router ID breaking ties. Priority 0 cannot win either role. However, a higher-priority newcomer does not simply preempt an established DR. The lab therefore brings R1 online first and confirms its DR role before enabling R2, then confirms the backup before enabling R3. This preserves a clear startup history rather than promising election solely from a final configuration snapshot.

sections.example: R3 sources the test from 198.51.100.35 and targets R2's 203.0.113.35. Its next hop should be 192.0.2.2. R2 independently learns the route back to R3's loopback. R1 may remain crucial to the control relationship while absent from this chosen data path.
sections.heading: Data forwarding follows its selected next hop
keyPoints: Keep control relationships and packet paths visually distinct.
The endpoint loopbacks are on R2 and R3; no hidden client devices exist.
sections.explanation: The DR participates in topology exchange, but the forwarding path is calculated from the destination and costs. R3 can send directly to R2 across SW1 when the remote loopback belongs to R2. The switch is a Layer 2 transit, not another IP routing hop. Use a destination-route lookup and, if desired, observed packet evidence to establish forwarding; never draw a mandatory detour through the DR just because it organizes OSPF.

sections.example: R3's LAN cost 10 plus R2's loopback cost 1 gives metric 11. Setting only R3's LAN cost 100 gives 101. R2's return calculation still uses its own outgoing cost 10 plus R3's loopback 1. A hypothetical second path totaling 20 would become preferable to 101, but no such path exists in this lab.
sections.heading: Cost is directional and cumulative
keyPoints: Cost need not be symmetric in opposite directions.
Changing cost does not change DR priority or guarantee an application performance improvement.
sections.explanation: OSPF cost represents an outgoing interface contribution. A path's cost adds the relevant contributions toward the destination, not the sum of every interface seen on a diagram. Traditional Cisco default reference bandwidth is 100 Mbps, so faster links can share the minimum cost unless the reference is adjusted consistently. The lab uses explicit costs to avoid hiding arithmetic behind interface bandwidth defaults. The bandwidth command itself is not a physical speed upgrade.

sections.example: This lesson supplies the broadcast DR/BDR portion of current v1.1 single-area OSPFv2. Together with 34 it covers both reserved network types. Announced v2.0 adds the OSPFv3 counterpart in 36; the metric exercise here is supporting path-selection practice, not a claim of executed production optimization.
sections.heading: Repair a metric error with matching evidence
keyPoints: A healthy ping can coexist with an incorrect routing metric.
Predicted numeric results must be checked on the actual image before being called runtime evidence.
sections.explanation: The deliberate fault is a deviation from the intended cost plan, not a fabricated outage. After changing R3 to 100, record the route's higher metric, the unchanged next hop, the stable neighbor roles and the same ping. Restore the exact cost 10 and verify metric 11 returns. Do not clear OSPF, renumber interfaces or change priorities to repair a cost mistake.

content.metaTitle: CCNA Day 35: OSPF DR, BDR and Path Cost
takeaways: DR and BDR organize topology exchange on a segment.
Priority 0 prevents election, not normal routing.
Existing DR roles are not simply preempted by newcomers.
Forwarding does not require a DR detour.
Path cost is directional arithmetic, not latency.
A cost-plan fault can exist while packets still arrive.
objectives: Explain DR, BDR and DROTHER scope on a broadcast segment.
Distinguish priority, router ID and cost.
Predict metric 10 plus destination-loopback cost 1.
Verify the selected next hop does not require a DR detour.
Restore one deliberately incorrect interface cost and retest.
content.plainAnswer: On a broadcast OSPF segment, DR and BDR roles organize topology exchange. Priority and router ID influence election, while outgoing interface cost influences path calculation. These are different decisions: a data packet can go directly to another router on the shared LAN without passing through the DR. Verify roles, next hop and metric separately.

terms.meaning: An OSPF mode for a shared multiaccess segment such as this Ethernet VLAN. It elects a DR and BDR to organize topology exchange.
The designated router and backup designated router coordinate adjacency and flooding on one broadcast segment. They are not automatically every packet's next hop.
A router that is neither DR nor BDR on the segment. It becomes fully adjacent to those two roles, not necessarily to every other DROTHER.
An election value from 0 through 255. Higher eligible priority is preferred during election; zero makes the interface ineligible for DR or BDR.
An established DR is not displaced merely because a new router arrives with a higher priority. Existing roles and startup history matter.
A directional routing metric assigned to an outgoing interface. OSPF selects lower total-cost paths within the applicable route class; cost is not milliseconds.

teachingPrelude.explanation: Ask two independent questions: who coordinates OSPF exchange on this segment, and which adjacent router receives this particular data packet? The first is an election question. The second follows the destination route and its metric. Keeping them separate prevents treating the DR as a default gateway for every router.
teachingPrelude.labBoundary: One VLAN, three routers and one switch. No alternative routed path exists. The cost fault changes a metric, not necessarily connectivity; no failover, throughput or convergence timing is measured.
