glossary.meaning: OSPF version 3 retains link-state routing, areas and SPF while changing protocol structures for IPv6. This lesson uses its IPv6 function; later address-family extensions are outside the lab.
A dotted-decimal OSPF identity that remains 32 bits even when all carried routes and interfaces are IPv6. It does not assign an IPv4 address.
An adjacent IPv6 router address associated with an output interface. OSPFv3 normally uses link-local sources for link communication and learns scoped next-hop information.
Two OSPF network types. Point-to-point forms direct full adjacency without DR/BDR; broadcast elects those roles on a shared segment.
A Link LSA describes link-specific information including a link-local address. Intra-Area-Prefix LSAs carry IPv6 prefixes associated with the topology.
The Cisco process number is local configuration bookkeeping. The on-link OSPFv3 Instance ID separates protocol conversations and must be compatible; this lab leaves it at its default.
Neighbor-facing interfaces assigned to different OSPF areas reject each other's intended adjacency. Correct IP addressing alone does not correct the mismatch.
Full indicates completed adjacency synchronization. A learned OSPF route and a successful fixed-source probe provide separate evidence for the desired destination.

sections.example: The v2.0 list reserves neighbor adjacencies, point-to-point, broadcast DR/BDR selection and router ID. This lesson configures both link types. It does not add an authentication requirement: the announced neighbor objective explicitly excludes authentication.
sections.heading: Know which exam window this chapter serves
keyPoints: Keep current and announced mappings distinct.
An authoring checklist does not prove that a learner executed the configurations.
sections.explanation: The current CCNA v1.1 blueprint names single-area OSPFv2, while announced v2.0 explicitly includes OSPFv2 for IPv4 and OSPFv3 for IPv6. v1.1 remains current through February 2, 2027; v2.0 begins February 3. This chapter is therefore a labeled v1.1 extension and a direct v2.0 bridge, not a retroactive claim that the old objective named OSPFv3.

sections.example: R1 advertises 2001:db8:1::1/128 with identity 1.1.1.1. Its direct-link neighbor address is fe80::11 on Gi0/1, while its shared-LAN address is fe80::1 on Gi0/0. Inspect the output interface alongside each link-local next hop to identify which link a route actually uses.
sections.heading: Keep identities while changing address semantics
keyPoints: Do not configure an unnecessary IPv4 address just to obtain a router ID.
A link-local address and an advertised global-prefix endpoint have different scopes.
sections.explanation: Router IDs and area IDs remain 32 bits. Neighbor identities are distinct from interface IPv6 addresses. OSPFv3 separates basic topology from prefix information, with Link and Intra-Area-Prefix LSAs serving different roles. You do not need to memorize every LSA encoding to understand why a neighbor identity is not itself the route being learned.

sections.example: The interface setting ipv6 ospf network point-to-point applies only to Gi0/1's two-router cable. Gi0/0 explicitly uses broadcast mode and priority. If your image lacks these documented commands, stop and use the paper alternative or an entitled compatible image; do not invent an accepted transcript.
sections.heading: Use one documented command family consistently
keyPoints: Record the full image build and parser behavior.
The local process number is not the on-wire OSPFv3 Instance ID.
sections.explanation: IOS supports the classic IPv6-specific OSPFv3 commands used here, and some platforms support newer address-family syntax. The command families must not be pasted together indiscriminately. This lab enables IPv6 forwarding, creates ipv6 router ospf 10, sets a router ID and enables interfaces with ipv6 ospf 10 area 0. Check the exact command family supported by the selected image.

sections.example: The initial point-to-point ping is taken before the LAN is enabled. Later, R3 has only the shared-LAN attachment and tests R1's loopback through that segment. R1 and R2 may have alternative equal-cost routes once both links exist; this lesson does not claim which parallel path their later traffic uses without inspecting actual output.
sections.heading: Verify both network types before comparing them
keyPoints: One physical router can have multiple adjacency relationships on separate links.
An observed role is scoped to its interface, not globally to every connection.
sections.explanation: On the direct link, R1 and R2 should reach Full without DR/BDR roles. On the broadcast VLAN, R1 and R2 also establish a separate adjacency on Gi0/0, with election roles scoped to that segment. Seeing the same router ID on two interfaces can therefore be legitimate. Always include the interface column when counting neighbors.

sections.example: During the fault, R3's address 2001:db8:36::3 can still reach R1's 2001:db8:36::1 across VLAN 36, but its route to 2001:db8:1::1 depends on the lost routing conversation. This difference narrows the fault without claiming that every possible IPv6 service is healthy.
sections.heading: An area fault can coexist with working IPv6
keyPoints: Check area, timers, instance, type and unique IDs before applying disruptive resets.
Do not describe a predicted recovery as measured convergence or a completed independent review.
sections.explanation: R3's planned fault replaces area 0 with area 1 on its only neighbor-facing interface. The local subnet and link-local addresses remain assigned, so a connected IPv6 ping can still work. OSPFv3 adjacency and learned remote loopbacks should disappear after processing and expiry. Restore the original area membership and repeat the same neighbor, route and fixed-source test; no broad protocol clear is needed.

content.metaTitle: CCNA Day 36: OSPFv3 for IPv6 on Both Network Types

Link-local communication and prefix advertisements have distinct roles.
Use one platform-appropriate command family consistently.
Verify point-to-point and broadcast interfaces separately.
An area mismatch can break routing while local IPv6 still works.
Map this lesson as v1.1 extension and direct announced v2.0 preparation.
objectives: Separate a 32-bit router ID from IPv6 interface addresses.
Build a point-to-point OSPFv3 adjacency and verify its remote endpoint.
Build a broadcast OSPFv3 segment with deliberate election roles.
Interpret a link-local next hop together with its interface.
Repair one area mismatch and repeat the original IPv6 test.
content.plainAnswer: OSPFv3 for IPv6 still uses areas, unique 32-bit router IDs and SPF calculations. Its adjacent link communication uses IPv6 link-local addresses, and IPv6 prefixes are carried separately from basic topology descriptions. Configure each interface explicitly, verify both point-to-point and broadcast behavior, and check remote routes as well as neighbor state.

firstPractice.expected: The router ID is a 32-bit protocol identity, not an IPv4 forwarding dependency. The learned destination and adjacency transport are IPv6.

beginnerGuide.startingPoint: Label R1's identity 1.1.1.1, loopback 2001:db8:1::1 and LAN neighbor address fe80::1 in separate columns. None is interchangeable with the others.

everydayComparison.whereItStops: OSPF identities are protocol fields, not human account credentials. The analogy does not reproduce link scope, database exchange or routing decisions.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: The staff number resembles OSPF's router ID. The IPv6 endpoint is the delivery destination, while a link-local neighbor identifies the immediate local handoff.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: An employee can retain a short staff number after the office changes to a new mailing-address format. The identity and the delivery address serve different purposes.

practiceQuestions.answer: Router IDs remain 32-bit dotted-decimal identities.
practiceQuestions.question: Why does OSPFv3 still show 1.1.1.1?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The identity field is not an IPv4 address assignment. An IPv6-only router can use an explicit ID without IPv4 forwarding.

practiceQuestions.answer: The output interface that identifies the correct local link.
practiceQuestions.question: What accompanies a link-local route next hop?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Link-local addresses are scoped to one link. The interface distinguishes the immediate neighbor from the globally described destination.

practiceQuestions.answer: The early test can use only the declared direct point-to-point link.
practiceQuestions.question: Why verify Gi0/1 before enabling Gi0/0?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Once both links exist, another route may be available. Staged verification avoids attributing later success to an unverified link.

practiceQuestions.answer: No; the same peer can form adjacencies over distinct links.
practiceQuestions.question: Are two neighbor entries with one peer ID always wrong?
practiceQuestions.explanation: This topology deliberately connects R1 and R2 through a direct cable and the shared LAN. Compare the interface and network-type fields.

practiceQuestions.answer: The IPv6 LAN address remains configured and connected.
practiceQuestions.question: Why can R3's connected ping survive the area fault?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Area membership controls the OSPF conversation. The remote loopback requires a learned route that the broken adjacency no longer supplies.

realWorldScenario.situation: In a hypothetical lab, R3's LAN interface is moved to area 1 while its peers remain in area 0. The learner sees working IPv6 addresses and assumes routing must work. The connected test succeeds, but the learned loopback route is absent.
walkthrough: Identify the exact source and destination used in the failed remote test.
Compare connected LAN reachability with the remote loopback route.
Inspect OSPFv3 area membership on the same interface as the connected neighbor.
Restore area 0 without altering IPv6 addresses or router IDs.
Wait for Full and repeat the original source-qualified exchange.

title: HSRP, VRRP, and first-hop resilience

lab.goal: Interpret supplied hypothetical HSRP and VRRP records, model a whole-router failure, restore the baseline and diagnose a physical-gateway mistake. Optional read-only checks can collect actual evidence on a prepared rack; none was executed during authoring.
setup: Required: draw the six named roles and mark every result HYPOTHETICAL. Use separate HSRP and VRRP worksheets; do not mix protocol versions or virtual-address ownership.

Baseline HSRP worksheet: version 2, groups 10 and 20, R1 priority 120 active for both, R2 priority 100 standby for both, preemption enabled on both, default hello/hold timers 3/10 seconds, no tracking.

Alternate VRRP worksheet: version 3 IPv4, VRIDs 10 and 20, same virtual IPs, R1 priority 120 Active and R2 priority 100 Backup, preemption enabled, neither router an address owner. No measured timing is supplied.

Optional instructor prepares exactly this isolated CML topology, addresses, access VLANs, IPv4 forwarding, host default routes and permitted ICMP before observation. This is not a from-factory build guide. No bridge, NAT connector, Internet link or production access is allowed.

Verify exact builds with show version. CML's CAT 8000V test table reports HSRP support; it does not establish VRRP validation. Use the optional VRRP commands only after the instructor verifies that exact release's capability and prepares a separate compatible variant; otherwise retain paper interpretation.

For optional Ubuntu consoles, verify ens2 against the prepared node's actual interface inventory; document any different interface name before proceeding. The instructor supplies authorized accounts, not credentials embedded in this lesson. Virtual timing is not hardware timing.

steps.why: A complete scope prevents first-hop redundancy from hiding an absent downstream endpoint.
steps.title: Draw both complete LANs
steps.instruction: Create the six devices, six cables and address ledger above. Label SW1 VLAN 10 and SW2 VLAN 20. Show .1 as a shared service on each LAN, not a third router, and write each host's exact default gateway.
steps.expectedResult: The model has named source, destination, both router paths and an explicit server return gateway.

steps.why: The word local changes with the console; two groups on separate interfaces need separate records.
steps.title: Interpret the HSRP baseline
steps.instruction: Write the hypothetical Gi1 group 10 records from section two. Add Gi2 group 20: R1 Active, priority 120, active local, standby 198.51.100.3, VIP 198.51.100.1; R2 Standby, priority 100, active 198.51.100.2, standby local, same VIP.
steps.expectedResult: R1 serves both virtual gateways, while R2 is the identified standby on both LANs.

steps.why: Read-only operational fields add evidence without inventing a configuration or a completed failover.
steps.title: Optional HSRP status collection
steps.instruction: Optional prepared rack only: select R1 in the CML workbench, open Console and connect with the instructor-authorized account. Start at > or #; use end if left in configuration mode. Repeat on R2 through its own Console. Only use the prepared HSRP variant. Record both interfaces and groups; compare observed fields with the paper baseline without assuming they match.
steps.expectedResult: A prepared matching rack should show both connected subnets and the planned two-group roles; retain actual deviations.
commandExplanations: Enter privileged EXEC using authorized access; do not bypass authentication.
Record the exact image, release and platform for this observation.
Compare interface, group, current role, peer addresses and virtual IP.
Inspect detailed priority, preemption, timers and any tracking.
Verify the route to the actual server, not just its gateway.
Verify the return-side route to the actual client.

steps.why: The operating system's selected route must use the virtual gateway before redundancy can help this host.
steps.title: Optional client baseline check
steps.instruction: Only on the prepared rack, select Client1, open its CML Console, log in with the authorized Ubuntu account and use its terminal. Do not type these commands into a router console. Otherwise write the expected route and test on paper.
steps.expectedResult: A correctly prepared client selects 192.0.2.1 via ens2 with source 192.0.2.10; successful replies remain unmeasured here.
commandExplanations: Inspect the selected next hop, output interface and source for Server1.
Send three ICMP echo probes to the final server; preserve actual replies or failure.

steps.why: Whole-router loss makes both request-side and reply-side failover explicit without an undeclared asymmetry.
steps.title: Remove R1 on the worksheet only
steps.instruction: Cross out R1 and both of its links on the HSRP worksheet. Leave R2, both switches, endpoints, addresses and host gateways unchanged. Do not power off a real router or run shutdown commands as part of this paper exercise.
steps.expectedResult: The only changed variable is availability of the entire R1 role; both R2 LAN attachments remain.

steps.why: A successful takeover restores one usable router path, not the original amount of redundancy.
steps.title: Predict the surviving HSRP roles
steps.instruction: After the modeled detection process, change both R2 group records to Active with active local. Mark the absent standby unknown. Keep virtual addresses .1 and R2's real addresses .3 unchanged; do not invent a precise recovery time.
steps.expectedResult: R2 now serves both virtual gateways, but no second operational standby remains in this two-router design.

steps.why: The client-facing Active label alone cannot establish Server1's return delivery.
steps.title: Trace request and reply after failure
steps.instruction: Trace Client1 to SW1 to R2 to SW2 to Server1. Then start at Server1's gateway 198.51.100.1 and trace the reply through SW2, R2 and SW1 to Client1. Check both destination subnets on R2.
steps.expectedResult: Both modeled directions terminate at the original endpoints through the surviving connected interfaces.

steps.why: Rollback includes topology, roles and end-to-end reasoning, not just erasing the failure mark.
steps.title: Restore and retest the original model
steps.instruction: Restore R1 and its two links with the original addresses and priorities. With the explicitly enabled preemption and readiness assumptions, predict R1 resuming both Active roles and R2 Standby. Retrace the original endpoint pair.
steps.expectedResult: The restored worksheet matches the original two-group baseline; no runtime recovery or zero-loss claim follows.

steps.why: This exercises both required operational interpretations without claiming the protocols interoperate as one group.
steps.title: Interpret the alternate VRRP design
steps.instruction: Use a separate clean worksheet with no HSRP. For each VRID, record R1 priority 120 Active or legacy Master and R2 priority 100 Backup, matching VIPs and owner false. Cross out R1, predict R2 Active for both VRIDs, then restore R1 with the stated preemption policy.
steps.expectedResult: The same host virtual gateways support the modeled transfer, but role names and protocol identity are VRRP-specific.

steps.why: A capability-qualified alternative preserves practical verification without asserting untested simulator support.
steps.title: Optional VRRP status collection
steps.instruction: Optional prepared rack only: select R1 in the CML workbench, open Console and connect with the instructor-authorized account. Start at > or #; use end if left in configuration mode. Repeat on R2 through its own Console. Use only the separately prepared, capability-verified VRRPv3 IPv4 variant. Do not enable VRRP beside HSRP on these virtual IPs. If unavailable, retain the paper records and mark runtime unsupported.
steps.expectedResult: Use the platform's actual state labels; unsupported commands are a boundary, not permission to fabricate output.
commandExplanations: Enter authorized privileged EXEC for read-only inspection.
Record the exact software used for this optional VRRP observation.
Read interface, VRID, address family, priority, preemption, role and group address.
Inspect detailed virtual addresses, current role, ownership, timers and priority.
Compare real interface addresses with the separate virtual service addresses.

steps.why: A numerical exercise teaches preference while keeping unexecuted health monitoring separate from observed state.
steps.title: Calculate a tracked priority separately
steps.instruction: Return to a copy of the baseline. Add a hypothetical failed health object with decrement 30 to R1's priority 120 for one named group. Compute 90, compare with R2's 100 and explicitly require R2 preemption. Then clear the hypothetical fault and restore 120.
steps.expectedResult: The effective priority changes from 120 to 90 and back; the baseline itself still contains no configured tracking.

steps.why: Two working redundancy records cannot compensate for a host pointed at an absent physical router.
steps.title: Diagnose the wrong physical gateway
steps.instruction: On the R1-failed copy, change only Client1's gateway from 192.0.2.1 to 192.0.2.2. Explain why R2 owning .1 does not make .2 available. Restore .1, then retrace request and reply to Server1 without changing either host address.
steps.expectedResult: The modeled client failure follows the wrong gateway; restoring the virtual address repairs that stated dependency.

steps.why: Honest evidence labels prevent a technically useful exercise from becoming a fabricated lab completion.
steps.title: Close with an evidence boundary
steps.instruction: Compare baseline, failure and restored worksheets for each protocol. For any optional rack observation, preserve real device versions, console fields and endpoint results separately. Do not record a measured outage duration unless an authorized future runtime test actually measures it.
steps.expectedResult: The report distinguishes paper predictions, optional collected outputs and unmeasured failure behavior.

quiz.explanation: The .1 address is the client LAN's virtual gateway. The .2 and .3 addresses belong to individual routers; the server is remote.

options: No standby is currently identified in that field.

glossary.meaning: The default gateway is the local router a host uses when no more-specific route matches a remote destination. First hop names that initial router, not the destination server.
A First Hop Redundancy Protocol lets participating routers present a shared gateway identity. The virtual IP address belongs to the logical service, not to an extra physical device.
The Ethernet identity used for the virtual router. Hosts can keep the same gateway IP while forwarding responsibility moves between participating routers.
Hot Standby Router Protocol selects an active router to serve the group and a standby ready to take over. Other HSRP states describe discovery or readiness, not equivalent forwarding roles.
Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol is an IETF standard. RFC 9568 says Active and Backup; older Cisco output may label the active role Master.
A group identifies one HSRP service on an interface. VRRP calls its group number a Virtual Router Identifier, or VRID. The number alone does not identify a router or destination.
Priority expresses election preference. Preemption permits a preferred available router to take over from a lower-priority incumbent; it is different from replacing a failed router.
Tracking observes a configured condition, such as interface state. A configured decrement can lower the effective election priority when that condition fails.
In VRRP, an address owner has the virtual address as its real interface address and uses priority 255. Our separate virtual .1 addresses have no address owner.
Failover transfers a role after failure detection. Convergence is the network settling into a usable state; neither term promises zero packet loss or a measured recovery time.

sections.example: R1 Gi1 is 192.0.2.2 and R2 Gi1 is 192.0.2.3; Client1 uses 192.0.2.1. The .1 address does not replace either router's real management identity. SW1 is a Layer 2 switch with no routing role in this model.
sections.heading: A virtual gateway is an identity, not another box
keyPoints: Count two real routers, not three routers because a virtual address exists.
Host gateway configuration is part of the redundancy dependency.
sections.explanation: Client1 is in 192.0.2.0/24 and Server1 is in 198.51.100.0/24, so their exchange needs routing. Each LAN has two real router interfaces and one virtual gateway address. The virtual IP is configured as the host's gateway. A virtual MAC supports the shared Ethernet identity while the current active router handles the handoff. No extra physical gateway is hidden in the diagram.

sections.example: Authored hypothetical record, not CLI capture: R1 Gi1, group 10, priority 120, Active, active local, standby 192.0.2.3, VIP 192.0.2.1. The matching R2 record is Standby with active 192.0.2.2 and standby local. Group 20 uses the server-facing addresses instead.
sections.heading: Interpret HSRP fields in interface and group context
keyPoints: A group number needs an interface and protocol context.
Compare both devices' records instead of trusting one healthy-looking line.
sections.explanation: Read interface, group, priority, state, active address, standby address and virtual IP together. The word local in an active-address field means the router whose console you are reading. A second router showing Standby supports the intended pair; an unknown standby does not prove a backup exists. Initial or discovery states should not be treated as the settled baseline.

sections.example: In the separate VRRP worksheet, R1 has VRID 10, priority 120, Active or legacy Master; R2 has priority 100 and Backup. Both agree on 192.0.2.1. This is an alternate protocol design, not an instruction to enable HSRP and VRRP on the same virtual address simultaneously.
sections.heading: Translate VRRP terminology without changing the meaning
keyPoints: Map a legacy Master label to the current active forwarding role.
Do not borrow VRRP owner priority 255 as an HSRP rule.
sections.explanation: VRRPv3 supports IPv4 and IPv6; this exercise uses IPv4 only. Current RFC 9568 uses Active and Backup, while Cisco versions may display Master for the active role. Read the actual software's vocabulary. A VRRP address owner uses priority 255; other eligible priorities are 1 through 254, with 100 the default. Our real addresses .2 and .3 differ from the virtual .1, so neither router is the address owner.

sections.example: Our worksheets explicitly enable preemption on both routers. After R1 returns healthy at priority 120, it is expected to resume the preferred role over R2 at 100, subject to readiness and configured delays. Without HSRP preemption, R2 may remain active after R1 returns; that alone is not a fault.
sections.heading: Separate failure replacement from preemption
keyPoints: Election preference is not a demand for instantaneous role change.
Failure detection, preemption and application recovery are separate events.
sections.explanation: A standby can replace a failed active router without preemption being enabled. Preemption concerns taking over from a still-operating lower-priority incumbent. HSRP preemption is not enabled by default; VRRP normally enables it, with special treatment for an address owner. Always inspect configuration and effective status rather than relying on a remembered default. Recovery may intentionally include a delay while the preferred router becomes ready.

sections.example: Separate paper calculation: R1's configured priority is 120 and a failed tracked condition subtracts 30. Its effective priority becomes 90, below R2's 100. With the stipulated preemption policy, R2 is preferred. This arithmetic is not evidence that tracking was configured or an upstream failure was executed.
sections.heading: Tracking changes preference, not the entire network
keyPoints: Inspect configured and current priority separately.
No tracked condition in the baseline means no automatic upstream-health guarantee.
sections.explanation: An active router can keep sending local redundancy messages while its useful destination path fails. Object tracking can connect a chosen health condition to a priority decrement, but the scope of that condition must be explicit. An interface-up check does not prove that a remote service answers. A changed priority also needs compatible preemption behavior to transfer the role from a still-live incumbent.

sections.example: The baseline path is Client1, SW1, R1, SW2, Server1. After the modeled R1 failure, both request and reply traverse R2. A ping to a virtual gateway alone is insufficient; VRRP handling of traffic addressed to the virtual IP can also depend on ownership and accept-mode behavior.
sections.heading: First-hop availability is narrower than service availability
keyPoints: Test the final endpoint and its return path, not only the gateway.
Current v1.1 objective 3.5 is conceptual; announced v2.0 objective 3.4 asks for HSRP and VRRP operational interpretation.
sections.explanation: This model survives one whole-router failure only while both switches, both endpoint links and the remaining router work. SW1 and SW2 are deliberate single points of failure. Both subnets are directly connected to each router, so no undeclared ISP, static default or remote routing protocol is needed. HSRP and VRRP do not replace destination routing, application checks or a redundant physical design.

content.metaTitle: CCNA Day 37: HSRP, VRRP and First-Hop Resilience
takeaways: Hosts must use the virtual gateway to benefit from the group.
Read protocol, interface, group, role and peer fields together.
HSRP preemption defaults differ from VRRP; inspect actual policy.
Tracking can change effective priority but does not prove application health.
Trace both forward and return paths through the surviving router.
Keep hypothetical status records distinct from captured output.
objectives: Distinguish each real interface address from its virtual gateway.
Interpret HSRP active/standby and VRRP active/backup status.
Calculate effective priority and explain preemption.
Trace request and reply paths when one router disappears.
Verify the same final endpoint without claiming measured failover.
content.plainAnswer: HSRP and VRRP let hosts use a stable virtual gateway while participating routers exchange responsibility for forwarding. The host must actually use the virtual IP, and the surviving router still needs a usable destination and return path. Read role, group, virtual address, effective priority and preemption together; a healthy first-hop role does not prove an application works.

visualStory.title: R1 or R2, never a serial router pair

stages.title: R1 serves both gateways
stages.explanation: Client1 192.0.2.10 uses gateway 192.0.2.1, then SW1, R1 and SW2 to Server1 198.51.100.20. Server1 uses gateway 198.51.100.1 for the reverse path.

stages.title: R2 takes both roles
stages.explanation: After modeled R1 loss, R2 serves both virtual gateways. The complete request path is Client1, SW1, R2, SW2, Server1; neither R1 nor an unnamed upstream router is traversed.

stages.title: Verify the return path
stages.explanation: After failover, the reply follows Server1, SW2, R2, SW1, Client1. Both virtual gateway addresses remain unchanged; the comparison does not measure recovery time.

visualStory.altText: Baseline: Client1, SW1, R1, SW2, Server1. After R1 loss: Client1, SW1, R2, SW2, Server1. Replies reverse the corresponding path. R1 and R2 are alternatives, never serial hops.
visualStory.boundary: Baseline-versus-failover role comparison, not a cabling diagram. The two records summarize the same six-device, two-LAN model; virtual gateways are not extra devices. No runtime or timing is measured.
visualStory.takeaway: Baseline uses R1; modeled failover uses R2. Both alternatives connect Client1 to Server1 while preserving both virtual gateways.

walkthrough.why: The client-facing and server-facing roles both matter to the complete exchange.
walkthrough.action: Read the baseline as a pair.

beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Two installed routers do not create useful redundancy unless hosts use the shared service and both routers can deliver traffic. Reading status becomes meaningful when it answers a specific endpoint question.

firstPractice.hint: Changing which router serves .1 does not transfer ownership of R1's separately configured .2 interface address.
firstPractice.task: Client1 uses gateway 192.0.2.2 instead of 192.0.2.1. R1 disappears and R2 serves the virtual gateway. Explain the remaining fault.
firstPractice.expected: Client1 still targets R1's physical address. Restore its gateway to the virtual .1 address in the model, then trace both directions again.

beginnerGuide.startingPoint: Draw Client1 and Server1 first. Their gateways are 192.0.2.1 and 198.51.100.1. Then draw R1 and R2 behind those virtual identities; do not add a third router for either virtual address.

checkUnderstanding.hint: Consider destination routes, interfaces, host gateways and the reply.
checkUnderstanding.answer: No. The label reports one local group role. Check both LANs, the selected destination route, the server's return gateway and a real final-endpoint test before claiming service.
checkUnderstanding.question: Does an HSRP Active label prove Server1 is reachable?

everydayComparison.whereItStops: Telephone shifts do not model Ethernet learning, protocol timers or return routes. The analogy explains stable identity only; it cannot predict packet loss.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: The published number resembles a virtual gateway, and the shift holder resembles the active role. Calling a private number resembles configuring the host with a single router's real address.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: A reception desk keeps one published telephone number while different staff members take the shift. Callers use the desk number rather than one employee's private number.

prerequisites: Know IPv4 subnet membership, default gateways and Ethernet address resolution.
Complete the required exercise on paper; no image, subscription or real router is needed.
Optional observation requires an instructor-prepared isolated CML project, entitlement and authorized console access.
content.learnerOutcome: You will interpret both protocols' operational fields, trace a complete modeled failover, and distinguish gateway redundancy from upstream reachability, return routing and measured service continuity.
content.metaDescription: Interpret HSRP and VRRP roles, virtual gateways, preemption and tracked priority with a complete two-LAN paper failover and optional read-only checks.

terms.meaning: The default gateway is the local router a host uses when no more-specific route matches a remote destination. First hop names that initial router, not the destination server.
A First Hop Redundancy Protocol lets participating routers present a shared gateway identity. The virtual IP address belongs to the logical service, not to an extra physical device.
The Ethernet identity used for the virtual router. Hosts can keep the same gateway IP while forwarding responsibility moves between participating routers.
Hot Standby Router Protocol selects an active router to serve the group and a standby ready to take over. Other HSRP states describe discovery or readiness, not equivalent forwarding roles.
Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol is an IETF standard. RFC 9568 says Active and Backup; older Cisco output may label the active role Master.
A group identifies one HSRP service on an interface. VRRP calls its group number a Virtual Router Identifier, or VRID. The number alone does not identify a router or destination.
Priority expresses election preference. Preemption permits a preferred available router to take over from a lower-priority incumbent; it is different from replacing a failed router.
Tracking observes a configured condition, such as interface state. A configured decrement can lower the effective election priority when that condition fails.
In VRRP, an address owner has the virtual address as its real interface address and uses priority 255. Our separate virtual .1 addresses have no address owner.
Failover transfers a role after failure detection. Convergence is the network settling into a usable state; neither term promises zero packet loss or a measured recovery time.

teachingPrelude.explanation: Start with the host's route, not a router's impressive-looking status. A laptop configured to use R1's physical .2 address will not automatically start using the group's .1 address. The two-LAN exercise deliberately gives the server its own virtual gateway so the return path is as explicit as the request.
teachingPrelude.labBoundary: Required: authored hypothetical status records and paper fault analysis, not captured CLI output. Optional commands are read-only on a prepared rack. No from-factory configuration, executed failover, packet-loss result or independent review is claimed.

practiceQuestions.answer: It is a shared logical identity served by participating real routers.
practiceQuestions.question: Why is the virtual gateway not a third physical router?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The topology contains only R1 and R2 as routers. Which one handles the virtual identity can change without adding a device.

practiceQuestions.answer: R2 itself currently serves that interface's group.
practiceQuestions.question: What does local mean in R2's active-address field?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Operational output is relative to the console being read. Pair the word with interface and group before identifying the forwarding device.

practiceQuestions.answer: No; preemption governs displacement of a live lower-priority incumbent.
practiceQuestions.question: Does failed-active replacement require preemption?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A standby replacing a missing active router is failure handling. A recovered preferred router taking the role back is a different decision.

practiceQuestions.answer: It is 90, lower than R2's unchanged priority 100.
practiceQuestions.question: What is R1's effective priority after a decrement of 30 from 120?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The configured preference and effective value differ while the tracked condition is down. Role change still depends on the applicable preemption rules.

practiceQuestions.answer: The reply needs a surviving first hop as well as the request.
practiceQuestions.question: Why does the model put a virtual gateway on Server1's LAN?
practiceQuestions.explanation: If Server1 remained pointed at failed R1's real address, client-side takeover could succeed while end-to-end communication still failed.

practiceQuestions.answer: Not necessarily; it can be the implementation's legacy name for the active role.
practiceQuestions.question: Does a VRRP Master label contradict RFC 9568 Active?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Translate the observed field with the platform documentation. Do not confuse vocabulary updates with proof that the running protocol is faulty.

realWorldScenario.title: Two routers, one incorrectly configured host
realWorldScenario.takeaway: Infrastructure redundancy is only useful to a host that uses it. Preserve the host route, router role and final-endpoint test as three separate pieces of evidence.
realWorldScenario.situation: In this hypothetical training network, the router pair correctly transfers both virtual gateways to R2. Client1 nevertheless fails because its default gateway is R1's real 192.0.2.2. The role election succeeded, but the host was never using the redundant identity.
walkthrough: Compare Client1's configured gateway with the virtual IP, not merely the router inventory.
Confirm R2's client-side and server-side group roles separately.
Trace Client1's request and Server1's reply across the surviving router.
Correct only the worksheet's host gateway to 192.0.2.1 and retrace the original endpoint pair.
For a real rack, record actual route selection and endpoint responses before claiming recovery.

title: DHCPv4 clients, servers, and relay

lab.goal: Configure Client1, Relay1 and Server1, obtain a lease, remove one helper, observe fresh-acquisition behavior, and restore it. All expected results are predictions. Authoring performed source and structural checks, not IOS execution.
setup: Use GNS3 2.2.55 and three fresh, independently entitled C8000v 17.12.1a instances with these exact ports. Stop if the available image differs; adapt only using its official documentation.
Create the two listed links and start the three nodes. Decline an initial configuration dialog on disposable nodes. Do not import employer configurations.
Capture clean-project snapshots and keep all three Consoles open. Use no external network adapters; a DHCP server must never leak into a shared LAN.
Paper alternative: draw the address table, simulate the DORA messages and diagnose the three fault cases. Mark every result predicted; no Cisco image execution is implied.

steps.why: The change is interpretable only when image, interfaces and initial configuration are known.
steps.title: Inspect the clean relay
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Relay1 and choose Console before typing. Start at > or # and inspect the device before making changes. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: The recorded ports match the topology; no existing service is overwritten.
commandExplanations: Enter privileged EXEC (#) from user EXEC (>); use only your authorized lab credentials.
Record the actual platform and IOS XE release; compare it with the reference image.
Inspect interface names, addresses and line/protocol states before connecting the configured roles.
Record the clean baseline privately; stop if unexpected configuration or secrets appear.

steps.why: Reversing these addresses would change relay subnet identification and break the planned route.
steps.title: Address both relay interfaces
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Relay1 and choose Console before typing. Start at #. Configure the client side first, then the transit side. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: Both planned addresses appear on the correct interfaces once peers are enabled.
commandExplanations: Enter global configuration mode from privileged EXEC (#); accepted changes affect the running device.
Select the exact port cabled to Client1 GigabitEthernet1.
Set the client subnet gateway using the /24 dotted-decimal mask.
Enable the selected client-facing interface.
Return from interface configuration to global configuration.
Select the port cabled to Server1 GigabitEthernet1.
Set the relay transit address with a /30 mask.
Enable the server-facing transit interface.
Return to privileged EXEC (#). This neither saves the configuration nor reverses accepted changes.

steps.why: A server can receive a relayed request yet fail to deliver its reply if its return routing is wrong.
steps.title: Address the server and return route
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Server1 and choose Console before typing. Start at > or #; Server1 must route replies back to the client subnet. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: Server1 has a connected transit route and a static route toward the client LAN.
commandExplanations: Enter privileged EXEC (#) from user EXEC (>); use only your authorized lab credentials.
Enter global configuration mode from privileged EXEC (#); accepted changes affect the running device.
Select the server port cabled to Relay1 GigabitEthernet2.
Configure Server1's directly connected transit address.
Enable the selected server interface.
Return to global configuration before entering a route.
Route the client /24 toward Relay1's adjacent transit address.
Return to privileged EXEC (#). This neither saves the configuration nor reverses accepted changes.

steps.why: The pool needs explicit values a beginner can compare with the plan; this lab deliberately offers no DNS service.
steps.title: Create a bounded address pool
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Server1 and choose Console before typing. Start at #. Reserve infrastructure addresses and define client settings. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: CLIENTS describes 192.0.2.0/24 with excluded infrastructure addresses and the correct gateway.
commandExplanations: Enter global configuration mode from privileged EXEC (#); accepted changes affect the running device.
Enable the IOS DHCP service; this is not a client address command.
Exclude the inclusive range .1 through .100 from dynamic allocation.
Create the local pool named CLIENTS and enter DHCP pool mode.
Select the client's /24 network, not the server transit subnet.
Offer Relay1's local client-facing address as the gateway.
Set a one-hour lease: zero days and one hour.
Return to privileged EXEC (#). This neither saves the configuration nor reverses accepted changes.

steps.why: A helper on the wrong interface cannot receive the intended local client broadcast.
steps.title: Enable the client-side relay
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Relay1 and choose Console before typing. Start at #. Apply the helper where Client1's initial broadcast arrives. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: The helper is on GigabitEthernet1, and Server1 should respond to the transit ping.
commandExplanations: Enter global configuration mode from privileged EXEC (#); accepted changes affect the running device.
Enable DHCP relay/server functionality on this clean lab router.
Choose the interface receiving broadcasts from Client1.
Forward supported UDP broadcasts, including DHCP, toward this exact server address.
Return to privileged EXEC (#). This neither saves the configuration nor reverses accepted changes.
Test Relay1's IP reachability to Server1 before testing DHCP.

steps.why: Using an IOS client explicitly practices client configuration instead of assuming an endpoint has already done it.
steps.title: Request a lease on an IOS client
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Client1 and choose Console before typing. Start at > or #. Do not assign a static address to this interface. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: A lease in the available 192.0.2.0/24 range should appear after exchange and address checks.
commandExplanations: Enter privileged EXEC (#) from user EXEC (>); use only your authorized lab credentials.
Enter global configuration mode from privileged EXEC (#); accepted changes affect the running device.
Select Client1's only cabled interface toward Relay1.
Ask DHCP to supply the interface address and supported options.
Enable the client interface so it can transmit requests.
Return to privileged EXEC (#). This neither saves the configuration nor reverses accepted changes.
Inspect the actual acquired lease, server and timing; do not invent the assigned address.
Compare the leased address with the planned subnet and interface status.

steps.why: A lease record alone does not prove the client applied the offer or that the remote path works.
steps.title: Record server and traffic baseline
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Server1 and choose Console before typing. Start at #. Capture pool, binding and route evidence before any fault. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: Server1's binding agrees with Client1's observed lease and the return route is present.
commandExplanations: Inspect available and allocated pool capacity; do not infer exhaustion from one failed client.
Record the actual client identifier, assigned address and lease expiry.
Inspect addresses marked conflicting without clearing them.
Check that the client subnet's route points toward 198.51.100.1.

steps.why: This provides a working baseline distinct from the mere presence of server configuration.
steps.title: Test the leased client's path
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Client1 and choose Console before typing. Start at #. Stop here if there is no lease or the subnet is wrong. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: Both tests should receive replies after initial address discovery; record actual results.
commandExplanations: Test the local gateway from the leased interface.
Test the remote DHCP server using the client's learned gateway and the server return route.

steps.why: This changes the initial broadcast forwarding dependency without changing the pool, routes or cables.
steps.title: Remove exactly one helper
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Relay1 and choose Console before typing. Start at # only after the working lease and pings were recorded. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: The helper line is absent, but both physical interfaces remain enabled.
commandExplanations: Enter global configuration mode from privileged EXEC (#); accepted changes affect the running device.
Select the same client-facing relay interface as before.
Remove only the known DHCP server helper destination.
Return to privileged EXEC (#). This neither saves the configuration nor reverses accepted changes.

steps.why: If the test still succeeds, inspect alternate helpers, duplicate servers, client state and actual requests instead of manufacturing failure.
steps.title: Test fresh acquisition after the fault
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Client1 and choose Console before typing. Start at #. First note the existing lease. Removing and reapplying DHCP is allowed only on this disposable client. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: Fresh acquisition should not complete through the removed helper. A retained lease before reset is not a contrary result.
commandExplanations: Record retained state before forcing a new acquisition attempt.
Enter global configuration mode from privileged EXEC (#); accepted changes affect the running device.
Select only the lab client's DHCP interface.
Remove DHCP address acquisition from this interface and its current DHCP-derived address state.
Restart DHCP acquisition on the same enabled interface.
Return to privileged EXEC (#). This neither saves the configuration nor reverses accepted changes.
Inspect whether a new lease was obtained; distinguish old display state from a new acknowledged lease.

steps.why: Rollback is a known inverse in this lab, not a broad reset of DHCP services or router configuration.
steps.title: Restore the relay baseline
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Relay1 and choose Console before typing. Start at #. Restore the one line removed; leave all other settings unchanged. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: The original helper destination is present again on the original interface.
commandExplanations: Enter global configuration mode from privileged EXEC (#); accepted changes affect the running device.
Return to the original client-facing interface.
Restore the exact server destination used by the working baseline.
Return to privileged EXEC (#). This neither saves the configuration nor reverses accepted changes.

steps.why: Successful retest supports this particular repair; DNS, applications and actual production reliability remain unmeasured.
steps.title: Reacquire and close the experiment
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Client1 and choose Console before typing. Start at #. Repeat acquisition after restoration, then inspect Server1 with the earlier baseline commands. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: A valid lease and the original reachability tests should recover; compare with Server1's binding.
commandExplanations: Enter global configuration mode from privileged EXEC (#); accepted changes affect the running device.
Select the same test client interface for a comparable acquisition.
Remove the test client's existing DHCP configuration before restarting it.
Request an address again through the restored relay path.
Return to privileged EXEC (#). This neither saves the configuration nor reverses accepted changes.
Record the newly observed lease and server rather than assuming the original address returns.
Retest the exact gateway used in the baseline.
Retest the exact remote server destination used in the baseline.

lab.title: Three IOS roles and one missing-helper fault
cleanup: Restore the helper and retain the final successful lease evidence; stop all three nodes after the exercise.
To return to a completely clean state, discard this disposable project or revert the prelab snapshots. Do not merge an old startup configuration as a claimed universal rollback.
devices: Client1: C8000v IOS XE 17.12.1a, one routed port.
Relay1: C8000v IOS XE 17.12.1a, two routed ports.
Server1: C8000v IOS XE 17.12.1a, one routed port.
lab.topology: Client1 GigabitEthernet1 -- Relay1 GigabitEthernet1; Relay1 GigabitEthernet2 -- Server1 GigabitEthernet1. Two direct Ethernet cables. No switch, bridge, Cloud or NAT node. GNS3 Console access is independent of both cables.

addressing.purpose: Client lease; actual host address is not predetermined.

verification: Record actual image releases, both cables, client lease and server binding; never substitute the guide's predicted values for output.
Check pool CLIENTS, exclusion range, correct default-router and Server1's return route to 192.0.2.0/24.
Show that fresh acquisition differs with the helper absent and restored while addresses and cables remain unchanged.
Repeat Client1's gateway and remote server pings after rollback and label any initial discovery loss.
State explicitly that no DNS, Internet, redundancy, encryption or other operating-system client behavior was tested.
lab.licensingNote: GNS3 does not provide Cisco software images. Use Cisco images only when the applicable license or entitlement permits this environment. Do not share or redistribute image files. Cisco Modeling Labs is an official alternative; its supplied reference images are licensed for CML, not automatically for export to GNS3. Use the labeled paper alternative when authorized software is unavailable. No emulator execution is claimed by this lesson.
troubleshooting: No client lease: inspect interface status and ip address dhcp, then helper placement, service dhcp, pool subnet and free addresses before blaming the server.
Binding exists but remote ping fails: compare the leased gateway and Server1's return route; DHCP success cannot repair a routing fault.
Missing-helper test still succeeds: check retained client state, duplicate servers and extra helper lines. Preserve evidence rather than broadening the fault.
Conflicting address: locate and remove the unauthorized duplicate in this isolated project before clearing a specific conflict; never clear a whole shared server database.

quiz.question: Where should the helper be placed in this topology?
quiz.explanation: The client-facing interface receives the initial broadcast. The server-facing port is not the ingress client LAN; a pool name and an unused loopback cannot relay this request.

options: A client lease matching a current server binding
quiz.question: Which observation best confirms a new lease?
quiz.explanation: Compare actual client state with the corresponding server binding and acquisition time. Link state, old state and an offer alone do not establish completed allocation.

quiz.question: What is the correct offered gateway here?
quiz.explanation: Relay1's client-facing address is locally reachable and routes onward. The server is remote, .255 is the /24 broadcast, and a free client address is not a configured router.

options: Change the helper to a public server
quiz.question: The pool has zero usable free addresses. What should you do first?
quiz.explanation: Determine why capacity is unavailable before changing it. Global clearing, interface shutdown and an unrelated server can disrupt users without addressing the cause.

glossary.meaning: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv4 supplies an address and related settings for a limited lease time. It does not carry the later web application traffic.
A client asks for settings. A server chooses and records a lease. A relay forwards DHCP messages between the client's local network and a server on another network.
A /24 subnet uses mask 255.255.255.0. Hosts in 192.0.2.0/24 use 192.0.2.1 here as their gateway, the next router for other networks.
A broadcast addresses the local broadcast domain. A unicast addresses one destination. An ordinary routed interface does not forward the client's initial local broadcast into another subnet.
A pool describes assignable settings for a subnet. An exclusion reserves addresses against dynamic allocation. A binding records a particular client's assigned address and lease.
Discover seeks a server, Offer proposes settings, Request identifies the selected offer, and Acknowledge confirms the lease. Renewal is not necessarily this complete four-message exchange.
User Datagram Protocol uses numbered application ports: DHCP clients use 68 and servers use 67. The DHCP gateway-address field, giaddr, lets the relay identify the client's subnet to the server.
The GNS3 Console is the node's text window. > is user EXEC, # is privileged EXEC, (config)# is global configuration and (config-if)# selects an interface. Type commands without these prompts.
Record working settings and actual tests first. A safe fault changes one known item only in this disposable lab. Rollback restores that item and repeats the original test.
A client asks to extend a lease before expiry. It can continue using a still-valid lease while a new broadcast path is broken, so an existing address is not proof that new allocation works.

sections.example: Imagine a client receives 192.0.2.101/24 with gateway 198.51.100.2. Its address could look plausible while the gateway is off-subnet. Inspect the offered options, not only the presence of an address. The correct default-router option points to Relay1 on the client's own LAN.
sections.heading: One service, three different responsibilities
keyPoints: DHCP configures an interface; it does not create every required route.
A router can perform a client role, a server role or a relay role.
sections.explanation: DHCP separates asking, assigning and forwarding. The client requests configuration; the server owns its pool and lease decisions; a relay carries messages across a routed boundary. The server's address is not the client's gateway merely because it supplied settings. In this lab the remote server is 198.51.100.2, but the client's gateway is the locally reachable 192.0.2.1.

sections.example: In our diagram the arrows show three roles, not a packet capture. Client1's initial Discover is local; Relay1 forwards toward Server1. The reply returns to the relay for delivery to Client1. Later renewal can be unicast toward the server, so deleting a helper does not necessarily break all existing clients immediately.
sections.heading: DORA is a starting exchange, not every DHCP packet
keyPoints: Inspect transaction state rather than assuming every message is a broadcast.
DHCP does not encrypt its ordinary address offers or prove server identity.
sections.explanation: During initial selection, Discover finds servers, Offer proposes a lease, Request identifies the chosen offer and Acknowledge confirms it. A client can hear multiple offers. Do not treat Offer alone as completed allocation. UDP ports identify the DHCP applications, not physical cable ports. Whether replies use broadcast or unicast depends on client state, flags and the relay path.

sections.example: Our pool CLIENTS contains network 192.0.2.0 with mask 255.255.255.0. Excluding .1 through .100 leaves .101 through .254 as potential dynamic host addresses, subject to existing bindings and conflict detection. Neither .0 nor .255 is a usable /24 host. The example does not promise which available address will be selected first.
sections.heading: Pool selection must match the client, not the server cable
keyPoints: Exclusions, active bindings and conflicts affect availability differently.
A pool for 198.51.100.0/30 would describe the transit network, not this client LAN.
sections.explanation: An IOS server pool declares a network and its mask. The excluded range keeps infrastructure addresses from dynamic assignment. Relay information tells the server which remote subnet is involved; a nonzero giaddr commonly supplies the client-facing relay address. The server also needs a route back toward that address. Pool naming is local organization, not a VLAN or a routing command.

sections.example: First ping 198.51.100.2 from Relay1 and inspect Server1's route to 192.0.2.0. Then enable the client. If Relay1 cannot reach the server, adding more DHCP pools is not a reasoned repair. If a pool exists but is exhausted, a perfectly working route still cannot create an unused lease.
sections.heading: Build both directions before judging the service
keyPoints: Configuration syntax, service state and tested behavior are separate evidence.
Keep service dhcp enabled on the server and relay in this lab.
sections.explanation: Relay1 has a connected route to each cable network. Server1 needs an explicit route to 192.0.2.0/24 via 198.51.100.1. Put ip helper-address on the interface receiving client broadcasts, not reflexively on the server-facing interface. On IOS the helper can forward additional UDP services; this isolated exercise is not a production hardening policy.

sections.example: The controlled fault removes only Relay1's helper. Fresh acquisition should fail while both cables remain up. Restore the helper and retry. Separately, use paper cases: an excluded entire pool produces no available address; a wrong pool network produces no matching scope; a wrong default-router option may allow a lease but break remote access.
sections.heading: Diagnose client, relay and server faults independently
keyPoints: Never clear every production lease to test one classroom client.
Record the actual address, client identifier, time and commands accepted.
sections.explanation: Start with the client's interface state and whether DHCP is configured. Then inspect the relay's client-facing address, helper destination and routes. Finally inspect server pools, bindings and conflicts. A missing address is a symptom, not a verdict against the server. An address conflict should be investigated before any record is cleared; deleting a warning does not remove the duplicate host.

sections.example: A complete lab note can say that one IOS client acquired a lease through one relay and reached the server in the disconnected project. It cannot claim public Internet access, a working DNS resolver, secure DHCP, high availability or Windows/macOS/Linux client verification. Label the paper fault matrix as reasoning, not runtime evidence.
sections.heading: State coverage and the limit of a successful lease
keyPoints: Inspect lease contents and connectivity rather than calling any address success.
Use the coverage record and assessment pointers, not a domain title, to track learning.
sections.explanation: CCNA v1.1 remains current through 2 February 2027; announced v2.0 starts 3 February 2027. This lesson addresses the DHCP portion of v1.1 4.3 and client/relay practice in 4.6. Server setup also supports v2.0 1.7 troubleshooting. These are authored exercises, not proof the learner executed every outcome or covered DNS, which is next.

content.metaTitle: CCNA Day 38: DHCP Clients, Servers and Relay
takeaways: DHCP client, server and relay are roles, not fixed device categories.
A relay identifies the client subnet and requires a routed return path.
Exclude infrastructure addresses and inspect actual pool capacity.
A valid existing lease can mask a broken initial acquisition path.
Verify the lease, the gateway and the remote destination separately.
Keep predicted lab results distinct from actual observations.
objectives: Trace Discover, Offer, Request and Acknowledge without assuming every message is broadcast.
Configure the IOS DHCP client, an excluded address range, a server pool and a client-facing relay.
Verify lease state, pool availability, helper placement and the return route.
Compare a missing-helper fault with wrong client settings and exhausted or mismatched pools.
Restore the known helper and reacquire a lease without clearing unrelated bindings.
content.plainAnswer: DHCPv4 leases an address and options to a client. A relay on the client-facing router interface forwards requests to a remote server and identifies the client subnet. Successful allocation needs the client, correct pool, available addresses and both routed directions. An old lease can remain usable after relay failure, so test a fresh acquisition as well as inspecting existing settings.

visualStory.title: DHCP crosses a router through a relay

stages.title: Ask from the client LAN
stages.explanation: Client1 has no static address. Relay1 receives the initial local request on its client-facing interface.

stages.title: Select the right pool
stages.explanation: Relay1 forwards toward Server1 and identifies the client subnet. Server1 chooses from 192.0.2.0/24, not the transit subnet.

stages.title: Return to Client1
stages.explanation: The server response returns through Relay1 to Client1. Check the confirmed client lease and matching server binding after the exchange.

visualStory.altText: Client1 sends through Relay1 to Server1. Server1 selects a client-subnet lease, and its response returns through Relay1 to Client1.
visualStory.boundary: Conceptual initial DHCP exchange on the two lab cables. Broadcast and unicast details vary by client state. This is not a capture, and existing leases may survive a relay fault.
visualStory.takeaway: The helper carries the request; the pool matches the client subnet; the reply must reach the client.

conceptSelection.selectionReason: The complete three-role exchange directly supports the missing-helper experiment; lease-state and pool details remain in the text.

walkthrough.why: The server-facing transit subnet is not the subnet from which this client should receive a lease.
walkthrough.action: Identify the subnet that needs an address.
walkthrough.whatHappens: Client1 has no static address on GigabitEthernet1. Relay1's attached interface is 192.0.2.1/24, so Server1 must offer from the 192.0.2.0/24 pool.

walkthrough.why: A route alone does not carry the initial local DHCP broadcast across the router.
walkthrough.action: Carry the request to the remote service.
walkthrough.whatHappens: The helper on Relay1 GigabitEthernet1 targets Server1 at 198.51.100.2. Server1 uses relay information and its configured pool to choose appropriate settings.

walkthrough.why: A server record and a client configuration are complementary evidence, not interchangeable claims.
walkthrough.action: Inspect both ends of the assignment.
walkthrough.whatHappens: Read Client1's address and lease, then compare Server1's binding and pool. Test Client1 to 192.0.2.1 and 198.51.100.2.

walkthrough.why: An already valid lease or unicast renewal can hide the missing initial broadcast relay.
walkthrough.action: Break only fresh acquisition, then restore it.
walkthrough.whatHappens: Remove the helper and remove/reapply DHCP on Client1. Compare acquisition with the working baseline, restore the helper and repeat the same process.

beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: An address assignment problem can stop work before a user can even reach a gateway. Changing a server pool blindly may miss a broken relay or return route and can introduce duplicate addressing.

firstPractice.hint: Choose the client's network, even though the server has its own interface address on a different network.
firstPractice.task: On paper, write Client1 beside 192.0.2.0/24, Relay1 beside 192.0.2.1 and Server1 beside 198.51.100.2. Circle which interface receives the client's broadcast and which subnet belongs in the server pool.
firstPractice.expected: The client-facing Relay1 GigabitEthernet1 receives the broadcast. The pool is 192.0.2.0/24, not the 198.51.100.0/30 transit link.

beginnerGuide.startingPoint: Begin with the address table and label each cable endpoint. A router can be a DHCP client on one interface; its device type does not force it to be the server. Keep every Console open so losing a lease cannot remove your control.

checkUnderstanding.hint: Ask whether the address was acquired before or after the change and whether its lease is still valid.
checkUnderstanding.answer: No. Existing lease state can remain valid, and renewal may use unicast. To evaluate the initial relay path, record the baseline and deliberately start a fresh acquisition on this isolated test client.
checkUnderstanding.question: A client still has an address after the helper is removed. Does that prove the helper was unnecessary?

everydayComparison.whereItStops: The analogy does not define packet destinations, timers or trust. A relay is not an approval authority, and receiving settings does not prove that a server is legitimate.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: The temporary assignment resembles a lease; the floor identifier resembles the relay's client-subnet information. The desk's list resembles the server binding record.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: A reception desk can temporarily assign a numbered locker. A messenger can carry a request from a different floor, while stating which floor needs the locker.

prerequisites: Recall that /24 means 255.255.255.0 and different subnets need routing.
Practice Day 15 Console access and Day 31 static routes before changing this isolated project.
Use three independently entitled C8000v IOS XE 17.12.1a instances in GNS3 2.2.55, or use the paper alternative.
content.learnerOutcome: Configure an IOS XE DHCP client, server pool and relay; compare a fresh lease with an existing lease, isolate a missing-helper fault, and explain what client, server and routing evidence establishes.
content.metaDescription: Build an isolated DHCP client, server and relay lab. Diagnose missing leases, wrong pools and return routes, then restore and verify the same client.
