teachingPrelude.explanation: Read the three roles separately before following the cables. Client1 is a router used as a DHCP client, Relay1 is its gateway, and Server1 runs the DHCP service. All result statements below are predictions to compare with your own observations, not recorded executions.
teachingPrelude.labBoundary: Three isolated IOS XE routers and two cables only. No Cloud, NAT node, physical adapter or production DHCP network. The client is an IOS interface, not a Windows PC. No DNS server or Internet service is provided.

practiceQuestions.answer: 192.0.2.0/24, the client subnet.
practiceQuestions.question: Which subnet belongs in the remote server's pool?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The server transit address is not the client's network. The relay identifies the client-facing subnet, allowing a matching pool to be selected.

practiceQuestions.answer: Its existing lease may remain valid.
practiceQuestions.question: Why can an old client work after a helper is removed?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The initial broadcast exchange and later client traffic are different operations. An existing lease or unicast renewal can hide a broken new-allocation path.

practiceQuestions.answer: No; the selected request and acknowledgement must follow.
practiceQuestions.question: Does an Offer prove the client has a confirmed lease?
practiceQuestions.explanation: An offer is a proposal. Multiple servers can offer settings, so the final accepted lease must be checked on the client and compared with server state.

practiceQuestions.answer: The exclusion range includes 192.0.2.1.
practiceQuestions.question: What keeps the gateway address out of this dynamic pool?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Infrastructure addressing must not be leased to an unrelated client. The pool name alone imposes no such restriction.

practiceQuestions.question: Which route is required on Server1?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The server's directly connected transit subnet does not include the relay's client-facing address or the assigned client address.

practiceQuestions.answer: No; this lab has no DNS service.
practiceQuestions.question: Does a successful server ping prove name resolution?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The test used a numeric address. DNS answers, web responses and secure server identity require their own tests and cannot be inferred from an ICMP reply.

realWorldScenario.title: Old clients work while new clients cannot join
realWorldScenario.takeaway: A retained lease can conceal a broken allocation path. A useful test starts from the state the affected learner actually has, follows one request through its dependencies, and verifies the restored result at both the client and server.
realWorldScenario.situation: In a fictional branch, already connected devices still reach an internal service, but a new client receives no lease. A recent change removed the helper from the client-facing interface. Existing leases make the network look healthy during a quick inspection. The operator must separate retained state from a fresh service transaction.
walkthrough: Ask when each client acquired its lease and record the affected subnet. Do not use the oldest working client as the sole service test.
Inspect the client-facing interface and compare its helper destination with the approved baseline. Keep the management console available.
Confirm the server pool contains available addresses for that subnet and has a return route toward the relay's client-facing address.
Restore only the approved helper line, then run a fresh acquisition on the disposable test client and compare both endpoint records.
Verify gateway and server reachability separately. Record any remaining DNS or application issue as a separate investigation rather than expanding the DHCP conclusion.

title: DNS records and name-resolution troubleshooting

lab.goal: Use a nonrecursive BIND fixture to inspect six record types and repair A data, then diagnose synthetic AAAA/MX/NS tickets with an optional private replay. No runtime was executed; DNS answers do not establish web, mail or IPv6 service health.
setup: Install BIND 9.18, dnsutils and nano in disposable Ubuntu images before isolating them. Record exact package versions with named -v and dig -v. No paid software or Cisco image is required.
Use fresh nodes whose sole lab NIC is ens3 and is not managed by DHCP or a competing network service. If the NIC differs, map it explicitly before substituting its name.
In nano, type the provided file text exactly, use Ctrl+O then Enter to save, and Ctrl+X to exit. Preserve dollar signs and trailing dots.

Create /tmp/qcs39 only for this lab. Run named in the foreground at the ordinary nonroot shell on unprivileged port 1053. Stop with Ctrl+C in DNS1's Console before editing; do not kill another system service.
Paper alternative: read the six fixture records and predict responses without starting BIND. Mark syntax and runtime checks unperformed; a worksheet does not verify a DNS daemon.

steps.why: Avoiding system configuration files and standard port 53 keeps the exercise bounded.
steps.title: Prepare the DNS interface
commands: sudo ip address add 192.0.2.53/24 dev ens3
sudo ip link set ens3 up
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click DNS1 and choose Console before typing. At the Linux shell, confirm ens3 and use only this disposable node. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: DNS1 has the planned address and a writable new fixture directory.
commandExplanations: Inspect interface names and existing addresses before selecting ens3.
Add the private DNS node address to the specified lab interface.
Enable ens3 without creating a default route.
Record the installed BIND version; these instructions target the 9.18 series.
Create a new disposable directory; stop if an existing directory needs ownership review.

steps.why: A failed basic local path should be repaired before interpreting a DNS timeout.
steps.title: Prepare the query client
commands: sudo ip address add 192.0.2.10/24 dev ens3
sudo ip link set ens3 up
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Client1 and choose Console before typing. At the Linux shell, inspect its interface and configure only the lab link. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: DNS1 should reply; no Internet route is needed.
commandExplanations: Check that ens3 is the isolated cable interface.
Assign the client's distinct /24 address on the same subnet.
Enable the client interface for the local cable.
Record the available DNS query tool version.
Send three ICMP tests to DNS1; this tests IP reachability, not DNS answers.

steps.why: Explicit private zones and an unprivileged port avoid depending on a public resolver or competing service.
steps.title: Create the authoritative server configuration
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click DNS1 and choose Console before typing. At DNS1's Bash shell, enter the complete multiline command below, including the closing QCS_FILE_END on its own unindented line. This here-document sends only the lines between its opening and closing markers into the named file. Keep the quotes around the opening marker so $TTL stays literal. A continuation prompt while entering these lines is normal; do not type the prompt. Enter no explanatory prose into the file. Use only the newly created private lab directory. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: The shell prompt returns after QCS_FILE_END; the file names match the next two fixtures. No system named.conf is changed.
commandExplanations: Create only the new lab named.conf. The redirection writes the bounded file text, without the delimiter lines. Its options disable recursion, bind the private listener and name the two zone files; no system configuration is changed.

steps.why: The code block preserves each record's line boundary and trailing dots; separating prose prevents invalid extra fields.
steps.title: Write the forward fixture
commands:
cat > /tmp/qcs39/forward <<'QCS_FILE_END'
$TTL 60
@ IN SOA ns.lab.test. admin.lab.test. (1 60 60 600 60)
@ IN NS ns.lab.test.
ns IN A 192.0.2.53
web IN A 192.0.2.80
web IN AAAA 2001:db8:39::80
www IN CNAME web.lab.test.
@ IN MX 10 mail.lab.test.
mail IN A 192.0.2.25
QCS_FILE_END
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click DNS1 and choose Console before typing. At DNS1's Bash shell, enter the complete multiline command below, including the closing QCS_FILE_END on its own unindented line. This here-document sends only the lines between its opening and closing markers into the named file. Keep the quotes around the opening marker so $TTL stays literal. A continuation prompt while entering these lines is normal; do not type the prompt. Enter no explanatory prose into the file. Use only the newly created private lab directory. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: The shell prompt returns; the file ends with mail IN A 192.0.2.25 on its own line, with no instruction prose appended.
commandExplanations: Write the quoted multiline forward zone verbatim. $TTL remains literal and sets 60 seconds; SOA supplies timers; NS, A, AAAA, CNAME and MX declare records. QCS_FILE_END is a shell delimiter, not a DNS record.

steps.why: A correct text file is necessary but must still be loaded by the intended running process.
steps.title: Write the reverse fixture and validate
commands:
cat > /tmp/qcs39/reverse <<'QCS_FILE_END'
$TTL 60
@ IN SOA ns.lab.test. admin.lab.test. (1 60 60 600 60)
@ IN NS ns.lab.test.
80 IN PTR web.lab.test.
QCS_FILE_END
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click DNS1 and choose Console before typing. At DNS1's Bash shell, enter the complete multiline command below, including the closing QCS_FILE_END on its own unindented line. This here-document sends only the lines between its opening and closing markers into the named file. Keep the quotes around the opening marker so $TTL stays literal. A continuation prompt while entering these lines is normal; do not type the prompt. Enter no explanatory prose into the file. Use only the newly created private lab directory. After the closing marker returns the ordinary prompt, run each validation command separately. Stop on any validation error before copying the baseline. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: Both zones should validate; stop and correct actual reported errors.
commandExplanations: Write only the reverse-zone text between the markers. Owner 80 expands beneath 2.0.192.in-addr.arpa; the markers are not stored in the file.
Check server configuration syntax; silence with successful exit is expected, not proof of running service.
Validate the forward zone and report parsing errors before starting the service.
Validate the independent reverse zone against its declared origin.
Only after all checks succeed, keep the exact working forward fixture for later bounded restoration.

steps.why: Keeping the process visible makes its stop action unambiguous: Ctrl+C in this same Console.
steps.title: Start the private DNS service
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click DNS1 and choose Console before typing. At the ordinary nonroot shell, start the foreground server. Leave this Console occupied while using Client1. Stop on permission or listener errors. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: Diagnostics should show both zones loaded and the private listener active. Do not invent a successful startup if errors appear.
commandExplanations: Run this exact BIND configuration in the foreground and print diagnostics; no system service is replaced.

steps.why: All named endpoints are data relationships, not hidden working servers omitted from the topology.
steps.title: Inspect every record relationship
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Client1 and choose Console before typing. At the Linux shell, retain complete answers including status and the responding server. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: Answers should match the fixture; the responding server is .53#1053. Neither web nor mail services exist.
commandExplanations: Ask DNS1 explicitly on lab port 1053 for the IPv4 address.
Ask for IPv6 data over the same IPv4 query path.
Inspect the alias target rather than assuming it is an address.
Inspect the preference and mail-target name.
Resolve the MX target to its separate fixture address.
Inspect the authoritative server name.
Construct and query the IPv4 reverse PTR name automatically.

steps.why: A status code and a network failure are different evidence and should not be collapsed into one error label.
steps.title: Compare three failure signatures
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Client1 and choose Console before typing. At the Linux shell, compare each test with the same functioning authoritative server. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: The first two are DNS responses; the unused-port test does not supply a valid DNS answer.
commandExplanations: Ask for an absent name; expect NXDOMAIN from this fixture.
Ask for a missing type at an existing name; expect NOERROR without an MX answer.
Ask an unused port with one one-second attempt; timeout or refusal differs from a DNS negative answer.

steps.why: Syntax validation cannot know the organization's approved destination address.
steps.title: Introduce one wrong A value
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click DNS1 and choose Console before typing. Press Ctrl+C in the foreground DNS Console first. At the restored shell, change only web's A from 192.0.2.80 to 192.0.2.81 and SOA serial 1 to 2; save and exit. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: The server should load the modified zone even though its A value is intentionally wrong.
commandExplanations: Edit the single A record and advance the zone serial; leave AAAA, CNAME and mail data unchanged.
Reject syntax errors before loading the deliberate, syntactically valid wrong value.
Restart only the foreground lab service using the changed fixture.

steps.why: A successful protocol response can still carry an operationally incorrect record.
steps.title: Observe and classify the wrong answer
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Client1 and choose Console before typing. At the Linux shell, use the same question and server as the recorded baseline. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: NOERROR can accompany the wrong A data; the original PTR remains unchanged.
commandExplanations: Compare the now-wrong .81 answer with the approved .80 baseline.
Follow the alias in an address query to inspect its target's changed data.
Show that the independent PTR was not automatically rewritten by the A change.

steps.why: Restoration is completed by a query from the client, not by accepting a file-copy command.
steps.title: Restore and reload the original record
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click DNS1 and choose Console before typing. Press Ctrl+C in the running server Console. At the shell restore the baseline file, set its SOA serial to 3, then validate and restart. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: The authoritative A should again be .80; the alias, AAAA, MX, NS and PTR retain their original relationships.
commandExplanations: Restore the exact lab forward data without touching other files.
Change only the restored SOA serial from 1 to 3 so revision numbering moves forward.
Validate the restored zone before serving it.
Start the private server with restored records and the newer serial.

steps.why: Independent fault/repair pairs reveal which record matters and avoid combining three faults into one ambiguous result.
steps.title: Replay and repair one additional ticket
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click DNS1 and choose Console before typing. First repeat the baseline queries in Client1's Console to verify the A repair, then return to DNS1. Ticket observations are synthetic. Optional replay follows serial 3 restoration: A6 uses serials 4 fault/5 corrected, MX1 6/7, NS1 8/9. Before each edit press Ctrl+C in this foreground server Console. Change only that ticket's specified record and SOA serial. Run these commands, perform the next client step, then repeat this step with the exact corrected line and next step again. Finish the pair before moving on; no parent delegation or application server is created. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: Each corrected trial must restore the approved AAAA, MX or NS data before the next trial; author observations remain unexecuted.
commandExplanations: Apply only the selected ticket's explicit fault or correction and its serial; preserve all unrelated records.
Validate the one edited zone; stop on a real error rather than serving an invalid fixture.
Restart only this private foreground service with the chosen ticket revision.

steps.why: The repeated question and dependent name lookups distinguish bad family data, a wrong MX target and misleading NS information.
steps.title: Re-query the ticket and its dependencies
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Client1 and choose Console before typing. At the shell, run these explicit questions before and after each optional ticket correction. For MX1 also inspect web's A/AAAA when the bad target is web; for NS1 inspect mail's A when the bad target is mail. Preserve status, AA flag, server and serial. On paper predict the differences instead of claiming execution. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: Corrected values match the ticket plan; mail AAAA remains absent. A direct authoritative response is not an HTTP, SMTP or recursive-delegation success.
commandExplanations: A6 checks the independent IPv6 record against ::80, not merely a successful A lookup.
Check A6's unchanged .80 data and MX1's incorrectly selected web target.
Check both preference and target; MX1 must return 10 mail.lab.test. after repair.
Resolve the correct mail target to .25; also expose NS1's wrong server target address.
Distinguish an existing mail name without IPv6 data from an absent name.
Check NS1 restores ns.lab.test. as the server name.
Verify the intended NS target resolves to the real DNS1 address .53.
Check the directly addressed authoritative zone and expected serial without requesting recursion.
Repeat the same direct authority check using TCP; this still does not test parent delegation.

steps.why: The final comparison checks collateral changes and keeps predicted behavior distinct from measured results.
steps.title: Repeat the baseline and stop cleanly
steps.instruction: In Client1's Console repeat every command from Inspect every record relationship and compare values. Then press Ctrl+C in DNS1's Console to stop only this foreground service. Stop both GNS3 nodes and retain the notes.
steps.expectedResult: All six record questions should match the planned data; record discrepancies and do not report application success.

lab.title: Private DNS records with one reversible wrong address
cleanup: Stop the foreground named process with Ctrl+C in DNS1's Console and verify it exits.
Stop or discard the two disposable nodes; never copy the private test zone into a public DNS service.
devices: DNS1: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, BIND 9.18, nano, nonroot user with sudo for interface setup.
Client1: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, dnsutils/dig and sudo for interface setup.
lab.topology: Client1 ens3 connects directly to DNS1 ens3 in GNS3 2.2.55. Both nodes are Ubuntu 24.04 LTS. No gateway, external bridge, Cloud or NAT node. DNS1 listens on 192.0.2.53 UDP/TCP 1053; explicit dig queries avoid changing system resolvers.

addressing.purpose: Actual query origin; no default gateway.
Records only; no corresponding endpoint nodes.
Record only; IPv6 forwarding is not configured.

verification: Compare name, type, status, answer and responding server for all six record types.
Confirm the wrong A produces a valid DNS response with wrong data, while PTR remains independent.
Distinguish NXDOMAIN, missing-type NOERROR and an unused-port timeout or refusal.
After restoration repeat alias, address, mail, authority and reverse questions, not only the edited A query.
For A6, MX1 and NS1 record synthetic expected/observed data, the exact corrected line and repeat queries; label optional replay unexecuted unless actually performed.
Explain why direct NS/SOA success does not prove parent delegation, and why correct DNS still needs separately prepared HTTP/TLS or SMTP service checks.
lab.licensingNote: GNS3 does not provide Cisco software images. Use Cisco images only when the applicable license or entitlement permits this environment. Do not share or redistribute image files. Cisco Modeling Labs is an official alternative; its supplied reference images are licensed for CML, not automatically for export to GNS3. Use the labeled paper alternative when authorized software is unavailable. No emulator execution is claimed by this lesson.
troubleshooting: named fails to start: inspect its actual diagnostics, directory ownership, AppArmor policy and listener conflicts. Do not disable host security globally; use an approved disposable image or the paper alternative.
Timeout on every query: confirm both ens3 addresses, server process and UDP/TCP 1053 reachability. A valid zone file does not prove a listener exists.
Wrong expanded target name: inspect trailing dots and the zone origin before changing the resolver or route.
Different answers through a caching resolver: compare direct authority and TTLs; this direct-query fixture does not reproduce public cache expiration.

quiz.question: A name exists but has no requested MX. Which result fits?
quiz.explanation: The name can exist while a type is absent. NXDOMAIN concerns the name; timeout concerns lack of response; HTTP redirects are application behavior.

quiz.question: Which MX preference is preferred first?
quiz.explanation: Lower numeric preference is preferred. Hostname length and address magnitude do not define MX preference.

quiz.question: What does www CNAME web establish?
quiz.explanation: CNAME supplies a DNS alias relationship. HTTP behavior, service health and certificate validity require separate application checks.

options: Forward and reverse zones are independent
quiz.question: Why can .80 PTR still return web after A changes to .81?
quiz.explanation: Separate record administration permits disagreement. It is not proof of caching corruption, immutability or an IPv6 interaction.

options: The queried records match the private plan
quiz.question: Which conclusion is supported by this fixture?
quiz.explanation: Only direct DNS records are tested. Public delegation, mail traffic and IPv6 forwarding need additional systems and evidence.

glossary.meaning: The Domain Name System stores typed records about names. A resolver asks DNS questions; an authoritative server answers from the zone data it controls.
A resource record has an owner name, type, time to live and data. A zone is an administered portion of the DNS namespace, not necessarily every name below a domain.
An A record supplies an IPv4 address. An AAAA record supplies an IPv6 address. The address family in the answer need not match the transport used to ask the question.
A canonical-name record makes one name an alias of another name. It is not an HTTP redirect and normally cannot coexist with other ordinary record types at the same owner.
A mail-exchanger record identifies a mail server name with a preference value; lower values are preferred. A name-server record identifies an authoritative server name for a zone.
A pointer record associates a reverse-DNS name with a target name. IPv4 reverse names reverse the octets under in-addr.arpa. Forward and reverse records are maintained separately.
Time to live is a cache lifetime in seconds, not a propagation guarantee. A cache retains a received answer temporarily, including certain negative answers.

NOERROR means the query was processed without a DNS error, but it may contain no requested record. NXDOMAIN means the queried name does not exist. SERVFAIL means resolution failed; timeout means no usable reply arrived.
Open a node's Console to reach its text window. Linux commands are entered at its shell prompt. An application port, such as UDP/TCP 53 or this lab's 1053, is not an Ethernet cable socket.

sections.example: Use web.lab.test. when comparing fixtures. In a zone file, web is relative to the lab.test zone, while web.lab.test. is absolute. Omitting the final dot from an intended absolute target can accidentally append the zone again, creating a wrong name that still passes basic text parsing.
sections.heading: Ask a name and a type, not whether DNS works
keyPoints: Record the exact question and responding server in your notes.
A name can have multiple address records; this fixture uses one of each family.
sections.explanation: A DNS request is more precise than the phrase DNS works. It names an owner and asks for a record type. A successful A lookup for web.lab.test tells you about IPv4 data for that name at that server and time. It says nothing by itself about an AAAA record, reverse lookup or mail destination. A fully qualified name ends at the DNS root; a trailing dot makes that explicit in zone data.

sections.example: The fixture gives www.lab.test a CNAME to web.lab.test. The target has A 192.0.2.80 and AAAA 2001:db8:39::80. A client may query either family using IPv4 transport to 192.0.2.53. Returning an IPv6 answer over IPv4 does not provide an IPv6 route to the returned address.
sections.heading: Addresses and aliases answer different questions
keyPoints: Inspect the alias and target when only one service name fails.
An address answer identifies data; verify the actual destination service separately.
sections.explanation: A maps a name to an IPv4 address; AAAA maps it to IPv6. CNAME points an alias to another name, which can then be resolved. A CNAME does not send an HTTP redirect response, move a browser to a new URL or change certificate requirements. Avoid ordinary records at a CNAME owner; an alias is not a convenient place to combine unrelated data.

sections.example: lab.test has MX 10 mail.lab.test., and mail.lab.test has A 192.0.2.25. The zone also has NS ns.lab.test., whose A record is the actual DNS node 192.0.2.53. This lab answers directly from that node with recursion disabled; it does not demonstrate root-to-zone delegation or a public recursive resolver.
sections.heading: Mail and authority records contain names
keyPoints: Do not put a raw IPv4 address where an MX or NS target name belongs.
A single local NS fixture is not a resilient production DNS design.
sections.explanation: MX identifies a mail-exchanger hostname and a preference number. Lower preference values are tried ahead of higher values according to mail delivery behavior; they are not probabilities. NS identifies the authoritative server names for a zone. Their names need usable address resolution. An authoritative answer comes from a server responsible for the zone; a recursive resolver can collect and cache answers for clients.

sections.example: Our forward A points web.lab.test to .80, and our PTR points .80 to web.lab.test. Editing the A record does not automatically edit the PTR. If they disagree, record both authoritative answers and identify their administrative owners. Reverse data is not cryptographic proof of ownership or trust.
sections.heading: Reverse DNS is a separate relationship
keyPoints: Forward and reverse lookups can be independently wrong or absent.
PTR absence does not mean the numeric IP address cannot exchange traffic.
sections.explanation: A PTR query asks for a name through the reverse namespace. For IPv4, 192.0.2.80 becomes 80.2.0.192.in-addr.arpa. The reverse zone in this exercise is 2.0.192.in-addr.arpa, with owner 80. IPv6 reverse names use reversed hexadecimal nibbles under ip6.arpa; this chapter explains that format but does not configure an IPv6 reverse zone.

sections.example: Query absent.lab.test A for a nonexistent name, then web.lab.test MX for an existing name without an MX. Compare those with an explicit query to port 1054, where this lab has no server. Keep status and answer sections rather than hiding them with output-shortening options during troubleshooting.
sections.heading: Distinguish status, empty answers and no response
keyPoints: Do not call an empty answer an unreachable DNS server.
Compare authoritative data with resolver data before blaming propagation.
sections.explanation: NXDOMAIN indicates that the queried name does not exist. NOERROR with no answer of the requested type can indicate that the name exists but lacks that record. SERVFAIL indicates a server-side resolution failure, which needs more diagnosis. A timeout is not a negative DNS answer at all. TTL controls cache use; negative answers can also be cached, so a correction may not immediately appear through every resolver.

sections.example: The safe fault changes web's A from .80 to .81 while leaving its AAAA, CNAME, MX and PTR unchanged. Query through www to notice how an alias can lead to the changed target, then restore .80. This covers v1.1 4.3's DNS role and a bounded portion of announced v2.0 4.4; real web/mail connections and public delegation remain untested.
sections.heading: Repair the record that the failing question uses
keyPoints: An authoritative wrong value needs a data repair, not a random resolver change.
Repeat all six record questions after repair to catch accidental collateral edits.
sections.explanation: A wrong A record can return NOERROR and still direct a client to an unintended address. Compare the record with the approved address plan, change only the lab record, validate zone syntax, restart the isolated server and repeat the identical query. Keep the original file and stop condition. Do not flush every cache as the first response to uncertain data.

sections.example: For each ticket, stop only the foreground named process in DNS1's Console with Ctrl+C. In that Console edit /tmp/qcs39/forward, validate using named-checkzone lab.test /tmp/qcs39/forward, then restart named -g -c /tmp/qcs39/named.conf. Client1's Console must re-query the same explicit .53 port 1053 server before and after correction. A6: query web.lab.test. AAAA and A. MX1: query lab.test. MX, then the returned target's A and AAAA. The corrected mail target has A .25 and NOERROR without AAAA in this fixture; absence of AAAA is not itself a mail failure. No mail or web application is running at any returned fixture address.
sections.heading: Tickets A6 and MX1: diagnose independent target data
keyPoints: Finish one ticket's correction and re-query before introducing another fault.
A correct address family or resolvable MX target is insufficient unless it matches the approved plan.
sections.explanation: These observations are synthetic, not captured output. A6 expected: web A 192.0.2.80 and AAAA 2001:db8:39::80. Observed: A is correct, but AAAA is 2001:db8:39::81 with NOERROR. A healthy IPv4 answer does not repair IPv6 data. For optional replay, change only web IN AAAA to ::81 with SOA serial 4; restore web IN AAAA 2001:db8:39::80 with serial 5. Do not put an IPv4 literal into AAAA or disable IPv6 to hide the discrepancy. MX1 expected: lab.test MX 10 mail.lab.test. and mail A 192.0.2.25. Observed: MX is 10 web.lab.test., which resolves successfully to the web fixture's .80 and ::80. The resolvable but wrong target is the fault, not its preference. Replay that MX with serial 6; restore @ IN MX 10 mail.lab.test. with serial 7, leaving both target address records untouched.

sections.example: Use the same DNS1 Console stop/edit/validate/restart procedure as the preceding tickets. From Client1 Console re-query lab.test. NS and the returned server name's A; then query lab.test. SOA directly at .53:1053 with recursion disabled and again using TCP. Require the expected name, .53 address and authoritative zone response. These direct tests do not exercise a parent referral, ordinary port 53 or a recursive lookup chain; no parent server exists here. Service decision: after correct A/AAAA, a real prepared endpoint still needs IPv4/IPv6 path and HTTP status/TLS checks. After correct MX and target addresses, an owned mail endpoint needs SMTP connection and controlled delivery/log checks. Those application tests remain paper-only here: do not probe the unhosted .80, .25 or IPv6 fixtures.
sections.heading: Ticket NS1: separate the authority record from delegation
keyPoints: Correct the record at the zone that owns the fault; a child answer does not prove its parent referral.
Record DNS correctness separately from HTTP availability, TLS identity and SMTP delivery.
sections.explanation: Synthetic NS1 expected: lab.test NS ns.lab.test., with ns A 192.0.2.53. Observed: lab.test NS mail.lab.test., with mail A 192.0.2.25; direct queries to .53 still answer authoritatively. The NS target is wrong even though the explicitly addressed server hosts the zone. Optional replay changes only @ IN NS mail.lab.test. with serial 8; correction restores @ IN NS ns.lab.test. with serial 9. Leave ns A .53 and the listener unchanged. NS targets identify DNS servers, not mail exchangers, and must not be aliases. For the separate paper delegation case, imagine a parent referral still naming mail.lab.test. while the child's own NS is correct: changing only the child cannot repair that parent. Its authorized owner must replace that referral with lab.test. NS ns.lab.test. and any required in-bailiwick glue with ns.lab.test. A 192.0.2.53.

content.metaTitle: CCNA Day 39: Diagnose DNS Records and Answers
takeaways: Choose the record type that answers the actual diagnostic question.
Follow alias and mail-target names to their address records.
Treat forward and reverse data as independently maintained.
Preserve status and responding server as well as answer values.
A correct DNS answer does not demonstrate a working application.
objectives: Choose A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, NS or PTR for a specific diagnostic question.
Read status, answer data, responding server and cache lifetime without inferring application health.
Follow an alias or mail-server name to its address record.
Build a private authoritative fixture and repair one wrong A record.
Explain why forward and reverse answers may disagree and why cached answers can differ.
Diagnose separate AAAA, MX and NS tickets, correct only the responsible record and repeat the relevant questions.
content.plainAnswer: DNS answers typed questions about names. Ask for the record type the application needs, check the responding server and status, then verify the record's target. An A answer does not prove the AAAA record, mail route or reverse lookup is correct. A valid DNS answer also does not establish that a web or mail service is running at the returned address.

visualStory.title: DNS records answer different questions

stages.title: Ask for an address
stages.explanation: A and AAAA return different address families. Check the requested type and answer without claiming the destination service is running.

stages.title: Follow the target name
stages.explanation: CNAME points to an alias target. MX identifies a mail target and preference. Resolve the relevant target address before testing its service.

stages.title: Check separate records
stages.explanation: NS identifies authoritative servers. PTR supplies a reverse name; editing an A record does not automatically update its PTR.

visualStory.altText: Six records compare A with IPv4, AAAA with IPv6, CNAME with an alias target, MX with a mail target, NS with authority and PTR with a reverse name.
visualStory.boundary: This is a record comparison, not a network wiring diagram. Returned web and mail addresses are fixture data, not working application servers.
visualStory.takeaway: Addresses, aliases, mail destinations, authority and reverse names are different relationships.

candidates.name: Six record relationships
candidates.scene: A six-cell comparison names each record and its returned data type.
candidates.limitation: Does not depict resolver delegation or an application connection.
candidates.teachingValue: Prevents treating every DNS answer as an IP address.

candidates.name: Resolver journey
candidates.scene: A client asks a resolver which follows authority referrals before answering.
candidates.limitation: The direct authoritative fixture does not execute this full path.
candidates.teachingValue: Explains the distributed lookup mechanism.

candidates.name: Wrong answer timeline
candidates.scene: Compare correct .80, faulty .81 and restored .80 responses.
candidates.limitation: Leaves the other five record types less visible.
candidates.teachingValue: Shows why NOERROR can contain wrong data.

conceptSelection.selectionReason: A record comparison fits this lesson's six-type diagnostic objective better than another router path.

walkthrough.why: Success for one address family cannot establish the other family's data or reachability.
walkthrough.action: Ask specifically for the web address.
walkthrough.whatHappens: The A query for web.lab.test returns the fixture's IPv4 address. The AAAA query asks independently for its IPv6 address.

walkthrough.why: An alias target and a mail target are names; neither is itself the numeric connection destination.
walkthrough.action: Follow a name rather than treating it as an address.
walkthrough.whatHappens: www.lab.test has a CNAME pointing to web.lab.test. The MX for lab.test points to mail.lab.test, whose A record must be checked separately.

walkthrough.why: This deliberately demonstrates that DNS data is not evidence of a running web or mail application.
walkthrough.action: Separate records from the services they describe.
walkthrough.whatHappens: The fixture returns 192.0.2.80 and 192.0.2.25 even though neither endpoint exists in this two-node project.

walkthrough.why: Different observations require different repairs; changing routing will not correct a valid but wrong zone record.
walkthrough.action: Compare a wrong answer with no answer.
walkthrough.whatHappens: A changed A record can produce a successful reply containing the wrong value. Querying an absent name produces a different status, while an unreachable port produces a timeout.

beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: A browser, mail sender and reverse lookup ask different questions. Replacing a resolver or flushing a cache without understanding the failed question can hide evidence while leaving the underlying record unchanged.

firstPractice.hint: Ask whether the expected data is an address, a name or a preference plus a name.
firstPractice.task: On paper, match these questions to record types: IPv4 address of web.lab.test; IPv6 address of that name; mail destination for lab.test; reverse name for 192.0.2.80. Then identify the extra lookup needed after an MX answer.
firstPractice.expected: Use A, AAAA, MX and PTR respectively. Resolve the MX target name with A or AAAA before attempting a mail connection.

beginnerGuide.startingPoint: Read one DNS answer like a labeled database row. First identify the requested name and record type. Then inspect status and the server that replied. Only after that interpret the returned value; a plausible-looking address can still be wrong.

checkUnderstanding.hint: Mail delivery may start with an MX query and then resolve the selected target name.
checkUnderstanding.answer: No. The successful A query may concern a different name. Check the domain's MX, its preference and its target's address records, then test mail-service reachability separately.
checkUnderstanding.question: An A query works but the mail server cannot be reached. Is DNS completely ruled out?

everydayComparison.whereItStops: DNS is distributed and cached. A directory analogy does not imply instant global updates, prove identity or mean that the application at an address will answer.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: DNS record types label different relationships. Address records identify addresses, aliases identify another name, and mail records identify a mail destination name plus preference.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: A directory may contain a person's telephone number, an alternate name and the office responsible for a department. Asking for an office does not return the same kind of information as asking for a telephone number.

prerequisites: Recall IPv4 /24 addressing and that an IPv6 address is a separate address family.
Use two disposable Ubuntu 24.04 LTS virtual machines in GNS3 2.2.55; install BIND 9.18 and dnsutils before disconnecting them.
Know how to open a node Console and use a text editor; nano controls are explained in the setup.
content.learnerOutcome: Interpret six DNS record types, follow alias and mail targets, separate response failures, repair a private A record and diagnose independent AAAA, MX and NS tickets with precise correction and re-query boundaries.
content.metaDescription: Read A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, NS and PTR records, distinguish DNS errors from application failures, and repair a wrong address in an isolated DNS lab.

teachingPrelude.explanation: Start with the question being asked: a name and a record type. The lab uses a private zone named lab.test and explicit queries to a private server. Names and addresses in its answers are records for inspection; no web server, mail server or IPv6 network is created.
teachingPrelude.labBoundary: Two Linux nodes, one cable and a private nonrecursive BIND server on port 1053. No Internet or public DNS changes. Returned web/mail/IPv6 addresses are deliberately unhosted fixtures; application reachability is not tested.

practiceQuestions.answer: AAAA returns IPv6 address data.
practiceQuestions.question: Which type returns an IPv6 address?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The query can travel over IPv4 or IPv6 independently of the address family returned. An IPv6 answer does not configure IPv6 connectivity.

practiceQuestions.answer: Resolve the mail-target name with A or AAAA.
practiceQuestions.question: What additional check follows an MX answer?
practiceQuestions.explanation: MX supplies a preference and a hostname. The sending application still needs a usable target address and a working mail service.

practiceQuestions.answer: The reverse-zone owner must restore 80 IN PTR web.lab.test.
practiceQuestions.question: A web A is correct at .80, but .80 PTR returns old.lab.test. What owns the repair?
practiceQuestions.explanation: In the private reverse file, correct only that PTR and advance its SOA serial, validate the reverse zone, restart the private server and repeat dig -x against .53:1053 plus the forward A. Do not change a correct A to match a wrong PTR.

practiceQuestions.answer: The requested type can be absent or its data can be wrong.
practiceQuestions.question: Why can NOERROR still be a problem?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A protocol status does not compare an address with your approved plan or prove the corresponding application is healthy.

practiceQuestions.answer: Different resolvers or authorities can return different data.
practiceQuestions.question: Why keep the server address in the evidence?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A comparison without the responding server loses the context needed to distinguish authoritative data from caching or split configuration.

practiceQuestions.answer: Detecting and repairing wrong authoritative A data.
practiceQuestions.question: What does the .81 fault actually test?
practiceQuestions.explanation: It does not measure a web outage because neither .80 nor .81 is a web endpoint in the private two-node topology.

practiceQuestions.answer: Restore only web's AAAA to 2001:db8:39::80 and re-query both families.
practiceQuestions.question: A6 returns the right A but AAAA ::81 instead of planned ::80. What changes?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Validate and reload the private zone with a newer serial. Do not disable IPv6 or overwrite the correct A. A repaired answer still does not establish an IPv6 route or web listener.

practiceQuestions.answer: A resolvable target can be the wrong mail exchanger; restore MX 10 mail.lab.test.
practiceQuestions.question: MX1 points to web.lab.test, which resolves. Why can mail still be misdirected?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Repeat MX and the returned target's A/AAAA after validation and reload. In this fixture mail has A .25 only; a real SMTP connection and controlled delivery remain separate, unperformed checks.

practiceQuestions.answer: Restore the zone's NS to ns.lab.test and verify its A is .53.
practiceQuestions.question: NS1's direct .53 answer works but NS names mail.lab.test. What must be corrected?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Re-query NS, server address and authoritative SOA over UDP/TCP. A separate stale parent referral belongs to the parent owner and is not repaired or exercised by this direct-query lab.

practiceQuestions.answer: Restore www IN CNAME web.lab.test. and query the alias plus target addresses.
practiceQuestions.question: www's CNAME is changed to absent.lab.test while web A remains correct. What next?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The broken alias can produce failure despite a healthy web A. Validate the corrected zone and repeat CNAME, www A and web AAAA using the same private authority; HTTP behavior remains untested.

realWorldScenario.title: The alias works, but points to the wrong destination
realWorldScenario.takeaway: DNS troubleshooting becomes manageable when the question and record type are explicit. Follow every returned name until you reach the required address, and keep DNS correctness separate from application availability.
realWorldScenario.situation: In a fictional maintenance window, an operator changes web.lab.test to the wrong IPv4 address. The public-facing alias remains spelled correctly, and its CNAME query succeeds. A learner concludes DNS cannot be involved because a name was returned. The useful next question is what address that target name resolves to, not whether the alias text exists.
walkthrough: Record the exact name, requested type, responding server and time. Preserve the full answer rather than reporting only that the command succeeded.
Follow the CNAME to the target's A and AAAA records; compare each value with the approved plan instead of assuming both families changed together.
Inspect the direct authoritative response separately from cached resolver data. A stale cached value and a wrong authoritative value require different interventions.
Restore the one wrong A record, validate the private zone, restart its isolated server and repeat the original alias and target queries.
Retain the PTR and mail-record checks as independent evidence. State that this fixture did not test HTTP, TLS, SMTP or IPv6 forwarding.

title: NAT and PAT from inside local to outside global

lab.goal: Compare static NAT, dynamic pool NAT and interface PAT on the same isolated IOS XE topology, then repair one selection fault. No runtime was performed by the author; preserve actual results and stop on unsupported syntax.
setup: Start fresh nodes with the two exact links. Record releases and interfaces; stop if the image or names do not match the reference platform.
Keep NAT1 and Outside1 Consoles open throughout. Capture prelab snapshots and do not save an intentional fault into startup configuration.
Only this disconnected lab may use clear ip nat translation *. It clears dynamic sessions on NAT1 and would disrupt users on a shared router.
Paper alternative: compute each table row and diagnose selector/pool/return-route faults without running IOS. Do not claim measured allocation, throughput or session sharing.

steps.why: The boundary determines which traversing traffic is eligible for this style of NAT.
steps.title: Build the inside and outside boundary
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click NAT1 and choose Console before typing. Start at > or # on the fresh router. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: Both ports have the intended roles and addresses.
commandExplanations: Enter privileged EXEC (#) from user EXEC (>); use only your authorized lab credentials.
Enter global configuration mode from privileged EXEC (#); accepted changes affect the running device.
Select the port cabled to PC1.
Set the inside gateway with the /24 mask.
Mark this interface as the inside side of traditional NAT.
Enable the selected inside port.
Return to global mode before selecting the other interface.
Select the cable toward Outside1.
Set the /30 outside transit address.
Mark this as the outside boundary.
Enable the outside port.
Return to privileged EXEC (#). This neither saves the configuration nor reverses accepted changes.

steps.why: A route and a translation are different objects and must be verified independently.
steps.title: Add the destination route
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click NAT1 and choose Console before typing. Start at # and inspect the initial state before any translation. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: The destination route exists; no client translation has yet been configured.
commandExplanations: Enter global configuration mode from privileged EXEC (#); accepted changes affect the running device.
Route the exact /32 destination through the adjacent outside router.
Return to privileged EXEC (#). This neither saves the configuration nor reverses accepted changes.
Record connected and static routes for the baseline.
Record the initially empty translation state.
Check inside/outside interface identification and current statistics.

steps.why: Explicit routing makes the reply path reproducible without depending on proxy ARP.
steps.title: Build the destination and return route
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Outside1 and choose Console before typing. Start at > or #. Do not add a route to the untranslated client LAN. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: Outside1 reaches the translation range through NAT1 and owns the loopback target.
commandExplanations: Enter privileged EXEC (#) from user EXEC (>); use only your authorized lab credentials.
Enter global configuration mode from privileged EXEC (#); accepted changes affect the running device.
Select the port cabled to NAT1's outside port.
Assign the adjacent transit address.
Enable the transit interface.
Return to global configuration.
Create the logical interface serving as the final test destination.
Assign the final destination as a /32 host address.
Return to global configuration before adding the return route.
Route the static/pool global range back to NAT1.
Return to privileged EXEC (#). This neither saves the configuration nor reverses accepted changes.

steps.why: This records a limited path baseline and distinguishes local connectivity from translated return reachability.
steps.title: Address PC1 and establish local baseline
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click PC1 and choose Console before typing. Use the VPCS prompt, not IOS configuration mode. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: The gateway should reply; the remote test should fail before NAT is configured.
commandExplanations: Assign PC1's source, /24 mask and NAT1 gateway.
Inspect PC1's actual settings before testing.
Test the inside cable and gateway.
Record the untranslated attempt; Outside1 has no route back to the client LAN.

steps.why: A fixed mapping can be configured without a flow, which differs from dynamic pool allocation.
steps.title: Configure static inside-source NAT
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click NAT1 and choose Console before typing. Start at #; this is the only active translation policy for PC1. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: The static relationship should appear; it does not itself prove a received reply.
commandExplanations: Enter global configuration mode from privileged EXEC (#); accepted changes affect the running device.
Fix the inside-local client to the inside-global lab address.
Return to privileged EXEC (#). This neither saves the configuration nor reverses accepted changes.
Inspect the static address relationship even before test traffic.

steps.why: Immediately inspect show ip nat translations in NAT1's Console at # and record actual roles; no sample output is fabricated.
steps.title: Test the static mapping from the client
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click PC1 and choose Console before typing. Use the VPCS prompt and the identical remote destination. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: Replies should arrive through the static translated return path.
commandExplanations: Generate inside-to-outside traffic and look for replies after initial discovery.

steps.why: Separate phases and explicit state checks prevent a lingering static translation from blocking removal or masking the new pool behavior.
steps.title: Replace static mapping with a pool
commands: no ip nat inside source static 10.40.0.10 198.18.0.100
show running-config | include ip nat inside source
ip nat inside source list 10 pool TWO
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click NAT1 and choose Console before typing. Start at # only after PC1's finite ping has returned to its VPCS prompt and no other node is generating traffic. Clear transient NAT state only on this exclusively owned, disconnected disposable NAT1. Check after clearing, then remove the exact static rule. Before the second configure terminal, require its absence from running-config and no remaining .100/.10 mapping. Stop on an in-use error or unexpected entry; do not answer a broad deletion prompt or continue installing the pool. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: The old static policy and mapping must be absent before the pool and rule are installed. New PC1 traffic is still required to demonstrate dynamic allocation.
commandExplanations: Clear transient translations only on this fully in-scope lab router; this disrupts active sessions and is not permission to clear a shared router.
Verify that transient ICMP child entries are gone. The configured static base relationship may remain at this point; stop if traffic recreates child entries.
Enter global configuration mode from privileged EXEC (#); accepted changes affect the running device.
Remove this exact static relationship after clearing its active children; stop if IOS reports it remains in use.
Return to privileged EXEC (#). This neither saves the configuration nor reverses accepted changes.
Require the old static .10-to-.100 rule to be absent before proceeding.
Require the removed mapping and its transient children to be absent. This is the mandatory checkpoint before installing a different policy.
Enter global configuration mode from privileged EXEC (#); accepted changes affect the running device.
Select only PC1 as eligible for dynamic translation; this is not an attached filter.
Define two routed global addresses in the /24 translation range.
Use ACL 10 to allocate non-overloaded addresses from pool TWO only after the static-removal checkpoint passes.
Return to privileged EXEC (#). This neither saves the configuration nor reverses accepted changes.

steps.why: One client demonstrates allocation only; two-address exhaustion and multiuser behavior remain paper predictions.
steps.title: Generate and read dynamic allocation
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click PC1 and choose Console before typing. At the VPCS prompt, send the same traffic; then inspect NAT1 promptly as described. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: Replies should arrive. In NAT1's Console at #, show ip nat translations and show ip nat statistics should identify .101 or .102, not an invented fixed choice.
commandExplanations: Cause the eligible inside host to request an on-demand pool mapping.

steps.why: Stopping traffic and clearing old state makes the new policy's effect observable.
steps.title: Replace the pool rule with PAT
commands: no ip nat inside source list 10 pool TWO
ip nat inside source list 10 interface GigabitEthernet2 overload
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click NAT1 and choose Console before typing. Start at # with PC1's test stopped. Clear dynamic state only because this router is disposable and exclusively in scope. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: New flows use 198.51.100.1 under overload instead of the removed pool.
commandExplanations: Remove dynamic translation state for this isolated phase change; never run this indiscriminately on shared devices.
Enter global configuration mode from privileged EXEC (#); accepted changes affect the running device.
Remove the non-overloaded pool rule before installing overload.
Delete the now-unused pool definition.
Translate eligible flows using the outside interface address with protocol-specific sharing.
Return to privileged EXEC (#). This neither saves the configuration nor reverses accepted changes.

steps.why: ICMP uses identifiers, not TCP ports; a one-client test does not measure simultaneous multiuser sharing.
steps.title: Test and inspect PAT baseline
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click PC1 and choose Console before typing. At the VPCS prompt, repeat the same destination; inspect NAT1 immediately afterward. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: Replies should arrive; NAT1's show ip nat translations should show the interface global address and ICMP-specific state while present.
commandExplanations: Generate an ICMP flow through interface overload.

steps.why: The experiment changes one policy decision; it does not install an interface deny rule.
steps.title: Introduce the wrong selector
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click NAT1 and choose Console before typing. Start at # after the test stops. Keep interfaces, routes and PAT rule unchanged. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: PC1 no longer matches the translation selection.
commandExplanations: Remove this isolated router's dynamic state so an old translation cannot hide the selector change.
Enter global configuration mode from privileged EXEC (#); accepted changes affect the running device.
Remove only this lab's dedicated NAT selection list.
Deliberately select a nonexistent host instead of PC1's .10 address.
Return to privileged EXEC (#). This neither saves the configuration nor reverses accepted changes.

steps.why: The result is not evidence of a NAT ACL firewall drop; combine selector, table and route observations.
steps.title: Observe the failed translated exchange
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click PC1 and choose Console before typing. At the VPCS prompt, compare local and remote tests without changing PC1. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: Gateway replies should persist; remote replies should fail because untranslated PC1 has no return route. Inspect NAT1 for the missing new translation.
commandExplanations: Confirm the unchanged inside gateway still responds.
Retry the same remote path while PC1 is not selected for translation.

steps.why: A narrow repair preserves the reason the experiment is interpretable.
steps.title: Restore the selector and verify state
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click NAT1 and choose Console before typing. Start at #. Restore the exact approved source rather than widening the match to any. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: The approved source match is restored without changing routing or the outside address.
commandExplanations: Enter global configuration mode from privileged EXEC (#); accepted changes affect the running device.
Remove the deliberate wrong host selector.
Restore PC1's exact source selection.
Return to privileged EXEC (#). This neither saves the configuration nor reverses accepted changes.
Check the corrected host match in the dedicated selector.
Confirm the intended NAT roles and overload policy remain configured.

steps.why: A completed repair needs both endpoint behavior and mapping evidence; neither result establishes DNS or application performance.
steps.title: Repeat the client test and close
steps.instruction: In PC1's Console, repeat ping 203.0.113.10. In NAT1's Console at #, immediately run show ip nat translations and show ip nat statistics. Retain the baseline, fault and restored observations, then stop all nodes.
steps.expectedResult: The same client flow should again receive replies and create the intended overload mapping.

lab.title: Three translation phases on one complete path
cleanup: Stop traffic and all three nodes after restoring the correct selector; preserve the observed table values privately.
Revert the clean-project snapshots to remove every lab change. Do not export the configuration into a real edge router.
devices: PC1: GNS3 VPCS 0.8.
NAT1 and Outside1: independently entitled C8000v IOS XE 17.12.1a in GNS3 2.2.55.
lab.topology: PC1 Ethernet0 -- NAT1 GigabitEthernet1; NAT1 GigabitEthernet2 -- Outside1 GigabitEthernet1. Outside1 Loopback0 (203.0.113.10/32) is the final ping destination. No switch or external bridge exists.

addressing.purpose: Final destination, not an Internet host.
Routed lab translation addresses; not extra nodes.

verification: Record the four address roles for static, pool and PAT phases; never invent selected ports or identifiers.
Confirm the static rule is absent before the pool phase and the pool rule is absent before PAT.
Match each observed entry to a PC1 test, not a router-originated ping.
Compare the wrong-selector failure with the restored exact host match and repeat the same remote destination.

Entry exists but no replies: inspect destination and return routes and outside host behavior before changing the translation rule.
Dynamic rule reports in use: stop the disposable client's traffic and inspect state; never clear unrelated production translations to continue this exercise.
Pool allocation absent: confirm the pool is referenced, the client matches and capacity is available. Static entries left from an earlier phase can mask the intended test.

quiz.question: Which address represents PC1 under static NAT?
quiz.explanation: The configured inside-global value is .100. The other choices are the remote destination, adjacent router and inside gateway.

options: The global representation and sharing policy
quiz.question: What changes when interface overload replaces the pool?
quiz.explanation: The client, cables and destination stay fixed; the translation policy now uses the outside interface address with overload.

quiz.question: An entry exists but no replies arrive. What remains necessary?
quiz.explanation: Mapping state is not end-to-end success. Routing and endpoint behavior still matter; NAT does not provide encryption.

options: New hosts can fail allocation when both addresses are occupied
quiz.question: A non-overloaded pool has two addresses. Which claim is sound?
quiz.explanation: Dynamic address resources are finite. Non-overloaded NAT does not imply unlimited sharing, duplication or a security filter.

options: PC1 ping to 203.0.113.10 plus immediate table inspection
quiz.question: Which test best exercises this client's NAT path?
quiz.explanation: The endpoint test traverses the configured boundary and can be correlated with state. Self-tests and saved configuration do not establish that path.

glossary.meaning: Network Address Translation changes address information as packets cross a configured boundary. This lesson uses traditional inside-source IPv4 NAT, not NAT64 or a firewall.
These are administrator-selected sides of a NAT boundary. Inside identifies our client LAN; outside identifies the other lab network, not necessarily the public Internet.

Inside local is the inside host's address in its own network. Inside global represents that same host toward the outside. Global describes the NAT role; it does not guarantee a publicly routed address.
Outside global identifies the outside host in its own network. Outside local is how that host appears inside. They are identical in this lab because outside addresses are not translated.

Static NAT configures a fixed address mapping. Dynamic pool NAT selects an available global address for an eligible inside host; without overload, separate simultaneous hosts require separate addresses.

Port Address Translation lets flows share a global address using protocol-specific identifiers, such as TCP/UDP ports. ICMP echo uses an identifier rather than a TCP port. IOS overload enables this sharing.

An access control list used by NAT selects traffic for translation. A host entry matches exactly one address. This selection is not an interface packet-filter policy unless separately attached as one.
Right-click the named GNS3 node and choose Console. IOS > is user EXEC, # is privileged EXEC and (config)# is configuration. VPCS has different commands. Predicted output is not a measured result.

sections.example: PC1 uses 10.40.0.10. Static NAT represents it as 198.18.0.100 toward Outside1, whose loopback is 203.0.113.10. All three ranges are isolated teaching addresses. The global role of .100 does not make it Internet-routable or prove an Internet provider has allocated it.
sections.heading: Names describe viewpoints, not public versus private
keyPoints: Read each column as host identity plus representation.
The outside node is the final recipient, not an omitted Internet cloud.
sections.explanation: Inside local and inside global describe two representations of the inside host. Outside local and outside global describe the outside host. In a simple inside-source design the outside address remains unchanged, so two columns legitimately contain the same address. Do not label every private address local and every public-looking address global without checking its role.

sections.example: The command maps 10.40.0.10 to 198.18.0.100. Outside1 routes 198.18.0.0/24 back to NAT1. That explicit route means the teaching exercise does not depend on undocumented proxy ARP behavior for a global address on the outside cable.
sections.heading: Static mapping fixes an address relationship
keyPoints: An entry that exists before traffic is not proof of a successful exchange.
Use a reachable translation range and a known return path.
sections.explanation: Static inside-source NAT configures a stable mapping between one inside-local address and one inside-global address. Its basic entry can appear without traffic, unlike an on-demand dynamic allocation. Static mapping does not create the internal host, guarantee a route or specify all security policy. Inbound reachability also depends on routing and filtering.

sections.example: Our pool contains 198.18.0.101 and 198.18.0.102. One PC can demonstrate allocation, but it cannot measure two-host exhaustion. On paper, if both addresses are allocated and another host needs a new mapping, no third address is available. Mark that example a prediction, not a captured test.
sections.heading: Dynamic pool NAT allocates a scarce resource
keyPoints: Traffic is needed to create an on-demand mapping.
Compare pool utilization and selection before changing unrelated routes.
sections.explanation: A pool defines candidate inside-global addresses. The NAT selection ACL identifies eligible inside sources. Without overload, ordinary dynamic address mapping does not allow unlimited inside hosts to share one pool address simultaneously. Pool exhaustion can therefore affect new allocations while existing translations continue. A pool name is not a route, and a NAT ACL deny means no match for that translation policy, not automatically a packet drop.

sections.example: The interface-overload phase uses NAT1's outside address 198.51.100.1. PC1 still sends from 10.40.0.10 toward 203.0.113.10. Inspect the protocol and identifier fields while traffic is active. Do not invent a TCP port number for an ICMP row or assume identifiers never change.
sections.heading: PAT shares an address, not an unlimited resource
keyPoints: A shared global address still needs per-flow state and correct return handling.
PAT is not encryption and is not a substitute for an explicit security policy.
sections.explanation: Overload permits flows to share an inside-global address using protocol-specific state. TCP and UDP use ports; ICMP echo can use identifiers. A protocol identifier is not a device's physical interface number. Capacity is finite and platform-dependent. A single ping verifies only a narrow flow, not a realistic NAT scale, throughput or application mix.

sections.example: With the selector changed to host 10.40.0.99, PC1 no longer matches. Outside1 intentionally lacks a route for 10.40.0.0/24, so untranslated client traffic has no valid return path. The failed ping alone does not prove an ACL packet drop. Compare the missing translation with the unchanged routes and interface status.
sections.heading: Evidence must separate mapping from successful delivery
keyPoints: Never clear a shared production translation table for this lesson.
Restore the exact host selector, then retest from PC1 rather than NAT1.
sections.explanation: Inspect interfaces and routes, the configured selection, translation entries and actual endpoint tests. A router-originated ping may not traverse the same inside-to-outside path as traffic from PC1, so it cannot replace the endpoint test. NAT counters can rise for traffic that later fails elsewhere. Existing state can also hide the impact of a changed policy.

sections.example: The static phase is removed before the pool phase, and the pool rule is removed before interface overload. Current v1.1 4.1 explicitly calls for static and pools; PAT extends that practice and maps to announced v2.0 4.3. Neither a structural check nor this one-client exercise establishes production NAT capacity or all IOS XE features.
sections.heading: Treat phases and cleanup as part of the change
keyPoints: Keep one active translation policy for this client during each phase.
v1.1 remains current through 2 February 2027; v2.0 begins 3 February 2027.
sections.explanation: Stop test traffic before removing a dynamic mapping. In this disposable project only, clearing dynamic translations makes policy replacement unambiguous; the command can disrupt sessions elsewhere. If IOS says a mapping is in use, do not force an unfamiliar production procedure. Confirm the isolated boundary, stop traffic and inspect state before continuing.

content.metaTitle: CCNA Day 40: Static NAT, Pools and PAT on IOS XE
takeaways: NAT roles describe viewpoint, not merely public versus private addressing.
Static, pool and overload policies have different allocation behavior.
A NAT selector is not automatically a packet filter.
Translation tables and endpoint replies answer different questions.
Routes and the reverse path remain necessary after translation.
objectives: Identify inside local, inside global, outside local and outside global in one exchange.
Configure and verify static inside-source NAT and a non-overloaded dynamic pool.
Replace the pool rule with IOS XE interface overload and inspect protocol-specific state.
Separate translation selection from routing and packet filtering.
Repair one known selector fault and repeat the original traffic and table checks.
content.plainAnswer: Static NAT fixes an address mapping, dynamic NAT allocates from a pool, and PAT lets flows share an address using protocol identifiers. All require the intended inside/outside boundary and working routes. A translation entry is evidence of a mapping, not proof of application success. A NAT selection ACL chooses traffic to translate; it is not automatically a firewall.

visualStory.title: Static, pool and PAT change different things

stages.title: Fix one mapping
stages.explanation: Static NAT maps PC1 10.40.0.10 to 198.18.0.100. The basic mapping exists even before traffic proves a successful exchange.

stages.title: Allocate from a pool
stages.explanation: Dynamic NAT chooses an available pool address for eligible traffic. Without overload, address capacity limits simultaneous host mappings.

stages.title: Share with flow state
stages.explanation: PAT uses 198.51.100.1 plus protocol-specific state. TCP/UDP ports or ICMP identifiers help associate replies with the inside flow.

visualStory.altText: Three records compare static NAT's fixed mapping, dynamic NAT's pool allocation and PAT's shared address with flow identifiers.
visualStory.boundary: Conceptual policy comparison, not physical wiring or measured scale. The full lab path ends at Outside1, and only one client is exercised.
visualStory.takeaway: Keep the client fixed; compare how its outside representation is chosen.

walkthrough.why: The setup makes a translated reply path explicit without claiming translation itself installs every route.
walkthrough.action: Prove the two local links first.
walkthrough.whatHappens: PC1 reaches NAT1 at 10.40.0.1, and NAT1 reaches Outside1. Outside1 has a return route for the translated pool, not for 10.40.0.0/24.

walkthrough.why: The four table headings are relative roles, not four necessarily different numerical addresses.
walkthrough.action: Read one static mapping in both directions.
walkthrough.whatHappens: 10.40.0.10 is represented by 198.18.0.100. The remote destination remains 203.0.113.10 before and after the inside-source translation.

walkthrough.why: Separate phases keep the observed entry attributable to one known policy.
walkthrough.action: Change only the translation policy.
walkthrough.whatHappens: Remove static NAT, test dynamic pool allocation, then replace it with interface overload using 198.51.100.1.

walkthrough.why: A wrong selector can leave routing and interfaces correct while preventing the intended translation.

beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Translation troubleshooting often fails when an operator treats routing, NAT selection and security policy as one thing. Keeping them separate lets a learner explain why a configured mapping may still produce no reply.

firstPractice.hint: First ask which host a column describes, then which side's representation it names.
firstPractice.task: On paper, fill four table columns for PC1 reaching Outside1 under static NAT: inside local, inside global, outside local and outside global. Use the exact address plan and explain why the last two are equal.
firstPractice.expected: The values are 10.40.0.10, 198.18.0.100, 203.0.113.10 and 203.0.113.10. This lab changes only the inside source.

beginnerGuide.startingPoint: Write two labels for the same inside host: its original 10.40.0.10 address and the address representing it outside. NAT does not create a second computer. Then write the unchanged destination 203.0.113.10 beside Outside1.

checkUnderstanding.hint: Identify whether the ACL is referenced by a NAT rule or attached as an interface filter.
checkUnderstanding.answer: No. The NAT rule uses this ACL to select translation candidates. Firewall policy and any separately attached interface ACL are separate controls; a NAT permit is not their approval.
checkUnderstanding.question: Does a permit in the NAT selector authorize all traffic through a firewall?

everydayComparison.whereItStops: NAT is not a human screening service or an encryption method. Protocol state and routing rules, not the analogy, determine which packets can be translated and delivered.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: The two address views resemble inside global and inside local. Additional flow identifiers let replies be associated with the correct internal exchange when an address is shared.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: A receptionist can use one published contact number while maintaining a list of internal extensions. The published number and an extension identify different views of a contact.

prerequisites: Recall Day 31 static routes and Day 15 IOS configuration modes; a route chooses the next hop.
Use GNS3 2.2.55 with two independently entitled C8000v IOS XE 17.12.1a routers and one VPCS 0.8 node.
Read the address table before connecting anything; all outside addresses remain inside this disconnected lab.
