glossary.meaning: Management access lets an authorized operator inspect or change a device. A local console, remote command session, web interface and cloud management service have different paths and trust dependencies.

Secure Shell protects a remote session. A server host key identifies the server to the client; a user credential identifies the operator to the server. Encryption without checking the intended host can protect a connection to the wrong system.

Secure Copy Protocol and SSH File Transfer Protocol are different file-transfer mechanisms using SSH. SFTP is not FTP with TLS. Modern OpenSSH scp commonly uses SFTP unless legacy SCP is explicitly requested.

Authentication, authorization and accounting answer identity, permission and activity-record questions. Virtual terminal lines are IOS remote-session entry points; their configured login and transport policy matters.

A configuration file records settings and can contain sensitive secrets or hashes. A software image contains executable device software. Copying either file does not install it or prove its trustworthiness.

A cryptographic digest summarizes file bytes to detect differences. Matching digests support integrity only relative to the compared copies; trusted provenance requires an authenticated source or signed verification.
Open the named GNS3 Console. IOS >, # and (config)# differ from the Linux shell and the sftp> interactive prompt. Type only commands, not prompt labels.
Removing a test file or restoring a service setting is different from restoring active device configuration. This lab never loads the copied configuration or installs a software image.

sections.example: A cloud dashboard being reachable does not prove its device control channel is healthy. Likewise, a local console is not automatically safe if an unauthorized person can access it. TACACS+ and RADIUS support centralized AAA decisions; they are not replacements for the encrypted SSH transport. Day 48 configures those client relationships.
sections.heading: Choose an administration path deliberately
keyPoints: Use secure supported access methods and restrict the management path.
Do not disable certificate or host-key checks to make a connection easier.
sections.explanation: Console provides local or out-of-band text access and remains valuable when the routed path fails, but physical access must be protected. Telnet and ordinary HTTP do not provide the session confidentiality expected for sensitive administration. SSH protects a command session, while HTTPS protects a web interface when its certificate is validated. Cloud management adds an external identity and service dependency.

sections.example: The isolated new lab allows a documented first-use acceptance only after you verify the complete private wiring and fresh node identity. Record that limitation. Files1's host fingerprint can be read directly from its Console and compared with the client prompt. Unexpected changes during the exercise are stop conditions, not invitations to bypass warnings.
sections.heading: Authenticate the server before trusting the session
keyPoints: User authentication and server identity solve different problems.
Keep the trusted Console open until remote access and rollback are verified.
sections.explanation: SSH authenticates a server host key and then authenticates the user. First-use trust is a bootstrap decision, not proof obtained from encryption alone. Production keys should be checked using an approved independent inventory or channel. A changed-key warning needs investigation; blindly deleting known_hosts or disabling checking discards important protection.

sections.example: Our selected IOS image is used as an SCP server; Files1's OpenSSH server provides SFTP. The Linux exercise uses put and get at an sftp prompt. This is a practical supported alternative, not proof that the same commands configure an IOS SFTP server. Newer platforms may have other supported SFTP client capabilities.
sections.heading: SCP and SFTP are separate capabilities
keyPoints: Do not diagnose every subsystem failure as a bad password.
Never force obsolete cryptographic algorithms just to conceal a compatibility problem.
sections.explanation: Both use SSH, but legacy SCP and SFTP are different protocols. OpenSSH 9 changed scp's default transfer protocol to SFTP. Cisco documents cases where IOS XE's SCP server needs the uppercase -O client option to request legacy SCP. That option changes the transfer protocol, not host-key verification or the SSH encryption requirement. Platform and release support must be checked.

sections.example: An isolated recovery environment might document a specific legacy transfer requirement under its own approved controls. This lesson does not configure FTP or TFTP and does not upload a real configuration through them. SFTP is the SSH file-transfer protocol, not a shorthand for secure FTP or FTPS.
sections.heading: Legacy FTP and TFTP have different capabilities
keyPoints: FTP, FTPS, SFTP and TFTP are not interchangeable names.
Prefer a supported secure transfer path for secrets and configuration backups.
sections.explanation: FTP supports authenticated file operations with separate control and data connections, but ordinary FTP does not encrypt its credentials or payload. TFTP is a simpler UDP-based transfer protocol without FTP's login model or general directory workflow. Their capabilities matter for understanding older network operations, not as recommendations for sensitive backups.

sections.example: Router1 records the backup's byte count, not a device-side digest. Admin1 retrieves the unchanged file twice, checks both sizes against that count and compares their Linux SHA-256 values. Later SFTP and recovery copies are compared with this local baseline. This checks read-back consistency, not independent source integrity, correct settings or an uncompromised router. No IOS hash switch is assumed for 17.12.1a. The separate software branch uses Linux SHA-512 against an authenticated vendor value; never compare SHA-256 with SHA-512.
sections.heading: A file transfer needs identity, path and integrity checks
keyPoints: Matching two copies checks consistency, not necessarily trustworthy origin.
Never distribute Cisco image files as part of a classroom transfer exercise.
sections.explanation: Before transfer, verify server identity, available storage, exact source and destination names and the account's permission. Treat configurations as sensitive even when passwords are hashed. Compare received bytes using a digest or equivalent approved verification. A file's existence does not establish completeness; a trusted vendor hash or signature adds provenance beyond comparing two copies.

sections.example: Disable only ip scp server enable, attempt the same file retrieval and inspect the actual error. Restore the service and repeat. This bounded difference isolates subsystem availability without changing credentials or host keys. v1.1 4.8 and 4.9 are addressed; v2.0 4.2 also has a conditional genuine-software staging exercise below. Installation and universal IOS SFTP support are not claimed.
sections.heading: Copying is not restoring, and service recovery is not password bypass
keyPoints: A transfer failure is not authorization to bypass identity controls.
v1.1 is current through 2 February 2027; v2.0 begins 3 February 2027.
sections.explanation: Copy running-config to a file creates a snapshot of current settings. It does not save startup configuration unless that is the chosen destination. Copying a file back into running configuration can merge commands and should not be described as a universal replacement. The lab tests a disabled SCP service while leaving SSH and the Console available.

sections.example: Privately prepare Admin1's /opt/qcs45-assets/c8000v-staging.bin before isolation, owned by its operator with mode 600 inside a private directory. This fixed local name is only an alias for the genuine downloaded bytes; retain the vendor filename-to-alias mapping in the private manifest. Do not rename day45.cfg into it. The device destination is exactly bootflash:qcs45-stage/c8000v-staging.bin. Files1 receives no software. Neither a GNS3 project nor a prepared VM containing the package may be redistributed. The worksheet records metadata and observations, never the software payload.
sections.heading: Software staging starts with entitlement and a trusted reference
keyPoints: The running lab router's entitlement does not automatically authorize every additional software download or use.
A trusted reference comes from the authenticated vendor channel, not from a hash supplied alongside an untrusted file.
sections.explanation: Staging means placing a software file in a temporary device directory without executing it. Before isolating this lab, the authorized operator must obtain a genuine C8000v consolidated .bin package from Cisco Software Download over certificate-validated HTTPS using their own entitlement. Record the actual product, release, original filename, byte count, download-page URL, retrieval date and Cisco-published SHA-512 value. A SHA-512 whole-file digest has 128 hexadecimal characters. Do not use a forum mirror, another learner's image, a renamed backup or an invented hash. No package is supplied by this lesson. If the file, entitlement or authenticated reference is unavailable, mark this branch unavailable and perform only the paper assessment.

sections.example: After copying, inspect the exact destination and its byte count. Retrieve that same staged file through SCP into Admin1's new software-returned.bin and compare both source and read-back SHA-512 values with the authenticated vendor value. This explicitly supported Linux hash calculation verifies the device file by read-back without assuming an IOS SHA-512 command. A match is not a boot test, signature validation or installation approval. Record any mismatch and stop; remove only this exercise's staged file, then its empty directory. Recheck bootflash and account for the private Linux copy. Never issue install, boot-setting, reload, erase, recursive deletion or redistribution actions.
sections.heading: Check capacity, verify staged bytes and remove only the new file
keyPoints: Use independent vendor comparison, not merely equality between two copies of an untrusted file.
Cleanup is limited to paths created by this branch; restore disposable snapshots after retiring all private artifacts.
sections.explanation: Let B be the authenticated package's byte count. Before transfer, require Router1 bootflash free bytes and Admin1's qcs45 filesystem available bytes each to exceed B plus 1,073,741,824 bytes. The extra one GiB is a conservative exercise reserve, not a Cisco installation requirement. Admin1 already holds the source elsewhere and needs room for one read-back copy. Confirm bootflash:qcs45-stage does not exist and ~/qcs45/software-returned.bin is absent. Stop on insufficient space or any collision; never delete existing boot images, packages or unrelated files to make room. Compare source size and SHA-512 with the vendor reference before copying through the recovered SCP service.

content.metaTitle: CCNA Day 45: SSH, SCP and SFTP Administration
takeaways: Check the intended host and user separately.
SCP and SFTP are different server capabilities despite sharing SSH.
Keep configuration copies private at every endpoint.
Compare file bytes without confusing integrity with trusted provenance.
A successful copy is not a configuration restore or software installation.
objectives: Compare console, Telnet, SSH, HTTP, HTTPS and cloud-managed administration.
Distinguish SSH server identity from user authentication and permission.
Configure local AAA, SSH-only VTY access and the IOS SCP server.
Retrieve a configuration with SCP and use SFTP on an explicitly supported Linux endpoint.
Compare backup read-backs on Linux and repair a disabled SCP service without weakening host checking.
Stage an entitled software file after capacity and vendor-hash checks; verify the device copy and perform scoped cleanup without installation.
content.plainAnswer: Secure administration requires the intended host, an authorized user, limited management exposure and verified file handling. SSH protects sessions; SCP and SFTP transfer files through SSH but are not interchangeable server capabilities. Verify identity, destination, permissions and copied bytes. Copying a configuration or software image does not restore settings, install software or prove the file is trusted.

visualStory.title: A private backup crosses two verified transfers

stages.title: Retrieve with SCP
stages.explanation: Admin1 retrieves Router1's private file using the documented SCP protocol. Host checking and user authorization remain required.

stages.title: Compare local read-backs
stages.explanation: Compare two SCP read-backs on Linux: sizes against Router1's count, then SHA-256 values with each other. Agreement checks copy consistency, not independent source integrity or permission to restore.

stages.title: Reach the SFTP endpoint
stages.explanation: Admin1 transfers the file to Linux Files1 and verifies a downloaded comparison copy. This does not claim SFTP-server support on Router1.

visualStory.altText: Router1's backup reaches Admin1 by SCP, then Files1 by SFTP. Switch1 carries the local traffic; the file is never applied as a restore.
visualStory.boundary: Logical file workflow, not direct cabling. All three hosts connect through Switch1. SFTP runs on Files1, not the selected IOS server; no software is installed.
visualStory.takeaway: Router1 supplies SCP; Admin1 verifies the copy; Files1 supplies the separate supported SFTP endpoint.

walkthrough.why: A remote-access mistake must not force password bypass or a blind reset.
walkthrough.action: Keep an independent recovery path.
walkthrough.whatHappens: Router1's GNS3 Console stays open while remote SSH and SCP are configured and tested.

walkthrough.why: A correct password does not establish that the server presenting the login is the intended device.
walkthrough.action: Verify the endpoint and user separately.

walkthrough.whatHappens: Router1 writes a private bootflash backup, and Admin1 retrieves it using legacy SCP mode where required.

beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: An encrypted transfer to the wrong host or path is still a mistake. A successfully copied configuration can contain sensitive data, and applying it blindly can remove management access. File handling needs checks beyond a progress bar.

firstPractice.hint: SSH is the protected transport; the requested application within that connection still needs to be available.
firstPractice.task: On paper, label Router1 as the SCP server, Admin1 as the client and Files1 as the SFTP server. Explain what happens if terminal SSH succeeds but the IOS SCP service is disabled.
firstPractice.expected: The terminal can remain usable while the file-transfer operation fails. Server subsystem support and authorization must be checked separately from SSH connectivity.

beginnerGuide.startingPoint: First separate logging into a device from transferring a file. Then identify who is the server for each connection. The same SSH transport can carry a terminal or a file-transfer subsystem, but successful terminal login does not prove every subsystem is enabled.

checkUnderstanding.hint: Integrity of bytes does not establish platform compatibility, intended settings or authorization.
checkUnderstanding.answer: No. The matching digest only compares the copies. Loading requires a separate approved change, compatible platform and interfaces, review of sensitive settings and a tested recovery plan.
checkUnderstanding.question: The backup digest matches after transfer. Is it now safe to load into a different router?

everydayComparison.whereItStops: Cryptographic protocols and file permissions are not physical seals. A digest from an untrusted sender cannot independently prove that a file is safe or genuine.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: Encryption protects the transfer, host identity identifies the recipient, permissions control access and file verification checks the received bytes. Applying a configuration remains a separate authorized action.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: A courier can carry a sealed envelope to a verified recipient. A sealed envelope alone does not prove the recipient is correct, the sender is trusted or the enclosed instructions should be carried out.

No copied configuration is applied, and no software is installed. Keep all backup files private because even a disposable configuration can contain credential material.
teachingPrelude.labBoundary: Router1, Admin1 and Files1 connect through one built-in switch. IOS XE 17.12.1a is the SSH/SCP endpoint; Linux Files1 supplies SFTP. No public cloud, Internet, production credentials, firmware installation or configuration restore is tested.

practiceQuestions.answer: No; the requested server subsystem must be supported.
practiceQuestions.question: Does SSH terminal success prove SFTP support?
practiceQuestions.explanation: SSH can carry different applications. The selected IOS release is used for SCP, while the Linux server explicitly supplies SFTP.

practiceQuestions.answer: It requests legacy SCP transfer protocol.
practiceQuestions.question: What does uppercase scp -O change?
practiceQuestions.explanation: It does not mean turning off host-key verification, encryption or authorization. It addresses the documented OpenSSH-to-IOS subsystem mismatch.

practiceQuestions.answer: Only relative byte consistency is established by this comparison.
practiceQuestions.question: Does a matching digest prove a file is trustworthy?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Trusted origin requires authenticated provenance or signed verification; compatibility and authorization to install remain separate.

practiceQuestions.answer: It preserves an independent authorized recovery path.
practiceQuestions.question: Why keep the Console open?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A remote management mistake should not require password bypass or blind resetting. Console security also requires physical or platform access controls.

practiceQuestions.answer: SFTP uses SSH; TFTP is a simpler UDP transfer protocol without that protection.
practiceQuestions.question: How is SFTP different from TFTP?
practiceQuestions.explanation: They are separate protocols with different features and security properties. Similar spelling is not a reason to use TFTP for sensitive backups.

practiceQuestions.answer: It creates a file snapshot without applying a restore.
practiceQuestions.question: What does copying running-config to bootflash do?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The destination is not startup-config. Copying and loading have different effects and need separate verification and authorization.

practiceQuestions.answer: No. This exercise requires more than 1,873,741,824 free bytes.
practiceQuestions.question: Paper ticket: B is 800,000,000 bytes and Router1 has 1,500,000,000 free. May staging start?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Add the explicitly chosen 1,073,741,824-byte reserve to B. Do not delete existing boot assets to force the gate to pass. This arithmetic is a worksheet, not measured device capacity or an installation requirement.

practiceQuestions.answer: Stop; equal copies of the wrong bytes do not pass vendor verification.
practiceQuestions.question: Source and read-back hashes agree, but both differ from the authenticated Cisco hash. What next?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Check that the manifest names this exact original package and algorithm. Record the mismatch, remove only the new staged file and empty directory, and obtain an authorized fresh source before retrying. Never install, reload or replace the reference with the observed hash.

realWorldScenario.title: SSH works but the backup transfer fails
realWorldScenario.takeaway: An SSH login is only one layer of a file-transfer workflow. Identify the requested subsystem, preserve identity checks and verify the received artifact before declaring the task complete.
realWorldScenario.situation: In a fictional maintenance exercise, Admin1 can open a router terminal, but a file retrieval fails after a workstation upgrade. The operator should inspect the requested transfer protocol and server subsystem before resetting credentials. A second controlled fault disables only the lab SCP service so the learner can distinguish protocol compatibility from service availability.
walkthrough: Record the exact client version, command, server identity and error without including a password in the transcript.
Check whether modern scp requested SFTP and whether the selected IOS release supports that server subsystem.
Use the documented legacy SCP option only for this supported endpoint; retain host-key checks and approved cryptography.
Verify SCP service and AAA authorization from the Console, restore the one disabled service setting and retry the original private file.
Compare the local read-back sizes, SHA-256 values and permissions. Record copy consistency, not independent router-source integrity, configuration restoration or software installation.

title: Threats, vulnerabilities, exploits, and risk

lab.goal: Demonstrate one control with paired positive and negative checks, then recover a deliberate configuration-drift fault. No runtime test or security assessment was performed during authoring.
setup: Create two fresh nodes and the one declared cable. Verify ens3 corresponds to that cable; if not, map the actual interface before entering commands.
Preinstall curl and Python 3.12 before isolation. No Cisco software or external service is needed.

Keep the same Asset1 Console shell open throughout. The server runs as a background job; server_pid records only its process ID. If that shell or variable is lost, stop and revert the disposable node rather than guessing a process to terminate.
Use only the new /tmp/qcs46 directory and the dummy text shown below; never serve your home directory, backups or credentials.
Do not change firewall rules to force a result. If a host firewall blocks the baseline, record it and use the paper alternative or a fresh prepared isolated image.
Paper alternative: predict the four baseline/fault/retest outcomes and complete the risk record. Label all service and network results unmeasured.

steps.why: The test remains bounded to a known isolated segment.
steps.title: Address the test client
commands: sudo ip address add 192.0.2.10/24 dev ens3
sudo ip link set ens3 up
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Admin1 and choose Console before typing. At the Linux shell, configure only the declared lab interface. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: Admin1 should own 192.0.2.10/24 without any default route.
commandExplanations: Assign the authorized test client's private address.
Enable the only cable to Asset1.

steps.why: The exercise demonstrates exposure without placing valuable information at risk.
steps.title: Prepare the harmless asset
commands: sudo ip address add 192.0.2.20/24 dev ens3
sudo ip link set ens3 up
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Asset1 and choose Console before typing. At the Linux shell, confirm /tmp/qcs46 does not already contain unrelated work before creating it. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: The new directory contains only the intended public classroom file.
commandExplanations: Assign the server's private cable address.
Enable the cable back to Admin1.
Create a fresh dedicated directory; stop if it already exists.
Create only a harmless public fixture, not a real configuration or secret.

steps.why: A specific address, directory and owned process make the scope and cleanup unambiguous.
steps.title: Observe the initial remote listener
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Asset1 and choose Console before typing. In the retained Console shell, start this background job and immediately capture its process ID. Wait until the listener appears before testing; inspect server.log and stop on a startup error. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: The owned job should run and the private listener should appear; no real output is supplied here.
commandExplanations: Serve only the dedicated directory on the private address, redirect diagnostics and return control to this shell.
Store the process ID of the job just started; do not replace it with a guessed ID.
Confirm this shell still owns the running lab job.
Verify the actual listener is on 192.0.2.20 before the remote request.

steps.why: This proves a service path when successful, not an exploit or a measured business risk.
steps.title: Record initial remote reachability
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Admin1 and choose Console before typing. At the Linux shell, issue one request only to the owned classroom endpoint. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: The response should contain Public classroom example. Record the actual result.
commandExplanations: Request the dummy page directly, bypassing any proxy and bounding the wait.

steps.why: A control should follow an explicit requirement rather than a blanket rule that every open port is unsafe.
steps.title: Choose the required use
steps.instruction: Record the lab owner as the learner and the required use as local access on Asset1 only. The response is to remove unnecessary remote exposure; local users remain within the residual-risk boundary. Write a separate fictional sensitive-backup risk statement without creating that file.
steps.expectedResult: The record names an asset, weakness, possible event, impact, owner, control and residual exposure.

steps.why: Changing the bind address preserves the local application while removing its direct remote path.
steps.title: Establish the restricted baseline
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Asset1 and choose Console before typing. Return to the same retained shell. Terminate and wait for only its owned job before restarting. A termination status from wait is expected here, not a configuration error. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: The server should now bind to 127.0.0.1:8080.
commandExplanations: Request termination of only the lab process whose ID this shell recorded.
Wait for that child process to exit before reusing its port; a terminated status is expected.
Restart the dummy service on loopback as a background job with private diagnostics.
Record the new owned process ID immediately for later cleanup.

steps.why: A negative remote result is meaningful only alongside evidence that the needed service still works.
steps.title: Check the retained local function
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Asset1 and choose Console before typing. Use the same Console shell while its background job runs. Wait for the intended listener to appear; inspect the log if it does not. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: The listener should be loopback-only and the local request should return the dummy text.
commandExplanations: Inspect the actual TCP listener address without inferring it from the command history.
Verify that Asset1 can still retrieve the intended local dummy page.

steps.why: A connection failure is distinct from an HTTP response denying a particular user.
steps.title: Check the excluded remote path
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Admin1 and choose Console before typing. At the Linux shell, repeat the exact remote request from the initial observation. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: The connection should fail; preserve the actual error instead of inventing an HTTP status.
commandExplanations: Test whether the removed direct remote listener remains unavailable.

steps.why: The fault represents configuration drift without adding secrets, malware or attack traffic.
steps.title: Introduce one safe drift fault
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Asset1 and choose Console before typing. In the same retained shell, stop the owned local-only job and deliberately restore the private cable binding. Keep the harmless directory unchanged. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: The server should again listen on the private cable address.
commandExplanations: Terminate only the currently owned loopback server.
Wait for that process to exit; its termination status is expected.
Reintroduce the original remote listener as the controlled configuration fault.
Track the replacement job immediately.
Wait for and verify the private cable listener before the next request.

steps.why: A recurring check needs to fail when the unwanted state returns, not merely pass once.
steps.title: Detect the reopened exposure
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Admin1 and choose Console before typing. At the Linux shell, make one bounded request to the same owned address. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: The dummy page should be reachable again, demonstrating that the negative check detects this drift.
commandExplanations: Repeat the acceptance test that should detect the deliberately reopened listener.

steps.why: This is the inverse of the one deliberate fault, with evidence of retained service.
steps.title: Restore and verify the local baseline
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Asset1 and choose Console before typing. Use the same retained Console shell to stop the owned fault job, start the loopback job and test it. Wait for the listener before curl. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: The listener should be loopback-only and local access should work again.
commandExplanations: Terminate only the owned remotely bound test server.
Wait for the child process to exit before restarting; termination status is expected.
Restore the agreed loopback-only service as a background job.
Record the restored job's process ID immediately.
Verify the restored loopback listener from the same shell.
Confirm the required local page still works.

steps.why: The conclusion covers this listener only, not the host's entire security posture.
steps.title: Retest remote exclusion
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Admin1 and choose Console before typing. At the Linux shell, repeat the same final check before calling the restoration successful. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: The request should fail while the preceding local request succeeded.
commandExplanations: Verify the restored baseline excludes the direct remote request once more.

steps.why: Rollback and cleanup return the isolated project to its clean state without leaving an unnecessary service running.
steps.title: Close the exercise and report precisely
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Asset1 and choose Console before typing. In the same retained shell, stop only the recorded job. Then stop both nodes and revert their disposable snapshots. Retain sanitized actual observations rather than invented logs. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: No classroom listener remains active. The report distinguishes predicted behavior, measured behavior and untested threats.
commandExplanations: Terminate only this exercise's current background server.
Wait for the owned child to exit; a termination status is expected.
Confirm that no classroom TCP 8080 listener remains.

lab.title: Reduce a harmless service's remote exposure
cleanup: Stop only the server recorded by server_pid in its original shell, then stop and revert both disposable nodes.
Retain sanitized observations and a risk decision, not real credentials or sensitive files.
devices: Admin1: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, curl installed.
Asset1: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS, Python 3.12 and curl installed.
GNS3 2.2.55; Linux images obtained from their official distribution with applicable licenses.
lab.topology: Admin1 ens3--Asset1 ens3 is the only cable. Each Ubuntu node has one lab NIC and local loopback. There is no switch, router, gateway, NAT node or Internet connection.

addressing.purpose: Local-only listener for the required local function.

verification: Initial private remote access should work; the loopback baseline should retain local access and exclude Admin1.
Reopening the cable listener should make the negative test detect drift; restoring loopback should reproduce both baseline checks.
Record threat, weakness, potential exploit, impact and owner without claiming an actual compromise.
Explain the residual local-process and physical-access boundaries and the difference between awareness and practiced response.
lab.licensingNote: GNS3 does not provide Cisco software images. Use Cisco images only when the applicable license or entitlement permits this environment. Do not share or redistribute image files. Cisco Modeling Labs is an official alternative; its supplied reference images are licensed for CML, not automatically for export to GNS3. Use the labeled paper alternative when authorized software is unavailable. No emulator execution is claimed by this lesson.
troubleshooting: No initial response: check cable, addresses, the owned job and existing firewall policy; do not call an untested control successful.
Local request fails after binding change: in Asset1's retained Console run cat /tmp/qcs46/server.log and inspect the listener before interpreting remote failure.
Remote request unexpectedly succeeds with a loopback listener: confirm the exact host, proxy bypass, other listeners and whether an old server was left running.
A service is actually required remotely: stop the lab analogy and design an approved authenticated service; loopback-only is not a universal production solution.

quiz.question: Which is the vulnerability in the fictional backup case?
quiz.explanation: The exposed access is the weakness; disclosure is a possible consequence. The owner and date support governance rather than create the weakness.

quiz.question: Which pair best verifies the intended control?
quiz.explanation: The control should remove the unwanted remote path while retaining the required local function.

quiz.question: A caller requests an unexpected sign-in approval. What is the safe response?
quiz.explanation: Use a known trusted channel and the approved reporting process. Do not disclose codes or approve an unexplained request.

quiz.question: What does v2.0 label 4.0 represent here?
quiz.explanation: The curriculum's broad domain label is not a specific objective. The lesson does not claim exact v2.0 configuration coverage from it.

options: Every port has the same risk
Risk depends on likelihood and impact in context
Risk equals the number of hosts
quiz.question: Which statement about risk is most accurate?
quiz.explanation: Data sensitivity, required operations, exposure and safeguards affect the assessment. Simple counts do not capture all consequences.

glossary.meaning: An asset is something worth protecting, such as a service, configuration or person. Confidentiality limits disclosure, integrity protects against unauthorized changes and availability keeps authorized use possible.
A threat is a potential harmful circumstance or event. Its source might be a malicious actor, an accidental action or an environmental event; not every threat is a hacker.

A vulnerability is a weakness that a threat can exploit or trigger. A missing access check, unsafe process or exposed console can matter even without a software defect or published vulnerability number.
An exploit is a method or action that takes advantage of a weakness. The weakness and the action using it are different concepts. This lesson describes that distinction without executing an exploit.
Risk combines uncertainty about harmful events with their consequences. Residual risk remains after controls are applied. A port number or vulnerability count alone cannot measure business risk.
A control is a safeguard or procedure. The risk owner is the accountable person who can approve the response and remaining risk; a junior operator should not silently accept risk for everyone.

A listener accepts connections on a protocol address and port. The loopback address 127.0.0.1 refers to the same host; binding there removes this IPv4 service's direct remote listener, not every possible local threat.
Awareness helps people recognize suspicious situations; training rehearses a specific safe action. A reporting channel, supportive response and physical-access procedure make both useful.
Open the named GNS3 Console to reach its Linux shell. Tests below request only a deliberately public classroom string from your own isolated hosts. They are not penetration tests or production scans.

sections.example: For a fictional backup server, an unauthenticated directory containing private backups is the weakness. Unauthorized retrieval is the possible event; using the exposed access to obtain a backup would exploit the weakness. Our lab serves only a dummy page and demonstrates reachability, not an actual disclosure incident.
sections.heading: Use the right term for each part of the problem
keyPoints: Name both the affected asset and the potential harm.
Do not infer exploitation merely from an open port.
sections.explanation: An asset has value; a threat could harm it; a vulnerability makes harm possible; an exploit uses a weakness. Risk connects the scenario to likelihood and consequences. These are not interchangeable labels. A configuration weakness can exist without a software bug, and a threat can be accidental or environmental rather than a deliberate attack.

sections.example: Compare a public classroom page with a payroll backup. Identical TCP ports do not imply identical consequences. Describe who could be affected, what operation would fail and what evidence supports the assessment. A fictional high or low label is a planning judgment, not a measured attack probability.
sections.heading: Impact depends on what the asset does
keyPoints: Treat the service's purpose and data sensitivity as part of the decision.
A control that breaks required work needs redesign or explicit approval.
sections.explanation: Confidentiality concerns who can read information, integrity concerns unauthorized alteration, and availability concerns authorized access when needed. One event can affect several objectives. An unnecessary public backup may threaten confidentiality; a mistaken shutdown of the only service may threaten availability even when intended as a security improvement.

sections.example: The fictional owner decides that remote access is unnecessary. The lab therefore binds the service to loopback. If remote access were required, the answer would be a supported authenticated service and reviewed network controls, not blindly closing the application. Insurance would not restore a broken access-control rule.
sections.heading: Select a response and keep an owner
keyPoints: State assumptions separately from measured observations.
Reassess when the service purpose, data or exposure changes.
sections.explanation: Possible responses include avoiding an unnecessary activity, reducing risk with safeguards, sharing some financial consequences and knowingly accepting residual risk. None should be a silent decision. Record the owner, chosen control, evidence needed, remaining exposure and review trigger. A numeric matrix can organize discussion but does not manufacture precise probabilities.

sections.example: A fictional caller asks an operator to approve an unexpected sign-in prompt. The operator denies it, contacts support using the known directory and reports the request without sending passwords or one-time codes. This is a tabletop discussion; no learner is phished, called or asked to submit real credentials.
sections.heading: Awareness teaches recognition; training rehearses a response
keyPoints: Never share passwords or approve an unexplained authentication prompt.
Measure whether the correct reporting action is understood, not whether people feel embarrassed.
sections.explanation: Social engineering manipulates trust or urgency to encourage unsafe actions. Awareness helps someone recognize a suspicious credential request. Training practices the next step: pause, verify through a known independent channel and report through the organization's approved process. Avoid blaming people for reporting early or using surprise deception without authorization.

sections.example: In a fictional visitor exercise, a person without a verified appointment asks to connect a laptop to a rack. The safe response is to follow the site's visitor process and contact the authorized host, not physically confront the visitor or grant access because the person sounds technical. Day 47 develops password, MFA, certificate and biometric distinctions.
sections.heading: Physical access and password handling are security controls too
keyPoints: A console is a privileged access path, including a virtual machine console.
Use paper scenarios unless a real exercise has explicit organizational authorization.
sections.explanation: Restrict equipment rooms and hypervisor consoles to authorized people, check visitor identity through the approved process and keep access records. Protect recovery media and configuration backups. Unique credentials, approved password storage and prompt revocation of unused access reduce avoidable exposure. Device hardening cannot compensate for an openly shared administrator account.

sections.example: A failed remote request alone could mean a dead server or wrong cable. A successful local request alongside the failed remote request supports the intended loopback-bound result. It still says nothing about malware, other ports or the safety of real data. v1.1 remains current through 2 February 2027; v2.0 begins 3 February 2027.
sections.heading: A useful test has a baseline, a fault and a limited conclusion
keyPoints: Pair a denied-path check with an allowed-function check.
Record residual scope instead of writing secure as a universal verdict.
sections.explanation: Establish the expected restricted state, deliberately reintroduce the one classroom exposure, observe the difference and restore the restriction. Keep every request bounded to your own nodes. Expected results are predictions until measured. The lesson addresses v1.1 5.1 and 5.2; the v2.0 4.0 label is a security domain, not a specific objective completed here.

content.metaTitle: CCNA Day 46: Threats, Weaknesses and Risk
takeaways: Separate the weakness from the harmful event and its consequence.
An open port is an observation, not proof of compromise.
Choose controls around required use and an accountable owner.
Verify the blocked path and the retained function.
Awareness, training and physical access complement technical safeguards.
objectives: Distinguish an asset, threat, vulnerability, exploit and risk in one scenario.
Explain confidentiality, integrity and availability as separate possible impacts.
Choose a control with an owner, acceptance criterion and residual-risk statement.
Practice awareness, reporting and physical-access decisions without deceptive real-world exercises.
Measure one service-exposure change using positive and negative checks.
content.plainAnswer: A threat is a possible harmful event, a vulnerability is a weakness, and an exploit is a way to use that weakness. Risk considers the likelihood and impact of harm to a specific asset. Choose controls that preserve required use, verify their effect and assign ownership of what remains. A reachable port alone proves neither a compromise nor a complete risk assessment.

visualStory.title: Does Asset1 need remote access?

stages.title: State the requirement
stages.explanation: The lab owner needs only Asset1-local access. Admin1's direct remote request is unnecessary exposure, not proof of a compromise.

stages.title: Compare alternatives
stages.explanation: Take the local-only case. A genuinely needed remote service would require a separate supported secure design and approval, not the next stop on a path.

stages.title: Verify both outcomes
stages.explanation: Admin1's remote request should fail while Asset1's local request succeeds. Local access remains within the residual-risk boundary.

visualStory.altText: Asset1 TCP 8080 has two alternative requirements: local-only use or remote access. The lab retains Asset1's local use and excludes Admin1; remote-required use needs a separate redesign.
visualStory.boundary: Independent alternatives, not a traffic path or serial decision chain. Admin1 and Asset1 are the complete lab endpoints. Only local-only use is practiced; secure remote redesign remains conceptual.
visualStory.takeaway: Choose the control from required use, then verify both the excluded path and the retained function.

candidates.name: Two mutually exclusive requirements
candidates.scene: Compare Asset1-local use with a separate remote-required case, with no arrows connecting the alternatives.
candidates.limitation: Only local-only use is practiced; remote redesign is a conceptual alternative.
candidates.teachingValue: Shows why the chosen control depends on required use without turning choices into a serial path.

candidates.name: Two-host listener change
candidates.scene: Admin1 tests Asset1 before and after a loopback-only binding.
candidates.limitation: A path alone does not explain the owner's risk decision.
candidates.teachingValue: Matches the real lab endpoints exactly.

candidates.name: Security vocabulary comparison
candidates.scene: Compare threat, weakness, exploit and risk using one backup scenario.
candidates.limitation: A table would omit the practical control decision.
candidates.teachingValue: Clarifies terms that beginners often confuse.

conceptSelection.selectionReason: Independent cases fit this either-or requirement: the local-only lab and a hypothetical remote-required design must not appear to be sequential steps.

walkthrough.why: The required use determines whether remote exposure is necessary before any control is chosen.
walkthrough.action: Name the asset and required use.
walkthrough.whatHappens: The fictional backup must stay private. In the actual lab, Asset1's harmless page is needed only by a process on Asset1 itself.

walkthrough.why: An accurate record avoids converting a small test into an unsupported security claim.
walkthrough.action: Separate observation from hypothesis.
walkthrough.whatHappens: A successful request from Admin1 establishes remote reachability. It does not establish an exploit, stolen data or a measured probability of attack.

walkthrough.why: Testing both outcomes checks that the control blocks the unwanted path without destroying the required function.
walkthrough.action: Reduce the specific exposure.
walkthrough.whatHappens: The server is restarted on 127.0.0.1 instead of the cable address. The remote request should fail while a local request still returns the dummy string.

walkthrough.why: A successful control does not mean the host has zero risk.
walkthrough.action: Record what remains.
walkthrough.whatHappens: Local users and processes can still reach the loopback service. The owner records that boundary and the need to review future configuration changes.

beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Calling every problem a threat hides important differences. Patching software does not fix an unlocked equipment room; closing a needed service may cause an availability incident. Accurate terms guide an appropriate change.

firstPractice.hint: Keep the potential event separate from the condition that would allow it.
firstPractice.task: Write four labels for a fictional private backup exposed by an unauthenticated web service: asset, weakness, possible harmful event and consequence. Do not claim it actually happened.
firstPractice.expected: The asset is the backup; the weakness is unnecessary unauthenticated exposure; the possible event is unauthorized retrieval; the consequence is disclosure of sensitive settings.

beginnerGuide.startingPoint: Start with what the owner needs to protect and who needs access. A security label becomes useful when it explains what could happen, why it could happen and how you would verify a sensible response.

checkUnderstanding.hint: Consider other services, local access, credentials, physical access and the limited test scope.
checkUnderstanding.answer: No. It verifies one exposure change. Other threats and weaknesses remain outside this experiment, and required local access must still be checked.
checkUnderstanding.question: Does closing TCP 8080 prove Asset1 is secure?

everydayComparison.whereItStops: Network access, cryptographic identity and software behavior need technical evidence. A door analogy does not prove that a specific port or protocol is vulnerable.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: The same separation applies to an unnecessary network listener and the information it exposes. A control should address the relevant access path while preserving authorized work.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: An unlocked storage room is a weakness. Someone taking a confidential folder is a harmful event. The consequence depends on the folder's contents and who needs it.

prerequisites: Review IP addresses, TCP ports and local versus remote communication.
Use GNS3 2.2.55 with two fresh Ubuntu 24.04 LTS nodes, Python 3.12 and curl installed before isolation.
No licensed Cisco image, public service, real secret, malware or exploit is needed for this lab.

teachingPrelude.explanation: We deliberately publish a harmless classroom string on an isolated service, then remove its unnecessary remote exposure. That is a control demonstration, not a discovered software vulnerability. The fictional business case uses sensitive backups only on paper; no such file enters the lab.
teachingPrelude.labBoundary: Admin1 ens3 connects directly to Asset1 ens3. Only a dummy file is served on TCP 8080. No external connection, credential collection, exploit, denial-of-service load or real physical-access test is authorized.

practiceQuestions.answer: It is a weakness that could permit a harmful event.
practiceQuestions.question: Is an unlocked console a threat or a weakness?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Unauthorized console use would be a possible threat event. The distinction helps choose a physical or platform-access control.

practiceQuestions.answer: No; it establishes only part of the reachable service surface.
practiceQuestions.question: Does an open port prove exploitation?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Evidence of successful unauthorized action is separate. The dummy HTTP request is authorized and contains no sensitive data.

practiceQuestions.answer: Availability of the required function must be preserved.
practiceQuestions.question: Why verify local access after removing remote exposure?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A stopped server can make a negative network test pass for the wrong reason. Pairing the two checks is more informative.

practiceQuestions.answer: The accountable authorized risk owner.
practiceQuestions.question: Who may accept residual business risk?
practiceQuestions.explanation: An operator can document observations and propose controls but should not silently approve organizational consequences.

practiceQuestions.answer: Recognition is different from rehearsing the safe action.
practiceQuestions.question: What makes awareness different from training?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A learner may recognize suspicious urgency yet still need practice using a known reporting channel without disclosing credentials.

practiceQuestions.answer: No; it changes one network listener's scope.
practiceQuestions.question: Does a loopback binding remove physical-access risk?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Local users, processes and console access remain relevant. The lesson intentionally does not claim complete hardening.

realWorldScenario.title: An internal convenience service outlives its purpose
realWorldScenario.takeaway: A clear risk statement leads to a testable control. The same open port can have different significance depending on data, access and operational purpose.
realWorldScenario.situation: A fictional operator discovers that a temporary file service still exposes a backup directory. The team must confirm the service owner and required use before changing it. The real lab uses only a public dummy string; it does not reproduce sensitive disclosure.
walkthrough: Inventory the service, its owner, data classification and authorized consumers before assigning risk.
Separate observed remote reachability from the hypothetical consequence of exposing private files.
Ask whether remote use is necessary; remove the listener if it is not, or plan a supported authenticated alternative if it is.
Check the unwanted access path and the required local function after the change.
Record residual local exposure, who approved it and a review trigger for future configuration changes.

title: Device hardening and management-plane boundaries

lab.goal: Verify local identity, privilege and a VTY source boundary, then recover a wrong permit address. All runtime outcomes are expected observations, not executed author evidence.
setup: Create exactly four nodes and three cables. Do not attach a Cloud, NAT node or production interface; no gateway is needed.
Keep R1 Console open. Use a fresh autonomous configuration without aaa new-model; do not remove AAA from an existing device to fit this exercise.

The executable profile uses VTY 0-4 and disables VTY 5-15. Confirm these ranges exist and no additional usable VTY range is present with show line; otherwise stop for an instructor-reviewed range adaptation or use the paper alternative.

Choose distinct private OPERATOR_SECRET and ENABLE_SECRET values, each randomly generated alphanumeric and at least 16 characters; replace placeholders before typing and never share the resulting configuration.

First-use host-key acceptance is restricted to this new disconnected topology after checking node identity and wiring. Production requires an approved independent identity check; stop on unexpected changed-key warnings.
Paper alternative: trace the source-rule decisions, factor categories and recovery sequence without licensed images. Mark account, SSH and ACL outcomes unmeasured.

steps.why: An incomplete line inventory can leave a management path outside the intended policy.
steps.title: Inventory and address R1
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click R1 and choose Console before typing. Start at > or #. Inspect show line and stop if the required VTY profile does not match before configuring the interface. Type each line without the prompt and press Enter. Stop on a syntax error; retain the console for recovery.
steps.expectedResult: The line inventory must match the setup gate, and R1 should own the planned address.
commandExplanations: Enter privileged EXEC (#) from user EXEC (>); use only your authorized lab credentials.
Inventory all console and VTY lines so no extra remote range is silently omitted.
Enter global configuration mode from privileged EXEC (#); accepted changes affect the running device.
Give the fresh router its intended identity.
Select the cable to Switch1 Ethernet0.
Assign the isolated management address.
Enable the local cable.
Return to privileged EXEC (#). This neither saves the configuration nor reverses accepted changes.

steps.why: Separate connectivity problems from later authentication and policy problems.
steps.title: Address Admin1

glossary.meaning: The management plane carries administration and monitoring traffic to or from the device, such as SSH. It differs from data-plane traffic forwarded through the device and control-plane protocols that build forwarding state.
Hardening reduces unnecessary exposure and unsafe settings. Least privilege gives an account only the permissions required for its task; a working login need not imply full administrator access.
Virtual terminal lines accept remote IOS sessions. A VTY access class filters which source addresses may reach those sessions. It is not an interface firewall for all traffic.
A local user authenticates against the router's own account database. The enable secret protects entry to a higher privilege level. Two passwords are still two examples of the same knowledge factor.

A password hash supports verification without storing a directly recoverable password. Encryption is reversible with its key. Type 7 obfuscation is weak; the lab explicitly selects Type 9 scrypt for local secrets.

Multi-factor authentication combines distinct factor categories: something known, possessed or inherent. A password plus another password is not MFA. Strong recovery and enrollment procedures are part of the design.

A certificate binds identity information to a public key under an issuer's signature. Authentication also needs proof of the corresponding private key and appropriate validation; copying the public certificate alone is not sufficient.

A biometric uses a physical or behavioral characteristic. It can activate a protected authenticator but requires privacy, accuracy and alternative-access considerations. A fingerprint is not a replaceable password.
A recovery path is an independent authorized way to restore access, such as a protected Console. It must be secured and tested rather than treated as permission to bypass authentication.
Right-click the named GNS3 node and choose Console. IOS > is user EXEC, # is privileged EXEC and (config)# is configuration mode; the Ubuntu shell runs ssh and ping.

sections.example: Admin1 and Guest1 share the lab segment. Only Admin1 may initiate an SSH session, but Guest1's ping can remain successful. That is not a contradiction. No interface ACL or control-plane policing is configured here, and there is no transit traffic to measure.
sections.heading: Protect the management path without confusing the planes
keyPoints: Inspect exactly where a policy is attached.
Do not claim complete hardening from a single passing SSH test.
sections.explanation: SSH to R1 is management traffic. Routing protocol exchanges maintain control-plane state, while ordinary packets crossing a router use its data plane. These functions interact but need appropriately scoped controls. Disabling unnecessary management services reduces exposure; a VTY access class is one small control, not a complete infrastructure firewall.

sections.example: The operator can inspect show privilege at the initial prompt. A separate enable secret permits the deliberate administrative transition. This is a simple lab demonstration, not a fine-grained enterprise role model; Day 48 explains centralized AAA and its permission decisions.
sections.heading: Use protected local secrets and limited starting privilege
keyPoints: Never publish real secrets or unredacted configurations.
Use a unique account and revoke access when the operator no longer needs it.
sections.explanation: A local username identifies the operator. The lab selects scrypt explicitly rather than relying on a release-dependent default. A one-way stored secret is different from reversible encryption and weak Type 7 obfuscation. Protect configuration copies anyway: hashes and network details remain sensitive. The account starts at privilege 1, not unrestricted level 15.

sections.example: For CLI safety, the lab asks for separate randomly generated alphanumeric secrets of at least 16 characters. That is an exercise input constraint, not a recommendation to prohibit spaces or require character mixtures in every system. Do not paste passwords into shared transcripts or shell command arguments.
sections.heading: A password policy includes lifecycle and storage
keyPoints: Separate a teaching placeholder from an actual secret.
Password transport, stored representation and account lifecycle each need attention.
sections.explanation: Choose long unique secrets, store them in an approved password manager, avoid default or compromised choices and revoke them on compromise or access changes. Current NIST guidance favors length and compromised-password screening over arbitrary composition rules and periodic changes without cause. Platform syntax and organizational requirements still need review; this IOS exercise does not implement a complete identity-policy engine.

sections.example: An unexpected approval request should be denied and reported through a known channel. Enrollment, lost-authenticator recovery and phishing resistance matter as much as the number of prompts. This lesson describes MFA; the local IOS username and enable secret do not implement it.
sections.heading: MFA is about distinct factors, not repeated questions
keyPoints: Count factor categories rather than login screens.
A successful password-only lab is not evidence of MFA enforcement.
sections.explanation: A knowledge factor is something you know, a possession factor is something you control and an inherent factor relates to a characteristic of you. A password followed by another password does not add a new category. A protected hardware authenticator activated by a PIN can combine possession with knowledge when the full system verifies that design.

sections.example: A fictional administrator presents an expired device certificate: knowing the username does not repair its validity. Another uses a fingerprint to unlock a hardware key: the fingerprint alone is not proof that every downstream application enforced MFA. Neither certificate enrollment nor biometric hardware is simulated here.
sections.heading: Certificates and biometrics need their own checks
keyPoints: Keep private keys private and validate the intended identity.
A biometric is not easily replaced after disclosure like a password.
sections.explanation: A certificate associates identity information with a public key under an issuer's signature. Validation considers trust, intended use, validity time and revocation as required by the system; authentication needs control of the private key. A public certificate is not a secret password. A biometric can activate a protected authenticator, but privacy, error rates and a suitable non-biometric alternative still matter.

sections.example: This lesson directly addresses v1.1 5.3 and describes 5.4; it supports the 5.2 human and physical controls from Day 46. v2.0 4.1 coverage is partial local-user configuration, and 4.2 is only secure-file-handling context here, not a transfer exercise. v1.1 is current through 2 February 2027; v2.0 begins 3 February 2027.
sections.heading: Keep a recoverable baseline and test new sessions
keyPoints: Every active remote line needs an explicit reviewed policy.
Console and hypervisor permissions are part of the management boundary.
sections.explanation: Keep a trusted Console, inventory every VTY range and close unused remote lines. Test a fresh connection after each change; an already established session is not a reliable test of admission policy. In this lab the wrong source permit is repaired from the Console. Do not disable password recovery, erase keys or reset the device to solve that small error.

content.metaTitle: CCNA Day 47: Device Hardening and Management Access
takeaways: Separate source admission, protected transport, user identity and permission.
Protect every usable VTY range and retain a secured recovery path.
Local secrets and configuration backups still need careful handling.
Two passwords are not two factor categories.
A narrow management test does not establish complete device hardening.
objectives: Distinguish management, control and data-plane exposure.
Configure local user and enable secrets with explicit protected storage.
Restrict SSH to the intended source while preserving a trusted Console.
Verify user versus privileged EXEC and diagnose a wrong-source ACL fault.
Compare password policy, MFA, certificates and biometrics with honest implementation boundaries.
content.plainAnswer: Device hardening combines a restricted management path, secure transport, verified identity, appropriate permissions and a recovery plan. A source ACL is not user authentication, SSH encryption is not least privilege, and two passwords are not MFA. Verify both the authorized session and the excluded source before accepting a management change.

everydayComparison.whereItStops: An IP address is not a physical identity badge. Address-based controls have limitations and need other protections; this small lab is not a complete enterprise access design.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: The source rule, SSH authentication and privilege level serve different purposes. A permitted address does not replace an individual account or a protected session.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: A visitor may enter a building, show identification and receive a badge for only one room. Admission, identity and permission are separate decisions.

title: AAA with local users, TACACS+, and RADIUS

lab.goal: Configure both client protocols against an explicit instructor-provisioned server, compare accept/reject evidence and recover one RADIUS reachability fault. No real server or runtime result was exercised during authoring.
setup: Build only the three declared links; no Cloud, NAT or Internet bridge. Use a clean R1 and keep its Console active. Gate the executable profile on VTY 0-15 only: use 0-4 and disable 5-15; stop for instructor adaptation if show line reveals a different usable range.

ISE1 must already be installed, running and licensed for Device Administration and the required RADIUS sessions, with enough vendor-specified compute. Its single-node services, private GUI trust and internal user store must work offline. Installation, DNS/NTP provisioning and entitlement acquisition occur before this isolated exercise; no external dependency may be required for these internal-user tests.

Server contract: define R1 as network device 192.0.2.1/32. Enable TACACS+ TCP 49 and RADIUS UDP 1812/1813 with distinct private TAC_KEY and RAD_KEY values. Match those values on R1. Existing server protections must not be disabled; if the old client cannot satisfy them, stop and use the paper alternative.

Create only the central internal user netop with a private unique secret. TACACS+ authentication accepts netop and its shell profile returns default privilege 1. RADIUS accepts netop with Service-Type NAS-Prompt-User and Cisco AV-pair shell:priv-lvl=1. Other identities, including breakglass, receive explicit rejection. No external directory or MFA is involved.

Enable server collection of EXEC session accounting and provide authorized access to TACACS/RADIUS live logs and accounting reports. Verify the GUI's certificate through the instructor's trusted fingerprint or CA process; never dismiss an unexplained warning.

Choose private randomly generated alphanumeric BREAKGLASS_SECRET, TAC_KEY and RAD_KEY values of at least 16 characters. netop's secret is separate. Replace placeholders before typing; no secrets belong in screenshots, chat, command-line test-password arguments or published configurations.

The SSH host key is new only on this fresh isolated router. Document first-use trust after checking wiring and identity, or use the instructor's verified fingerprint. Stop on an unexpected key change. Classic AAA protocols here are a disconnected learning fixture, not a production recommendation.

Without entitled ISE1, complete R1's local baseline and draw the two central flows on paper. Client definitions may be inspected, but do not attach central methods or claim accept/reject/accounting tests. Mark central configuration verification and outage behavior unmeasured.

glossary.meaning: Authentication checks identity, authorization decides permitted actions or services, and accounting records activity. A successful identity check does not establish permission or prove that an activity record was received.
For this device-administration exercise, R1 is the AAA client and ISE1 is the policy server. Admin1 is the SSH client to R1, not the device sending R1's AAA requests.

The local database stores accounts on R1 itself. It can provide a carefully controlled recovery method but creates per-device credential-management work and does not automatically centralize audit records.

Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus separates AAA exchanges and supports granular device-command authorization. Classic TACACS+ uses TCP 49; its legacy body obfuscation is not a substitute for a protected transport.

Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service carries authentication and authorization attributes, with accounting as a related function. This lab uses classic UDP 1812 for access and UDP 1813 for accounting, not TLS-protected RADIUS.

A method list is an ordered policy such as server group followed by local. A server group names the selected servers. Defining either does not apply it to a line until the matching line command is used.
A reject is an authoritative negative response. An error or unreachable service can permit trying the next method. Local fallback does not normally override a reachable server's rejection.
A shared secret is configured on the AAA client and server for their protocol relationship. It is not the user's login password. Protect it and match it to the exact client source address.
EXEC authorization decides whether a shell starts and which attributes it receives. EXEC accounting records session start/stop; it is not a record of every command.
Open the named GNS3 Console before commands. R1's local-only Console and breakglass account provide authorized recovery; the server-only netop account proves central authentication when it works.

sections.example: The lab expects netop to receive privilege 1 and records session start/stop. It does not configure per-command authorization or accounting. Seeing show clock succeed proves that small permission outcome, not that every privileged command is centrally controlled or logged.
sections.heading: Three decisions need three kinds of evidence
keyPoints: Check identity, effective privilege and received accounting separately.
Session accounting is not a complete command transcript.
sections.explanation: Authentication answers who the claimant is. Authorization determines what service or permission is granted. Accounting records activity. These can succeed or fail independently. A user authenticated by ISE1 can still be denied an EXEC shell; a shell can start while accounting delivery is unavailable. Do not use a login prompt or green authentication result as proof of all three.

sections.example: The appliance has one address, 192.0.2.20, but accepts two protocols. TACACS+ uses TCP 49; classic RADIUS access uses UDP 1812 and accounting uses UDP 1813. The client's local ephemeral source port need not equal the service destination port. All three systems are named endpoints; there is no invisible public identity service.
sections.heading: The router is the AAA client
keyPoints: Match the server's network-device definition to R1's actual source.
Do not confuse the SSH workstation with the router's AAA role.
sections.explanation: Admin1 speaks SSH to R1. R1 separately contacts ISE1 using its configured source interface. ISE1 must recognize that source as a network device and use the matching shared secret. The central user's password and the client/server shared secret have different purposes. A correct user password cannot repair a mismatched shared secret or wrong client address.

sections.example: Classic TACACS+ body protection is described as obfuscation in RFC 8907, and classic RADIUS does not encrypt the complete exchange. SSH protects Admin1-to-R1, not automatically R1-to-ISE1. Production deployments should use supported protected AAA transport and current vendor mitigations; this legacy-compatible isolated exercise does not claim TLS, IPsec or current production hardening.
sections.heading: TACACS+ and RADIUS are not the same permission model
keyPoints: Compare actual services and attributes, not slogans about which protocol encrypts everything.
Use the disconnected lab only with disposable credentials and no external bridge.
sections.explanation: TACACS+ separates authentication, authorization and accounting exchanges and is commonly used for detailed device-administration policy. RADIUS access responses can carry authorization attributes such as a privilege level, while its accounting service records sessions. This does not make RADIUS a drop-in replacement for TACACS+ per-command authorization. Either needs supported client and server policy.

sections.example: With group RAD_GRP local, ISE1 rejects breakglass because that identity is absent centrally. When the server link is suspended, R1 may eventually try its local database and authorize the local account. Timeout duration is measured, not promised. Accounting records during the outage are not assumed to arrive later.
sections.heading: Named method lists avoid accidental scope changes
keyPoints: Keep a tested local-only Console instead of depending solely on remote fallback.
Do not use none or if-authenticated as a shortcut to conceal policy failures.
sections.explanation: A method list specifies an order; a group selects servers; a line applies the list. The local-only Console is deliberately independent of the VTY method. Authentication and EXEC authorization each need their own fallback policy. A reachable server's reject is final for that method list; moving to local after no answer is a different case.

sections.example: For TACACS+, select an internal-user authentication rule and a shell profile returning default privilege 1 for netop. For RADIUS, return Access-Accept with Service-Type NAS-Prompt-User and Cisco AV-pair shell:priv-lvl=1. Reject other users. Configure accounting retention and verify logs are accessible. If the fixture or entitlement is absent, complete the local and paper path only; do not mark central testing passed.
sections.heading: Prepare the server before testing the clients
keyPoints: A preconfigured policy server is a declared prerequisite, not a fabricated lab result.
Do not weaken an existing production server's security policy to fit this fixture.
sections.explanation: This chapter configures network-device clients, not an ISE installation. An instructor must supply the exact ready server contract in the lab setup. On ISE, use Administration > Network Resources > Network Devices for R1's address and protocol secrets; internal users provide netop. Enable Device Admin on the policy-service node and create matching device-administration and network-access policies.

sections.example: A missing record could mean a service, policy, client-source, transport or collection problem. Diagnose from the retained Console and the server's actual reason. A wrong shared secret is not a safe substitute for the intentional outage because it can produce different errors and confusing evidence.
sections.heading: Read the server evidence and preserve secrets
keyPoints: Use actual received records rather than expected sample output.
A central audit outage remains a limitation even when local recovery works.
sections.explanation: For TACACS+, inspect Operations > TACACS > Live Logs and the Device Administration accounting reports. For RADIUS, inspect the RADIUS live-log details and accounting reports for the matching user, network device and session. An access result is not an accounting result. Record sanitized timestamps, result, source and session identifier; do not publish shared keys, passwords or packet payloads.

sections.example: The paper alternative can demonstrate reasoning about source, policy and fallback but cannot establish hands-on central AAA competence. v1.1 remains current through 2 February 2027 and v2.0 begins 3 February 2027. The parent and independent reviewer still own visual inspection and release decisions.
sections.heading: Limit the coverage claim to the procedure actually offered
keyPoints: Distinguish a complete client procedure from a measured working deployment.
Do not claim server installation, MFA or per-command policy coverage here.
sections.explanation: v1.1 5.3 covers the local-user configuration and 5.8 the AAA comparison. v2.0 4.1 is addressed by local users and both TACACS+ and RADIUS clients, conditional on the explicit test-server fixture. The RADIUS outage is tested procedurally; TACACS+ outage behavior is explained but not separately exercised. No author-side runtime is claimed.

content.metaTitle: CCNA Day 48: Local AAA, TACACS+ and RADIUS
takeaways: AAA identity, permission and records require separate evidence.
R1 is the AAA client even though Admin1 starts SSH.
A reject and an unreachable server have different fallback behavior.
A local-only Console is a deliberate recovery boundary.
A complete client procedure still requires a real compatible policy server.
Classic AAA transport in this isolated lab is not a production security endorsement.
objectives: Distinguish authentication, authorization and accounting evidence.
Identify the workstation SSH client, router AAA client and policy server.
Configure local users and named TACACS+ and RADIUS client groups.
Apply named login, EXEC authorization and accounting policies to a bounded VTY range.
Compare central rejection with unreachable-server fallback and restore the normal method.
content.plainAnswer: AAA separates identity, permission and activity records. For router administration, the router is the TACACS+ or RADIUS client even when a workstation starts the SSH session. An ordered method list can fall back to local credentials when a server cannot answer, but not simply because that server rejects a user. Keep a local Console path and verify server-side policy and accounting evidence separately.

visualStory.title: SSH client and AAA client are different roles

stages.title: Request the shell
stages.explanation: Admin1 opens SSH to R1. SSH protects this connection; it does not automatically protect the separate router-to-server AAA exchange.

stages.title: Ask the policy server
stages.explanation: R1 sends from .1 to ISE1 using the selected TACACS+ or RADIUS service. The server matches the device, secret, user and policy.

stages.title: Interpret the decision
stages.explanation: ISE1's reject ends the login attempt. With no usable server answer, the configured local method may run; authorization and accounting still need checks.

visualStory.altText: Admin1 opens SSH to R1, which separately queries ISE1 by TACACS+ or RADIUS. ISE1 returns a decision to R1. All physical traffic crosses Switch1.
visualStory.boundary: Logical protocol flow over the shared Switch1 segment. ISE1 supplies both separate services. Classic AAA is isolated; no TLS, external identity store or MFA is shown.
visualStory.takeaway: Admin1 asks R1 for a shell; R1 asks ISE1 for policy. A server reject is not the same as no answer.
