walkthrough.action: Verify the server contract.
walkthrough.whatHappens: ISE1 recognizes R1 at 192.0.2.1, has both services enabled, accepts netop and rejects the server-unknown breakglass identity.

walkthrough.why: Each protocol is configured and verified separately rather than assuming one working service validates the other.
walkthrough.action: Compare both central protocols.
walkthrough.whatHappens: The learner applies TACACS+ first and RADIUS second, checking a server-only login, privilege 1 and actual start/stop records.

walkthrough.why: The changed variable is server availability, not a new password or an override of an explicit deny.
walkthrough.action: Separate rejection from outage.
walkthrough.whatHappens: A reachable ISE1 rejects breakglass. During a deliberate ISE1 link suspension, RADIUS can time out and local fallback can accept that same local account.

beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: A working server address is not enough. The server must recognize the router's source, share the right protocol secret and return an appropriate policy. A password accepted centrally can still be followed by an authorization denial or missing accounting.

firstPractice.hint: The endpoint accepting the SSH connection is also the client of the central policy service.
firstPractice.task: Trace ssh netop@192.0.2.1. Name the source of R1's AAA request, its destination and the account store that must contain netop.
firstPractice.expected: R1 sends from 192.0.2.1 to ISE1 at 192.0.2.20. The account exists in ISE1's internal user store, not on Admin1 or R1.

beginnerGuide.startingPoint: Follow one login: Admin1 asks R1 for SSH access; R1 asks ISE1 about the user; R1 then decides whether to start the shell under the returned policy. The SSH session and the AAA exchange are different connections.

checkUnderstanding.hint: Distinguish a definitive negative answer from the absence of an answer.
checkUnderstanding.answer: No. A reject normally ends authentication. Local fallback is for an earlier method error or unavailability, so the separate local-only Console remains important.
checkUnderstanding.question: The method list ends in local. Must a valid local breakglass account work while ISE1 is reachable and rejects it?

everydayComparison.whereItStops: A network protocol has timeouts, source addresses and cryptographic limitations that the analogy does not model. A recorded visit also does not imply that every action inside was permitted or logged.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: R1 requests authentication, receives authorization attributes and sends accounting records. These are related but distinct tasks with different evidence.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: A receptionist checks a visitor with a central office, receives permission for a particular room and records when the visit starts and ends.

prerequisites: Review SSH identity and local privilege from Days 45 and 47; do not import an existing production AAA configuration.
Use GNS3 2.2.55, an entitled autonomous C8000v IOS XE 17.12.1a, Ubuntu 24.04 Desktop and an instructor-prepared Cisco ISE 3.3 Patch 4 appliance.
ISE provisioning, compute resources and valid Device Administration plus appropriate RADIUS entitlements are mandatory prerequisites, not included or assumed free.
content.learnerOutcome: Configure local recovery, named TACACS+ and RADIUS clients and method lists, compare central success with explicit rejection, and test bounded RADIUS outage fallback when the declared server is available.
content.metaDescription: Configure local users and both AAA clients with explicit server prerequisites, test reject versus outage behavior and verify authorization and session accounting.

terms.meaning: Authentication checks identity, authorization decides permitted actions or services, and accounting records activity. A successful identity check does not establish permission or prove that an activity record was received.
For this device-administration exercise, R1 is the AAA client and ISE1 is the policy server. Admin1 is the SSH client to R1, not the device sending R1's AAA requests.

The local database stores accounts on R1 itself. It can provide a carefully controlled recovery method but creates per-device credential-management work and does not automatically centralize audit records.

Terminal Access Controller Access-Control System Plus separates AAA exchanges and supports granular device-command authorization. Classic TACACS+ uses TCP 49; its legacy body obfuscation is not a substitute for a protected transport.

Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service carries authentication and authorization attributes, with accounting as a related function. This lab uses classic UDP 1812 for access and UDP 1813 for accounting, not TLS-protected RADIUS.

A method list is an ordered policy such as server group followed by local. A server group names the selected servers. Defining either does not apply it to a line until the matching line command is used.
A reject is an authoritative negative response. An error or unreachable service can permit trying the next method. Local fallback does not normally override a reachable server's rejection.
A shared secret is configured on the AAA client and server for their protocol relationship. It is not the user's login password. Protect it and match it to the exact client source address.
EXEC authorization decides whether a shell starts and which attributes it receives. EXEC accounting records session start/stop; it is not a record of every command.
Open the named GNS3 Console before commands. R1's local-only Console and breakglass account provide authorized recovery; the server-only netop account proves central authentication when it works.

teachingPrelude.explanation: One policy appliance supplies two separate AAA protocols. The netop account exists only on ISE1; breakglass exists only on R1. Their different locations make the tests interpretable. No server, license, user authentication or accounting outcome was executed or measured during authoring.
teachingPrelude.labBoundary: Admin1, R1 and ISE1 share Switch1. Classic AAA protocols are confined to this disconnected lab and are not presented as a production security baseline. No external identity store, MFA, command authorization or redundant server is tested.

practiceQuestions.answer: R1 is the AAA client; Admin1 is the SSH client.

practiceQuestions.explanation: R1 sends the central request from its configured .1 address. The two client roles belong to different protocol relationships.

practiceQuestions.answer: No; shell and command permissions require their own decisions.

practiceQuestions.explanation: The lab separately checks the resulting privilege. It does not configure or claim granular per-command authorization.

practiceQuestions.answer: The server returns a definitive rejection.
practiceQuestions.question: Why does breakglass fail while the server is reachable?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The trailing local method is for an earlier method's error or unavailability, not a general override of central policy.

practiceQuestions.answer: No; it belongs to the router/server protocol relationship.

practiceQuestions.explanation: User credentials authenticate the user. A matching client address and relationship secret are separate prerequisites.

practiceQuestions.explanation: It is not a full command transcript. Actual server receipt must be checked, and outage records cannot be assumed to arrive later.

practiceQuestions.answer: Local configuration and paper reasoning, not central runtime success.

practiceQuestions.explanation: The server's identity store, policy and accounting receiver are essential to the full tests; a nonexistent server cannot validate them.

practiceQuestions.explanation: The separate router-to-server protocol needs its own supported protection. This exercise is confined to a disconnected disposable lab.

realWorldScenario.title: The emergency account works only during a real outage
realWorldScenario.takeaway: A negative decision and an unavailable decision-maker are not interchangeable. A protected independent Console is more reliable than assuming every remote fallback scenario will work.
realWorldScenario.situation: A fictional operator expects a router-local recovery account to bypass a central denial because local appears last in the method list. A reachable policy server rejects the account, so the login fails. The retained local-only Console provides recovery while the operator investigates the actual result.
walkthrough: Identify the account's store and the exact applied login method before changing credentials.
Confirm a server-only netop session succeeds and receives the intended privilege through each protocol.

title: Standard IPv4 ACLs

lab.goal: Build one routed path, apply a source-only policy, observe a reversible ordering fault, and compare a numbered equivalent. All results below are predictions; neither CSR1000v nor VPCS was executed during authoring.
setup: Use fresh disposable nodes and save a stopped-project baseline. Confirm entitlement before obtaining or importing any Cisco image.
Record show version and actual port labels. The example requires the CSR GigabitEthernet1/2 mapping; if different, map and substitute consistently before starting.
Without that authorized image, perform the four-case host/wildcard worksheet. A practical alternative is an entitled CML router with mapped ports; its image must stay inside CML.
Enter one command at a time, omit prompts, and stop on errors. Do not save temporary faults or overwrite any shared startup configuration.

steps.why: Directly connected subnets make ACL behavior easier to separate from unrelated routing configuration.
steps.title: Build R1's two local networks
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click R1 and choose Console before typing. Use fresh routed ports with no existing ACLs. Inspect the release and map both cables, then configure the two gateway addresses. The connected routes remove any need for a static route in this experiment.
steps.expectedResult: Expect both ports to become up/up after the endpoints start; record actual states before proceeding.
commandExplanations: Enter privileged EXEC on this authorized lab device; stop if access is not authorized.
Record the actual CSR software release and platform.
Enter global configuration from privileged EXEC; changes affect the active configuration.
Select the routed port directly cabled to PC-A.
Set the gateway on the first /24 network.
Enable the selected isolated PC-A link.
Select the routed port directly cabled to PC-B.
Set the second subnet's local gateway.
Enable the PC-B link without changing other ports.
Return to privileged EXEC without saving or undoing the accepted changes.
Verify both mapped addresses and interface states.

steps.why: A destination can receive a request yet fail to reply when its gateway is wrong; that is not proof of an ACL denial.
steps.title: Address the destination endpoint
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click PC-B and choose Console before typing. Set the address and return gateway before testing from the other network. Check the displayed mask carefully; the reply must leave PC-B through R1.
steps.expectedResult: Expect PC-B's displayed values to match the addressing table exactly.
commandExplanations: Assign PC-B its address, /24 mask and local router gateway.
Read back PC-B's address, mask and gateway.

steps.why: Later differences are meaningful only when a previously working source, destination and route are known.
steps.title: Establish the unrestricted transit baseline
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click PC-A and choose Console before typing. Configure the permitted source and ping PC-B. Wait for neighbor resolution and repeat if needed. Do not attach a filter until this cross-subnet exchange works.
steps.expectedResult: Expect replies from PC-B before any ACL exists; stop if the baseline fails.
commandExplanations: Assign PC-A the intended permitted source and gateway.
Confirm this test really uses .10 in the first subnet.
Test PC-B through R1, including PC-B's return path.

steps.why: Creating a list alone does not filter this interface; direction and attachment complete the policy.
steps.title: Build and attach the named policy
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click R1 and choose Console before typing. From #, create the complete TO-B list before applying it outbound toward PC-B. Its explicit final denial provides a counter; it is not an extra permission. Keep the console open independently of data traffic.
steps.expectedResult: Expect TO-B as the outbound list, with the host permit before deny any.
commandExplanations: Enter global configuration from privileged EXEC; changes affect the active configuration.
Create a named standard source-only ACL.
Permit only the exact .10 IPv4 source at sequence 10.
Explicitly deny remaining IPv4 sources at sequence 20.
Leave ACL configuration for global configuration.
Select the outgoing PC-B-facing interface.
Attach the completed source filter in the outbound direction.
Return to privileged EXEC without saving or undoing the accepted changes.
Confirm the outbound ACL identifier and interface status.
Inspect entry ordering and current match counters.

steps.why: The two source cases test both sides of the requirement instead of treating any single failure as success.
steps.title: Measure permitted and denied sources
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click PC-A and choose Console before typing. First retest .10, then change only this isolated PC's address to the unused .20. Leave its mask and gateway unchanged. Record both test results before making any ACL edit.
steps.expectedResult: Expect .10 replies and .20 failure; a timeout alone is not sufficient without attachment and counter evidence.
commandExplanations: Check that the intended permitted source still gets replies.
Change only PC-A's source address to the denied test value.
Confirm .20 is active before interpreting the next result.
Send the same transit test from the denied source.

steps.why: This controlled failure changes .20's wildcard decision without changing addressing, routing or endpoint software.
steps.title: Capture counters and introduce the safe fault
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click R1 and choose Console before typing. Record counters after the .20 test. In this disconnected project only, insert wildcard permit 5 before wildcard deny 20. The .10 host lookup remains separate. Keep both original entries and do not save this fault.
steps.expectedResult: Expect wildcard permit 5 before wildcard deny 20. Source .20 has no host entry and can now match 5; .10 retains its host permit. Record actual output and counters; do not claim both original entries are shadowed.
commandExplanations: Record actual host-permit and explicit-denial counters after the baseline tests.
Enter global configuration from privileged EXEC; changes affect the active configuration.
Re-enter the exact named standard list.
Add wildcard permit 5 ahead of wildcard deny 20; this does not bypass .10's host lookup.
Return to privileged EXEC without saving or undoing the accepted changes.
Confirm entry 5 and unchanged entries 10/20; display order alone does not establish host matching or counters.

steps.why: An unintended success is a security failure even when connectivity appears healthier to the user.
steps.title: Observe the undesired permission
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click PC-A and choose Console before typing. Keep PC-A at .20 and repeat the same destination. If it still fails, preserve that observation and inspect the attachment and baseline rather than claiming the predicted outcome.
steps.expectedResult: Expect .20 replies: its host lookup misses and permit any precedes deny any in the wildcard list.
commandExplanations: Verify the supposedly denied source is still .20.
Test .20: after its host lookup misses, wildcard permit 5 is reached before wildcard deny 20.

steps.why: A narrow repair preserves the known policy and avoids replacing it with a new untested configuration.
steps.title: Remove only the known bad entry
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click R1 and choose Console before typing. Remove sequence 5, leaving the original permit and deny unchanged. Review the resulting list before returning to the endpoint. This is a specific inverse, not a general rollback method for unknown edits.
steps.expectedResult: Expect the original two entries with no broad earlier permit.
commandExplanations: Enter global configuration from privileged EXEC; changes affect the active configuration.
Select the same list containing the deliberate fault.
Remove the temporary sequence 5 entry only.
Return to privileged EXEC without saving or undoing the accepted changes.
Verify sequences 10 and 20 remain in their intended order.

steps.why: Restoration requires both intended access and intended denial, not just an accepted no command.
steps.title: Retest the restored policy
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click PC-A and choose Console before typing. Test .20 while it is still active, then restore .10 and test again. Preserve actual results and timestamps; the successful .10 result alone would not establish that the deny was restored.
steps.expectedResult: Expect .20 failure followed by .10 replies, matching the original policy matrix.
commandExplanations: Confirm the restored policy denies the .20 source.
Restore PC-A's intended permitted address.
Confirm the original source is allowed after the repair.

steps.why: Named and numbered are identifier styles; equivalent outcomes still require a repeated verification matrix.
steps.title: Replace the attachment with a numbered equivalent
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click R1 and choose Console before typing. Create number 10 completely while TO-B remains attached. Replace this interface's outbound attachment only after reviewing the numbered entries. No other interface or direction changes.
steps.expectedResult: Expect the interface to reference 10 and the numbered list to express the same source policy.
commandExplanations: Enter global configuration from privileged EXEC; changes affect the active configuration.
Create the numbered standard permit for the exact source.
Add the explicit denial to the numbered list.
Return to the same outbound filtering interface.
Replace the outbound attachment with number 10.
Return to privileged EXEC without saving or undoing the accepted changes.
Verify number 10, not TO-B, is now the outbound ACL.
Inspect the numbered policy before traffic tests.

steps.why: Equivalent configuration syntax is useful only when the installed policy and observed outcomes agree.
steps.title: Verify numbered behavior and restore the source
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click PC-A and choose Console before typing. Repeat both source cases for the numbered attachment, then leave PC-A at .10. Do not infer numbered behavior from the earlier named-list observations.
steps.expectedResult: Expect the same permitted and denied decisions as TO-B; record deviations instead of reporting equivalence automatically.
commandExplanations: Check the permitted source under numbered ACL 10.
Temporarily select the denied source again.
Check the numbered list rejects .20.
Restore the baseline PC-A address before cleanup.

steps.why: Detach-before-delete avoids relying on empty-list behavior and preserves a clear record of the intended cleanup.
steps.title: Detach the exercise policy and preserve evidence
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click R1 and choose Console before typing. Return the router to its unrestricted baseline in this disposable project. Detach first, then remove the two exercise lists. After this block, reopen PC-A Console and repeat its original ping manually as the final baseline check.
steps.expectedResult: Expect the baseline attachment state restored; the required PC-A retest should again receive replies.
commandExplanations: Enter global configuration from privileged EXEC; changes affect the active configuration.
Select the sole exercise attachment point.
Detach the numbered filter without resetting the interface.
Return to global configuration after detaching.
Remove the unused exercise numbered ACL.
Remove the unused named exercise ACL.
Return to privileged EXEC without saving or undoing the accepted changes.
Confirm no outbound exercise list remains.

lab.title: Compare two sources through a standard filter
cleanup: Remove the temporary sequence 5 before comparing named and numbered policies.
Detach the exercise ACL, remove only TO-B and number 10, restore PC-A .10, and repeat the baseline ping.
Keep private before/fault/repair notes and stop the disconnected nodes; do not distribute licensed images.
devices: R1: separately entitled CSR1000v IOS XE 17.3 with two mapped routed ports.
PC-A and PC-B: built-in VPCS 0.6.x nodes.
lab.topology: GNS3 2.2: PC-A Ethernet0 directly to R1 GigabitEthernet1; R1 GigabitEthernet2 directly to PC-B Ethernet0. R1 is CSR1000v IOS XE 17.3 with two routed NICs. No other links, adapters, NAT nodes or Internet access.

addressing.purpose: Permitted source; .20 is the temporary denied source.
PC-B gateway and outbound ACL attachment.

verification: Record R1's actual release, both cable mappings and successful unrestricted PC-A to PC-B replies.
For the named list, verify outbound attachment, explicit entries, .10 success and .20 failure together.
For the fault, record sequence 5 and the same .20 test before removing only that entry.
After repair and after numbered replacement, repeat the complete allow-and-deny matrix.
After detaching cleanup, reopen PC-A Console, run ping 198.51.100.10, and retain actual baseline-recovery evidence.
lab.licensingNote: GNS3 does not provide Cisco images. A license or entitlement must permit the image in the selected environment; do not share or redistribute image files. Cisco Modeling Labs is an official alternative. Its supplied Cisco reference images are licensed for use within CML, not automatically for export to GNS3. An unlicensed learner must use the explicitly labeled paper alternative, not report simulated Cisco execution.
troubleshooting: If neither endpoint works initially, fix the address, gateway, link or connected route before attributing anything to an ACL.
If .20 passes unexpectedly, inspect its source, attachment and wildcard permit 5. With no .20 host entry, permit 5 bypasses wildcard deny 20. Do not apply that explanation to .10's host lookup.
If counters do not change, verify that the tested traffic is transit traffic through the attached interface; avoid substituting a router-generated ping.
If sequence editing is rejected on a different image, stop and use the declared platform or a paper trace. Do not delete an active shared ACL experimentally.

quiz.question: Which field does a standard IPv4 ACL test?
quiz.explanation: Standard IPv4 matching is source-only. Do not borrow extended-ACL or application-firewall capabilities.

quiz.question: Which wildcard matches exactly one source?
quiz.explanation: Zero wildcard bits must match, so all-zero wildcard matching selects the specified address exactly.

quiz.question: Where is TO-B attached in this lab?
quiz.explanation: The filter sees transit requests leaving R1 toward PC-B. The return traffic travels in the other direction.

quiz.question: What is the deliberate fault's narrow inverse?
quiz.explanation: Only sequence 5 was introduced as the fault. Remove it and repeat both intended permit and deny tests.

glossary.meaning: An access control list (ACL) contains permit or deny tests. An access control entry (ACE) is one test. A standard IPv4 ACL examines source IPv4 addresses, not destination ports. Its host lookup and wildcard ordering both matter.
A zero bit in an ACL wildcard must match the address; a one bit is ignored. Thus 0.0.0.255 ignores the final octet, unlike a subnet mask used to define an interface network.

A hash table is an indexed lookup, not encryption. Cisco IOS XE 17 standard ACLs check exact 32-bit host entries there first. Only a host miss reaches wildcard rules in sequence order; their first match decides.
A packet matching neither a host entry nor a wildcard rule in an existing populated ACL is denied by an invisible final rule. Displayed sequence numbers alone do not predict host lookup or counters.
Direction is relative to the router interface. Inbound traffic enters that interface; outbound traffic leaves it. The label does not mean into or out of the entire company.
Transit packets pass through the router between other devices. A ping generated by the router is a different test and may not encounter an outbound ACL in the same way.
Console is the text window for a selected lab node. VPCS is a lightweight simulated PC, with its own ip and ping commands rather than the IOS configuration language.
A counter records matches reported by the device. A baseline records the intended configuration and observed working tests before a change; counters alone do not prove an application works.

sections.example: For PC-A to PC-B, the router sees source 192.0.2.10 and destination 198.51.100.10. The host entry matches .10 exactly. Moving PC-A to .20 changes the matching outcome, even though its cable and destination remain unchanged.
sections.heading: Turn the policy into a source test
keyPoints: A rule identifier is not its interface number or a subnet number.
Source addresses are not proof of user identity or trustworthy software.
sections.explanation: Our policy is deliberately narrow: permit PC-A at 192.0.2.10 toward PC-B's subnet and deny other sources on that exit. A standard ACL cannot express a destination or service test in each entry. This makes it suitable for learning source matching but unsuitable for saying that a user may browse one server while being denied SSH to it. Numbered standard lists use 1-99 or 1300-1999; a name such as TO-B describes intent more clearly than the number 10.

sections.example: Compare host 192.0.2.10 with 192.0.2.0 0.0.0.255. The first permits one source; the second permits every source whose first three octets match, including .20. Calculate the intended set before entering either rule.
sections.heading: Read wildcard bits in the correct direction
keyPoints: The any keyword covers every IPv4 source in a standard entry.
A wildcard describes matching; it does not assign addresses or create routes.
sections.explanation: The wildcard 0.0.0.0 requires all address bits to match. The host keyword expresses that exact-address test. A wildcard of 0.0.0.255 ignores the last eight bits, so 192.0.2.0 0.0.0.255 matches the entire /24. It is not a mask assigned to an interface. For a contiguous /24, subtracting each subnet-mask octet from 255 produces this wildcard; noncontiguous wildcard uses require separate reasoning.

sections.example: TO-B has 10 permit host 192.0.2.10 and 20 deny any. Adding 5 permit any changes .20 from wildcard deny 20 to wildcard permit 5 because .20 has no host entry. Source .10 retains its exact host permit. Remove only 5 and retest both sources; record actual counters rather than predicting them from display order.
sections.heading: Host lookup, wildcard order and final denial
keyPoints: Write the intended allow and deny examples before attaching a list.
A host lookup is distinct from first-match evaluation within the wildcard list.
sections.explanation: Cisco's IOS XE 17 Sequence Numbering Behavior documentation distinguishes exact 32-bit host entries, stored in a hash table, from wildcard entries ordered by sequence. The host lookup runs first; a miss reaches the wildcard list. Do not treat displayed sequence order as universal execution order. The implicit final deny drops traffic with no match; explicit deny any gives a visible counter. Build and inspect the entire list while unattached. Editing a live list affects traffic immediately; an empty or nonexistent attachment is not reliably fail-closed.

sections.example: The PC-B reply enters GigabitEthernet2 and leaves GigabitEthernet1. Our outbound attachment on GigabitEthernet2 sees the request, not that reply. Adding an inbound filter without considering reversed addresses would change the exercise and could break the return path.
sections.heading: Place a source-only filter with care
keyPoints: Direction is defined at the named interface, not from the viewer's perspective.
Use a transit endpoint test; router-originated pings do not duplicate this policy path.
sections.explanation: A customary starting point is to put standard filtering near the destination it protects, because denying a source near its origin can remove access to unrelated destinations. This is a design heuristic, not a law. In our two-subnet lab, outbound on R1 GigabitEthernet2 means traffic being routed toward PC-B. Inbound on the same interface would instead inspect packets arriving from PC-B. The list and the attachment must both be inspected.

sections.example: If .20 still passes, inspect whether TO-B is attached outbound on GigabitEthernet2 and whether sequence 5 remains. If neither counter changes, the traffic may not cross this router interface. If .10 fails too, first check the baseline addressing and the permit line.
sections.heading: Use several observations before diagnosing
keyPoints: Record observed output separately from this lesson's predicted behavior.
IPv4 ACL success says nothing about parallel IPv6 traffic or application authorization.
sections.explanation: An ACL counter increment supports the claim that traffic matched an entry, but other traffic may share that entry. Pair counters with the attachment display, exact source address, destination and test time. A failed ping could also come from bad masks, a stopped peer or an unavailable route. Establish the unrestricted baseline first, then compare allow and deny cases after attachment. Avoid clearing shared counters just to obtain a prettier result.

sections.example: The numbered pair access-list 10 permit host 192.0.2.10 and access-list 10 deny any has the same intended decisions as TO-B. Similar text does not establish equivalence until the attachment and both permitted and denied traffic tests are checked.
sections.heading: Recognize equivalent syntax and limited coverage
keyPoints: The course ledger must combine this partial coverage with the extended-ACL lesson.
A paper trace demonstrates reasoning, not successful execution on a Cisco platform.
sections.explanation: Named and numbered lists can represent the same source policy. They are not applied simultaneously in the same direction on this lab interface; first build number 10 while the named list is still active, then replace the attachment and repeat tests. This chapter addresses the standard named and numbered portion of v1.1 5.6 and announced v2.0 4.6. Extended ACLs are reserved for Day 50. The current v1.1 remains applicable through 2 February 2027; v2.0 starts on 3 February.

content.metaTitle: CCNA Day 49: Standard IPv4 ACLs Without Guesswork
takeaways: Standard ACLs inspect IPv4 source addresses, not services or destination ports.
A wildcard zero bit must match; a one bit is ignored.
On IOS XE 17, check the host lookup first, then wildcard order on a miss; no match means deny.
Validate the list and its interface direction as separate pieces of policy.
Test both allowed and denied traffic using real transit endpoints.
Coverage and deterministic checks are not claims of runtime or independent approval.
objectives: Explain the source-only boundary and why standard ACL placement matters.
Create and inspect named and numbered standard ACLs without mixing their identifiers.
Verify allowed and denied tests, rule order, counters and attachment direction.
Introduce one overbroad entry, observe its effect, remove it and repeat the original tests.
content.plainAnswer: A standard IPv4 ACL filters source addresses. Cisco IOS XE 17 checks exact host entries before ordered wildcard rules; unmatched traffic is implicitly denied. Build the complete list before attaching it, choose its interface and direction deliberately, and test allowed and denied sources.

visualStory.title: IOS XE 17 standard ACL lookup

stages.title: Exact-host case: .10
stages.explanation: Before and during the fault, .10 matches host permit 10. Do not infer that wildcard permit 5 replaced this lookup from display order.

stages.title: Wildcard case: .20
stages.explanation: No .20 host entry exists. Baseline: deny 20. Fault: permit 5 precedes deny 20 in the wildcard list, so .20 is wrongly permitted.

stages.title: Restore denial
stages.explanation: Remove only 5. Predict .20 denied by 20 and .10 still permitted by its host entry. Retest both; these are predictions, not measured counters.

visualStory.altText: Two source cases compare .10's exact-host hit with .20's host miss and wildcard decision, before and during the fault.
visualStory.boundary: IOS XE 17 standard ACL TO-B on R1's PC-B-facing exit. These are alternate source cases, not serial hops or observed counters.
visualStory.takeaway: TO-B: .10 keeps its host permit; fault entry 5 changes .20 from deny to permit.

candidates.name: Source decision comparison
candidates.scene: Two independent source records contrast a host hit with a host miss and changed wildcard decision.
candidates.limitation: It is not a packet capture or an observed counter table.
candidates.teachingValue: Explains why .20's permission changes while .10 retains its host permit.

candidates.name: Topology map
candidates.scene: Two PCs flank one router with the filtered exit marked.
candidates.limitation: Would not distinguish host lookup from wildcard ordering.
candidates.teachingValue: Would help locate the outbound attachment.

candidates.name: Wildcard bit table
candidates.scene: An address is paired with match and ignore bits.
candidates.limitation: Would omit the host-hash lookup and attachment.
candidates.teachingValue: Would clarify wildcard calculation.

conceptSelection.selectionReason: Explains why .20's permission changes while .10 retains its host permit.

walkthrough.why: Changing only the source makes the standard ACL's limited matching field directly visible.
walkthrough.action: Predict two source decisions before configuring.
walkthrough.whatHappens: PC-A at 192.0.2.10 should pass; the same isolated PC temporarily using .20 should fail. Both attempt to reach PC-B at 198.51.100.10.

walkthrough.why: A source-only rule placed inbound near PC-A would also affect its traffic toward other routed destinations.
walkthrough.action: Separate rule content from attachment.
walkthrough.whatHappens: The named list allows one host and denies the rest. The attachment is outbound on the port toward PC-B, so the filter protects only that exit in this topology.

walkthrough.why: The wildcard permit precedes wildcard deny any. Source .10 retains its separate host permit; sequence 5 does not prove that host entry was bypassed.
walkthrough.action: Repair the wildcard fault, then retest.
walkthrough.whatHappens: A temporary sequence 5 permit any makes .20 pass because .20 has no host entry. Remove only that sequence and repeat both source cases.

beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: A valid list can block the wrong traffic when attached too early in the path. For a source without a host entry, a broad wildcard permit before the intended wildcard deny also changes the policy. A small written test matrix separates these mistakes.

firstPractice.hint: Separate exact-host lookup from ordered wildcard rules. Do not infer the selected entry or an actual counter increment from the lowest displayed sequence number.
firstPractice.task: On paper, use TO-B: 10 permit host 192.0.2.10; 20 deny any. Evaluate .10 and .20 before and after adding 5 permit any. For all four cases, record host hit or miss, selected entry and permit or deny using the documented IOS XE 17 lookup order.
firstPractice.expected: Before: .10 host hit, sequence 10 permit; .20 host miss, sequence 20 deny. With the fault: .10 still uses host permit 10; .20 misses the host lookup and reaches wildcard permit 5 before wildcard deny 20.

beginnerGuide.startingPoint: Start with the packet's source address. For this Cisco IOS XE 17 standard ACL, check the exact-host lookup first. Only if it misses, read wildcard rules in sequence order until one matches. Mark that decision and stop; then identify the attached interface and direction.

checkUnderstanding.hint: Identify the fields available in a standard IPv4 entry, not the fields you wish it could inspect.
checkUnderstanding.answer: No. It sees the IPv4 source address, not TCP destination ports. Use an extended ACL for a protocol-and-port policy; placement can limit the affected destination path but cannot add port matching.
checkUnderstanding.question: Can a standard ACL allow .10 to one TCP port but deny it to another?

everydayComparison.whereItStops: An IP address is not an authenticated human identity. Addresses can change or be spoofed. An ACL neither encrypts a packet nor checks whether a permitted person should use a particular application.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: The directory resembles the standard ACL's host hash; the area rules resemble its wildcard list. The desk's location resembles the attached interface. Moving the same policy to another interface can affect different destinations.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: Imagine a reception desk checking a directory of individual addresses first. If an address has no directory entry, the clerk uses an ordered list of area-wide rules. This separates an exact lookup from the fallback rules.

prerequisites: Review IPv4 /24 addressing, routed interfaces and the IOS configuration modes.
Use GNS3 2.2 with a separately entitled CSR1000v IOS XE 17.3 image and two VPCS nodes.
Keep a direct console open; this disposable lab has no production, Cloud or NAT connection.
content.learnerOutcome: You will calculate a simple wildcard, configure equivalent named and numbered source filters, verify their attachment and counters, and remove an overbroad wildcard entry without changing unrelated routing.
content.metaDescription: Build named and numbered standard IPv4 ACLs, reason about source matching and direction, and repair a safe rule-order fault in an isolated lab.

terms.meaning: An access control list (ACL) contains permit or deny tests. An access control entry (ACE) is one test. A standard IPv4 ACL examines source IPv4 addresses, not destination ports. Its host lookup and wildcard ordering both matter.
A zero bit in an ACL wildcard must match the address; a one bit is ignored. Thus 0.0.0.255 ignores the final octet, unlike a subnet mask used to define an interface network.

A hash table is an indexed lookup, not encryption. Cisco IOS XE 17 standard ACLs check exact 32-bit host entries there first. Only a host miss reaches wildcard rules in sequence order; their first match decides.
A packet matching neither a host entry nor a wildcard rule in an existing populated ACL is denied by an invisible final rule. Displayed sequence numbers alone do not predict host lookup or counters.
Direction is relative to the router interface. Inbound traffic enters that interface; outbound traffic leaves it. The label does not mean into or out of the entire company.
Transit packets pass through the router between other devices. A ping generated by the router is a different test and may not encounter an outbound ACL in the same way.
Console is the text window for a selected lab node. VPCS is a lightweight simulated PC, with its own ip and ping commands rather than the IOS configuration language.
A counter records matches reported by the device. A baseline records the intended configuration and observed working tests before a change; counters alone do not prove an application works.

teachingPrelude.explanation: Write the policy in words before writing IOS syntax: only PC-A may reach the second subnet. Then identify what this ACL can actually inspect. Destination restrictions arise from where you attach this source-only filter, not from a hidden destination field in its rules.
teachingPrelude.labBoundary: One router joins two disconnected /24 networks. Two VPCS endpoints test transit ICMP only. No Internet, user identity, application security or IPv6 filtering is demonstrated.

practiceQuestions.answer: Source .20 has no host entry, so wildcard permit 5 precedes wildcard deny 20. Source .10 still uses host permit 10.
practiceQuestions.question: Why does TO-B's sequence 5 permit .20 without bypassing .10's host entry?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Cisco IOS XE 17 standard ACLs consult the host hash before ordered wildcard rules. Compare both source decisions; do not infer counters from numeric display order.

practiceQuestions.answer: All IPv4 sources with the first three octets 192.0.2.
practiceQuestions.question: What does 192.0.2.0 0.0.0.255 match?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The wildcard ignores the final octet. It is not the /24 interface mask and does not create a connected route.

practiceQuestions.answer: The exercise filters transit traffic leaving R1 toward PC-B.
practiceQuestions.question: Why test from PC-A rather than R1?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A locally generated packet is not the same forwarding case. Use the actual source endpoint and record its address.

practiceQuestions.answer: The implicit final deny rejects that packet.
practiceQuestions.question: What happens to an unmatched packet in the populated list?
practiceQuestions.explanation: An explicit deny is not needed to create the rejection, but provides visible evidence for the controlled test.

practiceQuestions.answer: Its source-only test could deny unrelated destinations if placed near the source.
practiceQuestions.question: Why attach TO-B near the protected destination?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Placement limits the paths affected; it does not turn a standard ACL into a destination-aware or port-aware filter.

practiceQuestions.answer: No; it records an address-based match, not an authenticated user.
practiceQuestions.question: Does a matching permit counter prove user authorization?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Authentication, application permissions and encryption require separate controls. Even an allowed ping has only a narrow reachability meaning.

realWorldScenario.title: The printer subnet disappeared after a source filter
realWorldScenario.takeaway: Policy is the combination of matching rules, their order and their place in the path. The source-only limitation is a reason to design carefully, not a reason to assume a standard ACL is broken.
realWorldScenario.situation: In a fictional branch change, an operator wants to stop a training workstation from reaching a printer subnet. They attach a source-only denial inbound on the workstation's gateway. Printing stops, but so do unrelated routed services from that workstation. The command was accepted; the placement implemented a broader policy than intended.
walkthrough: Draw the workstation, router interfaces and intended printer exit before considering any changes. Identify which paths cross the current inbound filter.
Read the list and interface attachment separately. Determine whether the rule denies the entire source or a destination-specific service.
Compare an affected printer test with an unrelated allowed service test from the same workstation. Record both source and destination addresses.
Design the correct destination-side placement or use an extended policy for destination and port matching. Obtain approval rather than moving a production ACL experimentally.
In a disconnected reproduction, verify the permitted and denied matrix, restore the baseline, and document precisely which traffic was tested.

title: Extended IPv4 ACLs

lab.goal: Build a harmless isolated web service, apply an extended filter, break one port match and restore it. This is a reproducible instruction set with predicted observations, not a report of executed router or VM tests.
setup: Use fresh VMs with only the named lab NIC and no preexisting routes or firewall rules blocking the baseline. Do not disable a production firewall.
Inspect ip -br link on each VM and show ip interface brief on R1. Substitute actual labels consistently if ens3 or the router ports differ.
Create an empty ~/ccna50-web directory in Server's file manager. Serve only that directory; never use a home directory containing private files.
Keep Server's foreground HTTP process running in its console during tests. Use the GNS3 VM console rather than a remote SSH path.
If the software or Cisco entitlement is unavailable, trace the tuple matrix on paper. An entitled CML router plus Linux hosts is a practical alternative with different port mappings.

steps.why: An explicit routed baseline prevents a missing path from being mistaken for an ACL decision.
steps.title: Configure the routed link baseline
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click R1 and choose Console before typing. Verify the release and cable labels before entering these commands on a fresh router. Both networks are directly connected; no NAT or static route is needed.
steps.expectedResult: Expect two enabled routed interfaces with the planned addresses.
commandExplanations: Enter privileged EXEC on this authorized lab device; stop if access is not authorized.
Enter global configuration from privileged EXEC; changes affect the active configuration.
Select the Client-facing routed port.
Assign the Client subnet gateway address.
Enable this isolated Client-facing port.
Select the Server-facing routed port.
Assign the Server subnet gateway address.
Enable the isolated Server-facing port.
Return to privileged EXEC without saving or undoing the accepted changes.
Check both addresses and link states before traffic tests.

sudo ip link set ens3 up

commandExplanations: Add Server's lab address to the verified data NIC.
Enable the Server lab NIC.
Give Server a return route through R1.
Serve only the empty lab directory on the lab address and TCP 8080.

commands: sudo ip address add 192.0.2.10/24 dev ens3
sudo ip link set ens3 up
sudo ip route add default via 192.0.2.1
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Client and choose Console before typing. In the Ubuntu shell, address the isolated NIC and test both protocols. Stop if either baseline fails; record the actual HTTP status and ping results before introducing a filter.

commandExplanations: Assign the permitted Client source address.
Enable Client's isolated NIC.
Set R1 as Client's default gateway.
Request HTTP headers with a five-second maximum duration.
Send three ICMP echo probes for the negative-control baseline.

steps.why: Matching fields and attachment jointly determine which traffic is examined.
steps.title: Install the named extended ingress filter
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click R1 and choose Console before typing. Create the entire WEB-IN list, then apply it inbound on the Client-facing port. This intentionally denies all other IPv4 traffic arriving there, so it belongs only in the disconnected exercise.
steps.expectedResult: Expect WEB-IN inbound on GigabitEthernet1 with the intended two entries.
commandExplanations: Enter global configuration from privileged EXEC; changes affect the active configuration.
Create the named extended IPv4 list.
Permit the exact Client-to-Server TCP destination service.
Deny remaining IPv4 input explicitly for visible counters.
Return from ACL mode to global configuration.
Select the interface where Client requests enter R1.
Attach WEB-IN to this inbound direction.
Return to privileged EXEC without saving or undoing the accepted changes.
Verify the installed inbound list name.

steps.why: The required result includes a working permitted service and a rejected previously working protocol.
steps.title: Test selective access
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Client and choose Console before typing. Repeat the exact two baseline tests. An HTTP response together with denied ping is the intended result, not evidence that the network is partly broken.
steps.expectedResult: Expect HTTP response and no echo replies; preserve the actual messages.
commandExplanations: Retest the allowed service using the same Client and URL.
Retest ICMP, which does not match the TCP permit.

steps.why: This single changed field isolates a common syntax mistake without changing the service process or topology.
steps.title: Record evidence and change only the port
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click R1 and choose Console before typing. Record counters, then replace sequence 10 with the wrong destination port 8081. Keep the explicit deny and the attachment unchanged; do not save this deliberately faulty state.
steps.expectedResult: Expect the list now permits 8081 rather than the real listening port 8080.
commandExplanations: Inspect permit and deny matches following both tests.
Enter global configuration from privileged EXEC; changes affect the active configuration.
Select the exact named list for the controlled experiment.
Remove only the original service permit entry.
Insert the deliberately incorrect destination-port permit.
Return to privileged EXEC without saving or undoing the accepted changes.

steps.why: Changing the test to match the mistake would conceal the regression instead of diagnosing it.
steps.title: Observe the actual service fail
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Client and choose Console before typing. Leave the Server process running. Request 8080 again, not the accidentally permitted 8081. Do not start a new service to make the wrong policy appear correct.
steps.expectedResult: Expect no completed HTTP response within the bounded test; exact error text can vary.
commandExplanations: Test the original required service against the wrong-port policy.

steps.why: A targeted inverse preserves the security boundary while repairing only the known mistake.
steps.title: Restore the correct destination-port match
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click R1 and choose Console before typing. Read the wrong entry, replace only sequence 10 with the original 8080 permit, and leave the final denial in place. Keep the source, destination and interface unchanged.
steps.expectedResult: Expect the original permit and deny policy restored in configuration.
commandExplanations: Enter global configuration from privileged EXEC; changes affect the active configuration.
Select the same list containing the wrong-port fault.
Remove only the faulty service permit.
Restore the intended destination TCP port.
Return to privileged EXEC without saving or undoing the accepted changes.
Verify the restored entry and retained explicit denial.

steps.why: Restoration means recovering the intended selective policy, not making every test pass.
steps.title: Retest the repaired service policy
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Client and choose Console before typing. Repeat both tests after repair. Record any unexpected result and inspect server availability before broadening permission or deleting the ACL.
steps.expectedResult: Expect HTTP recovery with ICMP still denied, matching the pre-fault policy.
commandExplanations: Verify HTTP returns after restoring destination 8080.
Verify unrelated ICMP remains denied.

steps.why: A name or number identifies a list; evidence must still establish installed behavior.
steps.title: Apply the numbered extended equivalent
commands: access-list 100 permit tcp host 192.0.2.10 host 198.51.100.10 eq 8080
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click R1 and choose Console before typing. Build ACL 100 while WEB-IN is still active, then replace only the inbound attachment. The numbered identifier does not change the port value in its permit.
steps.expectedResult: Expect ACL 100 on the ingress interface with equivalent matching conditions.
commandExplanations: Enter global configuration from privileged EXEC; changes affect the active configuration.
Build numbered extended ACL 100 with the same service allowance.
Add the equivalent explicit final IPv4 denial.
Select the existing Client ingress attachment point.
Replace WEB-IN with the completed numbered list.
Return to privileged EXEC without saving or undoing the accepted changes.
Confirm ACL 100 is attached inbound.
Inspect the numbered entries before retesting.

steps.why: The repeated matrix establishes the intended equivalence without relying on visual similarity of syntax.
steps.title: Verify the numbered matrix
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Client and choose Console before typing. Retest the same application and ICMP cases under ACL 100. Do not substitute a router-generated test or a different URL.
steps.expectedResult: Expect the same HTTP success and ICMP failure as the repaired named list.
commandExplanations: Check the permitted HTTP service under the numbered policy.
Check the denied control case under the numbered policy.

steps.why: Cleanup restores the declared baseline rather than leaving a permissive temporary rule hidden in an active list.
steps.title: Detach filters and restore unrestricted routing
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click R1 and choose Console before typing. In the disposable project, remove the attachment first and then only the two exercise lists. Leave both routed addresses intact for the final baseline check.
steps.expectedResult: Expect no exercise ACL attached; confirm with the interface display.
commandExplanations: Enter global configuration from privileged EXEC; changes affect the active configuration.
Select the only exercise attachment interface.
Detach the numbered inbound filter.
Return to global configuration.
Remove the now-unused numbered exercise list.
Remove the unused named exercise list.
Return to privileged EXEC without saving or undoing the accepted changes.

steps.why: The final check distinguishes ACL cleanup from accidentally stopping a service earlier in the experiment.
steps.title: Verify baseline recovery and stop the service
steps.instruction: In GNS3, right-click Client and choose Console before typing. Run the original two tests after detachment. Then open Server Console and press Ctrl+C to stop only the foreground HTTP process. Preserve notes and stop all three disposable nodes.
steps.expectedResult: Expect HTTP and ICMP both working before Server's process is stopped.

Confirm the original unrestricted echo baseline returns.

glossary.meaning: An extended access control list matches a protocol plus source and destination addresses. TCP and UDP entries can also match ports. All fields specified in one entry must match.

Transmission Control Protocol provides a reliable byte stream. A port identifies a transport endpoint. The lab server listens on destination TCP port 8080; the client normally chooses a different temporary source port.
Internet Control Message Protocol carries control and error messages. Ping uses echo messages, not TCP port 8080, so ping and a web request can have different filtering outcomes.
A basic extended ACL evaluates packets against entries without tracking an authenticated application session. The TCP established keyword tests certain flags; it is not a stateful firewall.
HTTP is an application request-and-response protocol. curl is a command-line client. This lab uses unencrypted HTTP only on an isolated synthetic network with no sensitive files.
The first matching ACL entry decides the action; unmatched IPv4 traffic is denied. Inbound means arriving on the specified router interface, not arriving at the final application.
A console opens a named device's text interface. IOS commands belong in R1; Ubuntu commands belong in that VM's Linux shell. sudo requests authorized local administrative privilege.

sections.example: The request TCP 192.0.2.10:49152 to 198.51.100.10:8080 matches our permit. The same addresses with destination 8081 do not. A ping between those addresses is ICMP and also does not match the TCP permit.
sections.heading: Read an extended entry as a complete condition
keyPoints: Every specified field must match; one matching address is insufficient.
Do not assume a client's temporary source port equals the server's listening port.
sections.explanation: An entry beginning permit tcp must match TCP as well as the source and destination conditions. A host keyword matches one address. The eq operator compares a port to one value; placed after the destination host, eq 8080 means destination TCP port 8080. Other protocol choices include udp, icmp and ip, where ip covers IPv4 rather than one application. A match still uses the first-entry rule learned in Day 49.

sections.example: Both curl and ping succeed before attachment. After attachment, curl should still work while ping should not. Trying another unused TCP port is not by itself a clean denial test because no server may be listening there even without an ACL.
sections.heading: Design the allowed and denied matrix
keyPoints: A negative control needs a known working baseline to isolate the filter's effect.
The lab does not infer IPv6 protection from an IPv4 ACL.
sections.explanation: Start with a small, explicit matrix: HTTP to server port 8080 allowed; ICMP echo to that server denied. This lab's deny ip any any intentionally rejects all remaining IPv4 input on the client-facing interface. A real deployment needs a broader requirements analysis including management, name resolution, control traffic and other applications. Do not transplant this educational policy into a production interface.

sections.example: If someone attaches the same list inbound on GigabitEthernet2 instead, the server response has source 198.51.100.10 and a temporary destination client port. It would not match the client-to-server permit. The unchanged command text would be applied to different traffic.
sections.heading: Placement changes the traffic under examination
keyPoints: Map both request and reply before adding a second attachment.
Direct console management remains available even when this lab blocks network traffic.
sections.explanation: Extended ACLs are often placed near the source to discard unwanted traffic before it consumes resources farther along the path. That is a starting heuristic, not a mandatory location. We use inbound on R1 GigabitEthernet1, directly facing the client. This attachment inspects client requests as they enter. The server response enters GigabitEthernet2 and leaves GigabitEthernet1, so it does not cross this one inbound list.

sections.example: An entry allowing destination TCP 8080 permits matching packets regardless of whether the server serves a useful page. curl may receive an HTTP error, or the service may be stopped. Separate ACL matching from TCP connection establishment and from application response interpretation.
sections.heading: Do not confuse flags with session validation
keyPoints: A TCP port number is a selector, not an identity guarantee.
Counters and flags need context rather than a blanket claim that traffic is trusted.
sections.explanation: A traditional extended ACL is stateless. The TCP established keyword matches packets with ACK or RST set; it does not prove a valid authenticated conversation was established through the router. A port permit also cannot ensure that the process listening on that port is the desired application. Stateful inspection and application security are distinct topics and are not silently supplied by this exercise.

sections.example: After changing eq 8080 to eq 8081, curl to 8080 should fail and the deny counter should increase. Restoring the original permit requires a new curl test; configuration text alone does not prove the server is still running.
sections.heading: Change named and numbered policies deliberately
keyPoints: Never remove a shared active list to experiment with syntax.
Read back the final entry order and attachment before interpreting tests.
sections.explanation: Named WEB-IN uses sequence entries; numbered extended lists use 100-199 or 2000-2699. The lab builds number 100 completely before replacing the attachment. Keep the same permit and explicit deny meanings and retest; the number is just an identifier, not the service port. For the wrong-port experiment, replace sequence 10 in the named list using an explicit removal followed by the new entry. The brief gap rejects requests under the final deny, so use only the isolated lab.

sections.example: A completed worksheet might contain the release, ingress interface, both entries, actual curl response and actual ping failure. Until these tests run, the expected result remains a prediction. Source checking and schema validation do not establish a functioning CSR or HTTP server.
sections.heading: State the version and evidence boundary
keyPoints: Preserve actual failures instead of replacing them with the expected answer.
Paper alternatives teach matching but cannot demonstrate configured hardware behavior.
sections.explanation: This chapter supplies extended named and numbered configuration practice for v1.1 objective 5.6 and announced v2.0 objective 4.6. Day 49 covers the standard-list portion; neither chapter claims IPv6 filtering or a full security architecture. v1.1 remains current through 2 February 2027, with v2.0 from 3 February. Technical documentation supplies syntax and limits, while the learner must supply actual observations.

content.metaTitle: CCNA Day 50: Extended IPv4 ACLs and Service Tests
takeaways: Read protocol, source and destination conditions together.
Destination service ports and temporary client source ports are different roles.
Named and numbered extended ACLs need deliberate interface attachment.
A denied ping can be correct while a permitted TCP service works.
Basic ACLs do not supply encryption, authentication or session validation.
Repeat allowed and denied tests after a narrow repair.
objectives: Read source and destination port positions correctly in an extended entry.
Build and verify named and numbered extended ACLs for one explicit service.
Use a working application baseline and a denied protocol test together.
Repair a destination-port fault and explain return-path and stateless-filter limitations.
content.plainAnswer: An extended IPv4 ACL can distinguish a service from other traffic between the same hosts. Specify protocol, source, destination and the correct port position, then verify the attached direction and both allowed and denied tests. A successful ping neither proves a TCP service is allowed nor proves the service is listening.

walkthrough.why: A stopped server and a dropped TCP request can both look like a failed application test.
walkthrough.action: Prove the server works before filtering.
walkthrough.whatHappens: Client curl receives an HTTP response from the isolated server; a baseline ping also works. The later denied ping can then be compared with this known start.

walkthrough.why: The policy must match the service field in its correct position and operate on the intended ingress interface.
walkthrough.action: Permit the complete request tuple.
walkthrough.whatHappens: The named entry permits TCP from the one client to the one server's destination port 8080. The next entry denies all other IPv4 traffic entering R1 from that client network.

walkthrough.why: The correct outcome is selective permission, not simply restoring every packet to an unrestricted state.
walkthrough.action: Change one field and retest precisely.
walkthrough.whatHappens: Replacing destination port 8080 with 8081 makes the real request miss the permit. Restore 8080 and verify HTTP succeeds while ping remains denied.

beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Putting a port test beside the source address instead of the destination can block every normal client request. More detail in an ACL gives more control, but also creates more ways to express a policy different from the one intended.

firstPractice.hint: A port operator follows the endpoint whose port it tests. Read the address and its nearby operator as a pair.
firstPractice.task: Compare permit tcp host 192.0.2.10 host 198.51.100.10 eq 8080 with permit tcp host 192.0.2.10 eq 8080 host 198.51.100.10. Decide which one matches a client request sourced from port 49152 and destined for 8080.
firstPractice.expected: Only the first expression matches that request; the second requires source port 8080.

beginnerGuide.startingPoint: Before touching a router, write a client request as TCP from 192.0.2.10 with a temporary source port to 198.51.100.10 port 8080. Mark the destination port. Now read the rule left to right and locate where eq 8080 belongs.

checkUnderstanding.hint: Compare the intended protocol allowance with what ping actually sends.
checkUnderstanding.answer: No. The intended policy permits TCP to destination 8080 and denies other IPv4 packets on this ingress path. ICMP echo does not match that permit. Record both results as selective behavior, not a general network outage.
checkUnderstanding.question: HTTP works but ping is denied after this policy. Is that automatically a fault?

everydayComparison.whereItStops: A port number does not authenticate the application, encrypt the payload or guarantee that the expected service is really running. A basic ACL only evaluates the fields it supports.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: The server IP resembles the building address, and the destination TCP port resembles the department. The client has its own return address and temporary port for the reply.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: Think of addressing a letter to a particular department at a street address. The address identifies the building, while the department selects where it should be delivered. This is only a memory aid for separate address and service fields.

prerequisites: Complete Day 49 source matching and first-match reasoning.
Use GNS3 2.2, an entitled CSR1000v IOS XE 17.3 and two fresh Ubuntu 24.04 VMs.
Install Python 3.12, curl, iproute2 and ping before disconnecting; use only synthetic data.
content.learnerOutcome: You will permit one isolated HTTP service, deny unrelated IPv4 traffic from that client path, identify a destination-port error, and verify equivalent named and numbered policies without mistaking packet filtering for session security.
content.metaDescription: Match protocol, source, destination and port in extended IPv4 ACLs, verify named and numbered policies, and repair a wrong-port fault safely.

terms.meaning: An extended access control list matches a protocol plus source and destination addresses. TCP and UDP entries can also match ports. All fields specified in one entry must match.

Transmission Control Protocol provides a reliable byte stream. A port identifies a transport endpoint. The lab server listens on destination TCP port 8080; the client normally chooses a different temporary source port.
Internet Control Message Protocol carries control and error messages. Ping uses echo messages, not TCP port 8080, so ping and a web request can have different filtering outcomes.
A basic extended ACL evaluates packets against entries without tracking an authenticated application session. The TCP established keyword tests certain flags; it is not a stateful firewall.
HTTP is an application request-and-response protocol. curl is a command-line client. This lab uses unencrypted HTTP only on an isolated synthetic network with no sensitive files.
The first matching ACL entry decides the action; unmatched IPv4 traffic is denied. Inbound means arriving on the specified router interface, not arriving at the final application.
A console opens a named device's text interface. IOS commands belong in R1; Ubuntu commands belong in that VM's Linux shell. sudo requests authorized local administrative privilege.

teachingPrelude.explanation: Write a packet as protocol, source address, source port, destination address and destination port. The service port belongs to the destination in the client's request. Reverse direction reverses these endpoint roles; never paste the same rule on both sides without reasoning.
teachingPrelude.labBoundary: Three isolated nodes test HTTP on TCP 8080 and ICMP echo. No production network, TLS, Internet, authentication, IPv6 filter or stateful firewall is implemented.

practiceQuestions.answer: The client normally uses a temporary source port, while 8080 is the destination service.
practiceQuestions.question: Why does source-port eq 8080 usually fail for this client?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Port operators attach to the preceding address condition. Inspect the request tuple rather than assuming both ports are the same.

practiceQuestions.answer: It covers IPv4 traffic, not just HTTP or TCP.
practiceQuestions.question: What does the ip protocol keyword cover here?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The explicit deny ip any any therefore catches ICMP too. IPv6 requires its own supported policy and is not filtered by this list.

practiceQuestions.answer: The policy permits TCP 8080 but has no ICMP permit.
practiceQuestions.question: Why can HTTP work while ping fails?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The protocols differ. A failed echo test cannot be used as proof that every application to the host fails.

practiceQuestions.answer: No; it tests ACK or RST flags in a basic extended ACL.
practiceQuestions.question: Does established prove a genuine authenticated TCP session?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Flags alone do not provide a stateful session table or application authentication. Avoid treating a stateless filter as a firewall replacement.

practiceQuestions.answer: It avoids exposing an incomplete policy while entries are being added.
practiceQuestions.question: Why build ACL 100 before changing the attachment?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Reviewing the full list first makes the change boundary clear. The final attachment and traffic matrix still need verification.

practiceQuestions.answer: Server replies do not cross the Client-facing inbound attachment.
practiceQuestions.question: Which return-path packets cross WEB-IN in this topology?
practiceQuestions.explanation: They enter the Server-facing port and leave the Client-facing port. A second ACL would require separately reasoned reverse-direction rules.

realWorldScenario.title: The application is down, yet someone keeps testing ping
realWorldScenario.takeaway: Troubleshoot the service the user needs. A selective policy can make one protocol work and another fail by design; only the declared test matrix can tell you whether that is correct.
realWorldScenario.situation: In a fictional help-desk case, a team added a service-specific ACL and now tests only ICMP echo. A blocked ping is reported as proof that the application is down, while the service itself has not been requested. Conversely, another team sees ping succeed before filtering and assumes TCP 8080 must work. Both reports substitute one protocol for another.
walkthrough: Ask for the actual application endpoint, protocol and listening port, then write the complete request tuple.
Confirm the server process and local response before treating a remote timeout as network filtering.
Inspect the installed ACL and its attachment; distinguish source and destination port operators.
Run the intended client request and the deliberately denied control test, preserving actual response text and counters.
Repair only the documented mismatch, repeat both tests and state the limited result rather than declaring every service healthy.

title: Port security, DHCP snooping, and Dynamic ARP Inspection

lab.goal: Configure port security, DHCP snooping and DAI on a dedicated Catalyst edge and correlate their state with one client. No physical hardware runtime is claimed; these instructions predict observations for an authorized isolated lab.
setup: Use only dedicated disconnected equipment. Back up configurations and keep direct serial/USB console access; never use production ports.
On each Cisco device use its documented console defaults, normally 9600 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit and no flow control. Verify actual settings and show version.
On Client, verify enp1s0 with ip -br link and ensure no NetworkManager or networkd DHCP client is managing that lab NIC. Do not stop management services on a real workstation.

No hardware is available here for execution. Paper alternative: trace lease, binding, ARP validation and the trust fault. Practical alternative: a licensed virtual platform explicitly documenting all three features, with its own port mapping.

Do not save the experiment over existing startup files. The final good state may be retained only as a dedicated lab configuration; restore the pre-lab backup through a separate approved workflow when dismantling.
