glossary.meaning: A MAC address identifies a local Ethernet interface. Port security limits which source MAC addresses may enter a switch port; it is not proof of a human identity.
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol leases IPv4 settings. DHCP snooping filters certain DHCP messages and learns a table linking a client's address, MAC, VLAN, interface and lease.
Address Resolution Protocol maps local IPv4 neighbors to MAC addresses. Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) checks incoming ARP on untrusted ports against permitted bindings or an explicit ARP policy.
Trust is specific to a feature. DHCP snooping trust permits server-side DHCP messages on that input; DAI trust bypasses ARP validation there. Neither means every attached device is safe.
A binding records a relationship between an address and a local attachment. A VLAN is a separate Layer 2 broadcast domain; this lab uses VLAN 10 on two access ports.

Port-security restrict drops violating traffic and reports violations without disabling the whole port. Shutdown mode can place a port in error-disabled state, requiring cause correction before recovery.
Sticky secure MAC learning adds learned addresses to the running configuration. They persist across restart only if saved appropriately; ordinary dynamic learning is a different state.

sections.example: We select restrict mode so the lab can inspect violation counters without deliberately disabling the port. Protect drops unknown sources without the same notification; shutdown can error-disable the port. No violation traffic is generated here, so no counter increment is claimed.
sections.heading: Port security constrains sources, not identities
keyPoints: Determine the expected source count before choosing a maximum.
Sticky entries in running configuration are not automatically saved startup state.
sections.explanation: On a static access port, port security can limit the number of allowed source MAC addresses and use static, dynamic or sticky learning. In this one-host lab the maximum is one. That value is not universal: a phone with a downstream PC or a virtualized host can legitimately introduce additional MAC addresses. Choose the limit from the actual port role. A copied MAC address also shows why this control is not a replacement for authenticated access.

sections.example: The router offers addresses in 192.0.2.0/24. Excluding .1 through .99 leaves an allocation range beginning at .100, but this lesson never assumes a particular lease. The client and switch outputs must agree on the actual address and attachment.
sections.heading: DHCP snooping builds evidence while enforcing roles
keyPoints: Server-facing trust follows topology, not an arbitrary uplink label.
A preexisting client lease may require a legitimate renewal before the switch learns it.
sections.explanation: Snooping must be enabled globally and for the intended VLAN. Ports start untrusted; the real server-facing port is deliberately trusted. The learned binding connects the client address to its MAC, VLAN and port. It is not the server's own lease database, and it is not simply the switch MAC table. A missing binding may result from enabling snooping after an existing lease was acquired, wrong VLAN selection or a failed DHCP exchange.

sections.example: Turning on DAI before the client binding exists can cause legitimate ARP to fail. A statically configured printer on an untrusted port needs a separately designed static ARP policy; making every endpoint trusted removes the validation rather than solving the missing evidence.
sections.heading: DAI checks ARP against permitted relationships
keyPoints: DAI concerns IPv4 ARP, not IPv6 neighbor discovery.
A trust bypass is a security boundary decision and needs an explicit reason.
sections.explanation: DAI is an ingress feature. On an untrusted port it validates ARP using suitable bindings or an explicitly configured ARP policy; a trusted port bypasses those checks. For our dynamically addressed client, snooping supplies the needed record. The static gateway is different: it does not acquire its interface address through DHCP. We trust only the directly connected, dedicated router port for its ARP traffic in this small topology.

sections.example: In the lab, option-82 insertion is disabled to keep the directly connected server experiment free from relay-information policy prerequisites. That is a scoped lab choice, not advice to disable relay information everywhere. No relay or upstream aggregation switch is present.
sections.heading: Operational dependencies need a restart plan
keyPoints: Do not reboot a protected access network as a diagnostic shortcut.
Preserve the exact trust state, VLAN and binding evidence with timestamps.
sections.explanation: Dynamic bindings are operational state. Their persistence across a switch restart needs a supported database-agent design, valid storage and careful platform review. This exercise does not configure or test that persistence. Saving the running switch configuration is not the same as preserving every current binding. Rate limits also matter: legitimate bursts can trigger protection, so arbitrary aggressive limits are not a substitute for measured baselines.

sections.example: After clearing only the client's isolated interface neighbor entries, ping should fail during the fault and return after restoring router-facing trust. Compare DAI drops with the actual test. The lab does not send forged ARP, prove resistance to every attack or measure line-rate behavior.
sections.heading: Diagnose a failed ARP exchange without weakening the edge
keyPoints: A valid lease does not prove local address resolution works.
Remove the known fault and retest before changing unrelated security controls.
sections.explanation: A host can retain a valid DHCP address while losing gateway reachability. Check the client neighbor cache, DAI counters, current binding and trust states before changing the addressing. In the controlled fault, only the dedicated router port loses DAI trust. Its static gateway address lacks a matching dynamic client binding, so fresh ARP from that router can be rejected. The repair restores the documented router-facing exception, not client trust.

sections.example: A learner with no dedicated hardware can complete a binding-and-trust worksheet and read the official command reference. They must label it paper practice. Merely accepting configuration text on an emulator would not establish the hardware forwarding or rate-limit behavior described by the vendor.
sections.heading: Map configuration practice without overstating it
keyPoints: Record platform and release before interpreting unsupported commands.
Runtime, independent review and rendered-visual inspection are separate from authored coverage.
sections.explanation: The lesson addresses the three controls named in v1.1 objective 5.7 and the corresponding subset of announced v2.0 objective 4.7. Storm control and RA guard are reserved for Day 52. v1.1 remains current through 2 February 2027; v2.0 begins 3 February. This physical lab is a practical alternative when a virtual switch lacks a supported implementation; the built-in GNS3 Ethernet switch has no equivalent IOS security CLI.

content.metaTitle: CCNA Day 51: Port Security, Snooping and ARP Inspection
takeaways: Source-MAC limits, DHCP validation and ARP inspection answer different questions.
Trust is feature-specific and follows a documented port role.
Verify the real binding before enabling dependent inspection.
Static-address devices require deliberate handling, not an assumed DHCP record.
Force fresh address resolution when testing an ARP-specific fault.
Restore the narrow known exception while keeping client ports untrusted.
objectives: Compare source-MAC limits, DHCP message validation and ARP binding checks.
Configure and inspect port security, DHCP snooping and DAI on their correct ports.
Recognize why a static gateway lacks a dynamically learned client binding.
Repair one server-facing DAI trust error and repeat address-resolution tests.
content.plainAnswer: Port security limits source MAC addresses, DHCP snooping controls DHCP messages and records leases, and Dynamic ARP Inspection validates local IPv4 address claims. They solve different problems and depend on correct port roles. Verify the client's binding before enabling inspection, and never fix a missing binding by trusting every edge port.

conceptSelection.selectionReason: Prevents confusing a learned MAC with a validated IPv4 binding.

walkthrough.why: DAI needs suitable evidence for an untrusted dynamic client before normal ARP traffic can be accepted.
walkthrough.action: Learn the real client binding first.
walkthrough.whatHappens: The client obtains a DHCP address and the switch records its actual MAC, leased IPv4 address, VLAN and ingress port. The exact lease is observed, not assumed.

walkthrough.why: Trusting the client would bypass the checks the lesson is supposed to establish.
walkthrough.action: Keep client and server roles distinct.
walkthrough.whatHappens: The router-facing port is trusted for DHCP replies and for its static gateway ARP. The client-facing port stays untrusted for both features.

walkthrough.why: An existing neighbor entry can hide an ARP problem; a repeat ping without fresh resolution may not exercise inspection.
walkthrough.action: Test fresh neighbor resolution after one fault.
walkthrough.whatHappens: Removing only router-facing DAI trust makes its unbound static ARP claim fail validation. Clearing the client's lab neighbor cache forces a fresh test.

beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Layer 2 controls can stop unwanted local traffic, but an incorrect trust boundary can also stop legitimate clients. A trustworthy rollout needs a binding baseline and an explicit explanation of which port may send server messages.

firstPractice.hint: Ask which device requested DHCP configuration and which device supplied it.
firstPractice.task: On paper, list the client MAC, leased address, VLAN and port that a snooping binding should contain. Then explain why the manually addressed router gateway should not be expected to appear as a DHCP client entry.
firstPractice.expected: The client record includes all four attachment facts; the statically addressed router did not obtain that address through a client lease.

beginnerGuide.startingPoint: Draw three boxes labeled source MAC, DHCP lease and ARP claim. Place each control beside the fact it checks. This prevents the common assumption that one security command verifies every aspect of a connected endpoint.

checkUnderstanding.hint: The two features inspect different protocols and have separate configuration commands.
checkUnderstanding.answer: No. DHCP snooping trust and ip arp inspection trust are separate controls. Inspect each state independently; an intended server-facing role may need both in this lab, but a client-facing port should not receive either as a shortcut.
checkUnderstanding.question: Does ip dhcp snooping trust automatically trust the port for DAI?

everydayComparison.whereItStops: A MAC address can be copied, DHCP can fail, and trusted ports bypass particular checks. This analogy does not turn these features into authenticated identity or encrypted transport.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: Port security resembles limiting presented identifiers; DHCP snooping supplies a lease-to-port record; DAI compares an IPv4-to-MAC claim against approved evidence. None of these checks alone validates the entire endpoint.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: Imagine three separate checks at a facility: a badge limit at a door, an equipment assignment register, and a check that a person claiming an item matches that register. The analogy is about separate records, not literal network authentication.

prerequisites: Review VLAN access ports, DHCP leases, IPv4 ARP and console configuration modes.
Use dedicated Catalyst 9200 IOS XE 17.12 and ISR4321 IOS XE 17.9 hardware with authorized software.
Use one Ubuntu 22.04 host with dhclient and iproute2 installed, with only its lab NIC managed manually.
content.learnerOutcome: You will build a single-client protected edge, correlate a DHCP lease with the switch binding, configure three complementary controls and repair a bounded DAI trust error while keeping the client edge untrusted.
content.metaDescription: Configure an isolated Layer 2 edge, verify DHCP bindings before ARP inspection, and distinguish port security from feature-specific trust.

terms.meaning: A MAC address identifies a local Ethernet interface. Port security limits which source MAC addresses may enter a switch port; it is not proof of a human identity.
Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol leases IPv4 settings. DHCP snooping filters certain DHCP messages and learns a table linking a client's address, MAC, VLAN, interface and lease.
Address Resolution Protocol maps local IPv4 neighbors to MAC addresses. Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) checks incoming ARP on untrusted ports against permitted bindings or an explicit ARP policy.
Trust is specific to a feature. DHCP snooping trust permits server-side DHCP messages on that input; DAI trust bypasses ARP validation there. Neither means every attached device is safe.
A binding records a relationship between an address and a local attachment. A VLAN is a separate Layer 2 broadcast domain; this lab uses VLAN 10 on two access ports.

Port-security restrict drops violating traffic and reports violations without disabling the whole port. Shutdown mode can place a port in error-disabled state, requiring cause correction before recovery.
Sticky secure MAC learning adds learned addresses to the running configuration. They persist across restart only if saved appropriately; ordinary dynamic learning is a different state.

teachingPrelude.explanation: Build the dependency chain deliberately: correct cabling and VLAN, working DHCP, an observed client binding, then ARP inspection. Port security is a parallel source-MAC control. Trust settings belong to each feature and must follow the actual role of the connected device.
teachingPrelude.labBoundary: A dedicated switch, dedicated DHCP router and one host share VLAN 10. No rogue traffic, flood generator, production port or Internet connection is used. Hardware tests remain unexecuted.

practiceQuestions.answer: The DHCP snooping binding with its IP, MAC, VLAN and port.
practiceQuestions.question: Which record does DAI use for this dynamic Client?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The ordinary forwarding MAC table alone does not establish the allowed IPv4-to-MAC relationship used in this exercise.

practiceQuestions.answer: The router did not obtain its gateway address through a DHCP client lease.
practiceQuestions.question: Why is the router's static address absent from dynamic client bindings?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Static nodes require an explicitly designed policy or justified trusted boundary rather than an assumed dynamic record.

practiceQuestions.answer: No; each feature has a separate command and trust meaning.
practiceQuestions.question: Does DHCP trust also configure ARP trust?
practiceQuestions.explanation: One permits legitimate DHCP server messages; the other bypasses ARP validation. Inspect both independently.

practiceQuestions.answer: It forces a new ARP exchange instead of reusing an old gateway mapping.
practiceQuestions.question: Why clear Client's neighbor cache in all three tests?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A cached address can allow traffic without testing the inspection path that the experiment is intended to evaluate.

practiceQuestions.answer: No; it reacts to source-MAC security violations and reports them.
practiceQuestions.question: Does restrict mode authenticate a user?
practiceQuestions.explanation: MAC-based limits do not prove identity, application permissions or encrypted communication.

practiceQuestions.answer: A verified binding persistence design and an actual restart test.
practiceQuestions.question: What is missing from a claim of reboot-safe protection here?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Saving configuration is not a substitute for preserving dynamic bindings, and this lesson does not perform a reboot.

realWorldScenario.title: The lease is valid, but the gateway will not answer
realWorldScenario.takeaway: Availability and security can fail together when dependencies are misunderstood. Inspect the binding and the protocol-specific trust boundary before removing the protection from the client edge.
realWorldScenario.situation: In a fictional classroom rollout, a learner enables ARP inspection after verifying DHCP. The client keeps its address, yet a fresh gateway ping fails. A peer suggests trusting the client port. The better investigation checks which ARP messages are being dropped and whether the gateway is statically addressed on a port whose trust state was accidentally changed.
walkthrough: Preserve the client's actual address, mask, gateway and MAC before assuming DHCP failed.
Compare the DHCP snooping binding with the client's VLAN and physical port; do not substitute the ordinary MAC table.
Inspect DAI trust on both used ports and compare drop counters before and after a bounded fresh-ARP test.
Restore only the known dedicated-router trust exception, keeping the client untrusted.
Repeat neighbor resolution and gateway ping, and document that no hostile-traffic or performance test was performed.

title: Storm control and IPv6 RA guard

lab.goal: Configure broadcast storm control and RA guard on dedicated hardware, observe legitimate advertisements and repair a role mismatch. The exercise avoids floods; neither hardware runtime nor measured suppression is claimed here.
setup: Start from backed-up dedicated equipment, not Day 51's active policy state. Only the two named ports are in scope.
Use direct USB/serial consoles with documented settings, usually 9600 8N1 and no flow control. Verify show version and port labels.
Enable ordinary host IPv6 reception on Client's dedicated NIC; verify forwarding is off and the lab NIC accepts RAs. No DHCPv6 server is needed.
Install rdisc6 before isolation. Paper alternative: evaluate policy roles and threshold math; this does not prove hardware enforcement.
The threshold is illustrative. No flood generator, multicast suppression, shutdown action or remote management path is part of this exercise.

commandExplanations: Enter global configuration from privileged EXEC; changes affect the active configuration.

steps.title: Create explicit host and router RA roles

show ipv6 nd raguard policy ROUTER52

Create the policy intended for the Client-facing port.
Declare that advertisements must not originate from this attached host role.
Return to global configuration for the other policy.
Create the policy for the legitimate router connection.
Declare the connected device to be an authorized router role.
Return to privileged EXEC without saving or undoing the accepted changes.
Read back the host policy definition.
Read back the router policy definition.

steps.title: Attach each role to its real ingress port
steps.instruction: Open SW1's direct USB or serial console in your terminal application before typing; confirm its hostname. Attach the host policy to Gi1/0/2 and router policy to Gi1/0/1. Inspect both interface configurations so a swapped cable label cannot go unnoticed.
steps.expectedResult: Expect correct roles on both actual cables, not just in the policy definitions.

Select the Client-facing ingress port.
Attach host-role RA protection at the client edge.
Select the R1-facing ingress port.
Attach the explicit router role to the legitimate RA source path.
Return to privileged EXEC without saving or undoing the accepted changes.
Check the router-facing attachment.

steps.title: Verify the protected advertisement path
steps.instruction: Open Client's local terminal console before typing. Repeat the same bounded solicitation after attaching the two policies. Keep the source router and prefix unchanged.
steps.expectedResult: Expect the same legitimate router and prefix as the unfiltered baseline.
commandExplanations: Verify fresh advertisements still arrive with the intended roles installed.

steps.why: This creates an ordinary configuration fault without generating rogue advertisements or traffic overload.
steps.title: Introduce a bounded router-role mistake

steps.instruction: Open SW1's direct USB or serial console in your terminal application before typing; confirm its hostname. In this disconnected lab only, detach ROUTER52 from the router-facing port and attach EDGE52 there. Leave the real Client port and the storm threshold unchanged.
steps.expectedResult: Expect the router-facing interface now references the host role.
commandExplanations: Enter global configuration from privileged EXEC; changes affect the active configuration.
Select only the legitimate router ingress.
Remove the correct role attachment from that one port.
Deliberately misclassify the router connection as host-facing.
Return to privileged EXEC without saving or undoing the accepted changes.

steps.why: This separates information reception from cached configuration and avoids a false instant-outage claim.
steps.title: Observe blocked fresh advertisements
steps.instruction: Open Client's local terminal console before typing. Repeat the original solicitation and allow its bounded retries to finish. Existing addresses or routes may remain valid; do not delete them simply to force a dramatic failure.
steps.expectedResult: Expect no fresh RA response through the misclassified router port, even if old addressing remains.
commandExplanations: Solicit fresh router information during the host-role misattachment.
Record that previously learned addressing may still exist.

steps.why: A narrow inverse repairs the mistake while preserving the intended edge protection.

steps.instruction: Open SW1's direct USB or serial console in your terminal application before typing; confirm its hostname. Remove only the wrong role from Gi1/0/1 and restore ROUTER52. Leave EDGE52 on the real host port and retain the illustrative storm threshold.
steps.expectedResult: Expect the protected baseline restored without broad trusted-port bypasses.

Select the same router-facing port affected by the experiment.
Remove the deliberate wrong host-role attachment.
Restore the known correct router role.

steps.title: Retest and document unmeasured behavior
steps.instruction: Open Client's local terminal console before typing. Repeat the same solicitation and record the actual response. Preserve all three observations, then leave the dedicated lab isolated or disconnect its data cables.

glossary.meaning: Storm control suppresses specified traffic categories when their measured rate crosses a threshold. It does not identify whether a sender is an authorized router.
The rising threshold starts suppression; a lower falling threshold permits recovery after traffic subsides. The gap reduces repeated switching between states near one value.
Broadcast targets all devices in an Ethernet broadcast domain. Multicast targets a group. IPv6 uses multicast for discovery rather than IPv4-style broadcast.
An IPv6 Router Advertisement (RA) conveys router and prefix information. A Router Solicitation (RS) asks routers to advertise. Both are ICMPv6 messages, not DHCPv4.
RA guard examines advertisements at a Layer 2 boundary and permits or blocks them according to policy. A host-facing role rejects router advertisements arriving from that port.
Stateless Address Autoconfiguration lets a host form IPv6 addresses from suitable advertised information. Advertised lifetimes mean old addresses or routes may remain after new RAs stop.
Ingress means traffic entering a particular interface. Hardware and software determine which packets a feature can inspect and how thresholds are enforced.

sections.example: At a nominal 1 Gbit/s, one percent corresponds to 10 Mbit/s mathematically. Actual hardware behavior, packet size and measurement windows still matter. Before a production choice, collect representative normal and burst traffic and assess which legitimate protocols could be affected.
sections.heading: Rate suppression needs a traffic baseline
keyPoints: Do not generate a flood to make this beginner lab appear complete.
Configured thresholds and measured suppression are separate claims.
sections.explanation: Storm control monitors a selected traffic class and compares it with a configured threshold. The platform supports percentage, bits-per-second and packets-per-second forms. Percentages depend on interface bandwidth, and hardware enforcement can be approximate. A rising value of 1.00 and falling value of 0.50 means a one-percent start and half-percent recovery point in our illustration, not one packet per second. These are teaching values, not universal safe settings.

sections.example: The host's IPv6 solicitation and the router's advertisement use IPv6 control traffic, commonly multicast. A broadcast threshold alone cannot decide whether the router is authorized. Conversely, an RA role policy does not cap unrelated broadcast traffic volume.
sections.heading: Traffic categories are not interchangeable
keyPoints: Choose the traffic category deliberately and inspect its installed value.
Avoid assuming every device implements identical unicast or multicast accounting.
sections.explanation: Broadcast, multicast and unicast controls operate on different traffic classes. Suppression of multicast can affect legitimate routing and discovery traffic as well as unwanted traffic. The exact exceptions and hardware behavior must come from the selected platform guide. Our lab configures broadcast only on the single-host port; it does not infer that this protects every IPv6 control message. A threshold of zero is not a harmless starting value.

sections.example: In the lab Gi1/0/1 receives advertisements from R1, and Gi1/0/2 receives host traffic. EDGE52 has device-role host and ROUTER52 has device-role router. Their names have no effect until the correct policy is attached to the correct port.
sections.heading: RA guard follows the ingress role
keyPoints: Port-role correctness is part of the security policy.
A downstream shared segment that bypasses the guard is outside this enforcement boundary.
sections.explanation: RA guard is deployed where advertisements traverse a controlled Layer 2 device. The simplest policy differentiates host-facing input, where router advertisements should not originate, from a legitimate router-facing input. Cisco's selected guide calls for explicit router roles on router-facing ports when host roles are used. This is not the same feature as DHCP snooping or IPv4 ARP inspection. It does not authenticate every IPv6 packet.

sections.example: When the real router is temporarily assigned the host role, the fresh solicitation should receive no RA through that input policy. Existing IPv6 addressing may still be visible. That combination is understandable and must not be rewritten as a fabricated immediate outage.
sections.heading: Test new information, not only cached state
keyPoints: Use the same interface and solicitation command in every comparison.
A local echo reply tests a different behavior from receiving a new RA.
sections.explanation: Hosts can retain previously advertised addresses, prefixes and default routers for their respective lifetimes. Removing new RAs does not necessarily make an existing local ping fail immediately. This lab therefore uses rdisc6 to send a bounded solicitation and report received advertisements, rather than flushing every host address or waiting for arbitrary timers. Record the actual router source and prefix before and after the policy change.

sections.example: A paper exercise can label allowed ports and predict a dropped advertisement. A dedicated compatible switch can exercise the documented commands. A generic emulator accepting a configuration line does not establish hardware-rate enforcement, parser depth or behavior for every IPv6 extension-header case.
sections.heading: Implementation limits are part of honest security
keyPoints: Do not claim universal rogue-router prevention from one successful test.
Separate policy configuration, ordinary traffic observation and specialized security validation.
sections.explanation: IETF guidance documents why implementations must inspect IPv6 header chains adequately and handle problematic fragmentation safely. A single ordinary RA test does not prove resistance to every evasion technique. Follow the supported software and hardware guidance, patching process and authorized test plan; this lesson provides no crafted evasion traffic. Nor does it claim that the GNS3 built-in switch implements Catalyst RA guard or hardware policers.

sections.example: A coverage record should point to the storm command and threshold question, then the RA policy, attachment fault and retest. It should also explicitly say that no load or evasion test ran. Those distinctions help a learner know what to practice next instead of interpreting a chapter title as proof.
sections.heading: Track the new blueprint scope explicitly
keyPoints: Keep configuration coverage and observed competence separate.
Do not relabel extension material as a named current-version objective.
sections.explanation: Storm control and RA guard extend beyond the specifically listed v1.1 5.7 controls, so this chapter is supporting extension for that version. They are named within announced v2.0 4.7. Day 51 supplies the companion port-security, DHCP-snooping and DAI instruction. v1.1 is current through 2 February 2027; v2.0 starts on 3 February. This mapping does not convert unperformed hardware tests into completed practical evidence.

content.metaTitle: CCNA Day 52: Storm Control and IPv6 RA Guard
takeaways: Volume protection and router-role protection solve different problems.
Threshold units and platform behavior matter as much as the configured number.
Attach host and router policies according to verified physical roles.
Fresh advertisements and cached IPv6 state are different observations.
Ordinary RA tests do not establish resistance to every implementation edge case.
No flood or hardware performance claim is needed to teach a safe configuration workflow.
objectives: Distinguish volume-based suppression from advertisement policy.
Read rising/falling thresholds without treating example values as production recommendations.
Configure host-facing and router-facing RA guard roles deliberately.
Observe a fresh RA baseline, introduce one role error, restore it and retest.
content.plainAnswer: Storm control asks how much of a traffic class enters a port; RA guard asks whether an IPv6 router advertisement is allowed to arrive there. Configure them for different purposes. Choose storm thresholds from measured traffic and assign RA roles from the actual topology, then verify fresh advertisements rather than relying only on an old address.

beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Overly low thresholds can discard useful traffic, while incorrect RA roles can hide the real gateway. Restoring connectivity by removing all protection leaves the design question unanswered.

firstPractice.hint: Classify the packet's purpose and destination type before choosing the control.
firstPractice.task: On paper, compare a quiet unauthorized RA with a high-rate broadcast stream. Choose the appropriate control for each, then explain why a one-percent broadcast limit is not evidence that unauthorized IPv6 RAs are blocked.
firstPractice.expected: RA guard addresses the role violation; storm control addresses the rate. IPv6 advertisements are not Ethernet broadcast traffic.

beginnerGuide.startingPoint: Separate two questions on your worksheet: Is the rate acceptable, and is this port allowed to send router advertisements? Write the expected router port before entering a policy name; a name does not automatically discover the device attached to it.

checkUnderstanding.hint: Consider the lifetimes of information already received rather than assuming every control message is required continuously.
checkUnderstanding.answer: Previously learned addresses and routes can remain valid until their lifetimes expire. Therefore an existing address or a successful local ping does not prove fresh advertisements pass. Use a new solicitation and inspect the response.
checkUnderstanding.question: Why might a host keep an IPv6 address after the router's new RAs are blocked?

everydayComparison.whereItStops: Network policies inspect supported packet fields and port roles, not human intent. Platform limits and topology determine whether packets actually cross the enforcement point.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: Storm control resembles the delivery-rate limit; RA guard resembles the notice-authority rule. A small number of unauthorized notices can matter even when total volume is low.

content.learnerOutcome: You will configure an illustrative broadcast threshold and explicit host/router RA roles, inspect their installed state, and repair a legitimate router misclassified as a host without generating a traffic storm.

terms.meaning: Storm control suppresses specified traffic categories when their measured rate crosses a threshold. It does not identify whether a sender is an authorized router.
The rising threshold starts suppression; a lower falling threshold permits recovery after traffic subsides. The gap reduces repeated switching between states near one value.
Broadcast targets all devices in an Ethernet broadcast domain. Multicast targets a group. IPv6 uses multicast for discovery rather than IPv4-style broadcast.
An IPv6 Router Advertisement (RA) conveys router and prefix information. A Router Solicitation (RS) asks routers to advertise. Both are ICMPv6 messages, not DHCPv4.
RA guard examines advertisements at a Layer 2 boundary and permits or blocks them according to policy. A host-facing role rejects router advertisements arriving from that port.
Stateless Address Autoconfiguration lets a host form IPv6 addresses from suitable advertised information. Advertised lifetimes mean old addresses or routes may remain after new RAs stop.
Ingress means traffic entering a particular interface. Hardware and software determine which packets a feature can inspect and how thresholds are enforced.

teachingPrelude.explanation: Two packets can both be undesirable for different reasons: one contributes to excessive traffic, while another falsely announces a router. A low-rate unwanted advertisement can evade a volume-only design. Conversely, a legitimate device can generate too much traffic without violating its role.
teachingPrelude.labBoundary: Three dedicated nodes in VLAN 52 test legitimate IPv6 advertisements. No floods, rogue advertisements or evasion packets are generated. Storm suppression performance is not measured.

glossary.meaning: A virtual private network creates a logical private connection across another network. Here IPsec supplies selected IP-layer security services; the word VPN alone does not specify encryption or authorization.

IPsec is a family of IP security mechanisms. An IPsec security association, or SA, holds one direction's security parameters and keys. Two-way protected traffic normally needs an SA in each direction.
Internet Key Exchange version 2 authenticates peers and negotiates security parameters. Its IKE SA protects negotiation; Child SAs carry the negotiated IPsec traffic protection.

Encapsulating Security Payload, ESP, can provide confidentiality and integrity. Authentication Header, AH, provides integrity and origin authentication but not confidentiality. The negotiated services matter.

Tunnel mode protects an original IP packet inside a new outer IP header. Transport mode retains the original IP header and protects upper-layer content; the exact integrity coverage depends on the protocol.
A traffic selector identifies traffic covered by a policy or negotiated SA using addresses and possibly protocols and ports. Matching a selector is not proof of successful cryptography.
NAT traversal carries ESP inside UDP so address translators can handle it. Common IKE and NAT-traversal UDP ports are 500 and 4500; native ESP is IP protocol 50, not TCP port 50.

sections.example: For the same server 10.53.2.200, a branch workstation may use Gateway-A without a client, while a traveling laptop negotiates directly with Gateway-B. Its virtual inner address and current outer access-network address serve different purposes.
sections.heading: Two VPN arrangements with different endpoints
keyPoints: Identify who terminates protection before drawing its boundary.
Remote-access VPN is not a synonym for unrestricted internal access.
sections.explanation: A site-to-site deployment places the IPsec function at gateways serving networks. Individual LAN hosts need not run a VPN client. Remote access instead terminates one side at a user's endpoint, often assigning it a virtual address and applying a user policy. Split tunneling sends only selected destinations through the VPN; full tunneling sends the policy's broader traffic set through it. Neither arrangement automatically authorizes all reachable resources.

sections.example: A capture label UDP/4500 may represent NAT-traversed IPsec traffic. A label ESP identifies native IPsec payload framing, not the selected encryption algorithm. Read the negotiated suite before claiming confidentiality, and do not infer the user's application from that outer label.
sections.heading: Protocol names are not interchangeable
keyPoints: AH does not supply encryption and is problematic with address translation.
This lesson identifies protocols; it does not recommend obsolete algorithm suites.
sections.explanation: IKEv2 establishes authenticated negotiation and IPsec parameters; it is not the encrypted application payload protocol. ESP can combine encryption with integrity, including authenticated-encryption suites. AH authenticates selected packet content and appropriate header fields but does not hide the payload. Native ESP and AH have IP protocol numbers 50 and 51. IKE commonly uses UDP 500; NAT traversal commonly uses UDP 4500. Do not create a firewall rule for TCP port 50 and call it ESP.

sections.example: For our site pair, the original packet is 10.53.1.10 to 10.53.2.200. The outer tunnel header is 192.0.2.1 to 198.51.100.1. After Gateway-B validates and removes ESP, it still needs a route and permitted path to Host-B.
sections.heading: Modes change which header remains outside
keyPoints: Transport and tunnel are encapsulation modes, not stronger and weaker passwords.
The unencrypted LAN portions remain outside this gateway-to-gateway IPsec boundary.
sections.explanation: With ESP tunnel mode, a new outer IP header carries a protected original IP packet between security endpoints. The original host addresses are inside the protected region when encryption is selected. ESP transport mode keeps the original IP header outside and protects upper-layer content. It is often associated with host-to-host protection, but deployment design determines the mode. Tunnel mode does not mean an application receives extra permission.

sections.example: A local selector 10.53.1.0/24 and remote selector 10.53.2.0/24 should correspond to the peer's opposite perspective. A typo selecting only 10.53.2.0/25 can exclude a server at .200 even when the IKE relationship exists.
sections.heading: Associations and selectors need both directions
keyPoints: A displayed SA is evidence about negotiated state, not every application's success.
The reverse direction reverses source and destination roles; it does not reuse an outbound SA blindly.
sections.explanation: An IPsec SA is directional. A normal bidirectional conversation uses corresponding protected directions, while an IKE SA secures the negotiation exchanges. IKE_SA_INIT negotiates initial parameters and key exchange; IKE_AUTH authenticates and normally establishes the first Child SA. IKEv2 should not be described as literally using IKEv1 Phase 1 and Phase 2 packet exchanges. Negotiated traffic selectors determine which traffic is covered.

sections.example: If Host-A's packets are counted as encapsulated but the peer never reports decapsulation, investigate the transit path and peer evidence. If both directions count and the application still fails, inspect the server and its policy. Neither observation alone identifies the final cause.
sections.heading: Troubleshoot the path without broadening trust
keyPoints: Record times and the precise tested flow so unrelated traffic does not confuse counters.
Retest a permitted flow and an intentionally unauthorized flow after a repair.
sections.explanation: Start with authorized evidence: endpoint addresses, route to the remote network, peer reachability, negotiation status and relevant logs. Then inspect negotiated selectors and matching encapsulation and decapsulation counters for a controlled flow. Check return routing and application authorization. Avoid solving a selector defect by permitting every network or weakening cryptography. Secrets, private keys and authentication material do not belong in shared troubleshooting notes.

sections.example: The instruction covers v1.1 5.5 and announced v2.0 4.5, including protocol and mode distinctions. Current v1.1 applies through 2 February 2027 and v2.0 starts 3 February. Runtime VPN configuration and proficiency are not claimed by this describe-level exercise.
sections.heading: Practice honestly at the available level
keyPoints: A paper trace is an available alternative when Python is unavailable.
Keep the observed-model result separate from any future real-tunnel evidence.

A practical next step is a separately authorized, crypto-capable CML or physical Cisco VPN lab with its release-specific guide, peer configuration and observed captures. content.plainAnswer: A site-to-site IPsec VPN protects selected traffic between gateways; remote access connects a user endpoint to a gateway. IKEv2 negotiates and authenticates, while IPsec SAs protect traffic. Tunnel mode adds an outer header; transport mode retains the original header. A working VPN does not grant unrestricted application trust.

visualStory.title: Where gateway VPN protection begins and ends

stages.title: Select the original flow
stages.explanation: Host-A sends to Host-B. Gateway-A checks the original addresses against policy before protecting the selected flow.

stages.title: Carry the inner packet
stages.explanation: ESP tunnel mode carries the original packet between the gateways. The outer header names Gateway-A and Gateway-B, not Host-B.

stages.title: Deliver after validation
stages.explanation: Gateway-B validates and decapsulates, then forwards toward Host-B. That LAN leg and the server's permissions require separate controls.

visualStory.altText: Host-A connects to Gateway-A, which carries protected traffic to Gateway-B for delivery to Host-B. The two LAN segments are outside the gateway IPsec boundary.
visualStory.boundary: This is a logical tunnel-mode path, not the executed worksheet or a measured tunnel. Transit hops, routing details and application authorization are omitted.
visualStory.takeaway: The original hosts remain the endpoints; only the gateway-to-gateway segment receives this IPsec protection.

everydayComparison.whereItStops: An envelope does not model cryptographic keys, anti-replay checks or authentication. Also, opening the outer parcel at the destination mailroom does not mean every employee may read every document.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: In tunnel mode, the outer IP addresses reach the security gateways. The protected inner packet still names the original hosts. After validation and decapsulation, normal forwarding must deliver that packet to its final destination.

glossary.meaning: A hypervisor allocates virtual hardware to virtual machines. Each VM runs its own guest operating system and kernel. A type 1 hypervisor runs directly on hardware; type 2 runs with a host operating system.

A container is an isolated running process environment using the host kernel. An image supplies its packaged filesystem and defaults. Two containers from one image are still separate running instances.

A virtual network interface connects a guest or container to a software network. A bridge forwards Ethernet frames between its attached ports; it does not automatically supply application authorization.
A Linux namespace gives processes a separate view of selected kernel resources, such as network interfaces and routes. A network namespace is not a complete independent guest kernel.
Virtual routing and forwarding gives groups of Layer 3 interfaces separate routing tables on a device. A VRF is neither a VM nor encryption; communication between VRFs requires an explicit design.
A cloud service allocates provider resources on demand. Responsibility for guest systems, network policy and applications depends on the service model, not merely on where a server is located.

sections.example: Our Ubuntu VM runs a guest Linux kernel. Docker inside that VM uses that kernel for both Alpine containers. The hypervisor's disconnected external adapter does not remove the bridge created entirely inside the guest.
sections.heading: Identify the kernel and hardware boundary
keyPoints: A VM's network attachment is distinct from its power state.
Resource sharing requires monitoring and capacity planning, not assumptions about unlimited performance.
sections.explanation: Virtualization presents logical resources on shared physical hardware. A VM receives virtual CPU, memory, disks and NICs and boots a guest kernel. A hypervisor manages these resources; type 1 and type 2 describe different hosting arrangements. A virtual NIC still needs an attachment to a virtual switch or other network. A powered-on guest is not proof of a connected network or correct address.

sections.example: The two Alpine instances can display the same kernel release because they use the Ubuntu VM kernel. That does not mean they share the same eth0 address. Their addresses belong to separate container network contexts connected through d54net.
sections.heading: Treat a container as a process environment
keyPoints: Never infer perfect isolation merely from the word container.
Deleting a container may discard its writable-layer data; persistence needs an explicit storage design.
sections.explanation: A container image supplies files and metadata; a running container adds processes and a writable layer. Linux containers share the host kernel while namespaces and other controls restrict their view and resource use. This is different from booting a complete separate guest kernel. Privileged flags, host networking and host filesystem mounts can weaken the intended boundary. We use none of those options.

sections.example: Here sudo docker exec d54-a ping sends from the container, not from the Ubuntu host. The destination .20 belongs to d54-b. The internal bridge has gateway .1, but the same-subnet test does not require forwarding through an external router.
sections.heading: Draw the actual forwarding path
keyPoints: The host-side virtual interface names are generated; inspect them rather than inventing fixed port names.
An internal bridge is not a strong boundary against an administrator controlling the Docker host.
sections.explanation: A software bridge is a Layer 2 forwarding element. In ordinary Docker Engine, a user-defined bridge network manages container attachments and address assignment. This differs from GNS3's direct use of containers as emulated endpoints, where its topology manages links and often requires manual interface configuration. Do not paste this Docker Engine procedure into a GNS3 container console and expect identical network ownership.

sections.example: An address 10.54.0.10 in a training VRF and the same address in a production VRF are not necessarily the same endpoint. Troubleshooting must name the routing context as well as the destination. Our Docker bridge does not prove either VRF works.
sections.heading: Keep VRFs separate from workload isolation
keyPoints: Ask which routing table owns the source interface.
VRF configuration is conceptual supporting instruction here, not a performed Cisco practical.
sections.explanation: A VRF associates Layer 3 interfaces with an independent routing table. Two VRFs may use overlapping addresses without automatically sharing routes. A route in the global table is not automatically usable inside every VRF. Deliberate interconnection or route leaking changes that separation and requires policy review. A VRF does not encrypt traffic, create a guest operating system or package an application.

sections.example: A local ping between .10 and .20 cannot establish that a remote cloud subnet has a return route, a correctly scoped policy or an available application. A cloud diagram without a named provider, resource and tested path remains an architectural sketch.
sections.heading: Cloud boundaries require their own evidence
keyPoints: No account, subscription, Internet gateway or billable resource is used in this lesson.
Cloud responsibility boundaries vary by service; verify current provider documentation before operating.
sections.explanation: Cloud computing includes on-demand shared resources and service models such as infrastructure, platform and software as a service. A VM running locally is not by itself a public cloud. Provider networks may add virtual subnets, routing, gateways and policy controls, with details defined by the provider. Reachability and responsibility depend on those exact resources and the service contract. Do not equate a local bridge success with cloud security validation.

sections.example: An error that a container name already exists means this fresh-lab assumption failed. Stop and choose a fresh disposable VM; do not delete an unknown workload. The cleanup below names only resources created by this exercise and never prunes the Docker installation.
sections.heading: Collect evidence at the right abstraction level
keyPoints: Evidence from this exercise is local Linux bridge evidence only.
A practical alternative is a paper path trace with no executed-network claim.
sections.explanation: Inspect image identity, container state, network membership and endpoint addresses before running a ping. Compare those facts after a single disconnection fault. Restore the same IP and network rather than replacing the entire environment. Current v1.1 through 2 February 2027 includes virtualization fundamentals at 1.12; announced v2.0 from 3 February includes relevant concepts at 1.2. VRF and cloud boundaries are labeled supporting where the exact subobjective is narrower.

content.plainAnswer: A VM has a guest kernel on virtual hardware; a container normally shares its host kernel while isolating processes and resources. A VRF separates routing tables, and a cloud network adds provider-specific controls. These boundaries solve different problems and do not make all attached workloads trusted.

beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: A running workload can still have a disconnected network. Conversely, a reachable container may expose an application that should not be public. Checking process state, attachment, addressing and policy separately avoids both mistaken outages and accidental exposure.

beginnerGuide.startingPoint: Imagine following one packet from a process rather than assuming that everything on one computer is connected. The process uses its container's interface; a virtual link attaches it to the bridge; the bridge reaches the other container only while that attachment exists.

checkUnderstanding.hint: Compare Layer 2 frame forwarding with separate Layer 3 routing contexts.
checkUnderstanding.answer: No. The bridge connects local Ethernet attachments. A VRF provides a separate routing table and associated Layer 3 interfaces. This lab configures the former, not the latter.
checkUnderstanding.question: Is a Docker bridge the same thing as a VRF?

everydayComparison.whereItStops: Rooms do not model kernel vulnerabilities, privileged access or virtual switches. Neither a VM nor a container guarantees perfect isolation, and a door label cannot replace verification of an actual network policy.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: A VM has a separate guest kernel, while containers on a Linux host share its kernel. Their network views can still be separate. The bridge is a deliberate connection between those views, not evidence that they share every resource.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: A building can contain independent furnished apartments or several rooms sharing common facilities. Both arrangements provide separation, but the shared facilities and the doors between rooms affect what is actually isolated.

glossary.meaning: The control plane determines forwarding information; the data plane forwards packets using that information. The management plane configures and observes the system. Actual distribution of these functions depends on the architecture.
A controller provides coordinated management or control through software interfaces. Logical centralization does not require one physical server or mean that every user packet traverses that server.

An application programming interface, API, is a defined software interaction. Northbound interfaces connect applications with the controller; southbound interfaces connect the controller with managed devices. These are architectural relationships, not compass directions.

The underlay supplies the underlying network reachability. An overlay creates logical connectivity over it, commonly using encapsulation. An overlay cannot bypass the need for an adequate underlying path.

A fabric is a coordinated network architecture. In Cisco SD-Access, fabric commonly refers to the overlay across its routed underlay, with defined edge, border and control-plane roles. Not every fabric is the same product or topology.
Intent describes the desired outcome or policy. Assurance compares evidence with that desired outcome. A request being accepted is not the same as the intended behavior being verified.
A router loopback is a logical interface useful as a stable address. Selecting it as the ping source tests the return path to that address, not just the directly connected transit subnet.

sections.example: Suppose ten branch devices need the same intended NTP policy. A per-device operator may mistype one value; an automated job may propagate one wrong variable to all ten. Both need a known source of truth and post-change verification, not merely a successful job status.
sections.heading: Automation changes repetition and responsibility
keyPoints: Human responsibilities shift toward data quality, testing, permissions and exception handling.
Automation impact is explicitly covered here for v1.1 objective 6.1.
sections.explanation: Automation can collect inventory, generate consistent configuration, apply approved changes and repeat tests across devices. It reduces repetitive typing but does not remove the need for correct source data, review, credentials, version control or rollback planning. A faulty template can enlarge the blast radius compared with one mistaken manual command. Begin with read-only collection, small scopes and measurable outcomes before expanding changes.

sections.example: For a failed change, compare the intended policy, controller task details and actual device configuration. A task may be accepted but still pending or partially failed. A manual CLI correction can also create drift from controller intent unless the supported workflow reconciles it.
sections.heading: Compare management approaches fairly
keyPoints: Centralized policy does not guarantee atomic changes across all devices.
Use the product's supported ownership model to avoid competing configuration writers.
sections.explanation: Traditional networks often configure and inspect each device through its own CLI or management interface. Control protocols can still operate automatically and distributedly; traditional does not mean every forwarding decision is manual. Controller-based management offers a coordinated inventory, policy view and programmable workflow. It adds dependencies such as controller availability, compatibility, credentials and task processing. Neither approach removes the need to understand the device state.

sections.example: In Cisco SD-Access, Catalyst Center provides management orchestration and assurance; LISP supplies overlay endpoint mapping; VXLAN carries the fabric data. Calling Catalyst Center the device that forwards every user's packet would confuse these separate roles.
sections.heading: Separate planes and API directions
keyPoints: API direction is relative to the architectural role, not the method name.
A response status must be interpreted with task and device evidence.
sections.explanation: The data plane performs forwarding; control functions establish the information used for that forwarding; management functions configure and observe. A controller may coordinate these functions without physically hosting every routing protocol. Northbound APIs expose controller capabilities to applications. Southbound mechanisms communicate with devices and may include model-driven interfaces or other supported protocols. REST is not inherently northbound, and OpenFlow is not mandatory in every SDN system.

sections.example: Our lab pings from R1 Loopback0 to R2 Loopback0 over one routed link. That resembles one prerequisite of reaching remote infrastructure addresses. It does not create a VXLAN tunnel, prove an MTU budget or connect any user virtual network.
sections.heading: Underlay reachability supports overlay behavior
keyPoints: A successful small ping does not validate large encapsulated packets.
Do not repair an underlay outage by randomly changing overlay policy.
sections.explanation: The underlay connects infrastructure locations using physical links and IP forwarding. The overlay adds logical connectivity, commonly by encapsulating an original packet or frame with headers that reach remote tunnel endpoints. More headers also require an appropriate MTU, the maximum packet size supported by the path. Basic reachability is necessary but not sufficient: endpoint mapping, segmentation, policy and packet-size handling must also work.

sections.example: A conceptual endpoint-to-edge-to-underlay-to-edge-to-endpoint journey has a final destination beyond the tunnel. The receiving edge must deliver to the correct endpoint and apply policy. Stopping the diagram at an unnamed cloud would hide those remaining obligations.
sections.heading: Fabric names carry architectural context
keyPoints: Name the exact product before asserting its control or failure behavior.
This lesson describes fabrics but does not certify a complete fabric design.
sections.explanation: A fabric coordinates connectivity across defined roles. Cisco SD-Access includes fabric edges for endpoint attachment, control-plane nodes for mappings and borders for external connectivity. Other architectures may use different protocols and topology. Leaf-spine describes a physical connectivity pattern, not a universal synonym for every controller-managed campus. Overlay separation is also not encryption by itself.

sections.example: The source-specific ping below needs return routing to each /32 loopback. An ordinary ping sourced from a transit interface could succeed despite a missing loopback return route. Record the source explicitly so the verification actually tests the intended requirement.
sections.heading: Verify intent, state and behavior independently
keyPoints: Current v1.1 remains applicable through 2 February 2027; v2.0 begins 3 February.
An authored procedure and static validation are not a claim of observed device execution.
sections.explanation: Begin with the approved target and expected result. Inspect controller task state where a controller exists, then device state and the precise test flow. Preserve negative cases when the policy includes denial. Compare the same tests after rollback. The chapter owns v1.1 6.1, 6.2 and 6.3 instruction, including APIs and plane separation. Announced v2.0 5.3 receives partial controller and automation coverage, supplemented by later automation lessons.

content.plainAnswer: Controller-based networking coordinates intent, configuration and evidence through software interfaces. Devices still forward traffic. An overlay supplies logical connectivity over a reachable underlay; a fabric combines specific roles and mechanisms. Controller success, underlay success and endpoint application success require different evidence.

beginnerGuide.whyItMatters: Automation can repeat a correct design consistently, but it can also distribute a wrong variable rapidly. Good operators learn both the software workflow and the forwarding fundamentals needed to recognize a wrong result.

firstPractice.hint: A packet can arrive at a server whose application denies the user. Keep transport evidence narrower than authorization.
firstPractice.task: Sort these into intent, installed state or behavior: an approved policy request; a device's routing-table entry; a source-specific ping result. Then identify which item alone proves an application login works.
firstPractice.expected: The request is intent, the route is installed state, and the ping is limited behavior. None alone proves an application login.

beginnerGuide.startingPoint: Write three questions beside the same change: what did we ask for, what did the devices install, and what did the test flow do? Use a different piece of evidence for each. This makes controller-based operation understandable without assuming the controller handles every packet.

checkUnderstanding.hint: Separate the software control relationship from the data-forwarding path.
checkUnderstanding.answer: No. Devices generally forward using installed state. The specific product determines control distribution and failure behavior, so neither universal inline forwarding nor indefinite controller independence should be assumed.

everydayComparison.whereItStops: A network's control functions may remain distributed among devices, and availability behavior depends on the product. The analogy does not prove that forwarding continues forever after every controller failure.
everydayComparison.networkMeaning: The controller coordinates intent and configuration; forwarding devices carry the traffic; telemetry and tests supply feedback. These relationships explain why a completed software request and a healthy user journey are not identical.
everydayComparison.familiarSituation: A transit planner sets routes and schedules while vehicles move passengers. Reports from stations help check whether service matches the plan. The planning office is important, but passengers do not ride through the office.

realWorldScenario.title: A completed policy task with a broken prerequisite path
realWorldScenario.takeaway: Controller workflows do not repeal physical and IP dependencies. An evidence chain from intent through installed state to the actual flow is more useful than a single green status.
realWorldScenario.situation: In a fictional campus change, a policy workflow finishes but users across two fabric locations cannot communicate. A routed uplink was left administratively down during maintenance. The operator initially suspects the new overlay policy because that is the most recent dashboard event.
walkthrough: Record the intended source, destination and policy, then separate task status from actual forwarding evidence.
Check the infrastructure path and relevant interface states before editing the overlay.
Compare the failed location's underlay reachability with the baseline and identify the administratively down link.
Restore only the approved link state through the owning workflow, then verify infrastructure and endpoint tests.
Keep the final report precise: the cause was a prerequisite path; the full overlay still needs its own evidence.

title: REST APIs, CRUD, authentication, and HTTP evidence
moduleTitle: Cloud, Automation, AI, and the Capstone
v20Blueprint: Supporting automation; not a named objective

lab.goal: Use an actual local file server and curl to inspect a synthetic response, produce a wrong-path fault, repair it and observe an unsupported method. No authenticated REST service or device runtime is claimed.
setup: Open two Terminal windows from the VM console and label them A and B. Keep the VM external adapter disconnected.
Use a new temporary directory with only the synthetic fixture. Do not serve a home directory or add credentials.
If port 8056 is occupied, stop and identify your own conflicting process; do not terminate an unknown service.
With no local runtime, hand-annotate the request and predicted response and mark the exercise paper-only.

steps.why: Creating data locally avoids exporting device state or exposing unrelated files.
steps.title: Prepare a synthetic representation
steps.instruction: In VM console Terminal A, check Python and create a new temporary directory. Enter each command separately. The shell variable LAB56 stays in this Terminal A session for later cleanup.
steps.expectedResult: Expect a new directory containing device.json with synthetic fields.
commandExplanations: Record the actual interpreter version.
Create a uniquely named empty directory owned by this exercise.
Move into that directory before writing or serving anything.
Write only a synthetic JSON fixture; Python serializes True as JSON true.
Record the exact exercise directory for cleanup verification.

steps.why: The explicit bind and isolated directory define the exact exposure boundary.
steps.title: Start the loopback listener
steps.instruction: In the same VM console Terminal A, start the foreground server from the fixture directory. Leave this terminal running; use Terminal B for clients. Do not replace loopback with an all-interface address.
steps.expectedResult: Expect the listener to start; if it reports address in use, stop and resolve the local conflict.
commandExplanations: Serve the current fixture directory on TCP 8056 bound only to loopback.

steps.why: Status, headers and body belong together when interpreting the response.
steps.title: Read the baseline response
steps.instruction: In VM console Terminal B, inspect curl's version and send a bounded GET. Proxy bypass ensures even a configured proxy is not used for this local exercise.
steps.expectedResult: Expect 200 and the synthetic JSON body; record actual headers and protocol version rather than assuming them.
commandExplanations: Record the actual client version.
GET the fixture; -i displays response headers and body, --max-time bounds waiting.

steps.why: A method's semantics explain the result more reliably than looking only for text content.
steps.title: Compare HEAD with GET
steps.instruction: In VM console Terminal B, request metadata for the same target. Do not mistake the absent response body for missing JSON; HEAD intentionally differs from GET in that respect.
steps.expectedResult: Expect a successful status and metadata without the JSON body.
commandExplanations: Send HEAD and display response headers without requesting a response body.

steps.why: This isolates resource lookup from TCP reachability and credential questions.
steps.title: Introduce a safe path fault
steps.instruction: In VM console Terminal B, change only the target path to a nonexistent file. The server, port and method remain unchanged. Compare the result with a transport failure in your notes.
steps.expectedResult: Expect HTTP 404 and an error representation, not connection refused.
commandExplanations: Request a nonexistent resource while keeping the known listener unchanged.

steps.why: A server's implemented methods determine behavior; a generic CRUD table cannot create missing capabilities.
steps.title: Repair the path and verify the boundary
steps.instruction: In VM console Terminal B, restore the known path and then test one unsupported POST against the same local fixture. This server has no create handler; do not label the POST a CRUD deployment.
steps.expectedResult: Expect restored GET success, unsupported POST 501 and unchanged GET content.
commandExplanations: Repeat the baseline GET after correcting the path.
Ask the file handler for an unsupported method; no production endpoint is contacted.
Verify that the readable fixture still exists after the rejected method.

steps.why: Process shutdown and filesystem cleanup are distinct; no broad deletion or unknown process termination is needed.
steps.title: Stop and clean up the local fixture
steps.instruction: In VM console Terminal A, press Ctrl+C to stop only the foreground Python server. Then verify the recorded directory before deleting its single fixture and removing the now-empty directory. Retest from Terminal B afterward.
steps.expectedResult: Expect the listener stopped and only the exercise file/directory removed. In Terminal B repeat the baseline curl; expect connection failure, not HTTP 404.
commandExplanations: Confirm Terminal A is still in the exact recorded /tmp/ccna56 directory.
Remove only the synthetic file in the verified exercise directory.
Leave the directory before removing it.
Remove only the now-empty directory stored by this same shell session.

lab.title: Read an HTTP exchange on loopback only
cleanup: Stop the foreground server with Ctrl+C in Terminal A.
Verify the exact temporary directory, delete only device.json and use rmdir on the empty exercise directory.
Keep redacted observations; no credential or real device data should exist in this lab.
devices: Ubuntu VM: one disconnected guest with Python 3.12 and curl 8.x.
Server process in Terminal A and client process in Terminal B: same loopback network.
lab.topology: One offline Ubuntu 24.04 VM. Terminal A runs Python 3.12 http.server on lo 127.0.0.1 TCP 8056; Terminal B runs curl 8.x against that listener. No external NIC, router or remote API.

addressing.purpose: Local client; the OS selects its source TCP port.

verification: Record Python and curl versions and the loopback bind address.
Keep the baseline status, headers and synthetic fields together.
Compare HEAD without content, wrong-path 404 and restored GET.
Label POST 501 as unsupported by this fixture, not an authentication result.
After stopping the server, repeat the exact bounded curl from Terminal B and record connection failure; no runtime is asserted here.
lab.licensingNote: GNS3 does not provide Cisco images. A license or entitlement must permit the image in the selected environment; do not share or redistribute image files. Cisco Modeling Labs is an official alternative. Its supplied Cisco reference images are licensed for use within CML, not automatically for export to GNS3. An unlicensed learner must use the explicitly labeled paper alternative, not report simulated Cisco execution.
troubleshooting: If curl cannot connect, inspect the foreground server, bind address and port before discussing HTTP statuses.
If 404 appears, compare the exact path and server working directory; do not rotate credentials in this unauthenticated fixture.
If the body is HTML, read the status and Content-Type before feeding it to a JSON parser.
If real API TLS validation fails in a separate lab, repair trust and naming; do not normalize disabling certificate checks.

glossary.meaning: Representational State Transfer, REST, is an architectural style using resource representations and a uniform interface. A resource is the thing identified by a URI; a JSON body can represent it but is not the resource itself.
A request has a method, target and headers, with a body when applicable. A response has a status, headers and possibly a body. Transport success does not guarantee application success.

Create, read, update and delete describe data operations. APIs commonly use POST for create, GET for read, PUT or PATCH for update and DELETE for removal, but the documented resource contract decides exact behavior.
Each request supplies the context needed to understand it. Stateless interaction does not mean that the server stores no resources, authorization data or other persistent information.
Authentication establishes identity or credential possession. Authorization determines permitted actions. A valid credential can still lack permission to change a device.

A safe method does not request a state change. Idempotent means repeated identical requests have the same intended server effect as one, not that every response is identical or that the operation is harmless.
Accept states the response formats a client can handle. Content-Type describes the format of the body being sent. They answer different questions and must match the API contract.

sections.example: An inventory resource might represent a device with name and enabled fields. Retrieving that representation is different from logging into the device, changing its interface or observing its forwarding counters. Our file fixture teaches the exchange but not a complete REST implementation.
sections.heading: REST is more than JSON over a URL
keyPoints: A URI identifies the target; a representation describes it at a particular time.
RESTCONF is a specific network-management protocol using modeled data, not another name for all HTTP.
sections.explanation: REST describes resource-oriented interactions using representations and a uniform interface, with client-server separation, stateless requests, cache semantics and layered systems. Not every HTTP endpoint is fully RESTful. A server can keep resource state while each request carries the context needed for processing. JSON is one representation format, not a transport protocol or a requirement that every API must use.

sections.example: A retry after a timed-out create may produce a duplicate if the API does not provide an idempotency mechanism. Read the contract and inspect current state before retrying an uncertain write. Never assume that a second DELETE must return the same status as the first.
sections.heading: Match CRUD intent to the documented method
keyPoints: Do not send an incomplete PUT body when the API treats it as replacement.
The fixture's unsupported POST result is not a successful create demonstration.
sections.explanation: GET retrieves a representation; HEAD asks for corresponding response metadata without a response body. POST often creates a subordinate resource or invokes an operation. PUT creates or replaces the target according to its contract. PATCH applies a defined partial modification. DELETE requests removal of the target. GET and HEAD are safe; PUT and DELETE are idempotent in intended effect, but that does not make deletion harmless. POST and PATCH are not universally idempotent.

sections.example: A read-only token may retrieve inventory but be denied a configuration write. Do not paste it into a public example, URL query, screenshot or shared command history. Our loopback fixture deliberately sends no credential because it implements no authentication check.
sections.heading: Authenticate without confusing permission
keyPoints: Do not use curl -k as a routine fix for an untrusted server certificate.
Store and rotate secrets using the organization's approved mechanism, not hardcoded lesson examples.
sections.explanation: Basic authentication encodes a user and password; Base64 is not encryption. Bearer authentication presents a token whose possession permits its scoped use, so it must be protected. Some APIs use an API key in a documented header; others issue tokens through an authorization flow. Use TLS with certificate validation for real credentials. Authentication success does not establish permission for every resource or method.

sections.example: A curl process can exit successfully after receiving HTTP 404 unless configured to treat HTTP error statuses as failures. Our command shows the status with -i. A connection-refused error has no HTTP status because an HTTP response never arrived.
sections.heading: Interpret status and metadata together
keyPoints: Inspect actual Content-Type before parsing the body as JSON.
Accept describes desired response formats; request Content-Type describes the submitted body.
sections.explanation: Successful 2xx responses differ: 200 commonly includes a representation, 201 signals creation, 202 may indicate asynchronous acceptance, and 204 has no response content. A 400 suggests a bad request; 401 concerns authentication; 403 refuses the action; 404 means the target was not found or its existence is not disclosed. A 5xx response indicates a server-side inability to fulfill the request. Read the documented error body and request identifiers without leaking secrets.

sections.example: Change /device.json to /missing.json and compare 200 with 404 while the listener stays unchanged. Then restore the path. A deliberately unsupported POST should produce 501 with this handler; do not rewrite that observation into an invented authentication or permission failure.
sections.heading: Use a bounded local fixture for HTTP mechanics
keyPoints: A full authenticated API practical requires a separately authorized platform and its resource schema.
No paid service, sandbox credential or production API is needed for this exercise.
sections.explanation: Python's simple server serves files and supports GET and HEAD, not arbitrary CRUD writes. Binding it to 127.0.0.1 limits this demonstration to the VM's loopback. A new temporary directory prevents accidental exposure of unrelated files. The synthetic device.json is a teaching fixture, not an export of a real device. An offline VM and proxy bypass keep all requests on the declared local path.

sections.example: A practical next step is an entitled IOS XE RESTCONF lab using its current release guide, trusted certificate, least-privilege account and explicitly authorized read resource. The local fixture's transcript cannot be reused as device evidence.
sections.heading: Map the lesson without inventing exam coverage
keyPoints: A local validator verifies authored structure, not HTTP runtime or API permissions.
Keep expected results separate from the transcript you actually observe.

The announced v2.0 does not name the same standalone REST objective, so the material is supporting automation knowledge, not a claim that a new objective has been satisfied. content.plainAnswer: REST APIs expose resources through defined interactions, commonly over HTTP. Read the method, exact URI, authentication requirement, status, headers and body together. GET reads; POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE have different documented effects. A successful connection or a JSON-looking body alone does not prove a request succeeded.

stages.title: Repair the wrong path

walkthrough.why: A body must be understood in the context of its source, freshness and status.
walkthrough.action: Read the complete baseline exchange.
walkthrough.whatHappens: GET /device.json should return a successful status and a synthetic JSON representation. The file's enabled value is data, not live interface state.

walkthrough.why: A wrong path is a safe fault that separates HTTP handling from network reachability.
walkthrough.action: Change only the resource path.
